commit_msg:
The syzbot fuzzer found a bug in the p54 USB wireless driver.  The
issue involves a race between disconnect and the firmware-loader
callback routine, and it has several aspects.

One big problem is that when the firmware can't be loaded, the
callback routine tries to unbind the driver from the USB _device_ (by
calling device_release_driver) instead of from the USB _interface_ to
which it is actually bound (by calling usb_driver_release_interface).

The race involves access to the private data structure.  The driver's
disconnect handler waits for a completion that is signalled by the
firmware-loader callback routine.  As soon as the completion is
signalled, you have to assume that the private data structure may have
been deallocated by the disconnect handler -- even if the firmware was
loaded without errors.  However, the callback routine does access the
private data several times after that point.

Another problem is that, in order to ensure that the USB device
structure hasn't been freed when the callback routine runs, the driver
takes a reference to it.  This isn't good enough any more, because now
that the callback routine calls usb_driver_release_interface, it has
to ensure that the interface structure hasn't been freed.

Finally, the driver takes an unnecessary reference to the USB device
structure in the probe function and drops the reference in the
disconnect handler.  This extra reference doesn't accomplish anything,
because the USB core already guarantees that a device structure won't
be deallocated while a driver is still bound to any of its interfaces.

To fix these problems, this patch makes the following changes:

	Call usb_driver_release_interface() rather than
	device_release_driver().

	Don't signal the completion until after the important
	information has been copied out of the private data structure,
	and don't refer to the private data at all thereafter.

	Lock udev (the interface's parent) before unbinding the driver
	instead of locking udev->parent.

	During the firmware loading process, take a reference to the
	USB interface instead of the USB device.

	Don't take an unnecessary reference to the device during probe
	(and then don't drop it during disconnect).

Signed-off-by: Alan Stern <stern@rowland.harvard.edu>
Reported-and-tested-by: syzbot+200d4bb11b23d929335f@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
CC: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Acked-by: Christian Lamparter <chunkeey@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Kalle Valo <kvalo@codeaurora.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tusb_get_dev(udev);', '\t\tusb_put_dev(udev);'], 'added_lines': ['\tusb_get_intf(intf);', '\t\tusb_put_intf(intf);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.2.1. There is a use-after-free caused by a malicious USB device in the drivers/net/wireless/intersil/p54/p54usb.c driver.

code_evidence: The function takes a reference on the USB device (udev) with usb_get_dev, then passes priv as the callback context to request_firmware_nowait, which runs asynchronously after this function returns. The disconnect handler can free the interface/private data; the callback later dereferences priv, and on error usb_put_dev(udev) drops a device reference that does not keep the interface alive.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the callback references priv after disconnect may have released it, and the error path drops only the device reference, leaving the interface lifetime unguarded. This is a lifetime/ownership flaw, not merely a lock-ordering race.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The asynchronous firmware-loading callback receives priv while only the USB device, not the interface, is kept alive. Disconnect can free the interface and private structure before the callback runs, so the callback accesses freed memory, producing a use-after-free (crash or potentially unauthorized memory access).

commit_msg:
Integer Overflow in RAND commands can lead to assertion (CVE-2023-25155)

Issue happens when passing a negative long value that greater than
the max positive value that the long can store.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (getLongFromObjectOrReply(c,c->argv[2],&l,NULL) != C_OK) return;', '            if (l < LONG_MIN/2 || l > LONG_MAX/2) {'], 'added_lines': ['        if (getRangeLongFromObjectOrReply(c,c->argv[2],-LONG_MAX,LONG_MAX,&l,NULL) != C_OK) return;', '            if (l < -LONG_MAX/2 || l > LONG_MAX/2) {']}
description: Redis is an in-memory database that persists on disk. Authenticated users issuing specially crafted `SRANDMEMBER`, `ZRANDMEMBER`, and `HRANDFIELD` commands can trigger an integer overflow, resulting in a runtime assertion and termination of the Redis server process. This problem affects all Redis versions. Patches were released in Redis version(s) 6.0.18, 6.2.11 and 7.0.9.

code_evidence: Line 7 parses the count argument with getLongFromObjectOrReply, accepting any long including long values below LONG_MIN/2; line 13's guard uses LONG_MIN/2 (a negative bound), so a large negative count passes the check; line 18 forwards l to zrandmemberWithCountCommand, where negation of such a value overflows.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The flaw is an integer overflow/wraparound: a signed count is negated under the assumption the result fits, but the accepted range allows a value that wraps. This matches CWE-190, distinct from mere input validation since the defect is the arithmetic range assumption.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the count bound permits values whose negation exceeds LONG_MAX, because the lower guard uses LONG_MIN/2 rather than -LONG_MAX/2. Trigger: an authenticated SRANDMEMBER/ZRANDMEMBER/HRANDFIELD request with a specially crafted negative count. Consequence: integer wraparound in the count-handling routine leads to a runtime assertion and Redis server termination (DoS).

commit_msg:
PR22201, DW_AT_name with out of bounds reference

DW_AT_name ought to always have a string value.

	PR 22201
	* dwarf2.c (scan_unit_for_symbols): Ignore DW_AT_name unless it
	has string form.
	(parse_comp_unit): Likewise.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t  unit->name = attr.u.str;'], 'added_lines': ['\t  if (is_str_attr (attr.form))', '\t    unit->name = attr.u.str;']}
description: dwarf2.c in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.29, does not validate the DW_AT_name data type, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (bfd_hash_hash NULL pointer dereference, or out-of-bounds access, and application crash) via a crafted ELF file, related to scan_unit_for_symbols and parse_comp_unit.

code_evidence: In the DW_AT_name case, the code unconditionally assigns unit->name = attr.u.str without checking attr.form. attr.u is a union populated by read_attribute according to the attribute form; for a non-string form (e.g., DW_FORM_addr or a constant), attr.u.str does not hold a valid string pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing form validation lets a non-string attribute value be stored as a string pointer, leading to dereference of an invalid/NULL pointer, matching CWE-476. It is not merely a type-confusion label; the supported consequence is a NULL/invalid pointer dereference causing DoS.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: DW_AT_name is assumed to always carry a string form, so no is_str_attr(attr.form) guard precedes the union read. Trigger: a crafted ELF/DWARF unit supplies DW_AT_name with a non-string form, making attr.u.str an invalid or NULL pointer. Consequence: later use of unit->name (hashing/dereference) causes a NULL pointer dereference or out-of-bounds access and application crash.

commit_msg:
posix-timer: Properly check sigevent->sigev_notify

timer_create() specifies via sigevent->sigev_notify the signal delivery for
the new timer. The valid modes are SIGEV_NONE, SIGEV_SIGNAL, SIGEV_THREAD
and (SIGEV_SIGNAL | SIGEV_THREAD_ID).

The sanity check in good_sigevent() is only checking the valid combination
for the SIGEV_THREAD_ID bit, i.e. SIGEV_SIGNAL, but if SIGEV_THREAD_ID is
not set it accepts any random value.

This has no real effects on the posix timer and signal delivery code, but
it affects show_timer() which handles the output of /proc/$PID/timers. That
function uses a string array to pretty print sigev_notify. The access to
that array has no bound checks, so random sigev_notify cause access beyond
the array bounds.

Add proper checks for the valid notify modes and remove the SIGEV_THREAD_ID
masking from various code pathes as SIGEV_NONE can never be set in
combination with SIGEV_THREAD_ID.

Reported-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers3@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Reported-by: Alexey Dobriyan <adobriyan@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
Cc: John Stultz <john.stultz@linaro.org>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tsigev_none = (timr->it_sigev_notify & ~SIGEV_THREAD_ID) == SIGEV_NONE;'], 'added_lines': ['\tsigev_none = timr->it_sigev_notify == SIGEV_NONE;']}
description: The timer_create syscall implementation in kernel/time/posix-timers.c in the Linux kernel before 4.14.8 doesn't properly validate the sigevent->sigev_notify field, which leads to out-of-bounds access in the show_timer function (called when /proc/$PID/timers is read). This allows userspace applications to read arbitrary kernel memory (on a kernel built with CONFIG_POSIX_TIMERS and CONFIG_CHECKPOINT_RESTORE).

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: common_timer_set only computes a sigev_none boolean and arms the timer; it performs no buffer access, and the out-of-bounds read described occurs in show_timer, not in this function.

commit_msg: Guard binary expressions from too much recursion.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ["\twhile (jsP_accept(J, '|'))"], 'added_lines': ['\tSAVEREC();', "\twhile (jsP_accept(J, '|')) {", '\t\tINCREC();', '\t}', '\tPOPREC();']}
description: jsparse.c in Artifex MuJS through 1.0.2 does not properly maintain the AST depth for binary expressions, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (excessive recursion) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: bitor() parses a left operand via bitxor(), then loops while the '|' token is accepted, rebuilding the AST with EXP2(BITOR, a, bitxor(J, notin)). The loop has no depth accounting or bound; each accepted '|' triggers another bitxor() descent, so nesting of binary '|' expressions is not tracked against any recursion limit.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing depth counter around the recursive bitxor() calls in the '|' loop directly matches CWE-674: uncontrolled recursion consuming stack resources. It is not merely an input-size issue; the parser fails to constrain recursion depth.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the binary-expression parser does not maintain AST depth while looping over '|' operators, so recursive descent through bitxor() is unbounded. Trigger: a crafted input with a deeply nested/stacked '|' binary expression. Consequence: excessive recursion consumes the program stack, causing a denial of service (crash).

commit_msg:
x509: excessive resource use verifying policy constraints

A security vulnerability has been identified in all supported versions
of OpenSSL related to the verification of X.509 certificate chains
that include policy constraints.  Attackers may be able to exploit this
vulnerability by creating a malicious certificate chain that triggers
exponential use of computational resources, leading to a denial-of-service
(DoS) attack on affected systems.

Fixes CVE-2023-0464

Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Shane Lontis <shane.lontis@oracle.com>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/20569)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (level_add_node(level, data, NULL, tree) == NULL) {'], 'added_lines': ['    /* Limit the growth of the tree to mitigate CVE-2023-0464 */', '    tree->node_maximum = OPENSSL_POLICY_TREE_NODES_MAX;', '', '    if (level_add_node(level, data, NULL, tree, 1) == NULL) {']}
description:
A security vulnerability has been identified in all supported versions

of OpenSSL related to the verification of X.509 certificate chains
that include policy constraints.  Attackers may be able to exploit this
vulnerability by creating a malicious certificate chain that triggers
exponential use of computational resources, leading to a denial-of-service
(DoS) attack on affected systems.

Policy processing is disabled by default but can be enabled by passing
the `-policy' argument to the command line utilities or by calling the
`X509_VERIFY_PARAM_set1_policies()' function.

code_evidence: tree_init allocates a policy tree sized to the certificate chain (n+1 levels) and initializes the root level via level_add_node without any cap on the number of nodes created. The patch adds tree->node_maximum and a flag argument to level_add_node, showing the pre-patch code permitted unbounded node growth while constructing the policy tree from attacker-supplied certificates.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The flaw is in validation of attacker-supplied X.509 certificate chains: policy processing proceeds without bounding the constructed policy tree, so certificate validation is improperly constrained and resource-exhausting chains are accepted for processing. This is a certificate-validation defect (CWE-295); the DoS is its consequence, not a separate weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the policy tree built from chain certificates has no node limit, so a malicious chain with policy constraints causes exponential node expansion during verification. Trigger: verifying an attacker-crafted X.509 chain with policy processing enabled. Consequence: excessive CPU/memory consumption leading to denial of service.

commit_msg:
Fixed bug: line hooks in stripped functions

Line-hook handling was accessing debug info. without checking whether
it was present.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  return 0;  /* no line changes in the way */'], 'added_lines': ['  if (p->lineinfo == NULL)  /* no debug information? */', '    return 0;', '  return 0;  /* no line changes between positions */']}
description: ldebug.c in Lua 5.4.0 attempts to access debug information via the line hook of a stripped function, leading to a NULL pointer dereference.

code_evidence: The function loops calling p->lineinfo[oldpc] (line 3) without any prior NULL check on p->lineinfo; the only exit is the loop condition and the final return on line 6. The patched version adds an early guard, confirming the original dereference path was reachable when lineinfo is absent.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer expected to be valid but which can be NULL for stripped functions, matching CWE-476's null dereference pattern. Contrast with CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read): the defect is the absent NULL check, not an index bound.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: changedline dereferences p->lineinfo unconditionally. Trigger: a stripped function (no debug info) whose lineinfo is NULL reaches this hook with oldpc < newpc, so p->lineinfo[oldpc] dereferences NULL. Supported consequence: NULL pointer dereference causing a crash/DoS.

commit_msg: opj_j2k_write_sot(): fix potential write heap buffer overflow (#991)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['                                  OPJ_UINT32 p_total_data_size,', '', '    if (p_total_data_size < 12) {', '        opj_event_msg(p_manager, EVT_ERROR,', '                      "Not enough bytes in output buffer to write SOT marker\\n");', '        return OPJ_FALSE;', '    }']}
description: A size-validation issue was discovered in opj_j2k_write_sot in lib/openjp2/j2k.c in OpenJPEG 2.2.0. The vulnerability causes an out-of-bounds write, which may lead to remote denial of service (heap-based buffer overflow affecting opj_write_bytes_LE in lib/openjp2/cio.c) or possibly remote code execution. NOTE: this vulnerability exists because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2017-14152.

code_evidence: opj_j2k_write_sot writes a fixed 12-byte SOT segment into p_data without receiving or checking any output-buffer capacity.
It performs sequential opj_write_bytes calls at p_data, p_data+2, p_data+4, p_data+6 (after +=4) and p_data+7, then advances p_data and reports *p_data_written = 12.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes 12 bytes of marker data through p_data with no capacity constraint, so writes can exceed the intended buffer end, matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). This is a write-past-end issue, not merely a read overrun or NULL dereference.

evidence_lines.code: * p_data_written = 12;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function assumes the caller-provided p_data buffer holds at least 12 bytes and has no size parameter or bound check. Trigger: a caller passing a smaller or truncated output buffer causes opj_write_bytes to store past the allocation. Consequence: heap-based out-of-bounds write, corrupting adjacent memory and potentially causing a crash or code execution.

commit_msg: Fix bug #72606: heap-buffer-overflow (write) simplestring_addn simplestring.c
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['void simplestring_addn(simplestring* target, const char* source, int add_len) {', '         int newsize = target->len + add_len + 1;', '         int incr = target->size * 2;', '         newsize = newsize - (newsize % incr) + incr;'], 'added_lines': ['void simplestring_addn(simplestring* target, const char* source, size_t add_len) {', '   size_t newsize = target->size, incr = 0;', '', '      if((SIZE_MAX - add_len) < target->len || (SIZE_MAX - add_len - 1) < target->len) {', "    \t  /* check for overflows, if there's a potential overflow do nothing */", '    \t  return;', '      }', '', '         newsize = target->len + add_len + 1;', '         incr = target->size * 2;', '         if (incr) {', '            newsize = newsize - (newsize % incr) + incr;', '         }', '         if(newsize < (target->len + add_len + 1)) {', '        \t /* some kind of overflow happened */', '        \t return;', '         }']}
description: Integer signedness error in the simplestring_addn function in simplestring.c in xmlrpc-epi through 0.54.2, as used in PHP before 5.5.38, 5.6.x before 5.6.24, and 7.x before 7.0.9, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer overflow) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a long first argument to the PHP xmlrpc_encode_request function.

code_evidence: add_len is a signed int, so a negative value passes the target/source check and reaches the size arithmetic.

The size test target->len + add_len + 1 > target->size and the newsize/incr computations are performed in signed int, so the sums and the modulo by incr can overflow or wrap, yielding a small or negative newsize.
realloc allocates the wrapped newsize and target->size is set to it, so the buffer is smaller than target->len + add_len + 1.
memcpy copies add_len bytes to target->str + target->len and the terminator is written at target->len, both beyond the undersized allocation, producing the heap write overflow.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes past the allocated target->str boundary, which is precisely an out-of-bounds memory buffer operation as described by CWE-119. The integer overflow is the enabling cause, but the supported consequence is the buffer overflow write.

evidence_lines.code: void simplestring_addn(simplestring* target, const char* source, int add_len) {

target->str = (char*)realloc(target->str, newsize);
target->size = target->str ? newsize : 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is signed int arithmetic on add_len and target->len without an overflow/negative check, so newsize wraps to a small value. Trigger is a long (or negative) add_len reaching this growth path; the consequence is a heap buffer overflow write in the memcpy and terminator store.

commit_msg:
Disallow namespace nodes in XPointer ranges

Namespace nodes must be copied to avoid use-after-free errors.
But they don't necessarily have a physical representation in a
document, so simply disallow them in XPointer ranges.

Found with afl-fuzz.

Fixes CVE-2016-4658.

Use DefineOwnProperty instead of Set in for gin, including gin::Define.
Replace Set in v8_helpers as well, to avoid the same problem.
Also update callsites from JS to CHECK expected arguments, rather
than DCHECK (since receiving unexpected arguments likely means
executing untrusted code).

BUG=549986

Review URL: https://codereview.chromium.org/1433293004

Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#359460}
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  DCHECK(args.Length() == 5);', '  DCHECK(args[0]->IsString());', '  DCHECK(args[1]->IsString());', '  DCHECK(args[2]->IsString());', '  DCHECK(args[3]->IsString());', '  DCHECK(args[4]->IsBoolean());'], 'added_lines': ['  CHECK_EQ(5, args.Length());', '  CHECK(args[0]->IsString());', '  CHECK(args[1]->IsString());', '  CHECK(args[2]->IsString());', '  CHECK(args[3]->IsString());', '  CHECK(args[4]->IsBoolean());']}
description: The Extensions subsystem in Google Chrome before 49.0.2623.75 does not properly maintain own properties, which allows remote attackers to bypass intended access restrictions via crafted JavaScript code that triggers an incorrect cast, related to extensions/renderer/v8_helpers.h and gin/converter.h.

code_evidence: The function validates its JavaScript-supplied arguments only with DCHECK: argument count, string types for args[0..3], and boolean type for args[4]. DCHECKs are compiled out in release builds, so these constraints are absent in production.

After the compile-time-only checks, args[0..3] are dereferenced via v8::String::Utf8Value and args[4] via BooleanValue, and the values flow into WebDOMFileSystem::create and createV8Entry. With crafted JS passing non-string/non-boolean values, the type assumptions are unchecked at runtime.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing runtime enforcement of expected property/argument types lets untrusted JS bypass intended restrictions on the extension API, matching CWE-264's scope of improper permission/access-control maintenance. It is not a generic memory-safety flaw; the weakness is the absent runtime constraint enabling access-control bypass.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is reliance on debug-only DCHECKs to enforce argument count and type constraints on an exposed JS callback; in release builds no validation occurs. Trigger is crafted JavaScript invoking GetFileEntry with unexpected argument count or types, causing incorrect casts on the V8 values and consequent type confusion when constructing the file-system entry.

commit_msg:
Fix #383 (amendment)

When reading images in GD or GD2 format, we have to ensure that the
transparent color is not set, if it would refer to a non-extant palette
entry.

We back that up with respective regression tests.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t/* Make sure transparent index is within bounds of the palette. */', '\t\tif (im->transparent >= 256 || im->transparent < 0) {', '\t\t\tim->transparent = (-1);', '\t\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\t}', '\t/* Make sure transparent index is within bounds of the palette. */', '\tif (!(im->trueColor) && (im->transparent >= im->colorsTotal || im->transparent < 0)) {', '\t\tim->transparent = (-1);']}
description: In the GD Graphics Library (aka LibGD) through 2.2.5, there is a heap-based buffer over-read in tiffWriter in gd_tiff.c. NOTE: the vendor says "In my opinion this issue should not have a CVE, since the GD and GD2 formats are documented to be 'obsolete, and should only be used for development and testing purposes.'

code_evidence: In the non-GD2 branch, colorsTotal and transparent are read from the stream, and transparent is only rejected when >= 256 or < 0, without checking it against colorsTotal.
Later, the loop writes im->open[i] for i < im->colorsTotal, so a transparent value larger than colorsTotal is retained but not used as an index here.

commit_msg:
mm/rmap: Fix anon_vma->degree ambiguity leading to double-reuse

anon_vma->degree tracks the combined number of child anon_vmas and VMAs
that use the anon_vma as their ->anon_vma.

anon_vma_clone() then assumes that for any anon_vma attached to
src->anon_vma_chain other than src->anon_vma, it is impossible for it to
be a leaf node of the VMA tree, meaning that for such VMAs ->degree is
elevated by 1 because of a child anon_vma, meaning that if ->degree
equals 1 there are no VMAs that use the anon_vma as their ->anon_vma.

This assumption is wrong because the ->degree optimization leads to leaf
nodes being abandoned on anon_vma_clone() - an existing anon_vma is
reused and no new parent-child relationship is created.  So it is
possible to reuse an anon_vma for one VMA while it is still tied to
another VMA.

This is an issue because is_mergeable_anon_vma() and its callers assume
that if two VMAs have the same ->anon_vma, the list of anon_vmas
attached to the VMAs is guaranteed to be the same.  When this assumption
is violated, vma_merge() can merge pages into a VMA that is not attached
to the corresponding anon_vma, leading to dangling page->mapping
pointers that will be dereferenced during rmap walks.

Fix it by separately tracking the number of child anon_vmas and the
number of VMAs using the anon_vma as their ->anon_vma.

Fixes: 7a3ef208e662 ("mm: prevent endless growth of anon_vma hierarchy")
Cc: stable@kernel.org
Acked-by: Michal Hocko <mhocko@suse.com>
Acked-by: Vlastimil Babka <vbabka@suse.cz>
Signed-off-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tanon_vma->parent->degree--;', '\t\tvma->anon_vma->degree--;', '\t\tVM_WARN_ON(anon_vma->degree);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tanon_vma->parent->num_children--;', '\t\tvma->anon_vma->num_active_vmas--;', '\t\tVM_WARN_ON(anon_vma->num_children);', '\t\tVM_WARN_ON(anon_vma->num_active_vmas);']}
description: mm/rmap.c in the Linux kernel before 5.19.7 has a use-after-free related to leaf anon_vma double reuse.

code_evidence: When the interval tree for an anon_vma becomes empty, the code decrements anon_vma->parent->degree and skips freeing the avc (continue), leaving the child anon_vma attached to the VMA chain while its parent's degree no longer reflects the child relationship.

The single degree counter conflates child anon_vmas and VMAs using the anon_vma; decrementing vma->anon_vma->degree here does not distinguish the two, so degree can reach zero while a leaf anon_vma is still referenced.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is reuse of freed anon_vma memory through stale page->mapping pointers during rmap traversal, which matches CWE-416 (use after free). The defect is the ambiguous degree accounting, not merely a merge-logic error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: one degree field tracks both child anon_vmas and active VMAs, and the empty-tree branch abandons a leaf node without creating a new parent-child link. An anon_vma can therefore be reused for one VMA while still tied to another; is_mergeable_anon_vma() then wrongly assumes identical chains, and vma_merge() can leave dangling page->mapping pointers that are dereferenced during rmap walks, yielding a use-after-free.

commit_msg:
minizip: Check length of comment, filename, and extra field, in zipOpenNewFileInZip4_64

These are stored in 16-bit fields in the zip file format. Passing longer
values would generate an invalid file.

Passing very long values could also cause the computation of
zi->ci.size_centralheader to overflow, which would cause heap buffer
overflow on subsequent writes to zi->ci.central_header.

If the member also requires', '    // a Zip64 extra block, that will also need to fit within that 16-bit', '    // length, but that will be checked for later.', '    if ((size_extrafield_local>0xffff) || (size_extrafield_global>0xffff))', '        return ZIP_PARAMERROR;']}

NOTE: MiniZip is not a supported part of the zlib product. NOTE: pyminizip through 0.2.6 is also vulnerable because it bundles an affected zlib version, and exposes the applicable MiniZip code through its compress API.

code_evidence: size_comment and size_filename are computed via (uInt)strlen() without any upper bound on the input lengths.
size_centralheader is computed as SIZECENTRALHEADER + size_filename + size_extrafield_global + size_comment in uInt arithmetic, then used to size the ALLOC buffer.
The filename bytes are copied into central_header at offset SIZECENTRALHEADER for size_filename iterations.
The comment bytes are copied at offset SIZECENTRALHEADER + size_filename + size_extrafield_global for size_comment iterations.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The direct flaw is an unchecked integer addition that wraps, producing an undersized allocation; the later out-of-bounds writes are the consequence. This matches CWE-190 (integer overflow/wraparound) rather than a pure out-of-bounds-write label, since the missing constraint is on the length arithmetic.

size_comment = (uInt)strlen(comment);
size_filename = (uInt)strlen(filename);

zi->ci.size_centralheader = SIZECENTRALHEADER + size_filename + size_extrafield_global + size_comment;
zi->ci.central_header = (char*)ALLOC((uInt)zi->ci.size_centralheader + zi->ci.size_centralExtraFree);

for (i=0;i<size_filename;i++)
*(zi->ci.central_header+SIZECENTRALHEADER+i) = *(filename+i);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the sums for size_centralheader and the comment copy offset are 32-bit uInt values built from attacker-controlled lengths with no 16-bit/overflow check. Consequence: ALLOC reserves a small buffer while the copy loops write size_filename/size_comment bytes past it, yielding a heap-based buffer overflow.

commit_msg:
tools/xenstore: fix checking node permissions

Today chk_domain_generation() is being used to check whether a node
permission entry is still valid or whether it is referring to a domain
no longer existing. This is done by comparing the node's and the
domain's generation count.

In case no struct domain is existing for a checked domain, but the
domain itself is valid, chk_domain_generation() assumes it is being
called due to the first node created for a new domain and it will
return success.

This might be wrong in case the checked permission is related to an
old domain, which has just been replaced with a new domain using the
same domid.

Fix that by letting chk_domain_generation() fail in case a struct
domain isn't found. In order to cover the case of the first node for
a new domain try to allocate the needed struct domain explicitly when
processing the related SET_PERMS command. In case a referenced domain
isn't existing, flag the related permission to be ignored right away.

This is XSA-417 / CVE-2022-42320.

Signed-off-by: Juergen Gross <jgross@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (domain_alloc_permrefs(&perms) < 0)', '\t\treturn ENOMEM;', '\tif (perms.p[0].perms & XS_PERM_IGNORE)', '\t\treturn ENOENT;']}
description: Xenstore: Guests can get access to Xenstore nodes of deleted domains Access rights of Xenstore nodes are per domid. When a domain is gone, there might be Xenstore nodes left with access rights containing the domid of the removed domain. This is normally no problem, as those access right entries will be corrected when such a node is written later. There is a small time window when a new domain is created, where the access rights of a past domain with the same domid as the new one will be regarded to be still valid, leading to the new domain being able to get access to a node which was meant to be accessible by the removed domain. For this to happen another domain needs to write the node before the newly created domain is being introduced to Xenstore by dom0.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function's set-perms logic and the added domain_alloc_permrefs/ignore handling address stale domain-ID permission reuse (CWE-672/416-style access control), not incomplete cleanup of temporary or supporting resources after use.

commit_msg:
Since server IDs are basically indistinguishable from really big client
IDs at many points in the source, it's theoretically possible to overflow
a map and either overflow server IDs into the client ID space, or grow
client IDs into the server ID space. This would currently take a massive
amount of RAM, but the definition of massive changes yearly.

Prevent this by placing a ridiculous but arbitrary upper bound on the
number of items we can put in a map: 0xF00000, somewhere over 15 million.
This should satisfy pathological clients without restriction, but stays
well clear of the 0xFF000000 transition point between server and client
IDs. It will still take an improbable amount of RAM to hit this, and a
client could still exhaust all RAM in this way, but our goal is to prevent
overflow and undefined behaviour.

Fixes #224

Signed-off-by: Derek Foreman <derek.foreman@collabora.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (i > WL_MAP_MAX_OBJECTS)', '\t\treturn -1;']}
description: An internal reference count is held on the buffer pool, incremented every time a new buffer is created from the pool. The reference count is maintained as an int; on LP64 systems this can cause the reference count to overflow if the client creates a large number of wl_shm buffer objects, or if it can coerce the server to create a large number of external references to the buffer storage. With the reference count overflowing, a use-after-free can be constructed on the wl_shm_pool tracking structure, where values may be incremented or decremented; it may also be possible to construct a limited oracle to leak 4 bytes of server-side memory to the attacking client at a time.

code_evidence: The function derives the array index from the caller-supplied 'i': client IDs below WL_SERVER_ID_START index client_entries, while larger IDs are rebased by subtracting WL_SERVER_ID_START and index server_entries. Before the patch no upper bound constrained 'i' or the rebased value.

'count' is computed from entries->size, then compared with the unbounded 'i'. If 'count == i' wl_array_add grows the array, and start[i] is written. An excessively large 'i' can drive array growth and index arithmetic toward the server/client ID transition point.
The write start[i].data and start[i].next uses the unbounded index directly, so an attacker-chosen large ID can overflow the map's ID space and corrupt adjacent tracking state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's index and array-size calculations assume values remain within a bounded ID space; the missing bound permits integer overflow/wraparound of IDs and sizes, matching CWE-190. Use-after-free or memory disclosure are consequences, not the root cause.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the map index 'i' is trusted without an upper bound, so ID/array-size arithmetic can approach or exceed the server/client ID transition. Trigger: a client supplies or coerces a very large object ID, causing wl_array_add to grow entries and the index to overflow the intended ID space, potentially corrupting the wl_map tracking structure.

code_evidence: memdup_user allocates ym and returns it; only an IS_ERR check is performed before proceeding.

Trigger: an ioctl_cmd of SIOCYAMSMCS with user data whose cmd field is not SIOCYAMSMCS. Consequence: repeated calls leak heap memory, leading to resource exhaustion/DoS.

This overflow is controllable and could be abused for code execution, especially on 32-bit systems.

commit_msg:
Bug #700169 - unchecked type

Bug #700169 "Type confusion in setcolorspace"

In seticc() we extract "Name" from a dictionary, if it succeeds we then
use it as a string, without checking the type to see if it is in fact
a string.

Add a check on the type, and add a couple to check that 'N' is an integer
in a few places too.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (r_type(pnval) != t_integer)', '        return gs_note_error(gs_error_typecheck);']}
description: psi/zicc.c in Artifex Ghostscript before 9.26 allows remote attackers to bypass intended access restrictions because of a setcolorspace type confusion.

code_evidence: dict_find_string retrieves the "N" entry into pnval; success only means the key exists, not that its value is an integer. Line 17 reads pnval->value.intval directly, interpreting the ref's union as an integer regardless of the actual stored type.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is an unchecked reinterpreting of a ref's union as an integer, i.e., treating one type as another, which matches CWE-704 Incorrect Type Conversion or Cast. A type-confusion child category would also fit, but the target class-level 704 correctly captures the missing type check before the cast.

Trigger: a dictionary whose "N" entry exists but holds a non-integer ref (e.g., a string or name) reaches line 17. The union bytes are then reinterpreted as an int, giving an attacker-influenced ncomps value that flows into picc_profile->num_comps and later profile handling.

commit_msg:
ext4: fix data exposure after a crash

Huang has reported that in his powerfail testing he is seeing stale
block contents in some of recently allocated blocks although he mounts
ext4 in data=ordered mode. After some investigation I have found out
that indeed when delayed allocation is used, we don't add inode to
transaction's list of inodes needing flushing before commit. Originally
we were doing that but commit f3b59291a69d removed the logic with a
flawed argument that it is not needed.

The problem is that although for delayed allocated blocks we write their
contents immediately after allocating them, there is no guarantee that
the IO scheduler or device doesn't reorder things and thus transaction
allocating blocks and attaching them to inode can reach stable storage
before actual block contents. Actually whenever we attach freshly
allocated blocks to inode using a written extent, we should add inode to
transaction's ordered inode list to make sure we properly wait for block
contents to be written before committing the transaction. So that is
what we do in this patch. This also handles other cases where stale data
exposure was possible - like filling hole via mmap in
data=ordered,nodelalloc mode.

The only exception to the above rule are extending direct IO writes where
blkdev_direct_IO() waits for IO to complete before increasing i_size and
thus stale data exposure is not possible. For now we don't complicate
the code with optimizing this special case since the overhead is pretty
low. In case this is observed to be a performance problem we can always
handle it using a special flag to ext4_map_blocks().

CC: stable@vger.kernel.org
Fixes: f3b59291a69d0b734be1fc8be489fef2dd846d3d
Reported-by: "HUANG Weller (CM/ESW12-CN)" <Weller.Huang@cn.bosch.com>
Tested-by: "HUANG Weller (CM/ESW12-CN)" <Weller.Huang@cn.bosch.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Kara <jack@suse.cz>
Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (ext4_test_inode_state(inode, EXT4_STATE_ORDERED_MODE)) {', '\t\tret = ext4_jbd2_file_inode(handle, inode);', '\t\tif (ret) {', '\t\t\tunlock_page(page);', '\t\t\tput_page(page);', '\t\t\tgoto errout;', '\t\t}', '\t}', ''], 'added_lines': []}
description: fs/ext4/inode.c in the Linux kernel before 4.6.2, when ext4 data=ordered mode is used, mishandles a needs-flushing-before-commit list, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information from other users' files in opportunistic circumstances by waiting for a hardware reset, creating a new file, making write system calls, and reading this file.

code_evidence: Before writing/committing data in data=ordered mode, the function checks EXT4_STATE_ORDERED_MODE and calls ext4_jbd2_file_inode(handle, inode) to register the inode on the transaction's ordered flush list, ensuring block contents reach stable storage before the transaction commits. The subsequent block_write_end path attaches freshly allocated/delayed blocks to the inode without this ordered-flush registration.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an information exposure: filesystem metadata commits ahead of data, causing previously freed block contents belonging to other users to be disclosed to the new file's owner. CWE-200 fits as the supported confidentiality impact of this missing flush ordering, though the root cause is an ordering/flush omission rather than explicit data handling.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the ordered-mode flush registration in ext4_write_end is removed/absent, so newly allocated blocks are attached to the inode without forcing their contents to be written before the allocating transaction commits. Trigger: a local user writes to a file in data=ordered mode and a crash/reset occurs; the inode metadata can reach stable storage before block data. Consequence: stale block contents from other users' files are exposed when the file is read after remount.

commit_msg: XBM coder leaves the hex image data uninitialized if hex value of the pixel is negative
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        break;', '        break;'], 'added_lines': ['        {', '          data=(unsigned char *) RelinquishMagickMemory(data);', '          ThrowReaderException(CorruptImageError,"ImproperImageHeader");', '        }', '        {', '          data=(unsigned char *) RelinquishMagickMemory(data);', '          ThrowReaderException(CorruptImageError,"ImproperImageHeader");', '        }']}
description: ReadXBMImage in coders/xbm.c in ImageMagick before 7.0.8-9 leaves data uninitialized when processing an XBM file that has a negative pixel value. If the affected code is used as a library loaded into a process that includes sensitive information, that information sometimes can be leaked via the image data.

code_evidence: data is allocated for the full image (142-143) and p is set to its start (146). In both the version-10 loop (147-156) and version-11 loop (157-164), c=XBMInteger(...) is read and if c<0 the loop breaks, leaving the remaining bytes of data uninitialized.

After the loops, p is reset to data (170) and the pixel loop (171-195) reads *p++ (181) for every pixel without checking whether the decoding loops completed. Bytes never written by the decode loops are consumed as pixel data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function emits uninitialized heap contents as image pixel data, an information exposure to whoever receives the resulting image. CWE-200 fits because the weakness is disclosure of residual sensitive process memory; the underlying uninitialized-memory error (CWE-457) is the mechanism, but the supported consequence is the confidentiality leak described by the target.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a negative hex pixel value causes the decode loop to break early, so the tail of the allocated data buffer is never initialized. Trigger: an XBM file containing a negative pixel value. Consequence: the pixel loop reads uninitialized heap bytes and copies them into the output image, potentially exposing residual process memory when the image is later returned or saved.

commit_msg:
Fix tf.raw_ops.LoadAndRemapMatrix vulnerability with invalid `row_remapping`.

Check that `row_remapping` has the correct dims().

PiperOrigin-RevId: 445522800
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    OP_REQUIRES(', '        context, row_remapping_t->dims() == 1,', '        errors::InvalidArgument("The `row_remapping` tensor must be 1-D, got "', '                                "a tensor of shape ",', '                                row_remapping_t->shape().DebugString()));']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. Prior to versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4, the implementation of `tf.raw_ops.LoadAndRemapMatrix does not fully validate the input arguments. This results in a `CHECK`-failure which can be used to trigger a denial of service attack. The code assumes `initializing_values` is a vector but there is no validation for this before accessing its value. Versions 2.9.0, 2.8.1, 2.7.2, and 2.6.4 contain a patch for this issue.

code_evidence: The kernel fetches `row_remapping` and immediately converts it with `row_remapping_t->vec<int64_t>()`, which assumes a rank-1 tensor without checking `dims()` first.

The size check at line 7 only compares `row_remapping.size()` to `num_rows_`; it does not establish that the tensor is 1-D, and the subsequent loop indexes `row_remapping(i)` relying on that unchecked assumption.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to validate a required property (rank/dimensionality) of an input tensor before using it, matching CWE-20's improper input validation. The impact is availability (crash), not a memory-safety flaw such as out-of-bounds access, so a lower-level memory CWE is not supported by the shown code.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code assumes a caller-supplied `row_remapping` tensor is 1-D and calls `vec<int64_t>()`/element access without validating rank. Trigger: a crafted `row_remapping` with a rank other than 1 causes a `CHECK`-failure in the vector accessor. Supported consequence: process abort, i.e., denial of service; the patch adds a `dims() == 1` guard before the accessor.

description: An issue was discovered in drivers/scsi/qedi/qedi_dbg.c in the Linux kernel before 5.1.12. In the qedi_dbg_* family of functions, there is an out-of-bounds read.

code_evidence: Local buffer nfunc is fixed at 32 bytes and zeroed before copying.

memcpy copies sizeof(nfunc)-1 (31) bytes from func regardless of the actual length of the caller-supplied string; if func is shorter, the read continues past its terminating null into adjacent memory.
The over-read nfunc is then passed as a %s argument to pr_warn in both the qedi->pdev branch and the fallback branch, exposing the copied bytes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is a read past the end of the intended source buffer (the short func string) during memcpy, matching CWE-125 Out-of-bounds Read. This is a read overrun, not an out-of-bounds write, since the destination nfunc is sized to the copy length.

evidence_lines.code:
pr_warn("[%s]:[%s:%d]:%d: %pV", dev_name(&qedi->pdev->dev),
nfunc, line, qedi->host_no, &vaf);
pr_warn("[0000:00:00.0]:[%s:%d]: %pV", nfunc, line, &vaf);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: an unconditional fixed-size memcpy copies 31 bytes from the source string func without checking its length. Trigger: a caller passes a string literal shorter than 31 bytes (e.g. __func__), so memcpy reads beyond the string's end. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read of global string data, reported by KASAN as a global-out-of-bounds read, with the excess bytes potentially printed.

commit_msg: RLE check for pixel offset less than 0 (heap overflow report from Craig Young).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    offset,', '          if (offset+((size_t) operand*number_planes) > pixel_info_length)', '          p=pixels+offset;', '          if (offset+((size_t) operand*number_planes) > pixel_info_length)'], 'added_lines': ['    offset,', '          if ((offset < 0) ||', '              (offset+((size_t) operand*number_planes) > pixel_info_length))', '          if ((offset < 0) ||', '              (offset+((size_t) operand*number_planes) > pixel_info_length))', '          p=pixels+offset;']}
description: Heap-based buffer overflow in the ReadRLEImage function in coders/rle.c in ImageMagick 6.9.4-8 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or have other unspecified impact via a crafted RLE file.

code_evidence: In ByteDataOp, offset is computed from attacker-controlled x, y, plane and image dimensions; the old check only rejected offset+operand*number_planes > pixel_info_length, so a negative offset (e.g. when y exceeds rows) passed, then p=pixels+offset and *p=pixel wrote before the buffer.
RunDataOp has the same pattern: offset computed at 252-253, p=pixels+offset at 254 before the bounds check at 255, allowing a negative offset to produce an out-of-bounds write via *p=pixel at 266.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes through a pointer derived from an unchecked offset, producing an out-of-bounds write to a heap buffer, which is an improper restriction of operations within a memory buffer (CWE-119). It is not merely a signedness issue in isolation; the supported consequence is memory-buffer boundary violation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: offset is a signed-derived value that can become negative when crafted RLE opcodes set y beyond image->rows, and the bounds check compares only the upper limit. Trigger: a crafted RLE file with SkipLinesOp moving y past rows followed by ByteDataOp/RunDataOp. Consequence: pixels+offset points before the allocated pixel buffer, and *p=pixel writes out of bounds, causing heap corruption or crash.

In mirror_iteration() we call mirror_wait_on_conflicts() with
`self` parameter set to NULL.

Starting from commit d44dae1a7c we dereference `self` pointer in
mirror_wait_on_conflicts() without checks if it is not NULL.

Buglink: https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=2001404

Signed-off-by: Stefano Garzarella <sgarzare@redhat.com>
Message-Id: <20210910124533.288318-1-sgarzare@redhat.com>

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                /*', '                 * If the operation is already (indirectly) waiting for us, or', '                 * will wait for us as soon as it wakes up, then just go on', '                 * (instead of producing a deadlock in the former case).', '                 */', '                if (op->waiting_for_op) {', '                    continue;', '                self->waiting_for_op = op;', '                self->waiting_for_op = NULL;'], 'added_lines': ['                if (self) {', '                    /*', '                     * If the operation is already (indirectly) waiting for us,', '                     * or will wait for us as soon as it wakes up, then just go', '                     * on (instead of producing a deadlock in the former case).', '                     */', '                    if (op->waiting_for_op) {', '                        continue;', '                    }', '', '                    self->waiting_for_op = op;', '', '                if (self) {', '                    self->waiting_for_op = NULL;', '                }', '']}
description: A NULL pointer dereference issue was found in the block mirror layer of QEMU in versions prior to 6.2.0. The `self` pointer is dereferenced in mirror_wait_on_conflicts() without ensuring that it's not NULL. A malicious unprivileged user within the guest could use this flaw to crash the QEMU process on the host when writing data reaches the threshold of mirroring node.

code_evidence: The loop skips only the exact op == self (lines 19-21). When self is NULL, no in-flight op equals NULL, so overlap detection still proceeds. Line 28 writes self->waiting_for_op = op and line 30 writes self->waiting_for_op = NULL without any NULL check on self; both dereference the NULL self pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes through a pointer (self) that is not validated for NULL, directly matching NULL Pointer Dereference (CWE-476). The deadlock-avoidance logic in the same branch concerns op->waiting_for_op, not a separate weakness class, so CWE-476 is the fitting label.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: mirror_wait_on_conflicts() unconditionally dereferences its self parameter at lines 28 and 30, but callers can pass self as NULL. Trigger: an overlapping in-flight operation is found while self is NULL, so the overlap branch is entered and self->waiting_for_op is written. Supported consequence: NULL pointer dereference, crashing the QEMU process (availability impact).

commit_msg:
IOMMU: default to always quarantining PCI devices

XSA-302 relies on the use of libxl's "assignable-add" feature to prepare
devices to be assigned to untrusted guests.

Unfortunately, this is not considered a strictly required step for
device assignment. The PCI passthrough documentation on the wiki
describes alternate ways of preparing devices for assignment, and
libvirt uses its own ways as well. Hosts where these alternate methods
are used will still leave the system in a vulnerable state after the
device comes back from a guest.

Default to always quarantining PCI devices, but provide a command line
option to revert back to prior behavior (such that people who both
sufficiently trust their guests and want to be able to use devices in
Dom0 again after they had been in use by a guest wouldn't need to
"manually" move such devices back from DomIO to Dom0).

This is XSA-306.

Reported-by: Marek Marczykowski-Górecki <marmarek@invisiblethingslab.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Wei Liu <wl@xen.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        else if ( (val = parse_boolean("quarantine", s, ss)) >= 0 )', '            iommu_quarantine = val;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.12.x allowing attackers to gain host OS privileges via DMA in a situation where an untrusted domain has access to a physical device (and assignable-add is not used), because of an incomplete fix for CVE-2019-18424. XSA-302 relies on the use of libxl's "assignable-add" feature to prepare devices to be assigned to untrusted guests. Unfortunately, this is not considered a strictly required step for device assignment. The PCI passthrough documentation on the wiki describes alternate ways of preparing devices for assignment, and libvirt uses its own ways as well. Hosts where these "alternate" methods are used will still leave the system in a vulnerable state after the device comes back from a guest. An untrusted domain with access to a physical device can DMA into host memory, leading to privilege escalation. Only systems where guests are given direct access to physical devices capable of DMA (PCI pass-through) are vulnerable. Systems which do not use PCI pass-through are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: The parser now accepts a 'quarantine' boolean token via parse_boolean and assigns the result to iommu_quarantine. parse_boolean already constrains the token to a valid boolean value, so the new branch itself validates its input correctly.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 requires that the function accept input without correctly validating required properties. Here the added branch uses parse_boolean, which rejects non-boolean tokens, and only a recognized token is stored. The function does not perform insufficient validation, so the target CWE is not directly supported by this function.

evidence_lines.code:
else if ( (val = parse_boolean("igfx", s, ss)) >= 0 )
iommu_igfx = val;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function is a command-line parameter parser; it only maps a recognized boolean token to the iommu_quarantine global. The security-relevant behavior (defaulting to quarantine) is not enforced or validated here, and the parser does not introduce an unvalidated data path. No missing validation of attacker-controlled input occurs within this function.

commit_msg: mod_radius: copy _only_ the password
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  /* Clear the buffers. */', "  memset(pwhash, '\\0', sizeof(pwhash));", '  memcpy(pwhash, passwd, pwlen);'], 'added_lines': ['  /* Clear the buffers. */', "  memset(pwhash, '\\0', sizeof(pwhash));", '', '    /* pwlen is not a multiple of RADIUS_PASSWD_LEN, need to prepare a proper buffer */', '    memcpy(pwhash, passwd, pwlen);', '  } else {', '    /* pwlen is a multiple of RADIUS_PASSWD_LEN, we can just use it. */', '    memcpy(pwhash, passwd, pwlen);']}
description: mod_radius in ProFTPD before 1.3.7c allows memory disclosure to RADIUS servers because it copies blocks of 16 characters.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function uses only stack-allocated buffers (pwhash, calculated) and performs no heap allocation, so there is no allocated memory to fail to release; the described defect is an out-of-bounds copy/memory disclosure, not CWE-401.

commit_msg: Fix bug #71923 - integer overflow in ZipArchive::getFrom*
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tbuffer = zend_string_alloc(len, 0);'], 'added_lines': ['\tbuffer = zend_string_safe_alloc(1, len, 0, 0);']}
description: Multiple integer overflows in php_zip.c in the zip extension in PHP before 7.0.6 allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer overflow and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted call to (1) getFromIndex or (2) getFromName in the ZipArchive class.

code_evidence: The caller-controlled len is parsed from the optional "l" argument at lines 18/23; when len < 1 it is replaced with the archive entry size sb.size (lines 31-33), so len is attacker-influenced.

Line 42 allocates a buffer of size len with zend_string_alloc, which computes the allocation size without overflow checking; line 43 then passes ZSTR_LEN(buffer) as the read length and line 49 writes the terminator at index n.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is unchecked integer arithmetic in a size calculation used for memory allocation, matching CWE-190. The overflow is the cause; the heap buffer overflow is the downstream consequence, not the mapped weakness itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the buffer length len flows into zend_string_alloc, whose internal size arithmetic (header plus len) is unchecked, so a crafted large len can wrap the computed allocation size. Trigger: getFromIndex/getFromName with a very large len. Consequence: an undersized heap allocation followed by zip_fread writing into it and the terminator write at n, yielding a heap-based buffer overflow/crash.

A new dir entry can be created in get_subdir and its 'header->parent' is
set to NULL.  Only after insert_header success, it will be set to 'dir',
otherwise 'header->parent' is set to NULL and drop_sysctl_table is called.
However in err handling path of get_subdir, drop_sysctl_table also be
called on 'new->header' regardless its value of parent pointer.  Then
put_links is called, which triggers NULL-ptr deref when access member of
header->parent.

In fact we have multiple error paths which call drop_sysctl_table() there,
upon failure on insert_links() we also call drop_sysctl_table().And even
in the successful case on __register_sysctl_table() we still always call
drop_sysctl_table().This patch fix it.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tput_links(header);'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (parent)', '\t\tput_links(header);']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 5.0.6, there is a NULL pointer dereference in drop_sysctl_table() in fs/proc/proc_sysctl.c, related to put_links, aka CID-23da9588037e.

code_evidence: Line 3 caches header->parent into parent, and line 6 unconditionally calls put_links(header) without checking that the cached parent (and thus header->parent) is non-NULL.
Lines 10-11 test parent before recursing, showing the code already expects header->parent may be NULL, yet the earlier put_links call lacks this guard.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer (header->parent) expected valid but actually NULL, matching CWE-476. The fix guards put_links with the same parent check already used for recursion; this is not a use-after-free or type confusion.

evidence_lines.code:
struct ctl_dir *parent = header->parent;
put_links(header);

if (parent)
drop_sysctl_table(&parent->header);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: put_links(header) is invoked even when header->parent is NULL, as occurs in error paths where a new directory entry was created but insert_header failed. put_links then dereferences header->parent, causing a NULL-pointer dereference and kernel crash (DoS).

commit_msg: Fix issue #658
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['      ((YR_OBJECT_INTEGER*) copy)->value = UNDEFINED;', '      ((YR_OBJECT_STRING*) copy)->value = NULL;'], 'added_lines': ['      ((YR_OBJECT_INTEGER*) copy)->value = ((YR_OBJECT_INTEGER*) object)->value;', '      if (((YR_OBJECT_STRING*) object)->value != NULL)', '      {', '        ((YR_OBJECT_STRING*) copy)->value = sized_string_dup(', '            ((YR_OBJECT_STRING*) object)->value);', '      }', '      else', '      {', '        ((YR_OBJECT_STRING*) copy)->value = NULL;', '      }', '      break;', '', '    case OBJECT_TYPE_FLOAT:', '      ((YR_OBJECT_DOUBLE*) copy)->value = ((YR_OBJECT_DOUBLE*) object)->value;']}
description: The sized_string_cmp function in libyara/sizedstr.c in YARA 3.5.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (use-after-free and application crash) via a crafted rule.

code_evidence: *object_copy is initialized to NULL and a new object is created via yr_object_create, so on failure the caller's pointer remains NULL rather than a dangling reference.
For OBJECT_TYPE_STRING the copy's value is set to NULL instead of duplicating the source string, so the copy does not share or own the source buffer.

The structure branch recursively copies each member with yr_object_copy and, on failure, cleans up with yr_object_destroy(copy) and yr_free(o); the copied member objects are owned by the new structure, not aliased to the source.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 requires a reference to memory after it has been freed. The shown code initializes outputs to NULL, does not share string buffers, and performs cleanup only on error returns without subsequently using the freed objects, so the target weakness is not directly evidenced by this function.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function duplicates objects and, on copy failure, destroys the partially built copy and frees temporary members. The copy's string value is NULL rather than aliasing the source, and failure paths return an error after cleanup. No path in this function dereferences a pointer after its referenced allocation is freed, so a use-after-free is not demonstrated here.

commit_msg:
If the device node of dvb_frontend is open() and the device is
disconnected, many kinds of UAFs may occur when calling close()
on the device node.

The root cause of this is that wake_up() for dvbdev->wait_queue
is implemented in the dvb_frontend_release() function, but
wait_event() is not implemented in the dvb_frontend_stop() function.

So, implement wait_event() function in dvb_frontend_stop() and
add 'remove_mutex' which prevents race condition for 'fe->exit'.

[mchehab: fix a couple of checkpatch warnings and some mistakes at the error handling logic]

Link: https://lore.kernel.org/linux-media/20221117045925.14297-2-imv4bel@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Hyunwoo Kim <imv4bel@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Mauro Carvalho Chehab <mchehab@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tmutex_init(&fe->remove_mutex);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 6.0.9. drivers/media/dvb-core/dvb_frontend.c has a race condition that can cause a use-after-free when a device is disconnected.

code_evidence: The function takes the global frontend_mutex with mutex_lock_interruptible, but the newly added per-frontend remove_mutex is only initialized here and not used to guard fe->exit or the frontend teardown path.
Initialization publishes fe->frontend_priv, kref reference and the per-frontend wait queues before dvb_register_device exposes the device node to userspace.
dvb_register_device can fail; on error the code calls dvb_frontend_put and unlocks, but registration and later disconnect/release paths are not serialized against each other through remove_mutex.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the code exposes a shared frontend device to concurrent open/close and disconnect sequences without exclusive synchronization over fe->exit and teardown state. It is a race condition rather than a simple missing check; the consequence is UAF, but the target weakness is the improper synchronization.

evidence_lines.code:
if (mutex_lock_interruptible(&frontend_mutex))
return -ERESTARTSYS;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the frontend registration and teardown paths rely on frontend_mutex and refcounting, but fe->exit and the wait_queue wakeup are not consistently synchronized, so a disconnect can race with release/stop. Trigger: a userspace process opens the dvb frontend node and the device is disconnected while close() is in progress. Consequence: use-after-free of dvb_frontend structures, leading to crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg:
PR29925, Memory leak in find_abstract_instance

The testcase in the PR had a variable with both DW_AT_decl_file and
DW_AT_specification, where the DW_AT_specification also specified
DW_AT_decl_file.  This leads to a memory leak as the file name is
malloced and duplicates are not expected.

I've also changed find_abstract_instance to not use a temp for "name",
because that can result in a change in behaviour from the usual last
of duplicate attributes wins.

	PR 29925
	* dwarf2.c (find_abstract_instance): Delete "name" variable.
	Free *filename_ptr before assigning new file name.
	(scan_unit_for_symbols): Similarly free func->file and
	var->file before assigning.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  const char *name = NULL;', '\t\t  if (name == NULL && is_str_form (&attr))', '\t\t      name = attr.u.str;', '\t\t\t\t\t\t  &name, is_linkage,', '\t\t      name = attr.u.str;', '\t\t    *filename_ptr = concat_filename (unit->line_table,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t     attr.u.val);', '  *pname = name;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t  if (*pname == NULL && is_str_form (&attr))', '\t\t      *pname = attr.u.str;', '\t\t\t\t\t\t  pname, is_linkage,', '\t\t      *pname = attr.u.str;', '\t\t    {', '\t\t      free (*filename_ptr);', '\t\t      *filename_ptr = concat_filename (unit->line_table,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t       attr.u.val);', '\t\t    }']}
description: GNU Binutils before 2.40 was discovered to contain a memory leak vulnerability var the function find_abstract_instance in dwarf2.c.

code_evidence: In the DW_AT_decl_file case, concat_filename allocates a new string and its result is written directly to *filename_ptr without releasing any previously stored filename.

The DW_AT_specification case recurses into find_abstract_instance, passing filename_ptr along, so a nested DIE that also carries DW_AT_decl_file overwrites the same pointer and orphans the earlier allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because allocated filename memory is not released before the pointer is overwritten, leaving it unavailable for reuse. This is missing release of memory, not a use-after-free or double-free, since the stale allocation is simply lost.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: *filename_ptr is reassigned to a freshly malloced filename on each DW_AT_decl_file attribute, including through recursive DW_AT_specification resolution, with no free of the prior value. Trigger: a variable DIE and its referenced specification DIE both specify DW_AT_decl_file. Consequence: the earlier filename buffer becomes unreachable, leaking memory (availability/resource consumption).

commit_msg:
evtchn: address races with evtchn_reset()

Neither d->evtchn_port_ops nor max_evtchns(d) may be used in an entirely
lock-less manner, as both may change by a racing evtchn_reset(). In the
common case, at least one of the domain's event lock or the per-channel
lock needs to be held. In the specific case of the inter-domain sending
by evtchn_send() and notify_via_xen_event_channel() holding the other
side's per-channel lock is sufficient, as the channel can't change state
without both per-channel locks held. Without such a channel changing
state, evtchn_reset() can't complete successfully.

Lock-free accesses continue to be permitted for the shim (calling some
otherwise internal event channel functions), as this happens while the
domain is in effectively single-threaded mode. Special care also needs
taking for the shim's marking of in-use ports as ECS_RESERVED (allowing
use of such ports in the shim case is okay because switching into and
hence also out of FIFO mode is impossihble there).

As a side effect, certain operations on Xen bound event channels which
were mistakenly permitted so far (e.g. unmask or poll) will be refused
now.

This is part of XSA-343.

Reported-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Acked-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    unsigned long flags;', '    spin_lock_irqsave(&chn->lock, flags);', '    spin_unlock_irqrestore(&chn->lock, flags);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. There are evtchn_reset() race conditions. Uses of EVTCHNOP_reset (potentially by a guest on itself) or XEN_DOMCTL_soft_reset (by itself covered by XSA-77) can lead to the violation of various internal assumptions. This may lead to out of bounds memory accesses or triggering of bug checks. In particular, x86 PV guests may be able to elevate their privilege to that of the host. Host and guest crashes are also possible, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS). Information leaks cannot be ruled out. All Xen versions from 4.5 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.4 and earlier are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: Line 10 obtains chn via evtchn_from_port(d, port) without holding chn->lock, then line 11 dereferences chn->notify_vcpu_id and passes chn to evtchn_port_set_pending with no per-channel lock held.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the shared event-channel structure is accessed without synchronization, creating a timing window where a concurrent evtchn_reset() interfering sequence modifies it. The missing per-channel lock, not a mere missing check, is the root cause.

evidence_lines.code:
chn = evtchn_from_port(d, port);
evtchn_port_set_pending(d, chn->notify_vcpu_id, chn);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function reads chn->notify_vcpu_id and operates on the channel without acquiring the per-channel lock. A concurrent evtchn_reset() can change the port mapping or channel state between the lookup at line 10 and the use at line 11, so the pending notification is applied to a channel whose state or vcpu id has been modified. This violates the exclusivity required for channel state, allowing out-of-bounds accesses or failed internal assumptions.

commit_msg:
Remove access to the root FS from lua

On linux / is mounted to /rootfs in RageFile, which allows access to the
_whole_ filesystem from lua. This means themes and mod files can
re-write user data and extract files via USB profiles.

/rootfs was only added for internal use by the alsa, oss and memory card
drivers, so it can be easily replaced with direct fstream file access.
