commit_msg:
Fix invalid handling of verify errors in libssl

In the event that X509_verify() returned an internal error result then
libssl would mishandle this and set rwstate to SSL_RETRY_VERIFY. This
subsequently causes SSL_get_error() to return SSL_ERROR_WANT_RETRY_VERIFY.
That return code is supposed to only ever be returned if an application
is using an app verify callback to complete replace the use of
X509_verify(). Applications may not be written to expect that return code
and could therefore crash (or misbehave in some other way) as a result.

CVE-2021-4044

Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (s->verify_mode != SSL_VERIFY_NONE && i <= 0) {'], 'added_lines': ['    if (s->verify_mode != SSL_VERIFY_NONE && i == 0) {']}
description: Internally libssl in OpenSSL calls X509_verify_cert() on the client side to verify a certificate supplied by a server. That function may return a negative return value to indicate an internal error (for example out of memory). Such a negative return value is mishandled by OpenSSL and will cause an IO function (such as SSL_connect() or SSL_do_handshake()) to not indicate success and a subsequent call to SSL_get_error() to return the value SSL_ERROR_WANT_RETRY_VERIFY. This return value is only supposed to be returned by OpenSSL if the application has previously called SSL_CTX_set_cert_verify_callback(). Since most applications do not do this the SSL_ERROR_WANT_RETRY_VERIFY return value from SSL_get_error() will be totally unexpected and applications may not behave correctly as a result. The exact behaviour will depend on the application but it could result in crashes, infinite loops or other similar incorrect responses. This issue is made more serious in combination with a separate bug in OpenSSL 3.0 that will cause X509_verify_cert() to indicate an internal error when processing a certificate chain. This will occur where a certificate does not include the Subject Alternative Name extension but where a Certificate Authority has enforced name constraints. This issue can occur even with valid chains. By combining the two issues an attacker could induce incorrect, application dependent behaviour. Fixed in OpenSSL 3.0.1 (Affected 3.0.0).

code_evidence: ssl_verify_cert_chain returns i; a negative internal-error result (i == -1) sets s->rwstate = SSL_RETRY_VERIFY and returns WORK_MORE_A, causing the handshake state machine to retry. The subsequent guard uses i <= 0, so it treats non-zero negative results as verification failure only after the retry path; the changed condition i == 0 separates internal errors from verification failure.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the mishandled retry state can drive the application/handshake retry loop under an exit condition callers cannot reach, producing resource-consuming or infinite retry behavior. It is not merely improper error handling: the supported consequence is a non-terminating retry loop.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a negative internal-error return from chain verification is mapped to SSL_RETRY_VERIFY, a state meant only for application verify callbacks. Trigger: server certificate verification yields an internal error (e.g. OOM or the SAN/name-constraint bug). The handshake IO returns without success and SSL_get_error reports SSL_ERROR_WANT_RETRY_VERIFY, which callers do not expect; repeated retries can cause loops or incorrect application behavior.

commit_msg:
Masking direction as indicated via mask_to_left is considered to be
calculated once and then used to derive pointer limits. Thus, this
needs to be placed into bpf_sanitize_info instead so we can pass it
to sanitize_ptr_alu() call after the pointer move. Piotr noticed a
corner case where the off reg causes masking direction change which
then results in an incorrect final aux->alu_limit.

Fixes: 7fedb63a8307 ("bpf: Tighten speculative pointer arithmetic mask")
Reported-by: Piotr Krysiuk <piotras@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Borkmann <daniel@iogearbox.net>
Reviewed-by: Piotr Krysiuk <piotras@gmail.com>
Acked-by: Alexei Starovoitov <ast@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t      const struct bpf_reg_state *off_reg,', '\t\t\t      u32 *alu_limit, u8 opcode)', '\tbool off_is_neg = off_reg->smin_value < 0;', '\tbool mask_to_left = (opcode == BPF_ADD &&  off_is_neg) ||', '\t\t\t    (opcode == BPF_SUB && !off_is_neg);', '', '\tif (!tnum_is_const(off_reg->var_off) &&', '\t    (off_reg->smin_value < 0) != (off_reg->smax_value < 0))', '\t\treturn REASON_BOUNDS;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t      u32 *alu_limit, bool mask_to_left)']}
description: kernel/bpf/verifier.c in the Linux kernel through 5.12.7 enforces incorrect limits for pointer arithmetic operations, aka CID-bb01a1bba579. This can be abused to perform out-of-bounds reads and writes in kernel memory, leading to local privilege escalation to root. In particular, there is a corner case where the off reg causes a masking direction change, which then results in an incorrect final aux->alu_limit.

code_evidence: mask_to_left is derived here from off_reg sign and opcode, but this direction is only computed once; the later pointer move can change the effective sign via the offset register.
The bounds check rejects only a non-constant var_off whose smin/smax straddle zero; it does not guard against the offset sign changing after masking direction is fixed.
For PTR_TO_MAP_VALUE, ptr_limit is computed from smin_value or umax_value depending on mask_to_left, so a stale direction yields an incorrect limit.
The incorrect ptr_limit is written to *alu_limit when it passes the ptr_limit < max check, propagating the bad mask to speculative ALU sanitization.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The miscomputed alu_limit defeats the speculative pointer-arithmetic mask, enabling out-of-bounds reads/writes in kernel memory, matching CWE-787. The flaw is an incorrect bound computation feeding the mask rather than a type confusion.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: masking direction is computed once from off_reg sign but the offset register can change the sign after the pointer move, so the derived alu_limit is wrong. Trigger: a BPF program with a non-constant offset whose sign flips relative to the original masking direction. Consequence: the verifier under- or mis-limits pointer arithmetic, allowing out-of-bounds kernel memory access.

commit_msg:
When running concurrent iptables rules replacement with data, the per CPU
sequence count is checked after the assignment of the new information.
The sequence count is used to synchronize with the packet path without the
use of any explicit locking. If there are any packets in the packet path using
the table information, the sequence count is incremented to an odd value and
is incremented to an even after the packet process completion.

The new table value assignment is followed by a write memory barrier so every
CPU should see the latest value. If the packet path has started with the old
table information, the sequence counter will be odd and the iptables
replacement will wait till the sequence count is even prior to freeing the
old table info.

However, this assumes that the new table information assignment and the memory
barrier is actually executed prior to the counter check in the replacement
thread. If CPU decides to execute the assignment later as there is no user of
the table information prior to the sequence check, the packet path in another
CPU may use the old table information. The replacement thread would then free
the table information under it leading to a use after free in the packet
processing context-

Unable to handle kernel NULL pointer dereference at virtual
address 000000000000008e
pc : ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
lr : ip6t_do_table+0x5b8/0x89c
ip6t_do_table+0x5d0/0x89c
ip6table_filter_hook+0x24/0x30
nf_hook_slow+0x84/0x120
ip6_input+0x74/0xe0
ip6_rcv_finish+0x7c/0x128
ipv6_rcv+0xac/0xe4
__netif_receive_skb+0x84/0x17c
process_backlog+0x15c/0x1b8
napi_poll+0x88/0x284
net_rx_action+0xbc/0x23c
__do_softirq+0x20c/0x48c

This could be fixed by forcing instruction order after the new table
information assignment or by switching to RCU for the synchronization.

Fixes: 80055dab5de0 ("netfilter: x_tables: make xt_replace_table wait until old rules are not used anymore")
Reported-by: Sean Tranchetti <stranche@codeaurora.org>
Reported-by: kernel test robot <lkp@intel.com>
Suggested-by: Florian Westphal <fw@strlen.de>
Signed-off-by: Subash Abhinov Kasiviswanathan <subashab@codeaurora.org>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tprivate = table->private;'], 'added_lines': ['\tprivate = xt_table_get_private_protected(table);', '\tRCU_INIT_POINTER(table->private, NULL);']}
description: An issue was discovered in netfilter in the Linux kernel before 5.10. There can be a use-after-free in the packet processing context, because the per-CPU sequence count is mishandled during concurrent iptables rules replacement. This could be exploited with the CAP_NET_ADMIN capability in an unprivileged namespace. NOTE: cc00bca was reverted in 5.12.

code_evidence: xt_unregister_table reads table->private into private under the mutex, then releases the mutex at line 7 and returns private at line 11 for the caller to free. The function itself does not clear table->private or otherwise prevent other CPUs from still dereferencing the table info after the mutex is dropped.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The freed xt_table_info is subsequently dereferenced by the packet path, matching CWE-416 (referencing memory after free). This is a synchronization/ordering defect enabling the use-after-free, not merely a race without invalid access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the table pointer is published/consumed without ordering relative to the synchronization counter, so xt_replace_table may observe an even sequence count and free old table info while another CPU's packet path still uses it. Trigger: concurrent iptables replacement while packets traverse the table. Consequence: use-after-free in packet processing (crash/NULL deref, potential memory corruption).

commit_msg: Fixed bug #71331 - Uninitialized pointer in phar_make_dirstream()
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tif (keylen < (uint)dirlen || !strncmp(str_key, dir, dirlen)) {'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tkeylen = 0;', '\t\t\tif (keylen == 0 || keylen < (uint)dirlen || !strncmp(str_key, dir, dirlen)) {']}
description: The phar_make_dirstream function in ext/phar/dirstream.c in PHP before 5.6.18 and 7.x before 7.0.3 mishandles zero-size ././@LongLink files, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (uninitialized pointer dereference) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted TAR archive.

Line 17 passes &keylen to zend_hash_get_current_key_ex and only breaks on HASH_KEY_NON_EXISTENT; otherwise keylen is assumed set. Line 21 compares keylen to dirlen, and line 22 uses keylen in comparisons and strncmp; for a zero-size @LongLink entry the key may not be populated, so keylen remains uninitialized and drives a pointer/length decision.

The patch's keylen = 0 initialization confirms this is the uninitialized-variable root cause rather than a simple bounds error.

Trigger: a crafted TAR archive containing a zero-size ././@LongLink entry. diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tthe->stack->value.string = (txString)fxNewChunk(the, l + 1);'], 'added_lines': ['\ttxInteger m;', '\tm = 0;', '\t\tif (m <= l)', '\t\t\tm = l;', '\t\telse', '\t\t\tfxAbort(the, XS_NOT_ENOUGH_MEMORY_EXIT);', '\t\tthe->stack->value.string = (txString)fxNewChunk(the, fxAddChunkSizes(the, l, 1));']}
description: Moddable SDK v11.5.0 was discovered to contain a heap-buffer-overflow via the component __libc_start_main.

code_evidence: The first loop computes the required output length l by summing sizes for '$', '&', '`', '\'', capture references and group references; l is a txInteger that can overflow or diverge from the second pass.
The buffer is allocated with fxNewChunk(the, l + 1) using that computed l, then the second loop writes via *s++ for each replacement token.

In the default digit branch, the length accounting adds l++ twice (and a third for d) when the capture index is invalid, while the write pass emits '$', c, and optionally d; if the two passes disagree or l overflowed, s advances past the l+1 allocation, producing an out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates a heap buffer sized from a computed length and then writes through s without re-validating the bound, so writes can pass the end of the intended buffer. This is a direct out-of-bounds heap write, matching CWE-787 rather than a read-side or use-after-free weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that buffer size l is computed from the replacement string and capture/group lengths without a guard against integer overflow or pass mismatch, then the write pass emits bytes based on the same input. A crafted replacement string (e.g., large capture/group values or edge-case digit references) makes the second loop write beyond the allocated l+1 chunk, corrupting heap memory and potentially leading to crash or code execution.

commit_msg:
Avoid using stale UserScript pointers

BUG=625393
TEST=Manually. Compile Chrome with ASAN and follow the steps from the bug report.

Review-Url: https://codereview.chromium.org/2116923002
Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#403725}
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  // There is no harm in allowing the injection when the script is gone,', '  // because there is nothing to inject.', '  if (!script_)', '    return PermissionsData::ACCESS_ALLOWED;', '']}
description: Use-after-free vulnerability in extensions/renderer/user_script_injector.cc in the Extensions subsystem in Google Chrome before 52.0.2743.82 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service or possibly have unspecified other impact via vectors related to script deletion.

code_evidence: The function dereferences script_ unconditionally at line 5 (script_->consumer_instance_type()) and again at lines 9, 18, and 25 (script_->id(), script_->match_about_blank()).
The diff adds an early null check for script_ before any dereference, confirming that script_ can be null when the underlying UserScript has been deleted.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer whose referent was freed, which is exactly CWE-416 (use after free); the fix guards against the dangling pointer rather than addressing a separate weakness such as null dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the UserScriptInjector holds a raw script_ pointer that becomes stale when the UserScript is deleted, yet CanExecuteOnFrame dereferences it without a liveness check. Trigger: script deletion while injection is evaluated. Consequence: use-after-free read of freed memory, leading to crash/DoS or potentially other impact.

description: The event scripts in Automatic Bug Reporting Tool (ABRT) uses world-readable permission on a copy of sosreport file in problem directories, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information from /var/log/messages via unspecified vectors.

code_evidence: Line 12 defaults mode to DEFAULT_DUMP_DIR_MODE | S_IROTH, i.e. world-readable; only when world_readable_dump is false (lines 13-17) is the extra S_IROTH dropped and my_euid set to the caller's effective uid.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the dump directory mode defaults to adding S_IROTH (world-readable) and ownership defaults to the current user, with the restrictive branch only taken when world_readable_dump is false. Trigger: creating an oops dump when world_readable_dump is not set. Consequence: the problem directory and its contents, including copied sensitive data such as /var/log/messages excerpts, are readable by other local users, exposing sensitive information.

description: ARM mbed TLS before 1.3.21 and 2.x before 2.1.9, if optional authentication is configured, allows remote attackers to bypass peer authentication via an X.509 certificate chain with many intermediates. NOTE: although mbed TLS was formerly known as PolarSSL, the releases shipped with the PolarSSL name are not affected.

code_evidence: Verification delegates to x509_crt_verify_top, and any nonzero return aborts the chain check via goto exit.
The child-chain path likewise calls x509_crt_verify_child and jumps to exit on nonzero return.
The fallback top-verification call also aborts on nonzero return.

A callback returning the non-fatal VERIFY_FAILED code causes early exit, but that value is not treated as fatal, so the chain may be accepted despite failed peer authentication. Root cause is trusting a callback's non-fatal status as a chain-verification outcome; trigger is a malicious chain with many intermediates and optional auth; consequence is authentication bypass.

commit_msg:
Jonathan Looney reported that TCP can trigger the following crash
in tcp_shifted_skb() :

	BUG_ON(tcp_skb_pcount(skb) < pcount);

This can happen if the remote peer has advertized the smallest
MSS that linux TCP accepts : 48

An skb can hold 17 fragments, and each fragment can hold 32KB
on x86, or 64KB on PowerPC.

This means that the 16bit witdh of TCP_SKB_CB(skb)->tcp_gso_segs
can overflow.

Note that tcp_sendmsg() builds skbs with less than 64KB
of payload, so this problem needs SACK to be enabled.
SACK blocks allow TCP to coalesce multiple skbs in the retransmit
queue, thus filling the 17 fragments to maximal capacity.

CVE-2019-11477 -- u16 overflow of TCP_SKB_CB(skb)->tcp_gso_segs

Fixes: 832d11c5cd07 ("tcp: Try to restore large SKBs while SACK processing")
Signed-off-by: Eric Dumazet <edumazet@google.com>
Reported-by: Jonathan Looney <jtl@netflix.com>
Acked-by: Neal Cardwell <ncardwell@google.com>
Reviewed-by: Tyler Hicks <tyhicks@canonical.com>
Cc: Yuchung Cheng <ycheng@google.com>
Cc: Bruce Curtis <brucec@netflix.com>
Cc: Jonathan Lemon <jonathan.lemon@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tBUG_ON(tcp_skb_pcount(skb) < pcount);'], 'added_lines': ['\tWARN_ON_ONCE(tcp_skb_pcount(skb) < pcount);']}
description: Jonathan Looney discovered that the TCP_SKB_CB(skb)->tcp_gso_segs value was subject to an integer overflow in the Linux kernel when handling TCP Selective Acknowledgments (SACKs). A remote attacker could use this to cause a denial of service. This has been fixed in stable kernel releases 4.4.182, 4.9.182, 4.14.127, 4.19.52, 5.1.11, and is fixed in commit 3b4929f65b0d8249f19a50245cd88ed1a2f78cff.

code_evidence: Line 19 adds pcount into prev's 16-bit gso_segs counter via tcp_skb_pcount_add; line 20 then asserts the shifted skb still has at least pcount, and line 21 subtracts pcount from skb. The counter is 16-bit, so repeated SACK coalescing of many fragments can wrap it before line 20's check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an integer wraparound of a fixed-width counter (tcp_gso_segs) whose overflow violates an invariant assumed by the caller, fitting CWE-190. It is not a pure logic bug: the arithmetic overflow is the direct cause of the failed assertion and resulting DoS.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the 16-bit tcp_gso_segs counter is incremented without a saturation guard while SACK coalesces skbs, so a remote peer advertising minimal MSS can drive it past 65535 and wrap. The wrap makes tcp_skb_pcount(skb) appear smaller than pcount, tripping the BUG_ON (converted to WARN_ON_ONCE) and crashing the kernel, a remote denial of service.

commit_msg:
sys-utils/ipcutils: be careful when call calloc() for uint64 nmembs

Fix: https://github.com/karelzak/util-linux/issues/1395
Signed-off-by: Karel Zak <kzak@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!p || !p->sem_nsems || p->sem_perm.id < 0)'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!p || !p->sem_nsems || p->sem_nsems > SIZE_MAX || p->sem_perm.id < 0)']}
description: An integer overflow in util-linux through 2.37.1 can potentially cause a buffer overflow if an attacker were able to use system resources in a way that leads to a large number in the /proc/sysvipc/sem file. NOTE: this is unexploitable in GNU C Library environments, and possibly in all realistic environments.

code_evidence: Line 4 validates p, sem_nsems and sem_perm.id but does not bound sem_nsems against SIZE_MAX before line 6 calls xcalloc(p->sem_nsems, sizeof(struct sem_elem)). The allocation size is the product of an attacker-influenced count from /proc/sysvipc/sem and the element size; without the upper-bound check the multiplication can wrap, yielding a small allocation for a large count.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the flaw is an integer multiplication overflow in the size calculation feeding xcalloc, which then leads to an undersized allocation and out-of-bounds writes. The missing SIZE_MAX guard on sem_nsems is exactly the constraint whose absence permits the wraparound; the buffer overflow is the downstream consequence rather than the root weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: sem_nsems is used unchecked as the calloc element count, so the count-times-size multiplication can overflow size_t and allocate an undersized buffer. Trigger: a large sem_nsems value read from /proc/sysvipc/sem. Consequence: the loop at lines 7-22 writes elements past the small allocation, causing a heap buffer overflow (memory corruption/possible code execution).

description: A heap-based buffer overflow was discovered in the opj_t2_encode_packet function in lib/openjp2/t2.c in OpenJPEG 2.2.0. The vulnerability causes an out-of-bounds write, which may lead to remote denial of service or possibly unspecified other impact.

code_evidence: opj_write_bytes writes the 2-byte SOD marker into p_data, then p_data is advanced by 2 and l_remaining_data is computed as p_total_data_size - 4 without first verifying p_total_data_size is at least 4.
The caller-supplied p_total_data_size and the derived l_remaining_data are passed to opj_tcd_encode_tile as the output buffer capacity, so an underflowed remaining size misrepresents available space.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked size arithmetic leads to buffer writes beyond the intended allocation, which is the out-of-bounds write described by CWE-787. It is not merely an integer underflow: the supported consequence is memory corruption from writing past the buffer end.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function subtracts 4 from p_total_data_size without a lower-bound check, so a small output buffer yields a huge unsigned l_remaining_data. Trigger: callers supply p_total_data_size below 4 while the SOD marker and tile data are written. Consequence: writes past the end of the heap buffer (DoS or other impact), as the fix adds the p_total_data_size < 4 guard.

description: In Wireshark 2.2.0 to 2.2.1 and 2.0.0 to 2.0.7, the DCERPC dissector could crash with a use-after-free, triggered by network traffic or a capture file. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-dcerpc-nt.c and epan/dissectors/packet-dcerpc-spoolss.c by using the wmem file scope for private strings.

code_evidence: dcv->private_data is assigned the pointer str returned by dissect_SYSTEM_TIME via the out-parameter [7,8]. str is a local char* with no scope or lifetime guarantee shown in this function; the raw pointer is stored into call_data [9] for later use by the dissector. commit_msg:
KEYS: fix keyctl_set_reqkey_keyring() to not leak thread keyrings

This fixes CVE-2017-7472.

Running the following program as an unprivileged user exhausts kernel
memory by leaking thread keyrings:

	#include <keyutils.h>

	int main()
	{
		for (;;)
			keyctl_set_reqkey_keyring(KEY_REQKEY_DEFL_THREAD_KEYRING);
	}

Fix it by only creating a new thread keyring if there wasn't one before.
To make things more consistent, make install_thread_keyring_to_cred()
and install_process_keyring_to_cred() both return 0 if the corresponding
keyring is already present.

Fixes: d84f4f992cbd ("CRED: Inaugurate COW credentials")
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # 2.6.29+
Signed-off-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\treturn -EEXIST;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\treturn 0;']}
description: The KEYS subsystem in the Linux kernel before 4.10.13 allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) via a series of KEY_REQKEY_DEFL_THREAD_KEYRING keyctl_set_reqkey_keyring calls.

code_evidence: When new->process_keyring is already set, the function returns -EEXIST instead of succeeding, so the caller's request to install the process keyring is reported as a failure even though a keyring already exists.

Otherwise it allocates a new keyring with keyring_alloc() (KEY_ALLOC_QUOTA_OVERRUN) and stores it in new->process_keyring; there is no path that releases or skips allocation when one is already present, so repeated calls can allocate again.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-404 covers improper resource release/reuse; here the resource (process keyring) is not correctly accounted for and re-allocated instead of reusing the existing one, leaking resources. The fix returns 0 when a keyring already exists, preventing repeated allocation.

evidence_lines.code:
if (new->process_keyring)
return -EEXIST;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the presence check returns an error rather than 0, and the allocation path does not recognize an already-installed keyring, so callers repeatedly trigger keyring_alloc(). Trigger: an unprivileged user repeatedly invoking keyctl_set_reqkey_keyring() with a def keyring type. Consequence: process/thread keyrings accumulate, exhausting kernel memory (DoS).

Both btrfs_find_device() and find_device() does the same thing except
that the latter does not take the seed device onto account in the device
scanning context. We can merge them.

Signed-off-by: Anand Jain <anand.jain@oracle.com>

Signed-off-by: David Sterba <dsterba@suse.com>

description: fs/btrfs/volumes.c in the Linux kernel before 5.1 allows a btrfs_verify_dev_extents NULL pointer dereference via a crafted btrfs image because fs_devices->devices is mishandled within find_device, aka CID-09ba3bc9dd15.

code_evidence: Lines 78-82 call btrfs_find_device for the source and target devices; the result is stored in dev_replace->srcdev and dev_replace->tgtdev without a NULL check before later use.
Lines 83-91 only set ret = -EIO when srcdev is NULL and the DEGRADED option is not set; execution continues when DEGRADED is set, leaving srcdev NULL.
Lines 92-100 apply the same conditional handling to tgtdev; when DEGRADED is set, tgtdev may remain NULL and execution proceeds.

Lines 101-113 enter the tgtdev branch and immediately dereference dev_replace->srcdev->total_bytes and related fields when srcdev is non-NULL only by the inner check, but the outer branch relies on tgtdev; the pairing allows a NULL srcdev path to be reached under DEGRADED.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the failure to find a device is converted only into an error return when DEGRADED is not set, so with the DEGRADED mount option a missing srcdev/tgtdev remains NULL. Trigger: mounting a crafted btrfs image whose dev-replace item references a missing device while DEGRADED is enabled. Consequence: subsequent dereference of the NULL device pointer causes a kernel NULL pointer dereference/DoS.

description: wolfSSL 5.x before 5.1.1 uses non-random IV values in certain situations. This affects connections (without AEAD) using AES-CBC or DES3 with TLS 1.1 or 1.2 or DTLS 1.1 or 1.2. This occurs because of misplaced memory initialization in BuildMessage in internal.c.

code_evidence: BuildMessage generates the per-record CBC/block-cipher IV with wc_RNG_GenerateBlock at line 166, but line 169 immediately overwrites the freshly generated random bytes with XMEMSET(args->iv, 0, args->ivSz), zeroing the IV before it is copied into the output at lines 182-184.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function is intended to supply a random IV for CBC encryption but instead emits a fixed zero value, so the security-relevant value is insufficiently random. This directly matches CWE-330 (Use of Insufficiently Random Values); it is not merely a memory-safety issue, since the buffer is valid but its contents are predictable.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the zeroing call after RNG generation destroys the random IV. Trigger: any non-AEAD TLS 1.1/1.2 or DTLS 1.1/1.2 connection using AES-CBC or DES3, where args->ivSz > 0. commit_msg:
[turbofan] Bailout if LoadBuffer typing assumption doesn't hold.

The LoadBuffer operator that is used for asm.js heap access claims to
return only the appropriate typed array type, but out of bounds access
could make it return undefined. So far we tried to "repair" the graph
later if we see that our assumption was wrong, and for various reasons
that worked for some time. But now that wrong type information that is
propagated earlier is picked up appropriately and thus we generate wrong
code, i.e. we in the repro case we feed NaN into ChangeFloat64Uint32 and
thus get 2147483648 instead of 0 (with proper JS truncation).

This was always considered a temporary hack until we have a proper
asm.js pipeline, but since we still run asm.js through the generic
JavaScript pipeline, we have to address this now. Quickfix is to just
bailout from the pipeline when we see that the LoadBuffer type was
wrong, i.e. the result of LoadBuffer is not properly truncated and thus
undefined or NaN would be observable.

R=mstarzinger@chromium.org, jarin@chromium.org
BUG=chromium:589792
LOG=y

Review URL: https://codereview.chromium.org/1740123002

Cr-Commit-Position: refs/heads/master@{#34322}
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['              if (access.machine_type().representation() !=', '                  MachineRepresentation::kFloat64) {', '                // TODO(bmeurer): See comment on abort_compilation_.', '                if (lower()) lowering->abort_compilation_ = true;', '              }', '          // TODO(bmeurer): See comment on abort_compilation_.', '          if (lower()) lowering->abort_compilation_ = true;', '']}
description: The LoadBuffer implementation in Google V8, as used in Google Chrome before 50.0.2661.75, mishandles data types, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service or possibly have unspecified other impact via crafted JavaScript code that triggers an out-of-bounds write operation, related to compiler/pipeline.cc and compiler/simplified-lowering.cc.

code_evidence: For kLoadBuffer, the operator's machine_type representation is used directly to construct output_info (lines 299-300 and 304-306) without verifying it matches the actual value produced for out-of-bounds access. The else branch (lines 307-309) unconditionally assigns Float64 output, and the outer else (lines 311-313) assigns AnyTagged. The patch adds abort_compilation_ checks when representation != kFloat64 and in the outer else, but the original function lacks any bailout, so wrong type information is propagated.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs buffer access lowering without a bounds/type-consistency constraint, allowing out-of-bounds heap access to be mishandled, which matches CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The type-confusion flavor is a mechanism, but the supported weakness is improper restriction within a memory buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the LoadBuffer lowering assumes the typed-array representation holds even though out-of-bounds access can yield undefined, and the function has no bailout when the assumption is violated. Trigger: crafted JavaScript performing an out-of-bounds asm.js heap read. Consequence: incorrect type information reaches later lowering, producing wrong code (e.g., NaN fed into ChangeFloat64Uint32 yielding 2147483648 instead of 0), supporting the described DoS/unspecified impact.

commit_msg:
Chain binding only requires the rule addition/insertion command within
the same transaction. Removal of rules from chain bindings within the
same transaction makes no sense, userspace does not utilize this
feature. Replace nft_chain_is_bound() check to nft_chain_binding() in
rule deletion commands. Replace command implies a rule deletion, reject
this command too.

Rule flush command can also safely rely on this nft_chain_binding()
check because unbound chains are not allowed since 62e1e94b246e
("netfilter: nf_tables: reject unbound chain set before commit phase").

Fixes: d0e2c7de92c7 ("netfilter: nf_tables: add NFT_CHAIN_BINDING")
Reported-by: Kevin Rich <kevinrich1337@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Pablo Neira Ayuso <pablo@netfilter.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (nft_chain_is_bound(chain))'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (nft_chain_binding(chain))']}
description:
A use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux kernel's netfilter: nf_tables component can be exploited to achieve local privilege escalation.

Addition and removal of rules from chain bindings within the same transaction causes leads to use-after-free.

We recommend upgrading past commit f15f29fd4779be8a418b66e9d52979bb6d6c2325.

code_evidence: The cleanup loop iterates every chain in the table and skips a chain only when nft_chain_is_bound(chain) is true, then sets ctx.chain and releases each rule via list_del and nf_tables_rule_release.
The guard tests the bound flag rather than whether the chain is a binding chain, so a chain that is a binding but not flagged bound is not skipped and its rules are released during table teardown.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function frees rule objects and leaves a dangling reference usable through the chain binding, which is exactly CWE-416: memory is referenced after being freed. This is not merely a double-free; the defect is reuse of freed memory via the retained binding reference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the teardown path decides whether to free a chain's rules using the wrong chain state predicate (is_bound instead of binding), so rules belonging to binding chains can be released while still reachable through the binding. Trigger: releasing a table that contains such a chain. Consequence: the binding still references freed rule memory, giving a use-after-free that can escalate to local privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
The driver for XillyUSB devices maintains a kref reference count on each
xillyusb_dev structure, which represents a physical device. This reference
count reaches zero when the device has been disconnected and there are no
open file descriptors that are related to the device. When this occurs,
kref_put() calls cleanup_dev(), which clears up the device's data,
including the structure itself.

However, when xillyusb_open() is called, this reference count becomes
tricky: This function needs to obtain the xillyusb_dev structure that
relates to the inode's major and minor (as there can be several such).
xillybus_find_inode() (which is defined in xillybus_class.c) is called
for this purpose. xillybus_find_inode() holds a mutex that is global in
xillybus_class.c to protect the list of devices, and releases this
mutex before returning. As a result, nothing protects the xillyusb_dev's
reference counter from being decremented to zero before xillyusb_open()
increments it on its own behalf. Hence the structure can be freed
due to a rare race condition.

To solve this, a mutex is added. It is locked by xillyusb_open() before
the call to xillybus_find_inode() and is released only after the kref
counter has been incremented on behalf of the newly opened inode. This
protects the kref reference counters of all xillyusb_dev structs from
being decremented by xillyusb_disconnect() during this time segment, as
the call to kref_put() in this function is done with the same lock held.

There is no need to hold the lock on other calls to kref_put(), because
if xillybus_find_inode() finds a struct, xillyusb_disconnect() has not
made the call to remove it, and hence not made its call to kref_put(),
which takes place afterwards. Hence preventing xillyusb_disconnect's
call to kref_put() is enough to ensure that the reference doesn't reach
zero before it's incremented by xillyusb_open().

It would have been more natural to increment the reference count in
xillybus_find_inode() of course, however this function is also called by
Xillybus' driver for PCIe / OF, which registers a completely different
structure. Therefore, xillybus_find_inode() treats these structures as
void pointers, and accordingly can't make any changes.

Reported-by: Hyunwoo Kim <imv4bel@gmail.com>
Suggested-by: Alan Stern <stern@rowland.harvard.edu>
Signed-off-by: Eli Billauer <eli.billauer@gmail.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20221030094209.65916-1-eli.billauer@gmail.com
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 6.0.9. drivers/char/xillybus/xillyusb.c has a race condition and use-after-free during physical removal of a USB device.

code_evidence: The disconnect path clears the interface data and xdev->dev, then calls kref_put(&xdev->kref, cleanup_dev) to drop the device reference, which can free xdev when the count reaches zero. This kref_put is the shared-resource decrement that races with xillyusb_open incrementing the same reference count after xillybus_find_inode releases its global mutex.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because concurrent disconnect and open sequences access the shared kref without mutual exclusion, creating a timing window. The use-after-free is the downstream consequence, not the weakness itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the reference-count decrement in xillyusb_disconnect is not synchronized with the lookup-and-increment sequence in xillyusb_open, so xdev can be freed between lookup and kref_get. Trigger: physical USB removal concurrent with opening the device node. Consequence is a use-after-free of xdev, causing memory corruption or crash.

description: When ImageMagick 7.0.6-1 processes a crafted file in convert, it can lead to a heap-based buffer over-read in the WriteUILImage() function in coders/uil.c.

code_evidence: The matte_image buffer is allocated with image->columns*image->rows bytes and filled while index i increments once per pixel across all rows, ending at i == columns*rows.
Later, when transparent is true, the loop reads matte_image[i] for each pixel, but i still holds columns*rows (the value after the fill loop), so the first read is one past the end of the buffer.
The buffer is only freed after this loop, so the out-of-bounds read at matte_image[i] occurs while it is live; the patch clamps i with a decrement before use.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Reading matte_image at index columns*rows, one past the allocated columns*rows buffer, is a direct out-of-bounds read. This is CWE-125 rather than a write, since the operation only reads the byte to test matte_image[i] != 0.

evidence_lines.code:
if (matte_image != (unsigned char *) NULL)
matte_image=(unsigned char *) RelinquishMagickMemory(matte_image);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the fill loop leaves i equal to the total pixel count, and the subsequent transparency pass indexes matte_image[i] using that stale value instead of a per-pixel index. Trigger: a crafted image with matte and a transparent pixel reaches the second loop. Consequence: a heap-based out-of-bounds read of matte_image, supporting CWE-125.

commit_msg:
only allow dynamic UnregisterHandler for external handlers, thereby fixing DoS

Trying to unregister an internal handler ended up in a SEGFAULT, because
the tcmur_handler->opaque was NULL. Way to reproduce:

dbus-send --system --print-reply --dest=org.kernel.TCMUService1 /org/kernel/TCMUService1/HandlerManager1 org.kernel.TCMUService1.HandlerManager1.UnregisterHandler string:qcow

we use a newly introduced boolean in struct tcmur_handler for keeping
track of external handlers. As suggested by mikechristie adjusting the
public data structure is acceptable.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\ttcmur_unregister_handler(handler);'], 'added_lines': ['\ttcmur_unregister_dbus_handler(handler);']}
description: tcmu-runner version 1.0.5 to 1.2.0 is vulnerable to a dbus triggered NULL pointer dereference in the tcmu-runner daemon's on_unregister_handler() function resulting in denial of service

code_evidence: The callback takes an arbitrary user_data and immediately casts it to struct tcmur_handler *, then reads handler->opaque into info without checking handler or the opaque value.

info is dereferenced at line 8 (info->register_invocation) and again at lines 13-14, and handler is passed to tcmur_unregister_handler at line 17. For internal handlers the opaque field is NULL, so the dereference of info is a NULL pointer access.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences info, derived from handler->opaque, while that pointer can be NULL, exactly matching CWE-476. The fix routes external handlers through tcmur_unregister_dbus_handler, confirming the NULL-opaque case was the defect rather than a generic use-after-free.

evidence_lines.code:
struct tcmur_handler *handler = user_data;
struct dbus_info *info = handler->opaque;

if (info->register_invocation) {
tcmur_unregister_handler(handler);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: on_handler_vanished assumes every handler has a non-NULL opaque dbus_info and dereferences handler->opaque unconditionally. Trigger: a handler whose opaque is NULL (internal handlers) reaching this path, e.g. via a D-Bus triggered unregister. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference causing a crash/SEGFAULT, i.e., denial of service.

commit_msg:
list-objects: pass full pathname to callbacks

When we find a blob at "a/b/c", we currently pass this to
our show_object_fn callbacks as two components: "a/b/" and
"c". Callbacks which want the full value then call
path_name(), which concatenates the two. But this is an
inefficient interface; the path is a strbuf, and we could
simply append "c" to it temporarily, then roll back the
length, without creating a new copy.

So we could improve this by teaching the callsites of
path_name() this trick (and there are only 3). But we can
also notice that no callback actually cares about the
broken-down representation, and simply pass each callback
the full path "a/b/c" as a string. The callback code becomes
even simpler, then, as we do not have to worry about freeing
an allocated buffer, nor rolling back our modification to
the strbuf.

This is theoretically less efficient, as some callbacks
would not bother to format the final path component. But in
practice this is not measurable. Since we use the same
strbuf over and over, our work to grow it is amortized, and
we really only pay to memcpy a few bytes.

Signed-off-by: Jeff King <peff@peff.net>
Signed-off-by: Junio C Hamano <gitster@pobox.com>

commit_msg:
VMA with VM_GROWSDOWN or VM_GROWSUP flag set can change their size under
mmap_read_lock().  It can lead to race with __do_munmap():

	Thread A			Thread B
__do_munmap()
  detach_vmas_to_be_unmapped()
  mmap_write_downgrade()
				expand_downwards()
				  vma->vm_start = address;
				  // The VMA now overlaps with
				  // VMAs detached by the Thread A
				// page fault populates expanded part
				// of the VMA
  unmap_region()
    // Zaps pagetables partly
    // populated by Thread B

Similar race exists for expand_upwards().

The fix is to avoid downgrading mmap_lock in __do_munmap() if detached
VMAs are next to VM_GROWSDOWN or VM_GROWSUP VMA.

[akpm@linux-foundation.org: s/mmap_sem/mmap_lock/ in comment]

Fixes: dd2283f2605e ("mm: mmap: zap pages with read mmap_sem in munmap")
Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Kirill A. Shutemov <kirill.shutemov@linux.intel.com>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
Reviewed-by: Yang Shi <yang.shi@linux.alibaba.com>
Acked-by: Vlastimil Babka <vbabka@suse.cz>
Cc: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Cc: Matthew Wilcox <willy@infradead.org>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>	[4.20+]
Link: http://lkml.kernel.org/r/20200709105309.42495-1-kirill.shutemov@linux.intel.com
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tdetach_vmas_to_be_unmapped(mm, vma, prev, end);'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!detach_vmas_to_be_unmapped(mm, vma, prev, end))', '\t\tdowngrade = false;']}
description: An issue was discovered in mm/mmap.c in the Linux kernel before 5.7.11. There is a race condition between certain expand functions (expand_downwards and expand_upwards) and page-table free operations from an munmap call, aka CID-246c320a8cfe.

code_evidence: After detach_vmas_to_be_unmapped() detaches VMAs from the rbtree, the code unconditionally calls mmap_write_downgrade(mm) when downgrade is true, releasing exclusive write access while the detached VMAs have not yet been unmapped by unmap_region()/remove_vma_list().
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-362: a shared resource (the mm address space/VMA structures) is accessed without exclusive synchronization during a timing window between detach and unmap. The missing constraint is that downgrade must be skipped when detached VMAs border growable VMAs, which the patch adds.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the write lock is downgraded to read before the detached region is fully zapped, so concurrent expand_downwards()/expand_upwards() can modify an adjacent VM_GROWSDOWN/VM_GROWSUP VMA under the read lock and populate pages overlapping the detached range. Trigger: another thread faults on the growable VMA during this window. Consequence: unmap_region() then zaps page tables concurrently being populated, a race that can corrupt page tables or cause instability/crash.

description: global heap buffer overflow in skip_range in GitHub repository vim/vim prior to 8.2.4763. This vulnerability is capable of crashing software, Bypass Protection Mechanism, Modify Memory, and possible remote execution

code_evidence: When the command begins with "'<,'>", eap->cmd is advanced by 5 and cmd_start points to the remaining command buffer; has_visual_range is set.
If the command is empty in Ex mode, eap->cmd is reassigned to the string literal "+", so cmd_start no longer points into the writable command buffer.

The visual-range relocation uses mch_memmove(cmd_start - 5, cmd_start, eap->cmd - cmd_start) and writes ":'<,'>" at eap->cmd - 1; after the "+" substitution these offsets and lengths are computed against the literal rather than the original buffer, producing out-of-bounds writes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe mch_memmove and memmove write past the bounds of a heap-allocated command buffer, matching CWE-122's heap-based buffer overflow. It is not merely a null-pointer or use-after-free issue; the writes themselves exceed the allocation due to the stale pointer arithmetic.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that cmd_start and eap->cmd can refer to different buffers after the empty Ex command is replaced by the literal "+", yet the relocation still computes offsets and lengths as if both pointed into the same command buffer. Triggering "'<,'>" followed by an empty Ex-mode command causes mch_memmove and the subsequent 6-byte write to operate outside the intended heap-allocated command buffer, corrupting heap memory and potentially crashing or enabling code execution.

Trying to fix some invalid left shift operations

Fixes issue #16
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\treturn (iw_int32)(iw_uint32)(b[0] | (b[1]<<8) | (b[2]<<16) | (b[3]<<24));'], 'added_lines': ['\treturn (iw_int32)(iw_uint32)((unsigned int)b[0] | ((unsigned int)b[1]<<8) |', '\t\t((unsigned int)b[2]<<16) | ((unsigned int)b[3]<<24));']}

commit_msg:
core: tee_entry: fix array out of bounds check in cleanup_shm_refs()

cleanup_shm_refs() can be called with num_params larger than what has
been used by copy_in_params(). If num_params is larger than
TEE_NUM_PARAMS copy_in_params() will return an error and
cleanup_shm_refs() is called to clean up.

This leads to accessing uint64_t saved_attr[TEE_NUM_PARAMS] in
entry_invoke_command() or entry_open_session() out of bounds and
possibly also the u[TEE_NUM_PARAMS] array in struct tee_ta_param.

So fix this by capping num_params TEE_NUM_PARAMS in cleanup_shm_refs().

Fixes: b05cd886e06d ("core: enable non-contiguous temporary reference parameters")
Reviewed-by: Jerome Forissier <jerome.forissier@linaro.org>
Signed-off-by: Jens Wiklander <jens.wiklander@linaro.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tfor (n = 0; n < num_params; n++) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tfor (n = 0; n < MIN((unsigned int)TEE_NUM_PARAMS, num_params); n++) {']}
description: OP-TEE Trusted OS is the secure side implementation of OP-TEE project, a Trusted Execution Environment. Versions prior to 3.19.0, contain an Improper Validation of Array Index vulnerability. The function `cleanup_shm_refs()` is called by both `entry_invoke_command()` and `entry_open_session()`. The commands `OPTEE_MSG_CMD_OPEN_SESSION` and `OPTEE_MSG_CMD_INVOKE_COMMAND` can be executed from the normal world via an OP-TEE SMC. This function is not validating the `num_params` argument, which is only limited to `OPTEE_MSG_MAX_NUM_PARAMS` (127) in the function `get_cmd_buffer()`. Therefore, an attacker in the normal world can craft an SMC call that will cause out-of-bounds reading in `cleanup_shm_refs` and potentially freeing of fake-objects in the function `mobj_put()`. A normal-world attacker with permission to execute SMC instructions may exploit this flaw. Maintainers believe this problem permits local privilege escalation from the normal world to the secure world. Version 3.19.0 contains a fix for this issue. There are no known workarounds.

code_evidence: The loop bound is the caller-supplied num_params with no upper-bound check against TEE_NUM_PARAMS.
saved_attr[n] and param->u[n] are indexed with the same unbounded n; param->u is the fixed-size uint64_t/u array of TEE_NUM_PARAMS.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function uses an untrusted index/loop bound to access fixed-size arrays without validating it against the array length, which is exactly CWE-129 (Improper Validation of Array Index). The missing constraint on num_params, not the array access itself, is the root cause.

evidence_lines.code: for (n = 0; n < num_params; n++) {

switch (saved_attr[n]) {
mobj_put(param->u[n].mem.mobj);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: num_params originates from normal-world SMC and is only capped at OPTEE_MSG_MAX_NUM_PARAMS (127), not TEE_NUM_PARAMS. When num_params exceeds TEE_NUM_PARAMS, the loop reads saved_attr[n] and param->u[n] out of bounds and may pass a bogus mobj pointer to mobj_put(), causing out-of-bounds reads and potential freeing of fake objects.

commit_msg:
IKEv2: Do not attempt to encrypt a reply without established IKE SA

This is https://github.com/libreswan/libreswan/issues/246

Signed-off-by: D. Hugh Redelmeier <hugh@mimosa.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '\t/*', "\t * For encrypted messages, the EXCHANGE TYPE can't be SA_INIT.", '\t */', '\tswitch (exchange_type) {', '\tcase ISAKMP_v2_IKE_SA_INIT:', '\t\tPEXPECT_LOG("exchange type %s invalid for encrypted notification",', '\t\t\t    exchange_name);', '\t\treturn;', '\tdefault:', '\t\tbreak;', '\t}'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!IS_IKE_SA_ESTABLISHED(md->st)) { /* XXX Andrew? how to dig into ike_sa ike ? */', '\t\tloglog(RC_LOG_SERIOUS, "unable to respond to exchange type %s message with encrypted notification because there is no established IKE SA",', '\t\t\texchange_name);', '\t\treturn;', '\t}', '\t/*', "\t * For encrypted messages, the EXCHANGE TYPE can't be SA_INIT.", '\t * And the IKE SA must have been established', '\t */', '\tswitch (exchange_type) {', '\tcase ISAKMP_v2_IKE_SA_INIT:', '\tcase ISAKMP_v2_IKE_AUTH:', '\t\tloglog(RC_LOG_SERIOUS, "exchange type %s invalid for encrypted notification",', '\t\t\t    exchange_name);', '\t\treturn;', '\tdefault:', '\t\tbreak;', '\t}', '']}
description: In Libreswan 3.27 an assertion failure can lead to a pluto IKE daemon restart. An attacker can trigger a NULL pointer dereference by initiating an IKEv2 IKE_SA_INIT exchange, followed by a bogus INFORMATIONAL exchange instead of the normallly expected IKE_AUTH exchange. This affects send_v2N_spi_response_from_state() in programs/pluto/ikev2_send.c that will then trigger a NULL pointer dereference leading to a restart of libreswan.

code_evidence: The function proceeds to build an encrypted reply using md->hdr.isa_xchg and passes ike/md into open_v2_message and open_v2SK_payload, then calls encrypt_v2SK_payload(&sk). Only ISAKMP_v2_IKE_SA_INIT is rejected; the IKE SA's established state is not checked before these encrypted operations.

The reply is logged and constructed from ike->sa fields and md without first verifying that the IKE SA is established, so a request arriving before IKE_AUTH completion reaches the encryption path with an unestablished SA.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is a NULL pointer dereference leading to daemon restart, matching CWE-476. The missing established-SA check is the precondition that exposes the NULL dereference, not a separate weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function attempts to encrypt a notification reply without confirming that the IKE SA is established. Trigger: an attacker sends a bogus INFORMATIONAL request after IKE_SA_INIT but before IKE_AUTH. The encryption path then dereferences state that is still NULL, causing a crash/restart of pluto (DoS).

commit_msg:
crypto: user - fix leaking uninitialized memory to userspace

All bytes of the NETLINK_CRYPTO report structures must be initialized,
since they are copied to userspace.  The change from strncpy() to
strlcpy() broke this.  As a minimal fix, change it back.

Fixes: 4473710df1f8 ("crypto: user - Prepare for CRYPTO_MAX_ALG_NAME expansion")
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org> # v4.12+
Signed-off-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Herbert Xu <herbert@gondor.apana.org.au>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstrlcpy(racomp.type, "acomp", sizeof(racomp.type));'], 'added_lines': ['\tstrncpy(racomp.type, "acomp", sizeof(racomp.type));']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 4.19.3. crypto_report_one() and related functions in crypto/crypto_user.c (the crypto user configuration API) do not fully initialize structures that are copied to userspace, potentially leaking sensitive memory to user programs. NOTE: this is a CVE-2013-2547 regression but with easier exploitability because the attacker does not need a capability (however, the system must have the CONFIG_CRYPTO_USER kconfig option).

code_evidence: Local struct racomp is declared uninitialized at line 3. Line 4 copies only the short literal "acomp" into racomp.type using strncpy, which does not zero-fill the remainder of the fixed-size type buffer. Lines 5-6 then pass the entire sizeof(struct crypto_report_acomp) to nla_put, copying the whole struct including any uninitialized tail bytes of type into the netlink message returned to userspace.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function explicitly transfers a partially uninitialized structure into a message delivered to userspace, exposing memory the caller was never meant to see. This is a direct confidentiality exposure of sensitive internal data, matching CWE-200; the underlying uninitialized-memory defect is the cause, while the supported impact here is the information disclosure.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the stack-allocated report struct is not fully initialized, and strncpy leaves bytes of the type array untouched beyond the copied literal. Trigger: any userspace call that causes crypto_report_acomp to build a CRYPTOCFGA_REPORT_ACOMP message. Consequence: residual stack memory is copied into the netlink reply, leaking kernel data to an unprivileged caller.

commit_msg:
Issue 26393: morphapp_fuzzer: Divide-by-zero in blockconvLow
* Removed the code that allowed divide by zero for tiny pix
* Ditto for 4 other block convolution functions.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (wc < 0) wc = 0;', '    if (hc < 0) hc = 0;', '        wc = L_MIN(wc, (w - 1) / 2);', '        hc = L_MIN(hc, (h - 1) / 2);', '        L_WARNING("kernel too large; reducing!\\n", procName);', '        L_INFO("wc = %d, hc = %d\\n", procName, wc, hc);', '    if (wc == 0 && hc == 0)   /* no-op */', '        return pixCopy(NULL, pix);'], 'added_lines': ['    if (wc <= 0 || hc <= 0)', '        return pixCopy(NULL, pix);', '        L_ERROR("kernel is too large: w = %d, wc = %d, h = %d, hc = %d\\n",', '                procName, w, wc, h, hc);', '        return pixCopy(NULL, pix);  /* no-op */']}
description: An issue in the Leptonica linked library (v1.79.0) allows attackers to cause an arithmetic exception leading to a Denial of Service (DoS) via a crafted JPEG file.

code_evidence: Lines 11-12 clamp negative wc/hc to 0 but allow zero to persist. Lines 15-16 reduce wc/hc via (w-1)/2 and (h-1)/2 when the kernel exceeds the image, which can yield 0 for small dimensions. Line 20's no-op guard only fires when both wc and hc are zero, so a single zero half-width/height reaches the downstream block-convolution calls at lines 34-43.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is CWE-369 because a zero kernel dimension from insufficient size validation propagates into a division, producing a divide-by-zero crash. It is a distinct arithmetic-fault issue rather than a mere bounds or size check, since the supported consequence is the divide operation on zero.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size-reduction/clamping logic permits one of wc or hc to remain 0 for tiny images, and the no-op check requires both to be zero. Trigger: a crafted small JPEG drives wc or hc to 0 while the other stays positive. Consequence: the downstream gray block convolution divides by a zero kernel dimension, causing an arithmetic exception and DoS crash.

commit_msg:
ahci: Update byte count after DMA completion

Currently, DMA read/write operations neglect to update
the byte count after a successful transfer like ATAPI
DMA read or PIO read/write operations do.

We correct this oversight by adding another callback into
the IDEDMAOps structure. The commit callback is called
whenever we are cleaning up a scatter-gather list.
AHCI can register this callback in order to update post-
transfer information such as byte count updates.

We use this callback in AHCI to consolidate where we delete
the SGlist as generated from the PRDT, as well as update the
byte count after the transfer is complete.

The QEMUSGList structure has an init flag added to it in order
to make qemu_sglist_destroy a nop if it is called when
there is no sglist, which simplifies cleanup and error paths.

This patch fixes several AHCI problems, notably Non-NCQ modes
of operation for Windows 7 as well as Hibernate support for Windows 7.

Signed-off-by: John Snow <jsnow@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
Tested-by: Michael S. Tsirkin <mst@redhat.com>
Message-id: 1412204151-18117-3-git-send-email-jsnow@redhat.com
Signed-off-by: Stefan Hajnoczi <stefanha@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    /* free sglist that was created in ahci_populate_sglist() */', '    qemu_sglist_destroy(&s->sg);', '    /* update number of transferred bytes */', '    ad->cur_cmd->status = cpu_to_le32(le32_to_cpu(ad->cur_cmd->status) + l);'], 'added_lines': ['    /* free sglist, update byte count */', '    ahci_commit_buf(dma, l);']}
description: The ahci_commit_buf function in ide/ahci.c in QEMU allows attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL dereference) when the command header 'ad->cur_cmd' is null.

code_evidence: Line 16 unconditionally dereferences ad->cur_cmd to read and update its status field after the DMA transfer; nothing in this function verifies that ad->cur_cmd is non-NULL before the access. Line 15 destroys the SG list first, so a NULL ad->cur_cmd reaches the dereference on the success path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the code dereferences a pointer (ad->cur_cmd) assumed valid but not checked, and the supported impact is a crash/DoS. This is a direct NULL dereference, not a use-after-free or type confusion, so no other weakness applies.

evidence_lines.code:
qemu_sglist_destroy(&s->sg);
ad->cur_cmd->status = cpu_to_le32(le32_to_cpu(ad->cur_cmd->status) + l);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function updates the command header status through ad->cur_cmd without a NULL check. Trigger: a command path where the header pointer has not been set (or was cleared) yet ahci_dma_rw_buf runs to completion. Consequence: a NULL pointer dereference that crashes QEMU, causing denial of service.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['bool         CheckRegion(int nPos, int nSize)', '            return (nPos >= 0 && nPos + nSize >= nPos && nPos + nSize <= m_nLen);'], 'added_lines': ['bool         CheckRegion(const unsigned int& nPos, const unsigned int& nSize)', '            return (m_nLen >= nSize && nPos <= (m_nLen - nSize));']}
description: Onlyoffice Document Server v6.0.0 and below and Core 6.1.0.26 and below were discovered to contain a heap overflow via the component DesktopEditor/fontengine/fontconverter/FontFileBase.h.

code_evidence: CheckRegion takes signed int nPos and nSize; the only bound test is the overflow-prone expression nPos + nSize >= nPos and nPos + nSize <= m_nLen. Because nSize is signed, a negative value passes the sum checks, and nPos + nSize can wrap for large values, so the region validation can succeed for a range that actually extends outside the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the faulty validation permits indexing/writing beyond the intended buffer, consistent with the reported heap overflow in this font-conversion component. It is not merely integer overflow (CWE-190); the supported consequence is out-of-bounds write enabled by the flawed check.

evidence_lines.code:
bool         CheckRegion(int nPos, int nSize)
return (nPos >= 0 && nPos + nSize >= nPos && nPos + nSize <= m_nLen);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: bounds check uses signed addition that can overflow or accept negative sizes, so it fails to guarantee nPos and nPos+nSize lie within m_nLen. Trigger: a caller-supplied negative or large nSize/nPos. Consequence: the checked region can exceed the buffer, allowing later reads/writes past the end (heap overflow).

commit_msg:
Fix a null pointer exception in SVDF

This is due to not checking that `GetVariableInput` returns non-null tensor.

Also fix a potential null pointer exception in `GetVariableInput`.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 385160147
Change-Id: Iadf3f0705b036a9014d27caa5a8bbd91f4c4c401
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  TF_LITE_ENSURE(context, state != nullptr);']}
description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. In affected versions the implementation of SVDF in TFLite is [vulnerable to a null pointer error](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/lite/kernels/svdf.cc#L300-L313). The [`GetVariableInput` function](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/lite/kernels/kernel_util.cc#L115-L119) can return a null pointer but `GetTensorData` assumes that the argument is always a valid tensor. Furthermore, because `GetVariableInput` calls [`GetMutableInput`](https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/460e000de3a83278fb00b61a16d161b1964f15f4/tensorflow/lite/kernels/kernel_util.cc#L82-L90) which might return `nullptr`, the `tensor->is_variable` expression can also trigger a null pointer exception. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 5b048e87e4e55990dae6b547add4dae59f4e1c76. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.6.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.5.1, TensorFlow 2.4.3, and TensorFlow 2.3.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Line 16 obtains the state tensor via GetVariableInput without checking the returned pointer; the diff adds a null check here. The pointer returned by GetVariableInput can be nullptr, yet the code proceeds to use it.

Line 28 passes GetTensorData<float>(state) into EvalFloatSVDF; GetTensorData assumes a valid tensor and dereferences the null state pointer. Line 75 similarly passes GetTensorData<float>(state) in the hybrid path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the missing null check on state leads directly to dereferencing a NULL pointer via GetTensorData. This is a null dereference, not merely a missing validation, so CWE-476 is the appropriate label.

evidence_lines.code:
TfLiteTensor* state = GetVariableInput(context, node, kStateTensor);
GetTensorData<float>(state), GetTensorShape(output),
GetTensorData<int8_t>(input_quantized), GetTensorData<float>(state),

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return value of GetVariableInput is not validated for null before being dereferenced. Trigger: a model where the variable state tensor is unavailable so GetVariableInput returns nullptr. Consequence: GetTensorData dereferences the null tensor, causing a crash (denial of service).

description: GPAC version 0.7.1 and earlier has a Buffer Overflow vulnerability in the gf_sm_load_init function in scene_manager.c in libgpac_static.a.

code_evidence: The function copies caller-controlled strings into fixed-size fields of the stack-local CATEnum (cat_enum.szPath, szRad1, szRad2, szOpt) using unbounded strcpy without checking destination capacity: line 13 copies fileName into szPath, line 18 copies fileName into szRad1, line 20 copies sep+1 into szRad1, line 24 copies sep+1 into szRad2, and line 31 copies sep into szOpt. A long fileName or a long '*'/'%'/':' suffix causes writes past the intended buffer boundaries.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The writes occur outside the intended bounds of the destination buffers, matching CWE-119's improper restriction of operations within a memory buffer. A more specific child (e.g., CWE-121 stack-based overflow) would be a better fit, but the supplied target is CWE-119 and the out-of-bounds write is directly supported.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unbounded strcpy into fixed-size stack buffers with no length validation. Trigger: a fileName (or substring after a separator) longer than the destination field. Consequence: stack buffer overflow, corrupting adjacent CATEnum fields and potentially enabling memory modification or code execution / crash.

commit_msg:
Copy the silence flags when sending update notifications.

This fixes a crash bug in the silence module on some versions of GCC.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tPushParamRef(flags);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tPushParam(flags);']}
description: An issue was discovered in InspIRCd 3 before 3.1.0. The silence module contains a use after free vulnerability. This vulnerability can be used for remote crashing of an InspIRCd server by any user able to fully connect to a server.

code_evidence: Constructor takes mask and flags by const reference and stores flags via PushParamRef, preserving a reference to the caller's string instead of copying it. The fix replaces this with PushParam(flags), which copies the value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function stores a reference to memory that can be freed while the message still references it, which is the defining pattern of CWE-416. The fix to a value-copying PushParam removes the dangling reference, confirming the lifetime defect rather than a mere logic error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: PushParamRef retains a reference to the caller-provided flags string rather than owning a copy. If that string is temporary or freed before the message is serialized/sent, the stored reference dangles. Trigger: constructing a SilenceMessage with a flags argument whose lifetime ends before use; consequence is a use-after-free read, supporting remote crash (DoS) as described.

commit_msg:
Jan Kara's analysis of the syzbot report (edited):

  The reproducer opens a directory on FUSE filesystem, it then attaches
  dnotify mark to the open directory.  After that a fuse_do_getattr() call
  finds that attributes returned by the server are inconsistent, and calls
  make_bad_inode() which, among other things does:

          inode->i_mode = S_IFREG;

  This then confuses dnotify which doesn't tear down its structures
  properly and eventually crashes.

Avoid calling make_bad_inode() on a live inode: switch to a private flag on
the fuse inode.  Also add the test to ops which the bad_inode_ops would
have caught.

This bug goes back to the initial merge of fuse in 2.6.14...

Reported-by: syzbot+f427adf9324b92652ccc@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Miklos Szeredi <mszeredi@redhat.com>
Tested-by: Jan Kara <jack@suse.cz>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (is_bad_inode(inode))'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (fuse_is_bad(inode))']}
description: An issue was discovered in the FUSE filesystem implementation in the Linux kernel before 5.10.6, aka CID-5d069dbe8aaf. fuse_do_getattr() calls make_bad_inode() in inappropriate situations, causing a system crash. NOTE: the original fix for this vulnerability was incomplete, and its incompleteness is tracked as CVE-2021-28950.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only checks is_bad_inode and returns -EIO before delegating to fuse_do_ioctl; it contains no cleanup or resource-release logic, so it does not directly demonstrate incomplete cleanup (CWE-459).

description: An issue was discovered in the Tatsuya Kinoshita w3m fork before 0.5.3-33. w3m allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (segmentation fault and crash) via a crafted HTML page.

code_evidence: In the HTML_N_TEXTAREA_INT case, the guard checks only n_textarea >= 0 before indexing a_textarea[n_textarea] and dereferencing its url field; a_textarea may still be NULL when max_textarea was already nonzero at function entry (lines 41-45 skip allocation), so the pointer is dereferenced without a NULL check.

commit_msg:
Allow fuse device clones to refer to be distinguished.  This patch just
adds the infrastructure by associating a separate "struct fuse_dev" with
each clone.

Signed-off-by: Miklos Szeredi <mszeredi@suse.cz>
Reviewed-by: Ashish Samant <ashish.samant@oracle.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tgoto err_put_conn;', '\t\tgoto err_put_conn;', '\tfile->private_data = fuse_conn_get(fc);'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct fuse_dev *fud;', '\tfud = fuse_dev_alloc(fc);', '\tif (!fud)', '\t\tgoto err_put_conn;', '', '\t\tgoto err_dev_free;', '\t\tgoto err_dev_free;', '\tfile->private_data = fud;', ' err_dev_free:', '\tfuse_dev_free(fud);']}
description: Memory leak in the cuse_channel_release function in fs/fuse/cuse.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4 allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) or possibly have unspecified other impact by opening /dev/cuse many times.

code_evidence: fc is allocated with kmalloc and initialized with fuse_conn_init; ownership of this connection is transferred to file->private_data at line 83 via fuse_conn_get(fc).

On success file->private_data holds a reference to fc and fput(file) is called, but the connection reference associated with the device is only dropped through the file's release path; there is no explicit pairing of the alloc at line 39 with a free on the success path beyond the reference handed to the file.

The error labels err_put_conn/err_fput/err free resources for failure paths, but the success path at line 83-87 leaves the connection's lifetime tied to file->private_data without a separate device object, so repeated opens can accumulate connections if release does not free them.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-399 is a resource-management category; the observed pattern is improper lifetime/ownership accounting of an allocated connection leading to resource exhaustion, matching the category's scope. It is not a memory-safety corruption (e.g., CWE-416) because the evidence concerns resource not being released rather than use-after-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function associates the connection reference with file->private_data instead of a per-clone struct fuse_dev, so the lifetime accounting is coupled to the file rather than a distinct device object. Trigger: opening the device many times creates connections whose release path may not free the underlying resource. Consequence: unbounded memory consumption (resource exhaustion).

commit_msg:
x86/fpu/xsaves: Fix improper uses of __ex_table

Commit:

  f31a9f7c7169 ("x86/xsaves: Use xsaves/xrstors to save and restore xsave area")

introduced alternative instructions for XSAVES/XRSTORS and commit:

  adb9d526e982 ("x86/xsaves: Add xsaves and xrstors support for booting time")

added support for the XSAVES/XRSTORS instructions at boot time.

Unfortunately both failed to properly protect them against faulting:

The 'xstate_fault' macro will use the closest label named '1'
backward and that ends up in the .altinstr_replacement section
rather than in .text. This means that the kernel will never find
in the __ex_table the .text address where this instruction might
fault, leading to serious problems if userspace manages to
trigger the fault.

Trigger: processing certain frame dimensions/field-combination sequences causes writes past the end of tbuffer. Supported consequence: heap-buffer overflow leading to memory corruption and crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
We're holding the request reference, but we need to go one higher
to ensure that the ctx remains valid after the request has finished.
If the ring is closed with pending task_work inflight, and the
given io_kiocb finishes sync during issue, then we need a reference
to the ring itself around the task_work execution cycle.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org # v5.7+
Reported-by: syzbot+9b260fc33297966f5a8e@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tpercpu_ref_get(&req->ctx->refs);', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.8.2. fs/io_uring.c has a use-after-free related to io_async_task_func and ctx reference holding, aka CID-6d816e088c35.

code_evidence: init_task_work() registers req->task_work, and io_req_task_work_add() queues it for later execution. The struct io_kiocb req is tied to req->ctx; the queued task_work references req after the issuing request completes, but no ctx reference is taken here.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the pending task_work dereferences ctx after its lifetime ends; the missing percpu_ref_get is the absent constraint. This is use-after-free, not merely a missing cleanup or double-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: task_work is scheduled without acquiring a reference on req->ctx, so the ring/ctx can be torn down while the task_work is still pending. Trigger: the ring is closed with task_work inflight and the io_kiocb finishes synchronously during issue. Consequence: the deferred task_work accesses freed ctx memory, a use-after-free (crash or memory corruption).

commit_msg: Fix out of bounds write
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '                        if( y >= m_height )', '                            break;']}
description: In opencv/modules/imgcodecs/src/utils.cpp, functions FillUniColor and FillUniGray do not check the input length, which can lead to integer overflow. If the image is from remote, may lead to remote code execution or denial of service. This affects Opencv 3.3 and earlier.

code_evidence: Line 10 computes width3 = m_width*nch without overflow checks; line 15/16 compute row pointer offsets from m_height and step.
Line 104 computes len = x_shift3 + ((y_shift * width3) & ...) where y_shift and width3 are attacker-influenced dimensions; the multiplication can overflow.
Lines 110-114 call FillUniGray with the overflowed len and only break after y >= m_height, so an out-of-range write can occur before the guard.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an integer overflow/wraparound in size computation (CWE-190), which then enables the out-of-bounds write. It is distinct from a pure out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) because the arithmetic wrap is the root cause, though the consequence is memory corruption.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is unchecked integer arithmetic on image dimensions (m_width*nch and y_shift*width3) that can wrap to a small or negative value. A crafted BMP RLE8 stream triggers the wrap in the absolute-mode branch, and the resulting length is passed to FillUniGray, causing an out-of-bounds write before the y>=m_height check is reached.
