commit_msg:
Fix buffer overflows occurring reading redis.conf.

There was not enough sanity checking in the code loading the slots of
Redis Cluster from the nodes.conf file, this resulted into the
attacker's ability to write data at random addresses in the process
memory, by manipulating the index of the array. The bug seems
exploitable using the following techique: the config file may be altered so
that one of the nodes gets, as node ID (which is the first field inside the
structure) some data that is actually executable: then by writing this
address in selected places, this node ID part can be executed after a
jump. So it is mostly just a matter of effort in order to exploit the
bug. In practice however the issue is not very critical because the
bug requires an unprivileged user to be able to modify the Redis cluster
nodes configuration, and at the same time this should result in some
gain. However Redis normally is unprivileged as well. Yet much better to
have this fixed indeed.

Fix #4278.

description: The clusterLoadConfig function in cluster.c in Redis 4.0.2 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds array index and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging "limited access to the machine."

code_evidence: The slot index is parsed with atoi(argv[j]+1) from the config file and used directly to index the migrating_slots_to/importing_slots_from arrays without any bounds check.
The direction char selects migrating_slots_to[slot] or importing_slots_from[slot]; a negative or oversized slot writes a node pointer outside the fixed CLUSTER_SLOTS array.

For range entries, start and stop come from atoi of attacker-controlled fields and drive while(start <= stop) clusterAddSlot(n, start++); with no range validation, so start/stop outside [0,CLUSTER_SLOTS) index out of bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs array indexing on fixed-size slot arrays using unvalidated config values, causing reads/writes outside the intended buffer boundary, matching CWE-119. The specific missing constraint is an index bounds check, distinguishing it from unrelated parsing errors.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: slot, start and stop values are taken from the nodes.conf file via atoi with no validation against CLUSTER_SLOTS, then used as array indices. Trigger: a modified cluster config supplies a negative or large slot value or range. Consequence: out-of-bounds writes of node pointers into cluster slot arrays, corrupting memory and enabling crash or arbitrary write.

commit_msg:
crypto/evp: harden AEAD ciphers.

Originally a crash in 32-bit build was reported CHACHA20-POLY1305
cipher. The crash is triggered by truncated packet and is result
of excessive hashing to the edge of accessible memory. Since hash
operation is read-only it is not considered to be exploitable
beyond a DoS condition. Other ciphers were hardened.

Thanks to Robert Święcki for report.

CVE-2017-3731

Reviewed-by: Rich Salz <rsalz@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['             * merge record sequence number as per', '             * draft-ietf-tls-chacha20-poly1305-03'], 'added_lines': ['                if (len < POLY1305_BLOCK_SIZE)', '                    return 0;', '             * merge record sequence number as per RFC7905']}
description: If an SSL/TLS server or client is running on a 32-bit host, and a specific cipher is being used, then a truncated packet can cause that server or client to perform an out-of-bounds read, usually resulting in a crash. For OpenSSL 1.1.0, the crash can be triggered when using CHACHA20/POLY1305; users should upgrade to 1.1.0d. For Openssl 1.0.2, the crash can be triggered when using RC4-MD5; users who have not disabled that algorithm should update to 1.0.2k.

code_evidence: Lines 67-68 read a 16-bit payload length from the caller-supplied AAD buffer; on the decrypt path (line 69), line 70 subtracts POLY1305_BLOCK_SIZE from that unsigned len without first checking it is at least the block size, so a truncated record (len < 16) underflows.

The wrapped length is stored into tls_payload_length (line 76) and the AAD is copied/processed; line 81 passes the 13-byte AAD into chacha20_poly1305_cipher, which then hashes according to the corrupted payload length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe operation is a read of memory beyond the intended buffer, matching CWE-125. It is not a write overflow (CWE-787) because the oversized hashing is read-only, consistent with the commit's DoS-only assessment.

evidence_lines.code:
unsigned char *aad = ptr, temp[POLY1305_BLOCK_SIZE];
chacha20_poly1305_cipher(ctx, NULL, aad, EVP_AEAD_TLS1_AAD_LEN);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is the missing lower-bound check on the record length before subtracting the tag size, causing unsigned underflow to a huge value. The trigger is a truncated TLS packet with a small length field; the resulting oversized payload length drives excessive hashing past the AAD buffer, producing an out-of-bounds read and a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
password: Use crypto_memneq() to compare hashes

Cryptographic verifications should be time-constant so that an attacker
cannot get information about the secrets used by observing the system,
so use crypto_memneq() rather than memcmp() to compare password hashes.

Signed-off-by: Sascha Hauer <s.hauer@pengutronix.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tif (strncmp(passwd1_sum, key, keylen) == 0)', '\t\tif (strncmp(passwd1_sum, passwd2_sum, hash_len) == 0)'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (!crypto_memneq(passwd1_sum, key, keylen))', '\t\tif (!crypto_memneq(passwd1_sum, passwd2_sum, hash_len))']}
description: common/password.c in Pengutronix barebox through 2021.07.0 leaks timing information because strncmp is used during hash comparison.

code_evidence: After computing the PBKDF2 hash into passwd1_sum, the code compares it against the stored key using strncmp(passwd1_sum, key, keylen); strncmp stops at the first differing byte, so comparison time depends on the matching prefix length.
The non-PBKDF2 branch likewise compares the computed digest passwd1_sum with the stored passwd2_sum via strncmp(passwd1_sum, passwd2_sum, hash_len), again terminating early on the first mismatch.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The early-exit comparison makes the function's observable execution time differ based on secret-dependent input, matching CWE-203's observable discrepancy. It is not merely a general timing flaw; the discrepancy is directly measurable by an unauthorized actor and leaks stored hash data.

evidence_lines.code:
if (strncmp(passwd1_sum, key, keylen) == 0)
ret = 1;

if (strncmp(passwd1_sum, passwd2_sum, hash_len) == 0)
ret = 1;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: secret hash bytes are compared with a non-constant-time strncmp. Trigger: an attacker repeatedly submits candidate passwords and measures response timing. Consequence: the number of leading matching hash bytes is leaked, enabling byte-by-byte recovery of the stored hash and eventual password verification bypass.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-13004/Juniper: Add a bounds check.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Forcepoint's security
researchers Otto Airamo & Antti Levomäki.

Add tests using the capture files supplied by the reporter(s).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['            ND_TCHECK_16BITS(p+l2info->cookie_len);']}
description: The Juniper protocols parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-juniper.c:juniper_parse_header().

code_evidence: Before the fix, line 144 performs EXTRACT_16BITS(p+l2info->cookie_len) without a bounds check. The preceding ND_TCHECK2 at line 135 only validates p[0] over cookie_len bytes, so the two-byte read at offset cookie_len lies just beyond the checked region. l2info->cookie_len is derived from packet-controlled pictype/cookie fields, so an attacker-crafted capture can set it so that p+cookie_len+1 exceeds the captured buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Reading EXTRACT_16BITS past the validated captured length is a direct out-of-bounds read, matching CWE-125. It is not CWE-787 (write) because no data is written out of bounds; the missing ND_TCHECK_16BITS is the specific unchecked read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the protocol field read at p+cookie_len is not covered by any ND_TCHECK. Trigger: a crafted Juniper capture whose cookie_len places the 16-bit extraction past the captured data. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read of up to two bytes, causing tcpdump to read beyond the packet buffer (crash/info leak).

description: OpenThread before 2019-12-13 has a stack-based buffer overflow in MeshCoP::Commissioner::GeneratePskc.

code_evidence: The guard uses strlen(aNetworkName) <= OT_NETWORK_NAME_MAX_SIZE to validate aNetworkName, but strlen reads until a NUL terminator and does not bound the read to the buffer size; a non-terminated or oversized name is not safely constrained before use.

The validated length is not the length used for the copy: memcpy(salt + saltLen, aNetworkName, strlen(aNetworkName)) recomputes the length and writes that many bytes into the fixed salt buffer, past its end when the name is long.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe memcpy writes attacker-influenced data past the end of the stack-allocated salt buffer, which is exactly an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). It is a write overflow, not merely an over-read from strlen, since the destination buffer bounds are violated.

evidence_lines.code:
VerifyOrExit((strlen(aPassPhrase) >= OT_COMMISSIONING_PASSPHRASE_MIN_SIZE) &&
(strlen(aPassPhrase) <= OT_COMMISSIONING_PASSPHRASE_MAX_SIZE) &&
(strlen(aNetworkName) <= OT_NETWORK_NAME_MAX_SIZE),
error = OT_ERROR_INVALID_ARGS);

memcpy(salt + saltLen, aNetworkName, strlen(aNetworkName));
saltLen += static_cast<uint16_t>(strlen(aNetworkName));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the network name is copied into the fixed-size salt array using an unbounded strlen-derived length, with no clamp to the remaining salt capacity. Trigger: a caller supplies an aNetworkName whose length pushes saltLen (prefix + PAN ID + name) beyond OT_PBKDF2_SALT_MAX_LEN. Consequence: a stack-based out-of-bounds write corrupting adjacent stack memory.

commit_msg:
scsi: lsi: exit infinite loop while executing script (CVE-2019-12068)

When executing script in lsi_execute_script(), the LSI scsi adapter
emulator advances 's->dsp' index to read next opcode. This can lead
to an infinite loop if the next opcode is empty. Move the existing
loop exit after 10k iterations so that it covers no-op opcodes as
well.

Reported-by: Bugs SysSec <bugs-syssec@rub.de>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Prasad J Pandit <pjp@fedoraproject.org>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        /*', '         * FIXME: if s->waiting != LSI_NOWAIT, this will only execute one', '         * instruction.  Is this correct?', '         */', '        /*', '         * FIXME: if s->waiting != LSI_NOWAIT, this will only execute one', '         * instruction.  Is this correct?', '         */']}
description: In QEMU 1:4.1-1, 1:2.1+dfsg-12+deb8u6, 1:2.8+dfsg-6+deb9u8, 1:3.1+dfsg-8~deb10u1, 1:3.1+dfsg-8+deb10u2, and 1:2.1+dfsg-12+deb8u12 (fixed), when executing script in lsi_execute_script(), the LSI scsi adapter emulator advances 's->dsp' index to read next opcode. This can lead to an infinite loop if the next opcode is empty. Move the existing loop exit after 10k iterations so that it covers no-op opcodes as well.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only writes registers and conditionally invokes lsi_execute_script; the infinite loop and its exit condition reside in lsi_execute_script, not in this function, and the diff only adds comments.

commit_msg:
The imperfect hash area can be updated while packets are traversing,
which will cause a use-after-free when 'tcf_exts_exec()' is called
with the destroyed tcf_ext.

CPU 0:               CPU 1:
tcindex_set_parms    tcindex_classify
tcindex_lookup
                     tcindex_lookup
tcf_exts_change
                     tcf_exts_exec [UAF]

Stop operating on the shared area directly, by using a local copy,
and update the filter with 'rcu_replace_pointer()'. Delete the old
filter version only after a rcu grace period elapsed.

Fixes: 9b0d4446b569 ("net: sched: avoid atomic swap in tcf_exts_change")
Reported-by: valis <sec@valis.email>
Suggested-by: valis <sec@valis.email>
Signed-off-by: Jamal Hadi Salim <jhs@mojatatu.com>
Signed-off-by: Pedro Tammela <pctammela@mojatatu.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20230209143739.279867-1-pctammela@mojatatu.com
Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (cp->perfect)', '\telse', '\t\tr = tcindex_lookup(cp, handle) ? : &new_filter_result;', '\tif (r == &new_filter_result) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tbool update_h = false;', '\tif (cp->perfect) {', '\t} else {', '\t\t/* imperfect area is updated in-place using rcu */', '\t\tupdate_h = !!tcindex_lookup(cp, handle);', '\t\tr = &new_filter_result;', '\t}', '\tif (update_h) {', '\t\tstruct tcindex_filter __rcu **fp;', '\t\tstruct tcindex_filter *cf;', '', '\t\tf->result.res = r->res;', '\t\ttcf_exts_change(&f->result.exts, &r->exts);', '', '\t\t/* imperfect area bucket */', '\t\tfp = cp->h + (handle % cp->hash);', '', '\t\t/* lookup the filter, guaranteed to exist */', '\t\tfor (cf = rcu_dereference_bh_rtnl(*fp); cf;', '\t\t     fp = &cf->next, cf = rcu_dereference_bh_rtnl(*fp))', '\t\t\tif (cf->key == handle)', '\t\t\t\tbreak;', '', '\t\tf->next = cf->next;', '', '\t\tcf = rcu_replace_pointer(*fp, f, 1);', '\t\ttcf_exts_get_net(&cf->result.exts);', '\t\ttcf_queue_work(&cf->rwork, tcindex_destroy_fexts_work);', '\t} else if (r == &new_filter_result) {']}
description:
Use After Free vulnerability in Linux kernel traffic control index filter (tcindex) allows Privilege Escalation. The imperfect hash area can be updated while packets are traversing, which will cause a use-after-free when 'tcf_exts_exec()' is called with the destroyed tcf_ext. A local attacker user can use this vulnerability to elevate its privileges to root.
This issue affects Linux Kernel: from 4.14 before git commit ee059170b1f7e94e55fa6cadee544e176a6e59c2.

code_evidence: For the imperfect hash area, the code resolves r via tcindex_lookup(cp, handle) and then writes r->res and tcf_exts_change(&r->exts, &e) directly into the shared filter result before rcu_assign_pointer(tp->root, cp).
This in-place mutation of the existing result object (r) happens while readers may concurrently call tcf_exts_exec on the same exts, so the exts can be destroyed/replaced under a reader.
The else branch only destroys new_filter_result.exts and never defers freeing the old result, leaving the stale pointer reachable.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function frees/replaces tcf_exts memory that a concurrent classifier still references, which is exactly CWE-416 use-after-free. It is not merely a race condition (CWE-362); the supported weakness is use of memory after it has been freed.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: tcindex_set_parms updates the imperfect hash filter result in place (r->res and r->exts) rather than replacing it with a new object. Trigger: a concurrent tcindex_classify/tcf_exts_exec reads the same tcf_exts while the update path frees/replaces it. Consequence: use-after-free of the tcf_ext, enabling memory corruption and potential privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
PR22205, .debug_line file table NULL filename

The PR22200 fuzzer testcase found one way to put NULLs into .debug_line
file tables.  PR22205 finds another.  This patch gives up on trying to
prevent NULL files in the file table and instead just copes with them.
Arguably, this is better than giving up and showing no info from
.debug_line.  I've also fixed a case where the fairly recent DWARF5
support in handling broken DWARG could result in uninitialized memory
reads, and made a small tidy.

	PR 22205
	* dwarf2.c (concat_filename): Return "<unknown>" on NULL filename.
	(read_formatted_entries): Init "fe".
	(decode_line_info <DW_LNE_define_file>): Use line_info_add_file_name.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t  if ((table->num_files % FILE_ALLOC_CHUNK) == 0)', '\t\t    {', '\t\t      struct fileinfo *tmp;', '', '\t\t      amt = table->num_files + FILE_ALLOC_CHUNK;', '\t\t      amt *= sizeof (struct fileinfo);', '\t\t      tmp = (struct fileinfo *) bfd_realloc (table->files, amt);', '\t\t      if (tmp == NULL)', '\t\t\tgoto line_fail;', '\t\t      table->files = tmp;', '\t\t    }', '\t\t  table->files[table->num_files].name = cur_file;', '\t\t  table->files[table->num_files].dir =', '\t\t    _bfd_safe_read_leb128 (abfd, line_ptr, &bytes_read,', '\t\t\t\t\t   FALSE, line_end);', '\t\t  line_ptr += bytes_read;', '\t\t  table->files[table->num_files].time =', '\t\t    _bfd_safe_read_leb128 (abfd, line_ptr, &bytes_read,', '\t\t\t\t\t   FALSE, line_end);', '\t\t  line_ptr += bytes_read;', '\t\t  table->files[table->num_files].size =', '\t\t    _bfd_safe_read_leb128 (abfd, line_ptr, &bytes_read,', '\t\t\t\t\t   FALSE, line_end);', '\t\t  line_ptr += bytes_read;', '\t\t  table->num_files++;'], 'added_lines': ['      unsigned int dir, xtime, size;', '\t\t  dir = _bfd_safe_read_leb128 (abfd, line_ptr, &bytes_read,', '\t\t\t\t\t       FALSE, line_end);', '\t\t  line_ptr += bytes_read;', '\t\t  xtime = _bfd_safe_read_leb128 (abfd, line_ptr, &bytes_read,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t FALSE, line_end);', '\t\t  line_ptr += bytes_read;', '\t\t  size = _bfd_safe_read_leb128 (abfd, line_ptr, &bytes_read,', '\t\t\t\t\t\tFALSE, line_end);', '\t\t  line_ptr += bytes_read;', '\t\t  if (!line_info_add_file_name (table, cur_file, dir,', '\t\t\t\t\t\txtime, size))', '\t\t    goto line_fail;']}
description: dwarf2.c in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.29, mishandles NULL files in a .debug_line file table, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and application crash) via a crafted ELF file, related to concat_filename. NOTE: this issue is caused by an incomplete fix for CVE-2017-15023.

code_evidence: In DW_LNE_define_file, read_string may return NULL for a malformed .debug_line entry; the result is stored into table->files[num_files].name without any NULL check ([246,247,248,258,271]).
Prologue file-table parsing likewise accepts cur_file from read_string and passes it to line_info_add_file_name without validating it ([160,161,162,170,171]).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function stores a possibly-NULL pointer and permits its later dereference, matching CWE-476's definition of dereferencing a pointer expected to be valid but NULL. This is distinct from an out-of-bounds read: the defect is the unvalidated NULL value, not an index beyond the buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a NULL filename returned by read_string (from a crafted ELF .debug_line file table) is admitted into the file table unchecked. Later code such as concat_filename dereferences the stored name, so a crafted ELF triggers a NULL pointer dereference and crash, giving a denial of service. The missing NULL constraint is the cause; the crash is the consequence.

commit_msg: Fix an invalid delete error
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            for (dsize = 0; dsize < size; dsize++) *m_nalBuffer++ = *src++;'], 'added_lines': ['            std::copy(src, src + size, m_nalBuffer);']}
description: Buffer Overflow in tsMuxer 2.6.16 allows attackers to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) by running the application with a malicious WAV file.

code_evidence: Line 3-4 deletes the previous m_nalBuffer and line 5 allocates a new buffer of exactly size bytes.
For the size<4 branch, the loop at line 9 copies size bytes into m_nalBuffer via post-increment, advancing the buffer pointer away from the allocation start.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The copy writes exactly size bytes into a size-byte buffer, so the destination bound is not exceeded; the defect is pointer corruption during buffer copy rather than a classic unchecked buffer copy. CWE-120 is not directly supported; the concrete issue is misuse/invalid free of the shifted pointer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The buffer is allocated with new uint8_t[size], but the small-size copy branch advances m_nalBuffer itself instead of a separate write index, so the stored pointer no longer refers to the allocation. Subsequent operations on m_nalBuffer (such as a later delete) act on a shifted pointer, and the original allocation bookkeeping is corrupted, causing invalid deallocation/crash.

commit_msg:
virpci: Resolve leak in virPCIVirtualFunctionList cleanup

Repeatedly querying an SR-IOV PCI device's capabilities exposes a
memory leak caused by a failure to free the virPCIVirtualFunction
array within the parent struct's g_autoptr cleanup.

Valgrind output after getting a single interface's XML description
1000 times:

==325982== 256,000 bytes in 1,000 blocks are definitely lost in loss record 2,634 of 2,635
==325982==    at 0x4C3C096: realloc (vg_replace_malloc.c:1437)
==325982==    by 0x59D952D: g_realloc (in /usr/lib64/libglib-2.0.so.0.5600.4)
==325982==    by 0x4EE1F52: virReallocN (viralloc.c:52)
==325982==    by 0x4EE1FB7: virExpandN (viralloc.c:78)
==325982==    by 0x4EE219A: virInsertElementInternal (viralloc.c:183)
==325982==    by 0x4EE23B2: virAppendElement (viralloc.c:288)
==325982==    by 0x4F65D85: virPCIGetVirtualFunctionsFull (virpci.c:2389)
==325982==    by 0x4F65753: virPCIGetVirtualFunctions (virpci.c:2256)
==325982==    by 0x505CB75: virNodeDeviceGetPCISRIOVCaps (node_device_conf.c:2969)
==325982==    by 0x505D181: virNodeDeviceGetPCIDynamicCaps (node_device_conf.c:3099)
==325982==    by 0x505BC4E: virNodeDeviceUpdateCaps (node_device_conf.c:2677)
==325982==    by 0x260FCBB2: nodeDeviceGetXMLDesc (node_device_driver.c:355)

Signed-off-by: Tim Shearer <tshearer@adva.com>
Reviewed-by: Ján Tomko <jtomko@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    g_free(list->functions);']}
description: A vulnerability was found in libvirt. This security flaw ouccers due to repeatedly querying an SR-IOV PCI device's capabilities that exposes a memory leak caused by a failure to free the virPCIVirtualFunction array within the parent struct's g_autoptr cleanup.

code_evidence: The loop frees only the per-element addr and ifname members (lines 8-9), then frees the list struct itself (line 11). The functions array pointer, allocated in virPCIGetVirtualFunctionsFull, is never released, so its backing storage becomes unreachable when list is freed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Fits CWE-401: allocated memory (the functions array) remains unreleased after its effective lifetime, with no remaining pointer, causing a persistent leak. This is a missing-release weakness, not use-after-free or double free, since the memory is simply never freed.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the cleanup routine releases element members and the parent struct but omits g_free(list->functions), the array holding those elements. Trigger: each capability query allocates the array; cleanup leaves it unfreed, so repeated queries accumulate leaked memory and eventually cause resource-consumption DoS. The added g_free(list->functions) before g_free(list) is the fix.

commit_msg:
media: usb: fix memory leak in af9005_identify_state

In af9005_identify_state when returning -EIO the allocated buffer should
be released. Replace the "return -EIO" with assignment into ret and move
deb_info() under a check.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-13043/BGP: fix decoding of MVPN route types 6 and 7

RFC 6514 Section 4.6 defines the structure for Shared Tree Join (6) and
Source Tree Join (7) multicast VPN route types. decode_multicast_vpn()
didn't implement the Source AS field of that structure properly, adjust
the offsets to put it right.

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Bhargava Shastry,

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).

commit_msg:
ax25: Fix UAF bugs in ax25 timers

There are race conditions that may lead to UAF bugs in
ax25_heartbeat_expiry(), ax25_t1timer_expiry(), ax25_t2timer_expiry(),
ax25_t3timer_expiry() and ax25_idletimer_expiry(), when we call
ax25_release() to deallocate ax25_dev.

One of the UAF bugs caused by ax25_release() is shown below:

      (Thread 1)                    |      (Thread 2)
ax25_dev_device_up() //(1)          |
...                                 | ax25_kill_by_device()
ax25_bind()          //(2)          |
ax25_connect()                      | ...
 ax25_std_establish_data_link()     |
  ax25_start_t1timer()              | ax25_dev_device_down() //(3)
   mod_timer(&ax25->t1timer,..)     |
                                    | ax25_release()
   (wait a time)                    |  ...
                                    |  ax25_dev_put(ax25_dev) //(4)FREE
   ax25_t1timer_expiry()            |
    ax25->ax25_dev->values[..] //USE|  ...
     ...                            |

We increase the refcount of ax25_dev in position (1) and (2), and
decrease the refcount of ax25_dev in position (3) and (4).
The ax25_dev will be freed in position (4) and be used in
ax25_t1timer_expiry().

The fail log is shown below:
==============================================================

[  106.116942] BUG: KASAN: use-after-free in ax25_t1timer_expiry+0x1c/0x60
[  106.116942] Read of size 8 at addr ffff88800bda9028 by task swapper/0/0
[  106.116942] CPU: 0 PID: 0 Comm: swapper/0 Not tainted 5.17.0-06123-g0905eec574
[  106.116942] Hardware name: QEMU Standard PC (i440FX + PIIX, 1996), BIOS rel-14
[  106.116942] Call Trace:
...
[  106.116942]  ax25_t1timer_expiry+0x1c/0x60
[  106.116942]  call_timer_fn+0x122/0x3d0
[  106.116942]  __run_timers.part.0+0x3f6/0x520
[  106.116942]  run_timer_softirq+0x4f/0xb0
[  106.116942]  __do_softirq+0x1c2/0x651
...

This patch adds del_timer_sync() in ax25_release(), which could ensure
that all timers stop before we deallocate ax25_dev.

Signed-off-by: Duoming Zhou <duoming@zju.edu.cn>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Abeni <pabeni@redhat.com>

commit_msg: * FIX [mqtt_parser] fix https://github.com/emqx/nanomq/issues/1181 in conn_handler
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tint      max;', '\tmax = limit + *pos;', '\t\t\tif (*pos >= max) {', '\t\t\t\tnng_free(dest, *str_len + 1);', '\t\t\t\t*str_len = -1;', '\t\t\t\treturn NULL;', '\t\t\t}']}
description: NanoMQ 0.17.5 is vulnerable to heap-buffer-overflow in the conn_handler function of mqtt_parser.c when it processes malformed messages.

code_evidence: The 16-bit length is read from src+*pos and *pos is advanced by 2. The only bound check compares *str_len against limit-2, i.e. the remaining length relative to limit, but does not account for the absolute offset *pos into src.

After the length check, memcpy copies *str_len bytes from src+*pos and writes a NUL at dest[*str_len]. Because the check used limit rather than the actual remaining bytes at the current offset, a length that is valid relative to limit can still exceed the source buffer when *pos is nonzero.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unchecked length leads to writing (and reading) past the intended buffer boundaries at [21,22]. The weakness is an out-of-bounds write/read caused by a missing offset-aware bound check, not a type or encoding flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the length validation in [10,11,12,13] ignores the current offset *pos, so *str_len can pass the check while src+*pos+*str_len lies past the end of src. Trigger: a malformed MQTT string with a large length field and nonzero *pos. Consequence: the memcpy in [21] reads out of bounds (heap-buffer-overflow), and the write at [22] can also overrun dest if allocation size is mismatched.

commit_msg:
Handle empty Tight gradient rects

We always assumed there would be one pixel per row so a rect with
a zero width would result in us writing to unknown memory.

This could theoretically be used by a malicious server to inject
code in to the viewer process.

Issue found by Pavel Cheremushkin from Kaspersky Lab.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    /* First pixel in a row */', '    pf.rgbFromBuffer(pix, &inbuf[y*rectWidth], 1);', '    for (c = 0; c < 3; c++)', '      pix[c] += prevRow[c];', '    memcpy(thisRow, pix, sizeof(pix));', '    pf.bufferFromRGB((rdr::U8*)&outbuf[y*stride], pix, 1);', '    /* Remaining pixels of a row */', '    for (x = 1; x < rectWidth; x++) {'], 'added_lines': ['    for (x = 0; x < rectWidth; x++) {', '      /* First pixel in a row */', '      if (x == 0) {', '        pf.rgbFromBuffer(pix, &inbuf[y*rectWidth], 1);', '        for (c = 0; c < 3; c++)', '          pix[c] += prevRow[c];', '        memcpy(thisRow, pix, sizeof(pix));', '        pf.bufferFromRGB((rdr::U8*)&outbuf[y*stride], pix, 1);', '        continue;', '      }', '']}
description: TigerVNC version prior to 1.10.1 is vulnerable to heap buffer overflow, which occurs in TightDecoder::FilterGradient. Exploitation of this vulnerability could potentially result into remote code execution. This attack appear to be exploitable via network connectivity.

code_evidence: For each row y, the code unconditionally reads one pixel at inbuf[y*rectWidth] and writes pix into outbuf[y*stride] and thisRow, with no check that rectWidth > 0.

The inner loop runs only for x >= 1, so when rectWidth is 0 the per-row first-pixel writes still execute but no valid pixel exists for that row; thisRow/prevRow indexing and outbuf writes proceed on an empty row.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes to thisRow and outbuf (and reads inbuf) at positions derived from y*rectWidth/y*stride without ensuring a pixel exists for the row, matching CWE-787 out-of-bounds write. This is not merely an integer overflow; the missing width constraint directly permits out-of-bounds memory access.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the row loop lacks a precondition that rectWidth is at least one, so a zero-width gradient rect still triggers the first-pixel read/write path. Trigger: attacker-supplied Tight gradient rectangle with width 0. Supported consequence: writes/reads using row offsets for a nonexistent pixel, corrupting memory beyond the intended buffer (heap out-of-bounds write).

description: Buffer overflow in the ImagingLibTiffDecode function in libImaging/TiffDecode.c in Pillow before 3.1.1 allows remote attackers to overwrite memory via a crafted TIFF file.

code_evidence: Line 6 declares the scanline size as a signed int, so a TIFFScanlineSize value larger than INT_MAX can wrap to a negative number.
Lines 56-63 assign TIFFScanlineSize to that int and guard only with `size > state->bytes`; a negative wrapped size passes this check unchanged.
Line 65 then calls TIFFReadScanline with state->buffer, which was sized from the unchecked value, allowing the library to write beyond the intended buffer.

if (TIFFReadScanline(tiff, (tdata_t)state->buffer, (uint32)state->y, 0) == -1) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the signed int cannot represent the attacker-influenced TIFFScanlineSize, and the bounds check compares the wrapped value instead of the true size. commit_msg:
A race condition may occur between the .disconnect function, which
is called when the device is disconnected, and the dvb_device_open()
function, which is called when the device node is open()ed.
This results in several types of UAFs.

The root cause of this is that you use the dvb_device_open() function,
which does not implement a conditional statement
that checks 'dvbnet->exit'.

So, add 'remove_mutex` to protect 'dvbnet->exit' and use
locked_dvb_net_open() function to check 'dvbnet->exit'.

Fixed missing input buffer length check in urbdrc

(cherry picked from commit 497df00f741dd4fc89292aaef2db7368aee45d0d)

description: FreeRDP is a free remote desktop protocol library and clients. Affected versions of FreeRDP are missing input length validation in the `urbdrc` channel. A malicious server can trick a FreeRDP based client to read out of bound data and send it back to the server. This issue has been addressed in version 2.9.0 and all users are advised to upgrade. Users unable to upgrade should not use the `/usb` redirection switch.

code_evidence: OutputBufferSize is read from the attacker-controlled stream at line 26 without validating that adding 4 stays within UINT32_MAX. Line 29 then computes OutputBufferSize + 4, which can wrap to a small value when OutputBufferSize is near UINT32_MAX, so urb_create_iocompletion allocates a buffer sized from the wrapped value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked size arithmetic leads to an undersized buffer that is subsequently accessed beyond its intended bounds, matching CWE-125 out-of-bounds read/write on the output stream. The fix adds an explicit OutputBufferSize > UINT32_MAX - 4 guard, confirming the missing constraint is the allocation-size overflow rather than a generic length issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing upper-bound check on OutputBufferSize before the arithmetic OutputBufferSize + 4. Trigger: a malicious server sends an io-control message with OutputBufferSize near UINT32_MAX, causing integer wrap in the allocation size. Consequence: a too-small output stream is created, so later buffer operations (e.g., query_device_port_status writing through Stream_Pointer(out) at line 45) can exceed the intended buffer, yielding out-of-bounds access on the output buffer.

It is a missing-presence check rather than a bounds or type confusion issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function assumes skb_dst(skb) is always set and dereferences dst->dev unconditionally in the else branch. Trigger: a fragmented IPv6 packet reaches icmp6_send (via icmpv6_param_prob) before a route lookup, leaving skb_dst NULL. commit_msg:
Trap for overly large input to XmlRPCPP which could cause problems with int <-> size_t conversions.

 - In XmlRpcClient, XmlRpcServerConnection and XmlRpcSocket, recognize when incoming or outgoing data is too large, generate an error and discard the data when practical.
 - Use the safe strtol() rather than atoi() to decode an incoming content-length header, and generate an error if the length is invalid or too large.
 - In XmlRpcUtil, prevent attempts to parse overly large XML input.
 - Add tests where they can reasonably be inserted into existing test routines.

Although this fix could be cleaner the update is written to make the update ABI compatible.

This fix addresses CVE-2020-16124 / Integer overflow in ros_comm.

Signed-off-by: Sid Faber <sid.faber@canonical.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  _contentLength = atoi(lp);', '  if (_contentLength <= 0) {', '    XmlRpcUtil::error("XmlRpcServerConnection::readHeader: Invalid Content-length specified (%d).", _contentLength);'], 'added_lines': ['  // avoid overly large or improperly formatted content-length', '  long int clength = 0;', '  clength = strtol(lp, nullptr, 10);', '  if ((clength < 0) || (clength > __INT_MAX__)) {', '    XmlRpcUtil::error("XmlRpcServerConnection::readHeader: Invalid Content-length specified.");', '  _contentLength = int(clength);']}
description: Integer Overflow or Wraparound vulnerability in the XML RPC library of OpenRobotics ros_comm communications packages allows unauthenticated network traffic to cause unexpected behavior. This issue affects: OpenRobotics ros_comm communications packages Noetic and prior versions. Fixed in https://github.com/ros/ros_comm/pull/2065.

code_evidence: Line 13 detects the attacker-controlled 'Content-length: ' header in the received data and line 14 sets lp to the following text, which is later decoded.
Line 32 parses that text with atoi() into the int _contentLength; lines 33-36 only reject values <= 0, so a large decimal value that exceeds int range is not detected before conversion.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs an integer conversion of attacker-controlled input and assumes the resulting int reflects the true length; the missing upper-bound check before narrowing is the integer overflow/wraparound weakness described by CWE-190.

evidence_lines.code:
if ((ep - cp > 16) && (strncasecmp(cp, "Content-length: ", 16) == 0))
lp = cp + 16;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the Content-length header is converted with atoi() into an int with only a non-positive check, so an oversized value overflows/wraps to an unintended or negative int. Trigger: an unauthenticated network client sends a very large Content-length. Consequence: the wrapped length drives subsequent request-size handling, producing unexpected behavior such as incorrect allocation/read logic.

commit_msg:
realpath: Set errno to ENAMETOOLONG for result larger than PATH_MAX [BZ #28770]

realpath returns an allocated string when the result exceeds PATH_MAX,
which is unexpected when its second argument is not NULL.  This results
in the second argument (resolved) being uninitialized and also results
in a memory leak since the caller expects resolved to be the same as the
returned value.

Return NULL and set errno to ENAMETOOLONG if the result exceeds
PATH_MAX.  This fixes [BZ #28770], which is CVE-2021-3998.

Reviewed-by: Adhemerval Zanella  <adhemerval.zanella@linaro.org>
Signed-off-by: Siddhesh Poyarekar <siddhesh@sourceware.org>

description: A heap-based buffer over-read was discovered in the get_le32 function in bele.h in UPX 4.0.0 via a crafted Mach-O file.

code_evidence: Lines 25-31 read e_shoff and e_shnum from the header and compute last_Shdr, but the pre-patch check only guards wrap-around and file_size; it does not require e_shoff to lie after the program headers or before EOF, so shdri at line 43 can point outside file_image.

Lines 39-45 allocate file_image of file_size, read the whole file, then set shdri = (Elf64_Shdr *)(e_shoff + file_image) with only the weak bound above; a crafted e_shoff yields shdri past the allocated buffer.

Lines 46-51 call elf_find_section_type over shdri and then index shdri[t] after only checking e_shnum <= t; because shdri is not proven within file_image, these reads can access memory beyond the buffer.

commit_msg:
mm: migrate dirty page without clear_page_dirty_for_io etc

clear_page_dirty_for_io() has accumulated writeback and memcg subtleties
since v2.6.16 first introduced page migration; and the set_page_dirty()
which completed its migration of PageDirty, later had to be moderated to
__set_page_dirty_nobuffers(); then PageSwapBacked had to skip that too.

No actual problems seen with this procedure recently, but if you look into
what the clear_page_dirty_for_io(page)+set_page_dirty(newpage) is actually
achieving, it turns out to be nothing more than moving the PageDirty flag,
and its NR_FILE_DIRTY stat from one zone to another.

It would be good to avoid a pile of irrelevant decrementations and
incrementations, and improper event counting, and unnecessary descent of
the radix_tree under tree_lock (to set the PAGECACHE_TAG_DIRTY which
radix_tree_replace_slot() left in place anyway).

Do the NR_FILE_DIRTY movement, like the other stats movements, while
interrupts still disabled in migrate_page_move_mapping(); and don't even
bother if the zone is the same.  Do the PageDirty movement there under
tree_lock too, where old page is frozen and newpage not yet visible:
bearing in mind that as soon as newpage becomes visible in radix_tree, an
un-page-locked set_page_dirty() might interfere (or perhaps that's just
not possible: anything doing so should already hold an additional
reference to the old page, preventing its migration; but play safe).

But we do still need to transfer PageDirty in migrate_page_copy(), for
those who don't go the mapping route through migrate_page_move_mapping().

commit_msg:
checkout: fix bug that makes checkout follow symlinks in leading path

Before checking out a file, we have to confirm that all of its leading
components are real existing directories. And to reduce the number of
lstat() calls in this process, we cache the last leading path known to
contain only directories. However, when a path collision occurs (e.g.
when checking out case-sensitive files in case-insensitive file
systems), a cached path might have its file type changed on disk,
leaving the cache on an invalid state. Normally, this doesn't bring
any bad consequences as we usually check out files in index order, and
therefore, by the time the cached path becomes outdated, we no longer
need it anyway (because all files in that directory would have already
been written).

But, there are some users of the checkout machinery that do not always
follow the index order. In particular: checkout-index writes the paths
in the same order that they appear on the CLI (or stdin); and the
delayed checkout feature -- used when a long-running filter process
replies with "status=delayed" -- postpones the checkout of some entries,
thus modifying the checkout order.

When we have to check out an out-of-order entry and the lstat() cache is
invalid (due to a previous path collision), checkout_entry() may end up
using the invalid data and thrusting that the leading components are
real directories when, in reality, they are not. In the best case
scenario, where the directory was replaced by a regular file, the user
will get an error: "fatal: unable to create file 'foo/bar': Not a
directory". But if the directory was replaced by a symlink, checkout
could actually end up following the symlink and writing the file at a
wrong place, even outside the repository. Since delayed checkout is
affected by this bug, it could be used by an attacker to write
arbitrary files during the clone of a maliciously crafted repository.

Some candidate solutions considered were to disable the lstat() cache
during unordered checkouts or sort the entries before passing them to
the checkout machinery. But both ideas include some performance penalty
and they don't future-proof the code against new unordered use cases.

Instead, we now manually reset the lstat cache whenever we successfully
remove a directory. Note: We are not even checking whether the directory
was the same as the lstat cache points to because we might face a
scenario where the paths refer to the same location but differ due to
case folding, precomposed UTF-8 issues, or the presence of `..`
components in the path. Two regression tests, with case-collisions and
utf8-collisions, are also added for both checkout-index and delayed
checkout.

Note: to make the previously mentioned clone attack unfeasible, it would
be sufficient to reset the lstat cache only after the remove_subtree()
call inside checkout_entry(). This is the place where we would remove a
directory whose path collides with the path of another entry that we are
currently trying to check out (possibly a symlink). However, in the
interest of a thorough fix that does not leave Git open to
similar-but-not-identical attack vectors, we decided to intercept
all `rmdir()` calls in one fell swoop.

This addresses CVE-2021-21300.

Co-authored-by: Johannes Schindelin <johannes.schindelin@gmx.de>
Signed-off-by: Matheus Tavares <matheus.bernardino@usp.br>

description: Git is an open-source distributed revision control system. In affected versions of Git a specially crafted repository that contains symbolic links as well as files using a clean/smudge filter such as Git LFS, may cause just-checked out script to be executed while cloning onto a case-insensitive file system such as NTFS, HFS+ or APFS (i.e. the default file systems on Windows and macOS). Note that clean/smudge filters have to be configured for that. Git for Windows configures Git LFS by default, and is therefore vulnerable. The problem has been patched in the versions published on Tuesday, March 9th, 2021. As a workaound, if symbolic link support is disabled in Git (e.g. via `git config --global core.symlinks false`), the described attack won't work. Likewise, if no clean/smudge filters such as Git LFS are configured globally (i.e. _before_ cloning), the attack is foiled. As always, it is best to avoid cloning repositories from untrusted sources. The earliest impacted version is 2.14.2. The fix versions are: 2.30.1, 2.29.3, 2.28.1, 2.27.1, 2.26.3, 2.25.5, 2.24.4, 2.23.4, 2.22.5, 2.21.4, 2.20.5, 2.19.6, 2.18.5, 2.17.62.17.6.

code_evidence: threaded_has_dirs_only_path delegates to lstat_cache with FL_DIR|FL_FULLPATH, returning whether the cached leading path resolves to directories. The function is the checkout cache probe: it reports 'all leading components are real directories' without itself re-validating on-disk state, so a stale cache entry can assert FL_DIR for a path component that has since been replaced by a symlink.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is improper link resolution before file access: a leading path component that is a symlink is not detected because the cached FL_DIR result is reused, so the subsequent file access follows the link outside the intended tree. This matches CWE-59 (link following), distinct from a mere cache-consistency bug because the exploited effect is following a link to an unintended resource.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the directory lstat cache is trusted across operations that can replace a cached directory with a symlink (path collisions on case-insensitive filesystems, out-of-order/delayed checkout). Trigger: checkout probes this function, receives FL_DIR from stale cache, and opens the file through the now-symlinked leading component, writing outside the repository. Consequence: arbitrary file write / unauthorized script execution during clone.

commit_msg:
Fix memory leak in AtomicModifyWrite

This patch fixes #4894.

JerryScript-DCO-1.0-Signed-off-by: Robert Fancsik robert.fancsik@h-lab.eu
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  ecma_free_value (idx);', '']}
description: There is an Assertion ''JERRY_CONTEXT (jmem_heap_allocated_size) == 0'' failed at /jerry-core/jmem/jmem-heap.c in Jerryscript 3.0.0.

code_evidence: The function acquires an ecma_value_t idx from ecma_validate_atomic_access; on success idx is a heap-allocated value reference that is never released.

The error path returns idx directly (lines 13-16). The success path computes indexed_position from idx via ecma_number_to_uint32 and then only marks locals JERRY_UNUSED; idx is never freed before the function returns 0.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The reachable assertion is a direct consequence of the unreleased idx allocation; the assertion terminates the application, matching CWE-617's reachable-assertion/DoS scope. The leak itself is the cause, but the supported observable weakness is the triggerable assertion.

evidence_lines.code:
uint32_t indexed_position = ecma_number_to_uint32 (idx) * element_size + offset;
JERRY_UNUSED (indexed_position);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the idx value obtained from ecma_validate_atomic_access is not released on the success path, leaking the allocation. Trigger: repeated AtomicModifyWrite calls on a valid typed array and index. Consequence: leaked heap allocations accumulate until the engine's heap accounting assertion JERRY_CONTEXT(jmem_heap_allocated_size) == 0 fires, aborting the process (DoS).

If loop_count is bigger than the array, truncate it to the array

commit_msg: Fix bug #72603: Out of bound read in exif_process_IFD_in_MAKERNOTE
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\texif_process_IFD_in_MAKERNOTE(ImageInfo, value_ptr, byte_count, offset_base, IFDlength, displacement TSRMLS_CC);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tif (!exif_process_IFD_in_MAKERNOTE(ImageInfo, value_ptr, byte_count, offset_base, IFDlength, displacement TSRMLS_CC)) {', '\t\t\t\t\tEFREE_IF(outside);', '\t\t\t\t\treturn FALSE;', '\t\t\t\t}']}
description: The exif_process_IFD_in_MAKERNOTE function in ext/exif/exif.c in PHP before 5.5.38, 5.6.x before 5.6.24, and 7.x before 7.0.9 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds array access and memory corruption), obtain sensitive information from process memory, or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted JPEG image.

code_evidence: The TAG_MAKER_NOTE case calls exif_process_IFD_in_MAKERNOTE with value_ptr and byte_count but ignores its return value, so a failure inside the MakerNote parser does not stop processing.
Before the call, value_ptr/byte_count are derived from attacker-controlled offset_val and components; the bounds checks here only validate the outer IFD tag, not the nested MakerNote structure.
The stream read fills value_ptr only up to byte_count and aborts on a short read, yet the MakerNote handler is still given the buffer and its advertised length to parse nested entries.

The bug and the fix were reported by https://hackerone.com/pnoltof

description: In versions of mruby up to and including 1.4.0, a use-after-free vulnerability exists in src/io.c::File#initilialize_copy(). An attacker that can cause Ruby code to be run can possibly use this to execute arbitrary code.

code_evidence: Lines 10-14: the existing DATA_PTR(copy) is obtained, finalized, and freed before the original object is validated.

Lines 15-16,21: the new struct is allocated and stored only after the freed block, then fptr_orig is fetched from orig and its fd duplicated; the ordering leaves the freed fptr_copy reachable while io_get_open_fptr runs.

If io_get_open_fptr on orig raises or triggers GC/re-entry before DATA_PTR is overwritten, the stale pointer is dereferenced, giving use-after-free; attacker-influenced Ruby code driving initialize_copy can corrupt memory or execute code.

commit_msg:
Add integer overflow check to the malloc wrappers

Add a check that the combined size of the buffer to allocate and
alloc_info_t does not exceed the maximum integer value representable
by size_t.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    alloc_info_t *alloc_info = (alloc_info_t *)__real__malloc_r(r, size + sizeof(alloc_info_t));'], 'added_lines': ['    alloc_info_t *alloc_info = NULL;', '    if (size <= SIZE_MAX - sizeof(alloc_info_t)) {', '        alloc_info = (alloc_info_t *)__real__malloc_r(r, size + sizeof(alloc_info_t));', '    }']}
description: ARM mbed-ualloc memory library version 1.3.0 is vulnerable to integer wrap-around in function mbed_krbs, which can lead to arbitrary memory allocation, resulting in unexpected behavior such as a crash or a remote code injection/execution.

code_evidence: Line 9 computes size + sizeof(alloc_info_t) as the allocation size for __real__malloc_r without any bound check on size, so a large size wraps around to a small value. Line 10 checks alloc_info != NULL, which succeeds because the wrapped request is small, and lines 11-13 then write header fields and return alloc_info + 1 as a buffer the caller believes holds size bytes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the unsafe operation is an unchecked integer addition whose wrapped result drives a memory allocation. This is a size-calculation wraparound leading to undersized allocation, not a separate bounds or null-check defect; the NULL check at line 10 does not address the wrap.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the addition size + sizeof(alloc_info_t) can wrap when size is near SIZE_MAX, and the result is used as the malloc request size. Trigger: a caller passes a huge size. Consequence: a small buffer is allocated but treated as size bytes, so subsequent caller writes overrun the heap, enabling memory corruption and potential code execution or crash.

commit_msg:
DNP3: fix reachable assertion and buffer over-read/overflow.

A DNP3 packet using a link layer header that specifies a zero length can
trigger an assertion failure if assertions are enabled.  Assertions are
enabled unless Bro is compiled with the NDEBUG preprocessor macro
defined.  The default configuration of Bro will define this macro and so
disables assertions, but using the --enable-debug option in the
configure script will enable assertions.  When assertions are disabled,
or also for certain length values, the DNP3 parser may attempt to pass a
negative value as the third argument to memcpy (number of bytes to copy)
and result in a buffer over-read or overflow.

Reported by Travis Emmert.

The loop at line 9 runs while len > 0; line 11 sets n = min(len,16), and line 12 checks CRC over data..data+n. Line 14 asserts data+n < buffer+buffer_len, an unchecked upper-bound relation that only guards the subsequent BufferData call at line 15 with range [data+transport, data+n). Line 17 advances data by n+2 without validating against buffer_len.

The specific assertion-to-check fix confirms the missing bound is the weakness, not merely a resource issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser derives chunk length from an attacker-controlled packet length and only uses an assertion to bound data+n against the endpoint buffer. With assertions disabled or certain length values, data+n and the BufferData range can exceed the buffer, producing an out-of-bounds read/write; with assertions enabled it aborts.

description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 6.3.4. fs/ksmbd/connection.c in ksmbd has an off-by-one error in memory allocation (because of ksmbd_smb2_check_message) that may lead to out-of-bounds access.

Trigger: a client sends a PDU whose parsed length reaches the accepted maximum. Consequence: one-byte out-of-bounds read/write on conn->request_buf, causing memory corruption or crash/DoS.

commit_msg:
pipe: limit the per-user amount of pages allocated in pipes

On no-so-small systems, it is possible for a single process to cause an
OOM condition by filling large pipes with data that are never read. A
typical process filling 4000 pipes with 1 MB of data will use 4 GB of
memory. On small systems it may be tricky to set the pipe max size to
prevent this from happening.

This patch makes it possible to enforce a per-user soft limit above
which new pipes will be limited to a single page, effectively limiting
them to 4 kB each, as well as a hard limit above which no new pipes may
be created for this user. This has the effect of protecting the system
against memory abuse without hurting other users, and still allowing
pipes to work correctly though with less data at once.

The limit are controlled by two new sysctls : pipe-user-pages-soft, and
pipe-user-pages-hard. Both may be disabled by setting them to zero. The
default soft limit allows the default number of FDs per process (1024)
to create pipes of the default size (64kB), thus reaching a limit of 64MB
before starting to create only smaller pipes. With 256 processes limited
to 1024 FDs each, this results in 1024*64kB + (256*1024 - 1024) * 4kB =
1084 MB of memory allocated for a user. The hard limit is disabled by
default to avoid breaking existing applications that make intensive use
of pipes (eg: for splicing).

commit_msg:
Fix a padding oracle in PKCS7_dataDecode and CMS_decrypt_set1_pkey

An attack is simple, if the first CMS_recipientInfo is valid but the
second CMS_recipientInfo is chosen ciphertext. If the second
recipientInfo decodes to PKCS #1 v1.5 form plaintext, the correct
encryption key will be replaced by garbage, and the message cannot be
decoded, but if the RSA decryption fails, the correct encryption key is
used and the recipient will not notice the attack.

As a work around for this potential attack the length of the decrypted
key must be equal to the cipher default key length, in case the
certifiate is not given and all recipientInfo are tried out.

The old behaviour can be re-enabled in the CMS code by setting the
CMS_DEBUG_DECRYPT flag.

Reviewed-by: Matt Caswell <matt@openssl.org>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/9777)

(cherry picked from commit 5840ed0cd1e6487d247efbc1a04136a41d7b3a37)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                if (pkcs7_decrypt_rinfo(&ek, &eklen, ri, pkey) < 0)', '            if (pkcs7_decrypt_rinfo(&ek, &eklen, ri, pkey) < 0)'], 'added_lines': ['                if (pkcs7_decrypt_rinfo(&ek, &eklen, ri, pkey,', '                        EVP_CIPHER_key_length(evp_cipher)) < 0)', '            if (pkcs7_decrypt_rinfo(&ek, &eklen, ri, pkey, 0) < 0)']}
description: In situations where an attacker receives automated notification of the success or failure of a decryption attempt an attacker, after sending a very large number of messages to be decrypted, can recover a CMS/PKCS7 transported encryption key or decrypt any RSA encrypted message that was encrypted with the public RSA key, using a Bleichenbacher padding oracle attack. Applications are not affected if they use a certificate together with the private RSA key to the CMS_decrypt or PKCS7_decrypt functions to select the correct recipient info to decrypt. Fixed in OpenSSL 1.1.1d (Affected 1.1.1-1.1.1c). Fixed in OpenSSL 1.1.0l (Affected 1.1.0-1.1.0k). Fixed in OpenSSL 1.0.2t (Affected 1.0.2-1.0.2s).

code_evidence: When pcert is NULL, the loop tries every recipient info and calls pkcs7_decrypt_rinfo(&ek, &eklen, ri, pkey) without validating the decrypted key length against the cipher's expected key length; each iteration only clears the error and continues.

The else branch handles a single pre-selected recipient with the same unvalidated pkcs7_decrypt_rinfo call, so a failed RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 decrypt can fall through to error clearing rather than a length check.

Later, eklen is compared to EVP_CIPHER_CTX_key_length(evp_ctx); on mismatch the code substitutes the random key tkey, so processing continues with a garbage key instead of failing, and the caller observes a decryption failure that leaks the oracle.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function relies on RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 decryption without a length constraint, and the observable padding-dependent behavior breaks the intended cryptographic protection. This is a risky/weak use of a cryptographic scheme rather than a memory-safety defect, so CWE-327 fits; CWE-208 would describe the timing side channel but not the underlying broken padding-check design.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the recipient-key decryption path does not enforce that the recovered key length equals the cipher default key length, and on mismatch it silently replaces the key with random bytes. Trigger: an attacker submits a CMS/PKCS7 message whose recipient info decrypts to PKCS#1 v1.5 plaintext of the wrong length. Consequence: distinct success/failure behavior forms a Bleichenbacher padding oracle enabling recovery of the transported encryption key.

number can trigger BUG(). Range check the epnum and returning
error instead of calling BUG().

Change caller stub_recv_cmd_submit() to handle the get_pipe()
error return.

Reported-by: Secunia Research <vuln@secunia.com>
Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Shuah Khan <shuahkh@osg.samsung.com>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (pipe == -1)', '\t\treturn;']}
description: The "get_pipe()" function (drivers/usb/usbip/stub_rx.c) in the Linux Kernel before version 4.14.8, 4.9.71, and 4.4.114 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) via a specially crafted USB over IP packet.

code_evidence: Line 8 passes attacker-controlled pdu->base.ep into get_pipe() and stores the result in pipe without validating the endpoint number.
Line 9 allocates priv and line 12 branches on usb_pipeisoc(pipe); line 39 then assigns the unvalidated pipe to priv->urb->pipe, so the invalid endpoint-derived value propagates into the URB.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The invalid endpoint number causes get_pipe() to read beyond the intended ep_in/ep_out arrays, which is an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) whose observed impact is a BUG()-induced denial of service. This is distinct from a write-based memory corruption, since the access is a read.

evidence_lines.code: int pipe = get_pipe(sdev, pdu->base.ep, pdu->base.direction);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the endpoint number from the received USB/IP packet is used to index the ep_in/ep_out arrays inside get_pipe() with no range check, so an out-of-range value reads past the array bounds and can hit the BUG(). The caller triggers this by submitting a cmd_submit PDU with a crafted endpoint; the supported consequence is a kernel crash/DoS, and the out-of-range read is the underlying out-of-bounds access.

description: The Electron framework lets you write cross-platform desktop applications using JavaScript, HTML and CSS. In affected versions of Electron IPC messages sent from the main process to a subframe in the renderer process, through webContents.sendToFrame, event.reply or when using the remote module, can in some cases be delivered to the wrong frame. If your app uses remote, calls webContents.sendToFrame, or calls event.reply in an IPC message handler then it is impacted by this issue. This has been fixed in versions 9.4.0, 10.2.0, 11.1.0, and 12.0.0-beta.9. There are no workarounds for this issue.

code_evidence: The function resolves the destination frame by scanning web_contents()->GetAllFrames() and matching only f->GetRoutingID() == frame_id, ignoring process identity.
The resulting iter is used directly to obtain the remote interface and deliver the message, with no check that the frame belongs to the intended process/control sphere.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function exposes a resource (the IPC message payload) to the wrong control sphere by failing to constrain frame selection to the intended process. This matches CWE-668's exposure of a resource to unintended parties; the identity-only-by-routing-ID lookup is the specific implementation mistake enabling cross-sphere delivery.

evidence_lines.code:
mojo::AssociatedRemote<mojom::ElectronRenderer> electron_renderer;
(*iter)->GetRemoteAssociatedInterfaces()->GetInterface(&electron_renderer);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the destination frame is selected solely by routing ID, which is not unique across processes, so a caller-supplied frame_id can resolve to a frame outside the intended control sphere. Trigger: an IPC handler passing a frame identifier. Consequence: the serialized message is delivered to the wrong frame, exposing data to unintended actors.

commit_msg:
sched/fair: Fix low cpu usage with high throttling by removing expiration of cpu-local slices

It has been observed, that highly-threaded, non-cpu-bound applications
running under cpu.cfs_quota_us constraints can hit a high percentage of
periods throttled while simultaneously not consuming the allocated
amount of quota. This use case is typical of user-interactive non-cpu
bound applications, such as those running in kubernetes or mesos when
run on multiple cpu cores.

This has been root caused to cpu-local run queue being allocated per cpu
bandwidth slices, and then not fully using that slice within the period.
At which point the slice and quota expires. This expiration of unused
slice results in applications not being able to utilize the quota for
which they are allocated.

The non-expiration of per-cpu slices was recently fixed by
'commit 512ac999d275 ("sched/fair: Fix bandwidth timer clock drift
condition")'. Prior to that it appears that this had been broken since
at least 'commit 51f2176d74ac ("sched/fair: Fix unlocked reads of some
cfs_b->quota/period")' which was introduced in v3.16-rc1 in 2014. That
added the following conditional which resulted in slices never being
expired.

if (cfs_rq->runtime_expires != cfs_b->runtime_expires) {
	/* extend local deadline, drift is bounded above by 2 ticks */
	cfs_rq->runtime_expires += TICK_NSEC;

Because this was broken for nearly 5 years, and has recently been fixed
and is now being noticed by many users running kubernetes
(https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/67577) it is my opinion
that the mechanisms around expiring runtime should be removed
altogether.

This allows quota already allocated to per-cpu run-queues to live longer
than the period boundary. This allows threads on runqueues that do not
use much CPU to continue to use their remaining slice over a longer
period of time than cpu.cfs_period_us. However, this helps prevent the
above condition of hitting throttling while also not fully utilizing
your cpu quota.

This theoretically allows a machine to use slightly more than its
allotted quota in some periods. This overflow would be bounded by the
remaining quota left on each per-cpu runqueueu. This is typically no
more than min_cfs_rq_runtime=1ms per cpu. For CPU bound tasks this will
change nothing, as they should theoretically fully utilize all of their
quota in each period. For user-interactive tasks as described above this
provides a much better user/application experience as their cpu
utilization will more closely match the amount they requested when they
hit throttling. This means that cpu limits no longer strictly apply per
period for non-cpu bound applications, but that they are still accurate
over longer timeframes.

This greatly improves performance of high-thread-count, non-cpu bound
applications with low cfs_quota_us allocation on high-core-count
machines. In the case of an artificial testcase (10ms/100ms of quota on
80 CPU machine), this commit resulted in almost 30x performance
improvement, while still maintaining correct cpu quota restrictions.
That testcase is available at https://github.com/indeedeng/fibtest.

Fixes: 512ac999d275 ("sched/fair: Fix bandwidth timer clock drift condition")
Signed-off-by: Dave Chiluk <chiluk+linux@indeed.com>
Signed-off-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
Reviewed-by: Phil Auld <pauld@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Ben Segall <bsegall@google.com>

Cc: Cong Wang <xiyou.wangcong@gmail.com>
Cc: Brendan Gregg <bgregg@netflix.com>
Link: https://lkml.kernel.org/r/1563900266-19734-2-git-send-email-chiluk+linux@indeed.com
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\texpire_cfs_rq_runtime(cfs_rq);'], 'added_lines': []}
description: kernel/sched/fair.c in the Linux kernel before 5.3.9, when cpu.cfs_quota_us is used (e.g., with Kubernetes), allows attackers to cause a denial of service against non-cpu-bound applications by generating a workload that triggers unwanted slice expiration, aka CID-de53fd7aedb1. (In other words, although this slice expiration would typically be seen with benign workloads, it is possible that an attacker could calculate how many stray requests are required to force an entire Kubernetes cluster into a low-performance state caused by slice expiration, and ensure that a DDoS attack sent that number of stray requests. An attack does not affect the stability of the kernel; it only causes mismanagement of application execution.)

code_evidence: __account_cfs_rq_runtime debits delta_exec from cfs_rq->runtime_remaining and, before the patch, calls expire_cfs_rq_runtime(cfs_rq) on every accounting step. The unconditional check on line 5 returns only while runtime_remaining stays positive; otherwise lines 7-8 assign more runtime or reschedule the current task.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-400 fits because the product fails to properly maintain and account a limited resource (CPU bandwidth quota): throttling is applied even though the quota remains available. The weakness is quota/slice accounting and expiration, not an unbounded allocation or a memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the per-cpu bandwidth slice is expired as soon as accounting runs, so a largely idle runqueue loses unused quota at the period boundary instead of retaining it. Trigger: a highly-threaded, non-CPU-bound workload under cpu.cfs_quota_us causes many per-cpu slices to expire unused. Supported consequence: the cgroup is throttled while its allocated quota is not consumed, degrading application throughput (DoS: Resource Consumption).

commit_msg: Fix stack overflow if interpreting a file full of '{' (fix #1448)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (!jspCheckStackPosition()) return 0;']}
description: Espruino before 1.99 allows attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) with a user crafted input file via a Buffer Overflow during syntax parsing because of a missing check for stack exhaustion with many '{' characters in jsparse.c.

code_evidence: When the token is '{', jspeStatement calls jspeBlock() to parse a nested block and then returns. In the pre-fix function there is no stack-depth guard before this call, so each nested '{' re-enters statement parsing through jspeBlock without any exhaustion check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function implements unbounded recursive descent on attacker-controlled nesting, matching CWE-674 (Uncontrolled Recursion): recursion depth is not controlled, leading to stack exhaustion. This is a recursion-depth weakness rather than a fixed-size buffer write, so CWE-674 fits better than a classic buffer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: jspeStatement recurses into jspeBlock for every '{' token without bounding recursion depth. Trigger: a crafted input file containing many consecutive '{' characters drives deep recursive descent; the stack is consumed until overflow, crashing the parser (DoS). The missing jspCheckStackPosition() guard is the cause; the crash is the consequence.

commit_msg: fixed crash on invalid input in http_parser
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tTORRENT_ASSERT(buf.begin <= buf.end);', '\t\tTORRENT_ASSERT(pos <= buf.end);', '\t\tif (chunk_size < 0) return true;', '']}
description: The parse_chunk_header function in libtorrent before 1.1.1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) via a crafted (1) HTTP response or possibly a (2) UPnP broadcast.

code_evidence: pos is initialized to buf.begin and advanced past optional CR/LF bytes only while guarded by pos < buf.end; the function then returns false when pos == buf.end, so the empty-input case is rejected before further use.
newline is derived from std::find over [pos, buf.end); if no newline is found the function returns false, and ++newline occurs only after that check.

The chunk length is parsed from the attacker-controlled header via strtoll(pos, 0, 16). The parsed value is stored in *chunk_size and immediately tested by the subsequent if (*chunk_size != 0) branch without any range or sign check on the parsed value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because the parsed chunk-size input is used to drive control flow without validation of its properties. The missing constraint is on the parsed quantity, not on pointer bounds, so this is improper input validation rather than an out-of-bounds weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
*chunk_size = strtoll(pos, 0, 16);
if (*chunk_size != 0)

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function parses an untrusted HTTP chunk-size token with strtoll and branches on the resulting value without validating that the parsed quantity is in an acceptable range. A crafted chunk header can yield a value the caller does not expect, which is the input that the surrounding parser must handle; the header bounds themselves are checked before parsing.

commit_msg:
usbip_host updates device status without holding lock from stub probe,
disconnect and rebind code paths. When multiple requests to import a
device are received, these unprotected code paths step all over each
other and drive fails with NULL-ptr deref and use-after-free errors.

The driver uses a table lock to protect the busid array for adding and
deleting busids to the table. However, the probe, disconnect and rebind
paths get the busid table entry and update the status without holding
the busid table lock. Add a new finer grain lock to protect the busid
entry. This new lock will be held to search and update the busid entry
fields from get_busid_idx(), add_match_busid() and del_match_busid().

match_busid_show() does the same to access the busid entry fields.

get_busid_priv() changed to return the pointer to the busid entry holding
the busid lock. stub_probe(), stub_disconnect() and stub_device_rebind()
call put_busid_priv() to release the busid lock before returning. This
changes fixes the unprotected code paths eliminating the race conditions
in updating the busid entries.

Reported-by: Jakub Jirasek
Signed-off-by: Shuah Khan (Samsung OSG) <shuah@kernel.org>
Cc: stable <stable@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t/* release the busid lock */', '\tput_busid_priv(bid);']}
description: In the Linux Kernel before version 4.16.11, 4.14.43, 4.9.102, and 4.4.133, multiple race condition errors when handling probe, disconnect, and rebind operations can be exploited to trigger a use-after-free condition or a NULL pointer dereference by sending multiple USB over IP packets.

code_evidence: get_busid_priv(buf) obtains a pointer to a shared bus_id_priv entry and returns -ENODEV if absent. The code then writes bid->status = STUB_BUSID_OTHER and passes the same bid to do_rebind without any synchronization visible in this function.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a concurrent access to a shared resource (bus_id_priv) with improper synchronization, matching CWE-362. The patch adds put_busid_priv(bid) to release a busid lock, confirming the unprotected window; the weakness is the missing exclusive access, not the pointer dereference itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the shared bus_id_priv entry is looked up and its status field mutated and used by do_rebind without holding a lock protecting that entry. Trigger: concurrent probe/disconnect/rebind paths or repeated imports operating on the same busid interleave. Supported consequence: the entry can be freed or changed between lookup and use, producing use-after-free or NULL-pointer dereference.

commit_msg:
CVE-2017-12897/ISO CLNS: Use ND_TTEST() for the bounds checks in isoclns_print().

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Kamil Frankowicz.

Don't pass the remaining caplen - that's too hard to get right, and we
were getting it wrong in at least one case; just use ND_TTEST().

Add a test using the capture file supplied by the reporter(s).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            isoclns_print(ndo, p, l2info.length, l2info.caplen);'], 'added_lines': ['            isoclns_print(ndo, p, l2info.length);']}
description: The ISO CLNS parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-isoclns.c:isoclns_print().

code_evidence: In the JUNIPER_LSQ_L3_PROTO_ISO case, the function passes l2info.length and l2info.caplen separately to isoclns_print(). The caplen argument is derived from the captured packet and was used by the ISO CLNS parser for bounds checks, but the commit states those checks were computed incorrectly, allowing the parser to read beyond the captured buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is reading memory beyond the intended captured buffer, matching CWE-125 (Out-of-bounds Read). It is not a write or integer issue; the unsafe operation is a read past the buffer end caused by improper bounds checking on caplen.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the caller forwards a caplen value that the callee's bounds checks mishandle, so isoclns_print() can index past the end of the captured data when parsing ISO CLNS content. Trigger: a crafted Juniper MLPPP packet with proto JUNIPER_LSQ_L3_PROTO_ISO whose ISO CLNS payload is truncated relative to length. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds read of packet buffer memory.

DO NOT MERGE mm-video-v4l2: venc: add checks before accessing heap pointers

Heap pointers do not point to user virtual addresses in case
of secure session.
Set them to NULL and add checks to avoid accesing them

Bug: 28815329

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                m_pOutput_pmem[i].buffer = (OMX_U8 *)SECURE_BUFPTR;'], 'added_lines': ['                m_pOutput_pmem[i].buffer = NULL;', '                    m_pOutput_pmem[i].buffer = NULL;']}
description: The secure-session feature in the mm-video-v4l2 venc component in mediaserver in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-08-01 mishandles heap pointers, which allows attackers to gain privileges via a crafted application, aka internal bug 28815329.

code_evidence: Lines 105-107 set the pmem size/offset and assign buffer to the SECURE_BUFPTR sentinel for the secure-session path; only when !secure_session (line 108) is a real mmap performed.
Lines 110/114 perform mmap into m_pOutput_pmem[i].buffer and line 118 checks MAP_FAILED, but on failure line 120 only closes the fd without resetting buffer to NULL, leaving MAP_FAILED stored.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because invalid heap pointer values (sentinel or MAP_FAILED) are used as buffer addresses, causing operations outside the intended buffer boundary. This is a pointer-validity/out-of-bounds access issue rather than a pure NULL dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the secure-session path stores a non-NULL sentinel (SECURE_BUFPTR) and the mmap-failure path leaves MAP_FAILED in m_pOutput_pmem[i].buffer, so downstream consumers treat these invalid addresses as valid heap pointers. Trigger: a secure session or a failed mmap. Consequence: out-of-bounds reads/writes through the invalid pointer, enabling privilege escalation.

description: Istio 1.4.x before 1.4.9 and Istio 1.5.x before 1.5.4 contain the following vulnerability when telemetry v2 is enabled: by sending a specially crafted packet, an attacker could trigger a Null Pointer Exception resulting in a Denial of Service. This also affects servicemesh-proxy where a null pointer exception flaw was found in servicemesh-proxy. When running Telemetry v2 (not on by default in version 1.4.x), an attacker could send a specially crafted packet to the ingress gateway or proxy sidecar, triggering a denial of service.

When that guard is absent, execution reaches line 5 and invokes wasm_->onResponseTrailers_(this, id_), calling into the VM even though the VM context was never created.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The fix adds a null/initialization guard before a pointer-mediated call, matching CWE-476: an expected-valid pointer or context is NULL and is dereferenced, causing a crash. This is a missing-state check, not a type or bounds error.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!wasm_->onResponseTrailers_) {
if (wasm_->onResponseTrailers_(this, id_).u64_ == 0) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: onResponseTrailers dispatches the trailers callback without verifying the VM context exists. Trigger: a crafted packet reaches trailer processing while telemetry v2 is enabled but the VM context is uninitialized, so the callback dereferences state tied to a missing context. Supported consequence: null pointer exception/crash leading to denial of service on the gateway or sidecar.
