commit_msg: Fix memleak in tcp server by wiping priority queues on deletion
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    crypto_memzero(con, sizeof(TCP_Secure_Connection));'], 'added_lines': ['    wipe_secure_connection(con);']}
description: The TCP Server module in toxcore before 0.2.8 doesn't free the TCP priority queue under certain conditions, which allows a remote attacker to exhaust the system's memory, causing a denial of service (DoS).

code_evidence: kill_TCP_secure_connection closes the socket via kill_sock(con->sock), then only clears the connection struct with crypto_memzero(con, sizeof(TCP_Secure_Connection)); the priority queue resources referenced by the connection are never freed before the struct is zeroed, leaving their allocations unreleased.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-404 covers failing to release a resource (the priority queue) on shutdown. The missing free before crypto_memzero is the improper release; the memory exhaustion is the consequence, not the weakness itself.

evidence_lines.code:
kill_sock(con->sock);
crypto_memzero(con, sizeof(TCP_Secure_Connection));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the teardown path zeroes the TCP_Secure_Connection without releasing resources it owns (the TCP priority queue). Trigger: a remote peer causes connections to be killed repeatedly. Consequence: leaked allocations accumulate, exhausting memory and causing denial of service.

description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.3 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.11, the IxVeriWave file parser could crash. This was addressed in wiretap/vwr.c by correcting the signature timestamp bounds checks.

code_evidence: find_signature returns sig_off, which is used to index m_ptr[sig_off] and passed to get_signature_ts without any check that sig_off is within rec_size; the only remaining guard checks sig_off + 15 <= msdu_length, but msdu_length is bounded by actual_octets <= rec_size - STATS_LEN, so a sig_off beyond the record can still satisfy it.

The earlier validation only rejects actual_octets > rec_size - vwr->STATS_LEN; it never constrains sig_off, so the subsequent m_ptr[sig_off] read and signature timestamp read can access memory outside the record buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads m_ptr at an attacker-influenced offset that can exceed the buffer's intended boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. This is a buffer-bounds root cause rather than merely a downstream crash.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: find_signature's returned offset is used as an index into m_ptr without a bounds check against rec_size, and the msdu_length comparison does not actually bound sig_off to the buffer. Trigger: a crafted IxVeriWave record where find_signature yields an offset past the record. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of the record buffer, which the description reports can crash the parser.

commit_msg:
usb: limit combined packets to 1 MiB (CVE-2021-3527)

usb-host and usb-redirect try to batch bulk transfers by combining many
small usb packets into a single, large transfer request, to reduce the
overhead and improve performance.

This patch adds a size limit of 1 MiB for those combined packets to
restrict the host resources the guest can bind that way.

Signed-off-by: Gerd Hoffmann <kraxel@redhat.com>
Message-Id: <20210503132915.2335822-6-kraxel@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                (totalsize == (16 * KiB - 36) && p->int_req)) {'], 'added_lines': ['                (totalsize == (16 * KiB - 36) && p->int_req) ||', '                /* Next package may grow combined package over 1MiB */', '                totalsize > 1 * MiB - ep->max_packet_size) {']}
description: A flaw was found in the USB redirector device (usb-redir) of QEMU. Small USB packets are combined into a single, large transfer request, to reduce the overhead and improve performance. The combined size of the bulk transfer is used to dynamically allocate a variable length array (VLA) on the stack without proper validation. Since the total size is not bounded, a malicious guest could use this flaw to influence the array length and cause the QEMU process to perform an excessive allocation on the stack, resulting in a denial of service.

code_evidence: The loop accumulates queued packets into a combined packet (lines 22-33) and computes totalsize from the combined iovec or current packet iovec (line 34). The only exit conditions before the patch (lines 35-37) do not cap totalsize, so a guest submitting many small packets can grow the combined size without bound before usb_device_handle_data is invoked.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-770 fits because the function allocates/accumulates a combined transfer resource on behalf of the guest without a size limit, which is exactly the missing throttling the patch addresses. This is resource exhaustion, not an out-of-bounds access, so memory-corruption CWEs do not apply.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the combination loop lacks an upper bound on the accumulated combined size. Trigger: a malicious guest queues many small bulk packets whose sizes pass the modulo/short_not_ok checks. Consequence: the combined transfer/iovec grows arbitrarily, leading to excessive host resource consumption and denial of service.

commit_msg:
Remove legacy workaround for parsing modulo operator

Fixes #2659
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    // Special case handling for `%` proceeding an interpolant.', "    if (lex< sequence< exactly<'%'>, optional< percentage > > >())", '    { return SASS_MEMORY_NEW(String_Constant, pstate, lexed); }', ''], 'added_lines': []}
description: In LibSass prior to 3.5.5, Sass::Eval::operator()(Sass::Binary_Expression*) inside eval.cpp allows attackers to cause a denial-of-service resulting from stack consumption via a crafted sass file, because of certain incorrect parsing of '%' as a modulo operator in parser.cpp.

code_evidence: The function accepts a bare '%' (or '%' followed by an optional percentage) and returns a String_Constant, short-circuiting the normal expression parsing. This special case at lines 55-56 is the legacy workaround removed by the patch, so the parser no longer treats a leading modulo sign as a complete value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's mis-parsing enables attacker-controlled input to exhaust process stack resources, which is the resource-consumption DoS described by CWE-400. It is not an injection flaw; the defect is uncontrolled resource consumption during parsing.

evidence_lines.code:
if (lex< sequence< exactly<'%'>, optional< percentage > > >())
{ return SASS_MEMORY_NEW(String_Constant, pstate, lexed); }

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: a special-case lexing of '%' as a value causes the parser to mis-handle '%' as a modulo operator, so crafted Sass input drives incorrect/recursive parsing paths. Trigger: a crafted .sass file containing such '%' constructs. Supported consequence: unbounded recursion / stack consumption leading to denial of service (crash).

commit_msg:
PackLinuxElf::canUnpack must checkEhdr() for ELF input

https://github.com/upx/upx/issues/485
	modified:   p_lx_elf.cpp
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (Elf32_Ehdr::ET_DYN==get_te16(&ehdri.e_type)) {', '        PackLinuxElf32help1(fi);', '    }'], 'added_lines': ['    if (checkEhdr(&ehdri)) {', '        return false;', '    }', '    // FIXME: ET_DYN same as 64-bit canUnpack ??', '    if (Elf32_Ehdr::ET_DYN==get_te16(&ehdri.e_type)) {', '        PackLinuxElf32help1(fi);', '    }']}
description: Null pointer dereference was found in upx PackLinuxElf::canUnpack() in p_lx_elf.cpp,in version UPX 4.0.0. That allow attackers to execute arbitrary code and cause a denial of service via a crafted file.

code_evidence: canUnpack() calls super::canUnpack() before any validation of the ELF header stored in ehdri; only afterward does it read ehdri.e_type via get_te16 and conditionally call PackLinuxElf32help1(fi). No checkEhdr() guard on ehdri precedes the super call or the e_type read.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The patch's added checkEhdr() guard and early return show the pre-fix path operated on an unvalidated header pointer, matching CWE-476 (NULL pointer dereference). Unlike a bounds/type-confusion issue, the weakness is using a pointer before confirming it is valid.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the ELF header ehdri is consumed (by the superclass canUnpack and by the ET_DYN test) without first validating it with checkEhdr(). Trigger: a crafted/truncated ELF input reaching this function. Supported consequence: dereference of header/pointer state that was never validated, leading to a crash (DoS) as reported; the fix moves checkEhdr() to the top and returns false on failure.

commit_msg: Prevent buffer overflow in SIXEL, PDB, MAP, and CALS coders (bug report from Donghai Zhu)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  packet_size=(size_t) (image->depth > 8 ? 2: 1);'], 'added_lines': ['  packet_size=(size_t) (image->depth > 8 ? 2 : 1);', '  status=SetQuantumDepth(image,quantum_info,image->depth > 8 ? 16 : 8);']}
description: Buffer overflow in the WriteMAPImage function in coders/map.c in ImageMagick before 6.9.5-8 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or have other unspecified impact via a crafted file.

code_evidence: packet_size is derived solely from image->depth (>8 gives 2, else 1), and scanline is allocated as image->columns*packet_size bytes.
quantum_info is acquired without constraining its quantum depth to match packet_size; the fix adds SetQuantumDepth(image,quantum_info,image->depth > 8 ? 16 : 8) to keep them consistent.

ExportQuantumPixels fills scanline, then the loop indexes scanline[x*packet_size], assuming each sample occupies exactly packet_size bytes; if quantum_info exports a wider depth than packet_size, this read exceeds the allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates a fixed-size scanline buffer but indexes it using a sample stride that may not match the buffer's intended bounds, producing an out-of-bounds memory access, which is the essence of CWE-119.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is a mismatch between the scanline buffer size (image->columns*packet_size) and the bytes per sample actually written by ExportQuantumPixels via quantum_info. When image depth pushes quantum export beyond packet_size, the read at scanline[x*packet_size] walks past the buffer, yielding an out-of-bounds read and possible crash.

commit_msg:
x86/spec-ctrl: Enumeration for MMIO Stale Data controls

The three *_NO bits indicate non-susceptibility to the SSDP, FBSDP and PSDP
data movement primitives.

FB_CLEAR indicates that the VERW instruction has re-gained it's Fill Buffer
flushing side effect.  This is only enumerated on parts where VERW had
previously lost it's flushing side effect due to the MDS/TAA vulnerabilities
being fixed in hardware.

FB_CLEAR_CTRL is available on a subset of FB_CLEAR parts where the Fill Buffer
clearing side effect of VERW can be turned off for performance reasons.

This is part of XSA-404.

Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Roger Pau Monné <roger.pau@citrix.com>

commit_msg:
[ Upstream commit ad0f75e5f57ccbceec13274e1e242f2b5a6397ed ]

When we clone a socket in sk_clone_lock(), its sk_cgrp_data is
copied, so the cgroup refcnt must be taken too. And, unlike the
sk_alloc() path, sock_update_netprioidx() is not called here.
Therefore, it is safe and necessary to grab the cgroup refcnt
even when cgroup_sk_alloc is disabled.

sk_clone_lock() is in BH context anyway, the in_interrupt()
would terminate this function if called there. And for sk_alloc()
skcd->val is always zero. So it's safe to factor out the code
to make it more readable.

The global variable 'cgroup_sk_alloc_disabled' is used to determine
whether to take these reference counts. It is impossible to make
the reference counting correct unless we save this bit of information
in skcd->val. So, add a new bit there to record whether the socket
has already taken the reference counts. This obviously relies on
kmalloc() to align cgroup pointers to at least 4 bytes,
ARCH_KMALLOC_MINALIGN is certainly larger than that.

This bug seems to be introduced since the beginning, commit
d979a39d7242 ("cgroup: duplicate cgroup reference when cloning sockets")
tried to fix it but not compeletely. It seems not easy to trigger until
the recent commit 090e28b229af
("netprio_cgroup: Fix unlimited memory leak of v2 cgroups") was merged.

description: The Linux kernel 4.9.x before 4.9.233, 4.14.x before 4.14.194, and 4.19.x before 4.19.140 has a use-after-free because skcd->no_refcnt was not considered during a backport of a CVE-2020-14356 patch. This is related to the cgroups feature.

code_evidence: sock_cgroup_ptr() reads skcd->val into v and only tests bit 0 (v & 1) before returning the default root cgroup; otherwise it casts the whole value to a struct cgroup pointer. The new no_refcnt bit (bit 1) is not masked out, so when that bit is set without bit 0, the tagged value is returned as a cgroup pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function returns a pointer to cgroup memory that may already have been freed because the missing reference count was not accounted for; dereferencing this result is a use-after-free, matching CWE-416. A mere type-confusion or bad-cast label would miss the freed-memory lifetime cause.

description:
Apptainer is an open source container platform for Linux. There is an ext4 use-after-free flaw that is exploitable through versions of Apptainer < 1.1.0 and installations that include apptainer-suid < 1.1.8 on older operating systems where that CVE has not been patched. That includes Red Hat Enterprise Linux 7, Debian 10 buster (unless the linux-5.10 package is installed), Ubuntu 18.04 bionic and Ubuntu 20.04 focal. Use-after-free flaws in the kernel can be used to attack the kernel for denial of service and potentially for privilege escalation.

Apptainer 1.1.8 includes a patch that by default disables mounting of extfs filesystem types in setuid-root mode, while continuing to allow mounting of extfs filesystems in non-setuid "rootless" mode using fuse2fs.

Some workarounds are possible. Either do not install apptainer-suid (for versions 1.1.0 through 1.1.7) or set `allow setuid = no` in apptainer.conf.  This requires having unprivileged user namespaces enabled and except for apptainer 1.1.x versions will disallow mounting of sif files, extfs files, and squashfs files in addition to other, less significant impacts.  (Encrypted sif files are also not supported unprivileged in apptainer 1.1.x.). Alternatively, use the `limit containers` options in apptainer.conf/singularity.conf to limit sif files to trusted users, groups, and/or paths, and set `allow container extfs = no` to disallow mounting of extfs overlay files. description: Buffer overflow in the ReadRLEImage function in coders/rle.c in ImageMagick before 6.9.4-4 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or have other unspecified impact via a crafted RLE file.

code_evidence: Lines 146-155: number_planes_filled is derived from the attacker-controlled number_planes (and alpha trait), and the pixel buffer is sized as columns*rows*number_planes_filled bytes. If number_planes is 1, number_planes_filled becomes 2, but the run/byte-data loops below still advance p by number_planes per pixel.

Lines 214-232: offset is computed from rows-y-1, columns, x, and number_planes; the bounds check compares offset+operand*number_planes against pixel_info_length. For a single-plane image the buffer is sized for 2 planes per pixel while the check uses 1, so the check under-constrains relative to the allocation and the writes at *p=pixel with p+=number_planes can run past the allocated region.

Lines 245-262: the RunDataOp path repeats the same offset computation and bounds check with number_planes, then writes pixel across operand iterations; the mismatch between the allocation stride (number_planes_filled) and the check stride (number_planes) leaves the write loop able to exceed the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes pixel data into a heap buffer without correctly restricting the write to the buffer's intended bounds, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. This is a bounds-restriction error; the incorrect stride between allocation and bounds check is the specific mechanism, not a separate resource or input-validation weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the pixel buffer is allocated using number_planes_filled (rounded up to at least 2), but offset/bounds checks and pointer advancement use number_planes, so for a 1-plane image the check permits writes that the allocation does not cover. Trigger: a crafted RLE file with number_planes=1 and large operand/x/y values. Consequence: out-of-bounds write past the heap buffer, causing crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg: Github Issue #522: Detect cycles in the ISO directory tree
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct file_info *file;', '\tuint64_t fsize;', '\tfile->offset = iso9660->logical_block_size * (uint64_t)location;'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct file_info *file, *filep;', '\tuint64_t fsize, offset;', '\t/* Sanity check that this entry does not create a cycle. */', '\toffset = iso9660->logical_block_size * (uint64_t)location;', '\tfor (filep = parent; filep != NULL; filep = filep->parent) {', '\t\tif (filep->offset == offset) {', '\t\t\tarchive_set_error(&a->archive, ARCHIVE_ERRNO_FILE_FORMAT,', '\t\t\t    "Directory structure contains loop");', '\t\t\treturn (NULL);', '\t\t}', '\t}', '', '\tfile->offset = offset;']}
description: bsdtar in libarchive before 3.2.0 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (infinite loop) via an ISO with a directory that is a member of itself.

code_evidence: The function derives location and fsize directly from the untrusted ISO directory record and only checks extent bounds against volume_block; it computes file->offset from location without checking whether that offset already appears among the parent chain.

file->parent is set to parent and file->offset is assigned the computed block offset; later a directory whose location equals an ancestor's offset is registered, so a self-referential directory record yields a file entry whose parent chain revisits the same offset.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser accepts a directory record whose extent offset duplicates an ancestor's offset, because it never validates the entry against the existing parent chain. Trigger: a crafted ISO image containing a directory that is a member of itself. Consequence: the directory tree becomes cyclic, and downstream traversal loops indefinitely, causing a denial of service.

commit_msg:
tools/xenstore: Fail a transaction if it is not possible to create a node

Commit f2bebf72c4d5 "xenstore: rework of transaction handling" moved
out from copying the entire database everytime a new transaction is
opened to track the list of nodes changed.

The content of all the nodes accessed during a transaction will be
temporarily stored in TDB using a different key.

The function create_node() may write/update multiple nodes if the child
doesn't exist. In case of a failure, the function will revert any
changes (this include any update to TDB). Unfortunately, the function
which reverts the changes (i.e. destroy_node()) will not use the correct
key to delete any update or even request the transaction to fail.

This means that if a client decide to go ahead with committing the
transaction, orphan nodes will be created because they were not linked
to an existing node (create_node() will write the nodes backwards).

Once some nodes have been partially updated in a transaction, it is not
easily possible to undo any changes. So rather than continuing and hit
weird issue while committing, it is much saner to fail the transaction.

This will have an impact on any client that decides to commit even if it
can't write a node. Although, it is not clear why a normal client would
want to do that...

Lastly, update destroy_node() to use the correct key for deleting the
node. Rather than recreating it (this will allocate memory and
therefore fail), stash the key in the structure node.

This is XSA-415 / CVE-2022-42310.

Signed-off-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
Reviewed-by: Juergen Gross <jgross@suse.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tTDB_DATA key;', '', '\tset_tdb_key(node->name, &key);', '\ttdb_delete(tdb_ctx, key);'], 'added_lines': ['\ttdb_delete(tdb_ctx, node->key);', '\t/*', '\t * It is not possible to easily revert the changes in a transaction.', '\t * So if the failure happens in a transaction, mark it as fail to', '\t * prevent any commit.', '\t */', '\tif ( conn->transaction )', '\t\tfail_transaction(conn->transaction);', '']}
description: Xenstore: Guests can create orphaned Xenstore nodes By creating multiple nodes inside a transaction resulting in an error, a malicious guest can create orphaned nodes in the Xenstore data base, as the cleanup after the error will not remove all nodes already created. When the transaction is committed after this situation, nodes without a valid parent can be made permanent in the data base.

code_evidence: destroy_node() deletes the TDB record using a key rebuilt from node->name via set_tdb_key(node->name, &key), rather than the key actually used when the node was created/updated during the transaction. The delete therefore targets the wrong record, so the temporary transaction-time entry is not removed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-459 fits because the weakness is incomplete cleanup of temporary transaction resources: the delete does not remove the record that was written. The primary defect is failure to properly clean up supporting data, distinct from a mere access-control or input-validation issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: cleanup deletes using a key derived from node->name instead of the key under which the transaction stored the node, so the delete misses the temporary/supporting record. Trigger: create_node() partially creates nodes inside a transaction and the failure path invokes destroy_node(). Consequence: orphaned/leftover nodes remain and can be committed into the database. The missing fail_transaction call also lets a damaged transaction proceed to commit.

description: In nDPI through 3.2, the packet parsing code is vulnerable to a heap-based buffer over-read in ndpi_parse_packet_line_info in lib/ndpi_main.c.

return(0);

description: Integer overflow in bcmath in Facebook HHVM before 3.15.0 allows attackers to have unspecified impact via unknown vectors, which triggers a buffer overflow.

code_evidence: The function accepts an int64_t scale parameter and only guards the negative case (scale < 0), replacing it with the global bc_precision; any large positive scale value passes through unchanged.
That unvalidated scale is then handed directly to bc_str2num for both operands, where it is consumed as a size/precision value that drives internal buffer handling.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an integer overflow/wraparound in size computation that becomes security-relevant because the result is used as a buffer size, matching CWE-190. It is not merely a logic bug in scale handling; the overflow directly drives a memory-corruption consequence.

evidence_lines.code:
int64_t scale ) {
if (scale < 0) scale = BCG(bc_precision);

bc_str2num(&first, (char*)left.data(), scale);
bc_str2num(&second, (char*)right.data(), scale);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the scale argument is trusted without bounding it to a safe range, so an oversized positive value is not rejected or clamped. Trigger: a caller supplies a very large scale; internal bcmath code multiplies/derives buffer sizes from it, producing an integer wraparound that yields a small or negative size. Consequence: undersized allocation followed by writes causes a buffer overrun.

commit_msg:
libblkid: care about unsafe chars in cache

The high-level libblkid API uses /run/blkid/blkid.tab cache to
store probing results. The cache format is

   <device NAME="value" ...>devname</device>

and unfortunately the cache code does not escape quotation marks:

   # mkfs.ext4 -L 'AAA"BBB'

   # cat /run/blkid/blkid.tab
   ...
   <device ... LABEL="AAA"BBB" ...>/dev/sdb1</device>

such string is later incorrectly parsed and blkid(8) returns
nonsenses. And for use-cases like

   # eval $(blkid -o export /dev/sdb1)

it's also insecure.

Note that mount, udevd and blkid -p are based on low-level libblkid
API, it bypass the cache and directly read data from the devices.

The current udevd upstream does not depend on blkid(8) output at all,
it's directly linked with the library and all unsafe chars are encoded by
\x<hex> notation.

   # mkfs.ext4 -L 'X"`/tmp/foo` "' /dev/sdb1
   # udevadm info --export-db | grep LABEL
   ...
   E: ID_FS_LABEL=X__/tmp/foo___
   E: ID_FS_LABEL_ENC=X\x22\x60\x2ftmp\x2ffoo\x60\x20\x22

Signed-off-by: Karel Zak <kzak@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tsafe_print(value, valsz, NULL);', '\t\tsafe_print(value, valsz, "\\"");'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tsafe_print(value, valsz, " \\\\\\"\'$`<>");', '\t\tsafe_print(value, valsz, "\\"\\\\");']}
description: Blkid in util-linux before 2.26rc-1 allows local users to execute arbitrary code.

code_evidence: In the export-list branch, value is written with safe_print(value, valsz, NULL), so no characters are escaped before being emitted to stdout as NAME=value.
In the default branch, value is wrapped in double quotes but safe_print only escapes '"'; backslash, backtick, $, and other shell metacharacters pass through unchanged.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function constructs output that is later consumed as a shell command string via eval, and it fails to neutralize special elements (backticks, $, quotes) that modify that command. This is command injection through a non-OS command-language boundary, matching CWE-77 rather than a plain output-encoding bug.

evidence_lines.code: safe_print(value, valsz, NULL);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: print_value emits externally supplied device metadata (e.g. a filesystem LABEL) into blkid output without neutralizing shell metacharacters. Trigger: an attacker sets a label containing characters such as $, `, or \ and a consumer runs eval $(blkid -o export ...). The unescaped value is interpreted by the shell, allowing command execution.

commit_msg:
libxl: restore passing "readonly=" to qemu for SCSI disks

A read-only check was introduced for XSA-142, commit ef6cb76026 ("libxl:
relax readonly check introduced by XSA-142 fix") added the passing of
the extra setting, but commit dab0539568 ("Introduce COLO mode and
refactor relevant function") dropped the passing of the setting again,
quite likely due to improper re-basing.

Restore the readonly= parameter to SCSI disks.  For IDE disks this is
supposed to be rejected; add an assert.  And there is a bare ad-hoc
disk drive string in libxl__build_device_model_args_new, which we also
update.

This is XSA-266.

Reported-by: Andrew Reimers <andrew.reimers@orionvm.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Signed-off-by: Ian Jackson <Ian.Jackson@eu.citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    assert(disk->readwrite); /* should have been checked earlier */']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen 4.7 through 4.10.x. libxl fails to pass the readonly flag to qemu when setting up a SCSI disk, due to what was probably an erroneous merge conflict resolution. Malicious guest administrators or (in some situations) users may be able to write to supposedly read-only disk images. Only emulated SCSI disks (specified as "sd" in the libxl disk configuration, or an equivalent) are affected. IDE disks ("hd") are not affected (because attempts to make them readonly are rejected). Additionally, CDROM devices (that is, devices specified to be presented to the guest as CDROMs, regardless of the nature of the backing storage on the host) are not affected; they are always read only. Only systems using qemu-xen (rather than qemu-xen-traditional) as the device model version are vulnerable. Only systems using libxl or libxl-based toolstacks are vulnerable. (This includes xl, and libvirt with the libxl driver.) The vulnerability is present in Xen versions 4.7 and later. (In earlier versions, provided that the patch for XSA-142 has been applied, attempts to create read only disks are rejected.) If the host and guest together usually support PVHVM, the issue is exploitable only if the malicious guest administrator has control of the guest kernel or guest kernel command line.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only builds qemu IDE drive strings and adds an assertion; it contains no handling of read-only/SCSI flags or any information exposure, so it does not support CWE-200.

commit_msg: https://github.com/ImageMagick/ImageMagick/issues/110
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (quantum != (extent/image->columns))'], 'added_lines': ['  if ((image->columns != 0) && (quantum != (extent/image->columns)))']}
description: The quantum handling code in ImageMagick allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (divide-by-zero error or out-of-bounds write) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: extent is computed as image->columns*quantum, then the overflow sanity check divides extent by image->columns. image->columns is not validated before this division; the patch adds an (image->columns != 0) guard, confirming the pre-fix division could have a zero divisor.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Line 28 directly performs extent/image->columns with no zero check, matching CWE-369's division by zero. The added guard in the diff corroborates this. It is not integer overflow (CWE-190), which is what the check itself guards against; here the missing constraint is the zero divisor.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the overflow check at line 28 divides by image->columns without confirming it is nonzero. Trigger: a crafted file yielding an image with columns == 0 reaches this function. Consequence: divide-by-zero, crashing the process (denial of service) before AcquireQuantumPixels runs.

commit_msg:
Fix invalid free() with oneof (#647)

Nanopb would call free() or realloc() on an invalid
(attacker controlled) pointer value when all the following
conditions are true:

- PB_ENABLE_MALLOC is defined at the compile time
- Message definition contains an oneof field, and the oneof
  contains at least one pointer type field and at least one
  non-pointer type field.
- Data being decoded first contains a non-pointer value for
  the oneof field, and later contains an overwriting pointer
  value.

Depending on message layout, the bug may not be exploitable in all
cases, but it is known to be exploitable at least with string and
bytes fields. Actual security impact will also depend on the heap
implementation used.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (PB_ATYPE(field->type) == PB_ATYPE_POINTER)', '    {', '        /* Initialize the pointer to NULL to make sure it is valid', '         * even in case of error return. */', '        *(void**)field->pField = NULL;', '        field->pData = NULL;', '    }', '']}
description: Nanopb is a small code-size Protocol Buffers implementation in ansi C. In Nanopb before versions 0.3.9.8 and 0.4.5, decoding a specifically formed message can cause invalid `free()` or `realloc()` calls if the message type contains an `oneof` field, and the `oneof` directly contains both a pointer field and a non-pointer field. If the message data first contains the non-pointer field and then the pointer field, the data of the non-pointer field is incorrectly treated as if it was a pointer value. Such message data rarely occurs in normal messages, but it is a concern when untrusted data is parsed. This has been fixed in versions 0.3.9.8 and 0.4.5. See referenced GitHub Security Advisory for more information including workarounds.

code_evidence: pb_release_union_field copies the current iterator into old_field, reads old_tag from *field->pSize, and on a tag change locates the previously active oneof member in old_field and calls pb_release_single_field(&old_field) at line 12. The function does not reset the pointer member's storage after release; the diff adds nulling only for PB_ATYPE_POINTER members, so before the fix a stale non-pointer value in the union storage could be treated as a pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-763 covers releasing an invalid pointer. Here the release routine is invoked on a union slot whose pointer-typed interpretation was never valid, matching the target weakness rather than a general memory leak or double free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: When a oneof first holds a non-pointer member and a later message overwrites it with a pointer member, the union storage contains attacker-controlled data that pb_release_single_field interprets as a pointer and passes to free()/realloc(), causing an invalid release. Trigger: decoding untrusted oneof data under PB_ENABLE_MALLOC; consequence: invalid free/realloc with possible memory corruption or crash.

commit_msg:
nbd: convert to use qio_channel_yield

In the client, read the reply headers from a coroutine, switching the
read side between the "read header" coroutine and the I/O coroutine that
reads the body of the reply.

In the server, if the server can read more requests it will create a new
"read request" coroutine as soon as a request has been read.  Otherwise,
the new coroutine is created in nbd_request_put.

Reviewed-by: Stefan Hajnoczi <stefanha@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Fam Zheng <famz@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Daniel P. Berrange <berrange@redhat.com>
Message-id: 20170213135235.12274-8-pbonzini@redhat.com
Signed-off-by: Stefan Hajnoczi <stefanha@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static void nbd_trip(void *opaque)', '    NBDRequest request;'], 'added_lines': ['static coroutine_fn void nbd_trip(void *opaque)', '    NBDRequest request = { 0 };    /* GCC thinks it can be used uninitialized */', '        nbd_client_put(client);', '    nbd_client_put(client);', '    nbd_client_put(client);']}
description: An assertion-failure flaw was found in Qemu before 2.10.1, in the Network Block Device (NBD) server's initial connection negotiation, where the I/O coroutine was undefined. This could crash the qemu-nbd server if a client sent unexpected data during connection negotiation. A remote user or process could use this flaw to crash the qemu-nbd server resulting in denial of service.

code_evidence: The NBD_CMD_DISC request type is handled by calling abort(), which terminates the process unconditionally when a client sends a disconnect request to this coroutine.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-617 fits because abort() is a reachable assertion-like termination primitive triggered by attacker-controlled request type, causing process exit more severe than necessary. It is not merely an unhandled input error; the code explicitly aborts on a valid client command.

evidence_lines.code:
case NBD_CMD_DISC:
abort();

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the request dispatch switch treats NBD_CMD_DISC by calling abort() instead of returning or closing the connection gracefully. Trigger: a remote NBD client sends a request with type NBD_CMD_DISC during negotiation/trip handling, reaching this case. Consequence: the qemu-nbd server process exits, dropping all connections (denial of service).

commit_msg: fix #342
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    AP4_Result result = data.SetDataSize(size);'], 'added_lines': ["    // check if there's enough data in the stream", '    AP4_LargeSize stream_size = 0;', '    AP4_Result result = m_DataStream->GetSize(stream_size);', '    if (AP4_SUCCEEDED(result)) {', '        if (size + offset > stream_size) {', '            return AP4_ERROR_OUT_OF_RANGE;', '        }', '    }', '    ', '    result = data.SetDataSize(size);']}
description: An issue was discovered in Bento4 1.5.1-627. AP4_Sample::ReadData in Core/Ap4Sample.cpp allows attackers to trigger an attempted excessive memory allocation, related to AP4_DataBuffer::SetDataSize and AP4_DataBuffer::ReallocateBuffer in Core/Ap4DataBuffer.cpp.

code_evidence: The function bounds the requested read only by the sample's own m_Size (line 6); it then passes the caller-supplied size directly to data.SetDataSize(size) (line 7), which resizes the destination buffer. No upper limit or stream-size check is applied before this allocation, so an attacker-controlled size reaches the buffer allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-770 fits because the function allocates a reusable resource (the data buffer) sized by an external actor's value without any intended size restriction. It is not a fixed-length overflow (CWE-121/122), since the weakness is the unbounded allocation size rather than a write past a fixed buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the size parameter is trusted for buffer allocation with only an m_Size comparison and no absolute cap or stream-length validation. Trigger: a crafted sample/container supplies a large size that satisfies m_Size >= size+offset. Consequence: AP4_DataBuffer::SetDataSize attempts an excessive memory allocation, enabling memory-exhaustion denial of service.

commit_msg:
When hdev->tx_sch_mode is HCLGE_FLAG_VNET_BASE_SCH_MODE, the
hclge_tm_schd_mode_vnet_base_cfg calls hclge_tm_pri_schd_mode_cfg
with vport->vport_id as pri_id, which is used as index for
hdev->tm_info.tc_info, it will cause out of bound access issue
if vport_id is equal to or larger than HNAE3_MAX_TC.

Also hardware only support maximum speed of HCLGE_ETHER_MAX_RATE.

So this patch adds two checks for above cases.

Fixes: 848440544b41 ("net: hns3: Add support of TX Scheduler & Shaper to HNS3 driver")

Signed-off-by: Peng Li <lipeng321@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: Huazhong Tan <tanhuazhong@huawei.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\tif (vport->vport_id >= HNAE3_MAX_TC)', '\t\treturn -EINVAL;']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.2.3. An out of bounds access exists in the function hclge_tm_schd_mode_vnet_base_cfg in the file drivers/net/ethernet/hisilicon/hns3/hns3pf/hclge_tm.c.

code_evidence: Line 4 obtains hdev from vport->back; line 7 passes vport->vport_id unvalidated as pri_id into hclge_tm_pri_schd_mode_cfg.
The loop at line 10 iterates i < kinfo->num_tc and line 11 indexes hdev->tm_info.tc_info[i] without bounding i against the array size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked index used to read hdev->tm_info.tc_info is a direct out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), not a write; the missing bound check on vport_id/num_tc is the root cause, and the read past the array is the consequence.

evidence_lines.code:
struct hclge_dev *hdev = vport->back;
ret = hclge_tm_pri_schd_mode_cfg(hdev, vport->vport_id);

for (i = 0; i < kinfo->num_tc; i++) {
u8 sch_mode = hdev->tm_info.tc_info[i].tc_sch_mode;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: vport_id is used as an index into hdev->tm_info.tc_info inside hclge_tm_pri_schd_mode_cfg without checking it is below HNAE3_MAX_TC; similarly num_tc drives a read of tc_info[i]. commit_msg:
Use a separate journal transaction if it turns out that we need to
convert an inline file to use an data block.  Otherwise we could end
up failing due to not having journal credits.

This addresses CVE-2018-10883.

https://bugzilla.kernel.org/show_bug.cgi?id=200071

Signed-off-by: Theodore Ts'o <tytso@mit.edu>
Cc: stable@kernel.org
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\text4_journal_stop(handle);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\text4_journal_stop(handle);']}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel's ext4 filesystem. A local user can cause an out-of-bounds write in jbd2_journal_dirty_metadata(), a denial of service, and a system crash by mounting and operating on a crafted ext4 filesystem image.

code_evidence: At line 17 a journal handle is started with only 1 credit. Line 30 checks ret == -ENOSPC and calls ext4_da_convert_inline_data_to_extent (lines 31-34) while the same handle is still active; ext4_journal_stop is only reached at line 35 after the conversion. The conversion can require additional journal credits that this handle does not reserve.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The target CWE-787 fits because the insufficient-credit condition propagates into jbd2_journal_dirty_metadata, which writes past the intended buffer bounds. This is a direct out-of-bounds write rather than merely a resource-exhaustion or NULL-dereference issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the inline-to-extent conversion runs within a transaction started with insufficient journal credits, so the conversion's metadata updates can exceed the reserved credit budget. Trigger: writing to an inline file whose data must be converted to an extent block while ret == -ENOSPC. Consequence: journal/block metadata accounting is corrupted, enabling an out-of-bounds write in jbd2_journal_dirty_metadata, leading to crash or memory corruption.

commit_msg: Implement push and pop in copying
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  struct Copier : public Visitor<Copier, Expression*> {', '      return Visitor<Copier, Expression*>::visit(curr);'], 'added_lines': ['  struct Copier : public OverriddenVisitor<Copier, Expression*> {', '      return OverriddenVisitor<Copier, Expression*>::visit(curr);', '    Expression* visitPush(Push* curr) {', '      return builder.makePush(curr->value);', '    }', '    Expression* visitPop(Pop* curr) {', '      return builder.makePop(curr->type);', '    }']}
description: An issue was discovered in Binaryen 1.38.32. Two visitors in ir/ExpressionManipulator.cpp can lead to a NULL pointer dereference in wasm::LocalSet::finalize in wasm/wasm.cpp. A crafted input can cause segmentation faults, leading to denial-of-service, as demonstrated by wasm2js.

code_evidence: copy() guards a NULL curr at lines 10-12 but otherwise dispatches through Visitor<Copier, Expression*>::visit(curr) at line 17; the diff replaces this base with OverriddenVisitor, so dispatch depends on a visit method being defined for the node kind.

visitLocalSet at lines 64-69 builds a LocalSet/LocalTee via builder.makeLocalSet(curr->index, copy(curr->value)); if copy returns nullptr for a malformed value, the builder stores a NULL value expression that later finalization dereferences.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The described behavior is a null pointer that is created and then dereferenced during finalization, matching CWE-476's null dereference for availability impact. It is not CWE-690 (unchecked return value) because the flaw is the missing null check before dereference, not merely an ignored status.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The copier does not guarantee that every expression kind has a dispatch handler; an unhandled or malformed input node can yield a null result from copy(), which is passed into builder.makeLocalSet as the value. Later finalize in wasm::LocalSet::finalize dereferences that null value, causing a segmentation fault and denial-of-service.

commit_msg:
Have a common routine for converting dates and times to strings.

Have a routine that takes a buffer, a strftime format, and a struct tm *
as arguments, and:

* checks whether the struct tm * is null and, if so, returns a string
indicating that the date and time couldn't be converted;

* otherwise, passes it to strftime(), along with the buffer and the
format argument and, if strftime() returns 0, meaning the string didn't
fit into the buffer and thus that the buffer's contents are undefined,
returns a string indicating that the date and time didn't fit into the
buffer;

* otherwise, returns a pointer to the buffer.

Call that routine instead of directly calling strftime() in printers;
that prevents printing a buffer with undefined data if the buffer isn't
big enough for the string.

Also, when generating file names using an strftime format, check the
return value of strftime() to make sure the buffer didn't overflow.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t    struct tm *lt;', '\t    char buffer[sizeof("Www Mmm dd hh:mm:ss yyyyy\\n")];', '\t\tlt = localtime(&t);', '\t\tif (lt != NULL) {', '\t\t    strftime(buffer, sizeof(buffer), "%a %b %e %T %Y%n", lt);', '\t\t    tstring = buffer;', '\t\t}', '\t\telse', '\t\t    tstring = "(Can\'t convert time)\\n";', '\t\ttstring = "NULL\\n";', '\t    ND_PRINT("%s", tstring);'], 'added_lines': ['\t    char buffer[sizeof("Www Mmm dd hh:mm:ss yyyyy")];', '\t\t    tstring = nd_format_time(buffer, sizeof(buffer), "%a %b %e %T %Y",', '\t\t    localtime(&t));', '\t\ttstring = "NULL";', '\t    ND_PRINT("%s\\n", tstring);']}
description: The SMB protocol decoder in tcpdump version 4.99.3 can perform an out-of-bounds write when decoding a crafted network packet.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the unchecked strftime can write past the fixed-size stack buffer when the formatted string exceeds sizeof(buffer); the missing return-value check removes the constraint preventing the overflow. commit_msg:
io_uring/msg_ring: check file type before putting

If we're invoked with a fixed file, follow the normal rules of not
calling io_fput_file(). Fixed files are permanently registered to the
ring, and do not need putting separately.

Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Fixes: aa184e8671f0 ("io_uring: don't attempt to IOPOLL for MSG_RING requests")
Signed-off-by: Jens Axboe <axboe@kernel.dk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tio_put_file(req->file);'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!(req->flags & REQ_F_FIXED_FILE))', '\t\tio_put_file(req->file);']}
description:
Use After Free vulnerability in Linux Kernel allows Privilege Escalation. An improper Update of Reference Count in io_uring leads to Use-After-Free and Local Privilege Escalation.
When io_msg_ring was invoked with a fixed file, it called io_fput_file() which improperly decreased its reference count (leading to Use-After-Free and Local Privilege Escalation). Fixed files are permanently registered to the ring, and should not be put separately.

We recommend upgrading past commit  https://github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/fc7222c3a9f56271fba02aabbfbae999042f1679 https://github.com/torvalds/linux/commit/fc7222c3a9f56271fba02aabbfbae999042f1679

code_evidence: The done path runs for every command outcome and unconditionally calls io_put_file(req->file) at line 23 before clearing req->file at line 24, with no check of REQ_F_FIXED_FILE. For a fixed-file request, req->file is a permanently registered file that must not be put here, so the reference count is decremented incorrectly and the file may be freed while the ring still references it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the improper reference-count update frees memory (the file object) that remains reachable through the ring's fixed-file table, and subsequent use of that dangling reference is a use-after-free; a mere refcount bug alone would not suffice without the later reuse of freed memory.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the unconditional io_put_file on the shared done path drops a reference that the caller does not own when the request uses a fixed file. Trigger: invoking io_msg_ring with a fixed file, reaching line 23. Consequence: premature release of the registered file can lead to use-after-free when later requests access it, enabling privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
list-objects: pass full pathname to callbacks

When we find a blob at "a/b/c", we currently pass this to
our show_object_fn callbacks as two components: "a/b/" and
"c". Callbacks which want the full value then call
path_name(), which concatenates the two. But this is an
inefficient interface; the path is a strbuf, and we could
simply append "c" to it temporarily, then roll back the
length, without creating a new copy.

So we could improve this by teaching the callsites of
path_name() this trick (and there are only 3). But we can
also notice that no callback actually cares about the
broken-down representation, and simply pass each callback
the full path "a/b/c" as a string. The callback code becomes
even simpler, then, as we do not have to worry about freeing
an allocated buffer, nor rolling back our modification to
the strbuf.

This is theoretically less efficient, as some callbacks
would not bother to format the final path component. But in
practice this is not measurable. Since we use the same
strbuf over and over, our work to grow it is amortized, and
we really only pay to memcpy a few bytes.

Signed-off-by: Jeff King <peff@peff.net>
Signed-off-by: Junio C Hamano <gitster@pobox.com>

commit_msg:
Use req::strndup in php_mb_parse_encoding_list to prevent oob memory write.

Summary:
Fix out of bounds write access in mb_detect_encoding.  Using strndup in
php_mb_parse_encoding_list will cause strings with embedded nulls to be
unexpectedly shortened.  The expected length of the string is tracked in
value_length but since strndup may copy fewer characters when there are
mbedded null this can lead to oob writes into tmpstr.

I've found a couple other places in this file that use strndup and replaced
them with req::strndup as well.  The use of strndup in mb_send_mail also seemed
to be a leak.

This replaces uses of strndup with req::strndup which can handle embedded
nulls properly.

It looks like I also accidentally fixed t11337047 at the same time.  Adding it to the list of tasks.

Reviewed By: paulbiss

Differential Revision: D3360065

endp is computed as tmpstr + value_length, so it can point past the allocation when tmpstr was truncated by an embedded null; the comma scan and the null-terminator write at *p = '\0' (p reaching endp) then write beyond the allocated buffer.
free(tmpstr) frees the buffer whose tracked length exceeds its real size, consistent with the truncated copy.

commit_msg:
posix-timers: Sanitize overrun handling

The posix timer overrun handling is broken because the forwarding functions
can return a huge number of overruns which does not fit in an int. As a
consequence timer_getoverrun(2) and siginfo::si_overrun can turn into
random number generators.

The k_clock::timer_forward() callbacks return a 64 bit value now. Make
k_itimer::ti_overrun[_last] 64bit as well, so the kernel internal
accounting is correct. 3Remove the temporary (int) casts.

Add a helper function which clamps the overrun value returned to user space
via timer_getoverrun(2) or siginfo::si_overrun limited to a positive value
between 0 and INT_MAX. INT_MAX is an indicator for user space that the
overrun value has been clamped.

Reported-by: Team OWL337 <icytxw@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
Acked-by: John Stultz <john.stultz@linaro.org>
Cc: Peter Zijlstra <peterz@infradead.org>
Cc: Michael Kerrisk <mtk.manpages@gmail.com>
Link: https://lkml.kernel.org/r/20180626132705.018623573@linutronix.de
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\ttimr->it_overrun = -1;', '\t\tinfo->si_overrun += timr->it_overrun_last;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\ttimr->it_overrun = -1LL;', '\t\tinfo->si_overrun = timer_overrun_to_int(timr, info->si_overrun);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel through 4.17.3. An Integer Overflow in kernel/time/posix-timers.c in the POSIX timer code is caused by the way the overrun accounting works. Depending on interval and expiry time values, the overrun can be larger than INT_MAX, but the accounting is int based. This basically makes the accounting values, which are visible to user space via timer_getoverrun(2) and siginfo::si_overrun, random. For example, a local user can cause a denial of service (signed integer overflow) via crafted mmap, futex, timer_create, and timer_settime system calls.

code_evidence: Line 11 copies the accumulated 64-bit overrun into it_overrun_last; line 14 then adds that value into info->si_overrun, which is a 32-bit int field exposed to userspace via siginfo. No clamp or range check exists before the addition, so a large it_overrun_last (overruns can exceed INT_MAX depending on interval/expiry) causes a signed integer overflow in si_overrun.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the defect is an arithmetic operation (si_overrun += it_overrun_last) that can exceed the int representation and wrap. It is not merely an information leak; the unchecked accumulation into a narrower signed type is the overflow cause, which the patch fixes by clamping via timer_overrun_to_int().
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the kernel accumulates overruns in a wider type but folds them into a 32-bit si_overrun with an unchecked add. Trigger: a timer configured with intervals/expiry such that accumulated overruns exceed INT_MAX. Consequence: si_overrun wraps to a negative or small value, making timer overrun accounting visible to userspace random/unreliable, supporting the reported DoS and integrity effects.

commit_msg:
Don't treat the packet length as unsigned.

The scanf family of functions are as annoyingly bad at handling unsigned
numbers as strtoul() is - both of them are perfectly willing to accept a
value beginning with a negative sign as an unsigned value.  When using
strtoul(), you can compensate for this by explicitly checking for a '-'
as the first character of the string, but you can't do that with
sscanf().

So revert to having pkt_len be signed, and scanning it with %d, but
check for a negative value and fail if we see a negative value.

Bug: 12396
Change-Id: I54fe8f61f42c32b5ef33da633ece51bbcda8c95f
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/15220
Reviewed-by: Guy Harris <guy@alum.mit.edu>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tguint\t\tpkt_len;', '\tguint\t\toffset = 0;', '\tif (sscanf(line, "%9d.%9d: %15[a-z0-9/:.-](%1[io]) len=%9u:%12s->%12s/",'], 'added_lines': ['\tint\t\tpkt_len;', '\tint\t\toffset = 0;', '\tif (sscanf(line, "%9d.%9d: %15[a-z0-9/:.-](%1[io]) len=%9d:%12s->%12s/",', '\t}', '\tif (pkt_len < 0) {', '\t\t*err = WTAP_ERR_BAD_FILE;', '\t\t*err_info = g_strdup("netscreen: packet header has a negative packet length");', '\t\treturn FALSE;']}
description: wiretap/netscreen.c in the NetScreen file parser in Wireshark 1.12.x before 1.12.12 and 2.x before 2.0.4 mishandles sscanf unsigned-integer processing, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) via a crafted file.

code_evidence: pkt_len is declared as guint and populated via sscanf with the %9u conversion, so a negative length field in the file header is silently interpreted as a large unsigned value.

The only guard is pkt_len > WTAP_MAX_PACKET_SIZE; the value is then assigned to phdr->len and passed to ws_buffer_assure_space(buf, pkt_len), driving buffer sizing and the later offset > pkt_len comparison.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to validate that a file-supplied length is non-negative before using it, which is exactly improper input validation of a numeric metadata property. The fix adds a signed parse and an explicit pkt_len < 0 check, confirming the missing constraint rather than a separate weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser accepts an attacker-controlled packet-length field without rejecting negative values, because the unsigned conversion and unsigned storage hide the sign. Trigger: a crafted NetScreen capture whose header length begins with a minus sign. Consequence: the length becomes a huge unsigned quantity used for buffer allocation and length checks, leading to a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Fix buffer overflows in TGA and troff exports (addresses #53, #54)

These were all caused by sprintf() appending a null char that was not actually used.
Fixes CVE-2021-30498 and CVE-2021-30499.

code_evidence: The output buffer is allocated with a fixed estimate *bytes = 1000 + height*(10 + width*(48+36+10+17)) and cur = data = malloc(*bytes); the estimate does not account for the extra NUL byte sprintf appends per conversion.

Line 164 appends a single character via sprintf(cur, "%c", ...), which writes 2 bytes (character plus terminating NUL) while only 1 byte of content is intended, so cur advances by 2 and the trailing NUL overwrites the next position.
The many sprintf-based appends accumulate; the final realloc at lines 201-204 uses the already-overrun cur-data size, so the heap write past the allocated region occurs before any size correction.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes data beyond the end of the allocated heap buffer because the allocation estimate omits sprintf's null terminators, which is exactly an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). It is not merely an integer overflow in size computation; the write itself crosses the buffer boundary.

*bytes = 1000 + cv->height * (10 + cv->width * (48 + 36 + 10 + 17));
cur = data = malloc(*bytes);

else if(linechar[x + i] < 0x00000080)
cur += sprintf(cur, "%c", (uint8_t)linechar[x + i]);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the buffer size estimate assumes each appended field consumes exactly its printed length, but sprintf always adds a terminating NUL that is not counted, and line 164's "%c" conversion appends an unused NUL. Trigger: exporting a canvas whose content makes the accumulated output reach the estimated allocation boundary. Consequence: a heap out-of-bounds write past the malloc'd buffer, risking memory corruption and crash.

tunnels: Don't apply GRO to multiple layers of encapsulation.

When drivers express support for TSO of encapsulated packets, they
only mean that they can do it for one layer of encapsulation.
Supporting additional levels would mean updating, at a minimum,
more IP length fields and they are unaware of this.

No encapsulation device expresses support for handling offloaded
encapsulated packets, so we won't generate these types of frames
in the transmit path. However, GRO doesn't have a check for
multiple levels of encapsulation and will attempt to build them.

UDP tunnel GRO actually does prevent this situation but it only
handles multiple UDP tunnels stacked on top of each other. This
generalizes that solution to prevent any kind of tunnel stacking
that would cause problems.

Fixes: bf5a755f ("net-gre-gro: Add GRE support to the GRO stack")
Signed-off-by: Jesse Gross <jesse@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tNAPI_GRO_CB(skb)->udp_mark = 0;'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tNAPI_GRO_CB(skb)->encap_mark = 0;']}
description: The IP stack in the Linux kernel before 4.6 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (stack consumption and panic) or possibly have unspecified other impact by triggering use of the GRO path for packets with tunnel stacking, as demonstrated by interleaved IPv4 headers and GRE headers, a related issue to CVE-2016-7039.

code_evidence: The GRO receive loop dispatches each packet to ptype->callbacks.gro_receive after resetting only per-packet state; the reset at line 24 initializes the old udp_mark field, not a general encapsulation-depth marker, so no limit on stacked tunnel layers is enforced before dispatch.
ptype->callbacks.gro_receive (line 40) is called unconditionally for any matching offload type, allowing nested IPv4/GRE headers to be processed recursively by GRO handlers.

When same_flow is false, the code appends the skb to napi->gro_list and increments napi->gro_count, evicting the oldest only when gro_count reaches MAX_GRO_SKBS; stacked tunnel packets keep being held and merged without bounding encapsulation depth.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to throttle or bound a limited processing resource (encapsulation depth/stack) when accepting remote packets, which matches CWE-400's uncontrolled resource consumption. It is not merely an out-of-bounds or parsing bug; the missing depth constraint is the actual weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: dev_gro_receive lacks any check on the number of encapsulation layers before handing a packet to gro_receive, and the per-packet mark reset only covers UDP tunneling. Trigger: remote packets with interleaved IPv4 and GRE headers traverse this path, causing GRO to stack frames. Consequence: unbounded stack consumption/recursion leading to kernel panic or resource exhaustion (DoS).

commit_msg:
Bug 699668: handle stack overflow during error handling

When handling a Postscript error, we push the object throwing the error onto
the operand stack for the error handling procedure to access - we were not
checking the available stack before doing so, thus causing a crash.

Basically, if we get a stack overflow when already handling an error, we're out
of options, return to the caller with a fatal error.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        *++osp = *perror_object;'], 'added_lines': ['        osp++;', '        if (osp >= ostop) {', '            *pexit_code = gs_error_Fatal;', '            return_error(gs_error_Fatal);', '        }', '        *osp = *perror_object;']}
description: In Artifex Ghostscript before 9.24, attackers able to supply crafted PostScript files could use insufficient interpreter stack-size checking during error handling to crash the interpreter.

code_evidence: Inside the non-interrupt error path, the code performs *++osp = *perror_object; incrementing the operand-stack pointer and writing without first verifying that osp is below ostop, so the write can land at or beyond the stack limit.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsafe pre-increment store writes one element beyond the intended operand-stack buffer, which is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The later patch adds the osp >= ostop check before writing, confirming the missing constraint; this is distinct from a mere read overflow or stack exhaustion.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing bounds check before pushing the error object onto the operand stack during error handling. Trigger: a crafted PostScript file causes an error while the operand stack is already full, so the pre-increment push writes past the stack end. Supported consequence: memory corruption/crash of the interpreter, consistent with the commit's stack-overflow crash.

commit_msg:
nfc: replace improper check device_is_registered() in netlink related functions

The device_is_registered() in nfc core is used to check whether
nfc device is registered in netlink related functions such as
nfc_fw_download(), nfc_dev_up() and so on. Although device_is_registered()
is protected by device_lock, there is still a race condition between
device_del() and device_is_registered(). The root cause is that
kobject_del() in device_del() is not protected by device_lock.

   (cleanup task)         |     (netlink task)
                          |
nfc_unregister_device     | nfc_fw_download
 device_del               |  device_lock
  ...                     |   if (!device_is_registered)//(1)
  kobject_del//(2)        |   ...
 ...                      |  device_unlock

The device_is_registered() returns the value of state_in_sysfs and
the state_in_sysfs is set to zero in kobject_del(). If we pass check in
position (1), then set zero in position (2). As a result, the check
in position (1) is useless.

This patch uses bool variable instead of device_is_registered() to judge
whether the nfc device is registered, which is well synchronized.

Fixes: 3e256b8f8dfa ("NFC: add nfc subsystem core")
Signed-off-by: Duoming Zhou <duoming@zju.edu.cn>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!device_is_registered(&dev->dev)) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (dev->shutting_down) {']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in the Linux kernel's NFC core functionality due to a race condition between kobject creation and delete. This vulnerability allows a local attacker with CAP_NET_ADMIN privilege to leak kernel information.

code_evidence: The function acquires device_lock, then calls device_is_registered(&dev->dev) to decide whether the device is still registered and bails out with -ENODEV. The registration state read by this check is not protected by device_lock against device_del(), whose kobject_del() clears state_in_sysfs outside that lock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-367 fits because the code checks a resource state (device_is_registered) before using the device, and that state can change between check and use due to a concurrent unregister path. This is a check-then-act race rather than a simple missing lock, since the check itself executes but its result becomes invalid.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the registration-state check is made under device_lock, but the state transition performed by kobject_del() in device_del() is not synchronized by the same lock. A concurrent nfc_unregister_device can pass the check and then clear the state, so the validated registration condition is stale when subsequent target deactivation proceeds, yielding a TOCTOU race on a shared device object.

description: GPAC MP4box 2.1-DEV-rev649-ga8f438d20 is vulnerable to buffer overflow in h263dmx_process filters/reframe_h263.c:609

code_evidence: When opid is not yet set, the code subtracts current from ctx->bytes_in_header without checking that current is at most bytes_in_header; a larger start-code offset underflows this unsigned counter.

In the frame-copy branch, current is subtracted from bytes_in_header before memcpy(pck_data, ctx->hdr_store, current); pck_data was allocated with size current, so the copy length is not constrained by the header store size or the subtraction result.

commit_msg:
evtchn/x86: enforce correct upper limit for 32-bit guests

The recording of d->max_evtchns in evtchn_2l_init(), in particular with
the limited set of callers of the function, is insufficient. Neither for
PV nor for HVM guests the bitness is known at domain_create() time, yet
the upper bound in 2-level mode depends upon guest bitness. Recording
too high a limit "allows" x86 32-bit domains to open not properly usable
event channels, management of which (inside Xen) would then result in
corruption of the shared info and vCPU info structures.

Keep the upper limit dynamic for the 2-level case, introducing a helper
function to retrieve the effective limit. This helper is now supposed to
be private to the event channel code. The used in do_poll() and
domain_dump_evtchn_info() weren't consistent with port uses elsewhere
and hence get switched to port_is_valid().

Furthermore FIFO mode's setup_ports() gets adjusted to loop only up to
the prior ABI limit, rather than all the way up to the new one.

Finally a word on the change to do_poll(): Accessing ->max_evtchns
without holding a suitable lock was never safe, as it as well as
->evtchn_port_ops may change behind do_poll()'s back. Using
port_is_valid() instead widens some the window for potential abuse,
until we've dealt with the race altogether (see XSA-343).

This is XSA-342.

Reported-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
Fixes: 48974e6ce52e ("evtchn: use a per-domain variable for the max number of event channels")
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Stefano Stabellini <sstabellini@kernel.org>
Reviewed-by: Julien Grall <jgrall@amazon.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    for ( port = 1; port < d->max_evtchns; ++port )', '        if ( !port_is_valid(d, port) )', '            continue;'], 'added_lines': ['    for ( port = 1; port_is_valid(d, port); ++port )']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.14.x. Out of bounds event channels are available to 32-bit x86 domains. The so called 2-level event channel model imposes different limits on the number of usable event channels for 32-bit x86 domains vs 64-bit or Arm (either bitness) ones. 32-bit x86 domains can use only 1023 channels, due to limited space in their shared (between guest and Xen) information structure, whereas all other domains can use up to 4095 in this model. The recording of the respective limit during domain initialization, however, has occurred at a time where domains are still deemed to be 64-bit ones, prior to actually honoring respective domain properties. At the point domains get recognized as 32-bit ones, the limit didn't get updated accordingly. Due to this misbehavior in Xen, 32-bit domains (including Domain 0) servicing other domains may observe event channel allocations to succeed when they should really fail. Subsequent use of such event channels would then possibly lead to corruption of other parts of the shared info structure. An unprivileged guest may cause another domain, in particular Domain 0, to misbehave. This may lead to a Denial of Service (DoS) for the entire system. All Xen versions from 4.4 onwards are vulnerable. Xen versions 4.3 and earlier are not vulnerable. Only x86 32-bit domains servicing other domains are vulnerable. Arm systems, as well as x86 64-bit domains, are not vulnerable.

code_evidence: The loop iterates port from 1 while port < d->max_evtchns, and only skips invalid ports via the port_is_valid() check inside the body before calling evtchn_from_port(d, port). The loop bound uses the recorded domain-wide max_evtchns rather than the effective per-bitness limit, so for 32-bit guests ports up to the too-high limit are still enumerated and indexed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function indexes event-channel structures using an over-large limit, producing accesses past the intended buffer, matching CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write). It is not merely an incorrect limit check; the enumeration bound enables writes beyond the 2-level shared-info array.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: d->max_evtchns is recorded too high for 32-bit x86 domains, exceeding the 1023-channel shared-info capacity. Trigger: a 32-bit guest causes event channels above the usable limit to exist; the loop then indexes evtchn_from_port() for ports past the 2-level shared-info bounds. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds access/write into the shared info and vCPU info structures, corrupting memory and enabling denial of service.

commit_msg:
list-objects: pass full pathname to callbacks

When we find a blob at "a/b/c", we currently pass this to
our show_object_fn callbacks as two components: "a/b/" and
"c". Callbacks which want the full value then call
path_name(), which concatenates the two. But this is an
inefficient interface; the path is a strbuf, and we could
simply append "c" to it temporarily, then roll back the
length, without creating a new copy.

So we could improve this by teaching the callsites of
path_name() this trick (and there are only 3). But we can
also notice that no callback actually cares about the
broken-down representation, and simply pass each callback
the full path "a/b/c" as a string. The callback code becomes
even simpler, then, as we do not have to worry about freeing
an allocated buffer, nor rolling back our modification to
the strbuf.

This is theoretically less efficient, as some callbacks
would not bother to format the final path component. But in
practice this is not measurable. Since we use the same
strbuf over and over, our work to grow it is amortized, and
we really only pay to memcpy a few bytes.

Signed-off-by: Jeff King <peff@peff.net>
Signed-off-by: Junio C Hamano <gitster@pobox.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tshow_object(obj, NULL, name, data);', '\t\t\t\t     NULL, path, data);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tshow_object(obj, name, data);', '\t\t\t\t     &base, path, data);']}
description: revision.c in git before 2.7.4 uses an incorrect integer data type, which allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code via a (1) long filename or (2) many nested trees, leading to a heap-based buffer overflow.

commit_msg:
gvariant: Don’t allow child elements to overlap with each other

If different elements of a variable sized array can overlap with each
other then we can cause a `GVariant` to normalise to a much larger type.

This commit changes the behaviour of `GVariant` with non-normal form data. If
an invalid frame offset is found all subsequent elements are given their
default value.

When retrieving an element at index `n` we scan the frame offsets up to index
`n` and if they are not in order we return an element with the default value
for that type.  This guarantees that elements don't overlap with each
other.  We remember the offset we've scanned up to so we don't need to
repeat this work on subsequent accesses.  We skip these checks for trusted
data.

Unfortunately this makes random access of untrusted data O(n) — at least
on first access.  It doesn't affect the algorithmic complexity of accessing
elements in order, such as when using the `GVariantIter` interface.  Also:
the cost of validation will be amortised as the `GVariant` instance is
continued to be used.

I've implemented this with 4 different functions, 1 for each element size,
rather than looping calling `gvs_read_unaligned_le` in the hope that the
compiler will find it easy to optimise and should produce fairly tight
code.

Fixes: #2121

description: A flaw was found in GLib. GVariant deserialization is vulnerable to an exponential blowup issue where a crafted GVariant can cause excessive processing, leading to denial of service.

code_evidence: gvs_tuple_is_normal iterates over each tuple member, computing child.data = value.data + offset (line 32) and child.size from the ending type, then recursing via g_variant_serialised_is_normal(child) (line 57). The only bound checks are end < offset and end > offset_ptr (line 52); there is no check that the new offset (end) is >= the previous member's end, so successive child ranges can overlap and offsets may not be monotonically increasing. The comment added in the diff ('All element bounds have been checked above') is therefore not sufficient to guarantee ordered, non-overlapping element frames for untrusted data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-502 fits because the function is the deserialization/normal-form validation path for untrusted serialized GVariant data, and it fails to sufficiently ensure the resulting structure is valid (non-overlapping, ordered frames). The missing ordering constraint is the deserialization-validation deficiency, not merely a generic bounds bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the normal-form validator accepts a serialized tuple whose child element frames overlap because it checks each element's end against offset_ptr but never enforces that end advances past the prior element's end. Trigger: a crafted untrusted GVariant with non-monotonic frame offsets is deserialized. Supported consequence: the tuple is treated as normal, allowing normalization to a much larger type and resource-consumption DoS (per description/commit).

This fixes a buffer over-read discovered by Kamil Frankowicz.

Don't pass the remaining caplen - that's too hard to get right, and we

description: The ISO CLNS parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 has a buffer over-read in print-isoclns.c:isoclns_print().

code_evidence: After the NULL_HDRLEN header is consumed, length and caplen are decremented and p is advanced by NULL_HDRLEN.
The ISO CLNS family branch calls isoclns_print(ndo, p, length, caplen) with the post-header pointer and both remaining lengths.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Passing a mismatched remaining-length value into isoclns_print() enables it to index beyond the intended buffer, matching CWE-125's read-past-end pattern. The defect is a bounds/offset mismatch, not an unbounded write, so out-of-bounds read rather than a write-based CWE applies.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The caller hands the sub-parser a pointer already advanced past the null header together with the remaining caplen. If the sub-parser's internal bounds checks are computed against the wrong length base, it can read past the captured buffer; the commit states the remaining caplen was being passed and got the checks wrong. Trigger: a crafted ISO CLNS packet whose caplen/length relationship exposes the miscalculated check. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds read of capture data.

commit_msg:
Bug 698158: prevent trying to reloc a freed object

In the token reader, we pass the scanner state structure around as a
t_struct ref on the Postscript operand stack.

But we explicitly free the scanner state when we're done, which leaves a
dangling reference on the operand stack and, unless that reference gets
overwritten before the next garbager run, we can end up with the garbager
trying to deal with an already freed object - that can cause a crash, or
memory corruption.
diff_func:
--- func_before
+++ func_after
@@ -5,6 +5,12 @@
     int code;
     ref token;
 
+    /* Since we might free pstate below, and we're dealing with
+     * gc memory referenced by the stack, we need to explicitly
+     * remove the reference to pstate from the stack, otherwise
+     * the garbager will fall over
+     */
+    make_null(osp);
     /* Note that gs_scan_token may change osp! */
     pop(1);                     /* remove the file or scanner state */

commit_msg:
LISP: Don't go past a LCAF payload length

The LISP Canonical Address Format has a payload length indicator.
Use that to create a payload tvb and don't dissect outside the
payload length. With fuzzed and malformed packets, this was causing
the same bytes to be dissected many times, particularly in the
recursive address types.

A LCAF would be dissected outside the payload region, but then
elsewhere the offset was only advanced by the payload length.

Fix #18900
