Trigger: an attacker-supplied URL whose path contains "../" reaches ServeFile. Supported consequence: the resolved path lies outside the intended directory and its contents are read and served, exposing files outside the root.

commit_msg:
Ensure array count consistency in kadm5 RPC

In _xdr_kadm5_principal_ent_rec(), ensure that n_key_data matches the
key_data array count when decoding.  Otherwise when the structure is
later freed, xdr_array() could iterate over the wrong number of
elements, either leaking some memory or freeing uninitialized
pointers.  Reported by Robert Morris.

CVE-2023-36054:

An authenticated attacker can cause a kadmind process to crash by
freeing uninitialized pointers.  Remote code execution is unlikely.
An attacker with control of a kadmin server can cause a kadmin client
to crash by freeing uninitialized pointers.

ticket: 9099 (new)
tags: pullup
target_version: 1.21-next
target_version: 1.20-next
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!xdr_array(xdrs, (caddr_t *) &objp->key_data,', '\t\t       &n, ~0, sizeof(krb5_key_data),', '\t\t       xdr_krb5_key_data_nocontents)) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tbool_t r;', '\tif (xdrs->x_op == XDR_DECODE && objp->n_key_data < 0) {', '\t\treturn (FALSE);', '\t}', '\tr = xdr_array(xdrs, (caddr_t *) &objp->key_data, &n, objp->n_key_data,', '\t\t      sizeof(krb5_key_data), xdr_krb5_key_data_nocontents);', '\tobjp->n_key_data = n;', '\tif (!r) {']}
description: lib/kadm5/kadm_rpc_xdr.c in MIT Kerberos 5 (aka krb5) before 1.20.2 and 1.21.x before 1.21.1 frees an uninitialized pointer. A remote authenticated user can trigger a kadmind crash. This occurs because _xdr_kadm5_principal_ent_rec does not validate the relationship between n_key_data and the key_data array count.

code_evidence: Line 55 decodes attacker-influenced n_key_data via xdr_krb5_int16 without checking it is non-negative; line 65 copies it into unsigned n; lines 66-68 pass &n as the element count to xdr_array with maxsize ~0, so the decoded array length is not tied to the declared n_key_data used later when freeing key_data.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The inconsistent count leads to key_data entries being treated as valid pointers when they were never initialized, and cleanup dereferences/frees them. That is access of an uninitialized pointer (CWE-824), not merely a memory leak.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The declared n_key_data is decoded but not constrained to match the actual number of key_data elements populated by xdr_array, and a negative value is accepted before being copied into unsigned n. The resulting inconsistent count causes later cleanup to iterate over more elements than were initialized, freeing uninitialized pointers and crashing kadmind.

commit_msg:
SOFT: Check the EC Key on C_CreateObject and C_DeriveKey

When constructing an OpenSSL EC public or private key from PKCS#11
attributes or ECDH public data, check that the key is valid, i.e. that
the point is on the curve.

This prevents one from creating an EC key object via C_CreateObject with
invalid key data. It also prevents C_DeriveKey to derive a secret using
ECDH with an EC public key (public data) that uses a different curve
or is invalid by other means.

Signed-off-by: Ingo Franzki <ifranzki@linux.ibm.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (!EC_KEY_check_key(ec_key)) {', '        TRACE_ERROR("EC_KEY_check_key failed\\n");', '        rc = CKR_FUNCTION_FAILED;', '        goto out;', '    }', '']}
description: A flaw was found in openCryptoki. The openCryptoki Soft token does not check if an EC key is valid when an EC key is created via C_CreateObject, nor when C_DeriveKey is used with ECDH public data. This may allow a malicious user to extract the private key by performing an invalid curve attack.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function only constructs an EC key from private-key bytes and lacks the added EC_KEY_check_key validation; it contains no code that exposes sensitive information, and the described invalid-curve attack consequence is a downstream confidentiality impact, not a CWE-200 root cause in this function.

The fuse xlator notify function tries to assign data object
to graph object without checking an event. In case of upcall
event data object represents upcall object so during access
of graph object the process is crashed for asan build.

Solution: Access the graph->id only while event is associated
          specific to fuse xlator

Fixes: #3954
Change-Id: I6b2869256b26d22163879737dcf163510d1cd8bf
Signed-off-by: Mohit Agrawal <moagrawa@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', '    gf_log("fuse", GF_LOG_DEBUG, "got event %d on graph %d", event,', '           ((graph) ? graph->id : 0));'], 'added_lines': ['    gf_boolean_t event_graph = _gf_true;', '            /* Set the event_graph to false so that event', '               debug msg would not try to access invalid graph->id', '               while data object is not matched to graph object', '               for ex in case of upcall event data object represents', '               gf_upcall object', '            */', '            event_graph = _gf_false;', '    gf_log("fuse", GF_LOG_DEBUG, "got event %d on graph %d", event,', '           ((graph && event_graph) ? graph->id : 0));']}
description: In Gluster GlusterFS 11.0, there is an xlators/mount/fuse/src/fuse-bridge.c notify stack-based buffer over-read.

code_evidence: The function unconditionally assigns the generic event payload to a graph pointer (graph = data) and then dereferences graph->id in the debug log without verifying that data actually points to a glusterfs_graph_t. For events whose data is a different object (e.g., a gf_upcall), graph->id reads past the intended object.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Dereferencing graph->id on a pointer that may reference a smaller, unrelated object is an out-of-bounds read, matching CWE-125. It is a read of memory beyond the intended buffer, not a write or use-after-free, so CWE-125 fits the target rather than a write-class weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the code assumes every notify event's data is a graph and dereferences graph->id before the event type is examined. Trigger: a notify event carrying a non-graph data object reaches this log statement. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read of the id field, causing an ASan crash / DoS rather than memory corruption.

commit_msg:
The functions that were used in the emulation of fxrstor, fxsave, sgdt and
sidt were originally meant for task switching, and as such they did not
check privilege levels.  This is very bad when the same functions are used
in the emulation of unprivileged instructions.  This is CVE-2018-10853.

The obvious fix is to add a new argument to ops->read_std and ops->write_std,
which decides whether the access is a "system" access or should use the
processor's CPL.

Fixes: 129a72a0d3c8 ("KVM: x86: Introduce segmented_write_std", 2017-01-12)
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t    kvm_read_guest_virt(&vcpu->arch.emulate_ctxt,', '\t\t\t\tkvm_get_linear_rip(vcpu), sig, sizeof(sig), &e) == 0 &&'], 'added_lines': ['\t    kvm_read_guest_virt(vcpu, kvm_get_linear_rip(vcpu),', '\t\t\t\tsig, sizeof(sig), &e) == 0 &&']}
description: A flaw was found in the way Linux kernel KVM hypervisor before 4.18 emulated instructions such as sgdt/sidt/fxsave/fxrstor. It did not check current privilege(CPL) level while emulating unprivileged instructions. An unprivileged guest user/process could use this flaw to potentially escalate privileges inside guest.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function handle_ud only reads the instruction stream to detect a forced emulation prefix; it contains no privilege-level or CPL check, and the privileged instruction emulation (sgdt/sidt/fxsave/fxrstor) occurs in other functions not shown here.

commit_msg:
f2fs: support swap file w/ DIO

Signed-off-by: Jaegeuk Kim <jaegeuk@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tstruct address_space *mapping = page->mapping;'], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct address_space *mapping = page_file_mapping(page);']}
description: In the Linux kernel 5.0.21, mounting a crafted f2fs filesystem image can cause a NULL pointer dereference in f2fs_recover_fsync_data in fs/f2fs/recovery.c. This is related to F2FS_P_SB in fs/f2fs/f2fs.h.

code_evidence: Line 3 reads page->mapping and stores it in mapping. Line 4 guards with if (mapping), so the local mapping is checked before line 5 dereferences mapping->host. The patch replaces page->mapping with page_file_mapping(page), and the surrounding guard still protects the subsequent dereference of mapping->host and the F2FS_I_SB(inode) path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 requires a pointer dereference without a validity check. Here the dereference of mapping is guarded by if (mapping), so the function does not directly support a NULL pointer dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function only dereferences mapping->host after confirming mapping is non-NULL, so the changed expression is not itself an unchecked NULL dereference. The patch alters how the mapping is obtained (page_file_mapping) rather than removing or bypassing the NULL check; no path in this function dereferences a pointer that the guard fails to cover.

commit_msg:
PR22186, divide-by-zero in decode_line_info

	PR 22186
	* dwarf2.c (decode_line_info): Fail on lh.line_range of zero
	rather than dividing by zero.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t      if (lh.line_range == 0)', '\t\tgoto line_fail;']}
description: decode_line_info in dwarf2.c in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.29, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (divide-by-zero error and application crash) via a crafted ELF file.

code_evidence: Line 124 reads attacker-controlled lh.line_range as a single byte from the crafted .debug_line section; no nonzero check is performed here.
In the DW_LNS_const_add_pc case, lines 347-348 compute (255 - lh.opcode_base) / lh.line_range with no guard, and lines 351-355 divide by lh.line_range again in the multi-op path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs division by the untrusted lh.line_range value, matching CWE-369's divide-by-zero with availability impact. It is not a generic input-validation issue; the specific unsafe operation is division by zero.

evidence_lines.code:
lh.line_range = read_1_byte (abfd, line_ptr, line_end);
line_ptr += 1;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: lh.line_range is read from the ELF DWARF data and used as a divisor without validating it is nonzero. Trigger: a crafted file sets line_range to 0 and includes a DW_LNS_const_add_pc opcode, causing integer division by zero. Supported consequence: crash/denial of service of the consuming application.

description: Stack-based buffer overflow vulnerability in frontend/main.c in faad2 before 2.2.7.1 allow local attackers to execute arbitrary code via filename and pathname options.

code_evidence: Three fixed 255-byte stack buffers aacFileName, audioFileName, adtsFileName are declared for user-controlled paths.
Case 'o' copies the -o optarg into the 255-byte audioFileName stack array via strcpy with no length check.
Case 'a' likewise strcpy's the -a optarg into the fixed adtsFileName stack buffer.
argv[optind] is copied into the fixed 255-byte aacFileName stack array via strcpy, without bounds checking.
When no outfile is set, aacFileName is copied into audioFileName and a file extension is strcat'ed, again unbounded on the fixed buffer.

This is distinct from a mere buffer overflow read or use-after-free; the unsafe strcpy/strcat into undersized fixed arrays directly supports CWE-787.

evidence_lines.code: strcpy(aacFileName, argv[optind]);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: command-line filename/pathname options (optarg and argv[optind]) are copied into fixed 255-byte stack buffers with strcpy/strcat and no length validation. Trigger: supplying an option or file path longer than 255 bytes. Consequence: an out-of-bounds stack write that can corrupt adjacent stack memory, crash the program, or potentially lead to arbitrary code execution.

code_evidence: At line 11 the parameter header is parsed, setting member_length from packet data. Line 13 passes that length to rtps_util_add_type_library, and line 14 advances offset by member_length without checking for overflow.

Line 15 parses another header, again setting member_length from the packet. Line 17 dissects the type id using the current offset, and line 19 adds member_length to offset unchecked before line 20 reads a guint32 at the resulting offset.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function's unsafe offset arithmetic lets crafted lengths cause repeated dissection loops without a sufficient iteration limit, directly supporting CWE-834 Excessive Iteration. The added check_offset_addition guards only the offset sum, not loop counts, so the underlying missing constraint remains.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: attacker-controlled member_length values from the packet are added to offset with no overflow or bounds check. When the sum wraps, offset becomes small or negative, causing the dissector to re-read the same region repeatedly and drive excessive iteration/resource consumption, matching the reported DoS.

commit_msg:
USB HID: Always use a format string.

Ensure that the second argument to wmem_strdup_printf is always a format
string.
Fixes #18384.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            str = "Button %u";', '            str = "Instance %u";', '        str = "Character U+%04X";', '        str = "ENUM_%u";', '    if (!str)', '', '    return wmem_strdup_printf(pool, str, id);'], 'added_lines': ['    const char *fmt_str = NULL;', '            fmt_str = "Button %u";', '            fmt_str = "Instance %u";', '        fmt_str = "Character U+%04X";', '        fmt_str = "ENUM_%u";', '    if (fmt_str) {', '        return wmem_strdup_printf(pool, fmt_str, id);', '    }', '    if (!str) {', '    }', '    return wmem_strdup_printf(pool, "%s", str);']}
description: Crash in the USB HID protocol dissector in Wireshark 3.6.0 to 3.6.8 allows denial of service via packet injection or crafted capture file on Windows

code_evidence: The function stores either a lookup result or a literal format string in the single variable `str`; for BUTTON_PAGE, when the lookup fails, `str` is set to the literal "Button %u".
UNICODE_PAGE unconditionally assigns the format literal "Character U+%04X" to `str`.
USB_ENUMERATED_VALUES_PAGE unconditionally assigns the format literal "ENUM_%u" to `str`.
After the switch, if `str` is still NULL it is replaced with "Reserved", then `str` is passed as the format argument to `wmem_strdup_printf(pool, str, id)` with `id` as the variadic argument.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-134 fits because a function that accepts a format string (wmem_strdup_printf) is called with a variable, `str`, rather than a fixed format literal; the value can be externally influenced through packet data and lookup results. The fix separates constant format literals into `fmt_str` and uses "%s" for plain strings, confirming the missing constraint that the format argument must be a constant.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that the format string passed to wmem_strdup_printf is the variable `str`, which may hold a non-constant value rather than a controlled format literal. When a lookup returns a string containing format specifiers, or when the fallback/literal paths are mixed with attacker-influenced data, the format string is not a fixed constant, allowing the format to be interpreted. The supported consequence is a crash/denial of service (as described) and potentially format-string-driven memory disclosure or corruption depending on the value.

commit_msg: Defensive coding to avoid 0x80000000/0xFFFFFFFF FPE.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        ok_ = (value_.at(n).second != 0 && INT_MIN < value_.at(n).first && value_.at(n).first < INT_MAX );'], 'added_lines': ['        ok_ = (value_.at(n).second > 0 && INT_MIN < value_.at(n).first && value_.at(n).first < INT_MAX );']}
description: Exiv2 is a command-line utility and C++ library for reading, writing, deleting, and modifying the metadata of image files. A floating point exception (FPE) due to an integer divide by zero was found in Exiv2 versions v0.27.4 and earlier. The FPE is triggered when Exiv2 is used to print the metadata of a crafted image file. An attacker could potentially exploit the vulnerability to cause a denial of service, if they can trick the victim into running Exiv2 on a crafted image file. Note that this bug is only triggered when printing the interpreted (translated) data, which is a less frequently used Exiv2 operation that requires an extra command line option (`-p t` or `-P t`). The bug is fixed in version v0.27.5.

code_evidence: Line 3 guards the divisor only with value_.at(n).second != 0 before setting ok_, so a zero denominator makes ok_ false and line 4 returns 0.
Line 5 divides value_.at(n).first by value_.at(n).second; this path is reached only when ok_ is true, i.e. when the denominator was non-zero at the check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code explicitly tests the denominator before dividing and returns early when it is zero, which is the missing-constraint control that CWE-369 describes; the function does not perform an unguarded division by zero. Because the guard is present in this version, the function does not itself demonstrate the weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
ok_ = (value_.at(n).second != 0 && INT_MIN < value_.at(n).first && value_.at(n).first < INT_MAX );
if (!ok_) return 0;
return value_.at(n).first / value_.at(n).second;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the divisor check on line 3 is separated from the division on line 5, and ok_ is the only gate. Trigger: a crafted Rational whose second member is zero is supplied to toLong, making ok_ false and returning 0 at line 4 instead of dividing. The commit message indicates the defensive check was added to avoid FPE from 0x80000000/0xFFFFFFFF, so this function's guard prevents the divide-by-zero rather than causing it.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!ND_TTEST2(cp, len)) {'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (ND_TTEST2(cp, len)) {']}
description: print-wb.c in tcpdump before 4.7.4 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (segmentation fault and process crash).

code_evidence: len is reduced by sizeof(*io)*nid from the packet-supplied nid (line 22), then cp is derived from id+nid (lines 23-24). The guard on line 25 uses !ND_TTEST2(cp,len), so fn_print on line 27 executes only when the bounds check fails, reading len bytes past the validated region.

The inverted check is the concrete validation defect; the out-of-bounds read and crash are consequences.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the packet-derived nid and len are not correctly validated against the capture buffer; the inverted ND_TTEST2 condition treats an out-of-bounds region as safe to print. Trigger: a crafted whiteboard packet with nid/len causing cp beyond the captured data. Consequence: fn_print reads out-of-bounds memory, causing a segmentation fault and process crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
Ensure IMAP connection is closed after a connection error.

During connection, if the server provided an illegal initial response,
Mutt "bailed", but did not actually close the connection.  The calling
code unfortunately relied on the connection status to decide to
continue with authentication, instead of checking the "bail" return
value.

This could result in authentication credentials being sent over an
unencrypted connection, without $ssl_force_tls being consulted.

Fix this by strictly closing the connection on any invalid response
during connection.  The fix is intentionally small, to ease
backporting.  A better fix would include removing the 'err_close_conn'
label, and perhaps adding return value checking in the caller (though
this change obviates the need for that).

This addresses CVE-2020-28896.  Thanks to Gabriel Salles-Loustau for
reporting the problem, and providing test cases to reproduce.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  imap_close_connection (idata);'], 'added_lines': ['  imap_close_connection (idata);']}
description: Mutt before 2.0.2 and NeoMutt before 2020-11-20 did not ensure that $ssl_force_tls was processed if an IMAP server's initial server response was invalid. The connection was not properly closed, and the code could continue attempting to authenticate. This could result in authentication credentials being exposed on an unencrypted connection, or to a machine-in-the-middle.

code_evidence: An illegal initial server response enters the else branch, reports the error, and jumps to bail; in the original code bail did not close the connection.
The err_close_conn label was the only site calling imap_close_connection (idata) before return, and it was guarded by #if defined(USE_SSL); bail only freed capstr and returned -1 without closing.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Proceeding with authentication on an unverified/unencrypted connection means the identity claim is not properly proven before credentials are transmitted, matching CWE-287. The flaw is the missing close on the error path enabling continued authentication, not a cryptographic defect itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the bail path on an invalid initial response returns -1 without closing the socket, leaving the connection open. The caller relied on connection status rather than the return value, so it could proceed to authentication, sending credentials over a connection where STARTTLS/TLS was never negotiated. The supported consequence is credential exposure to a machine-in-the-middle.

commit_msg:
Bug 759398: Heap use-after-free in xmlDictComputeFastKey <https://bugzilla.gnome.org/show_bug.cgi?id=759398>

* parser.c:
(xmlParseNCNameComplex): Store start position instead of a
pointer to the name since the underlying buffer may change,
resulting in a stale pointer being used.
* result/errors/759398.xml: Added.
* result/errors/759398.xml.err: Added.
* result/errors/759398.xml.str: Added.
* test/errors/759398.xml: Added test case.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    const xmlChar *end; /* needed because CUR_CHAR() can move cur on \\r\\n */', '    end = ctxt->input->cur;', '\tend = ctxt->input->cur;', '\t    end = ctxt->input->cur;', '    return(xmlDictLookup(ctxt->dict, end - len, len));'], 'added_lines': ['    size_t startPosition = 0;', '    startPosition = CUR_PTR - BASE_PTR;', '    return(xmlDictLookup(ctxt->dict, (BASE_PTR + startPosition), len));']}
description: Use-after-free vulnerability in the xmlDictComputeFastKey function in libxml2 before 2.9.4, as used in Apple iOS before 9.3.2, OS X before 10.11.5, tvOS before 9.2.1, and watchOS before 2.2.1, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted XML document.

code_evidence: Line 6 stores a raw pointer `end` into the parser input buffer, and line 11 initializes it to `ctxt->input->cur` after GROW.

Inside the loop, GROW at line 26 may reallocate/grow the input buffer; line 32 then refreshes `end = ctxt->input->cur`, but the pointer captured before the buffer change is stale once reallocation occurs.
Line 50 passes `end - len` to xmlDictLookup, dereferencing the potentially stale pointer after buffer growth.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function stores a pointer into memory that GROW can free/reallocate and later dereferences it via `end - len` in xmlDictLookup, exactly the reuse of freed memory described by CWE-416. This is not merely an out-of-bounds read because the pointer's target was freed by buffer reallocation before use.

evidence_lines.code: return(xmlDictLookup(ctxt->dict, end - len, len));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser keeps a raw pointer (`end`) into the input buffer across GROW calls that can move or reallocate that buffer. Trigger: a crafted long NCName causes GROW to reallocate the buffer while parsing; the stale `end` (and `end - len`) then references freed memory. Supported consequence: xmlDictLookup reads freed memory, yielding a use-after-free that can crash (DoS) and potentially leak or corrupt data.

commit_msg: Fix vulnerability around urls crafter as http://host/../secret.foo (#24)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if ((file_path.Find("/..") >= 0) || (file_path.Find("\\\\..") >= 0) ||'], 'added_lines': ['    if ((file_path.Find("../") >= 0) || (file_path.Find("..\\\\") >= 0) ||']}
description: Platinum Upnp SDK through 1.2.0 has a directory traversal vulnerability. The attack could remote attack victim by sending http://ip:port/../privacy.avi URL to compromise a victim's privacy.

code_evidence: file_path is an attacker-influenced request path passed by value into ServeFile and used to construct NPT_File file(file_path) at line 8 before any validation. The guard at lines 10-12 only searches for the literal substrings "/.." and "\\.."; it does not detect the sequence "../" that follows a directory segment (e.g. /dir/../secret) and does not canonicalize or resolve the path. On success, line 32 opens the file and line 43 streams it back.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function uses external path input to locate a file intended to be under a restricted root but fails to neutralize ".." elements, so a pathname can resolve outside that directory and be read. This is exactly CWE-22 path traversal; the check's substring-order flaw is the missing constraint, not a separate weakness class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the traversal check matches the wrong substring order, so relative parent-directory sequences embedded after a directory component escape the intended root. Trigger: a crafted URL path containing "../" that resolves outside the served directory. Consequence: the file is opened and streamed, disclosing files outside the restricted root to a remote client.

commit_msg: Added extra EOF check and some minor refactoring.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static void SkipRGBMipmaps(Image *image, DDSInfo *dds_info, int pixel_size)'], 'added_lines': ['static MagickBooleanType SkipRGBMipmaps(Image *image,DDSInfo *dds_info,', '  int pixel_size,ExceptionInfo *exception)', '      if (EOFBlob(image) != MagickFalse)', '        {', '          ThrowFileException(exception,CorruptImageError,"UnexpectedEndOfFile",', '            image->filename);', '          return(MagickFalse);', '        }', '  return(MagickTrue);']}
description: coders/dds.c in ImageMagick allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service via a crafted DDS file.

code_evidence: SkipRGBMipmaps trusts DDS header fields (ddscaps1, ddscaps2, mipmapcount, width, height) to decide whether and how far to skip mipmap data. It computes offset = w*h*pixel_size and advances the blob with SeekBlob without checking that the file actually contains that many bytes or that the offset stays within the blob. The loop condition w && h only guards against zero dimensions, not against truncated or inconsistent file contents.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is missing validation of attacker-controlled DDS header values (mipmapcount, dimensions, caps) before they drive offset computation and seeking, matching CWE-20's improper input validation. The EOF check added in the diff confirms the missing constraint; this is not merely an offset-arithmetic issue (CWE-190) but absent validation of file-derived metadata.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the crafted DDS file's mipmap metadata and dimensions are used to compute a seek offset without validating them against the actual blob length. Trigger: a truncated or malicious DDS whose declared mipmap/dimension data exceeds the file contents. Consequence: SeekBlob moves past end-of-file and later reads operate on invalid positions, causing a denial of service (crash) in ImageMagick.

description: Istio 1.4.x before 1.4.9 and Istio 1.5.x before 1.5.4 contain the following vulnerability when telemetry v2 is enabled: by sending a specially crafted packet, an attacker could trigger a Null Pointer Exception resulting in a Denial of Service. commit_msg:
vgacon: remove software scrollback support

Yunhai Zhang recently fixed a VGA software scrollback bug in commit
ebfdfeeae8c0 ("vgacon: Fix for missing check in scrollback handling"),
but that then made people look more closely at some of this code, and
there were more problems on the vgacon side, but also the fbcon software
scrollback.

We don't really have anybody who maintains this code - probably because
nobody actually _uses_ it any more.  Sure, people still use both VGA and
the framebuffer consoles, but they are no longer the main user
interfaces to the kernel, and haven't been for decades, so these kinds
of extra features end up bitrotting and not really being used.

So rather than try to maintain a likely unused set of code, I'll just
aggressively remove it, and see if anybody even notices.  Maybe there
are people who haven't jumped on the whole GUI badnwagon yet, and think
it's just a fad.  And maybe those people use the scrollback code.

If that turns out to be the case, we can resurrect this again, once
we've found the sucker^Wmaintainer for it who actually uses it.

commit_msg:
Bluetooth: hci_ldisc: Postpone HCI_UART_PROTO_READY bit set in hci_uart_set_proto()

task A:                                task B:
hci_uart_set_proto                     flush_to_ldisc
 - p->open(hu) -> h5_open  //alloc h5  - receive_buf
 - set_bit HCI_UART_PROTO_READY         - tty_port_default_receive_buf
 - hci_uart_register_dev                 - tty_ldisc_receive_buf
                                          - hci_uart_tty_receive
				           - test_bit HCI_UART_PROTO_READY
				            - h5_recv
 - clear_bit HCI_UART_PROTO_READY             while() {
 - p->open(hu) -> h5_close //free h5
				              - h5_rx_3wire_hdr
				               - h5_reset()  //use-after-free
                                              }

It could use ioctl to set hci uart proto, but there is
a use-after-free issue when hci_uart_register_dev() fail in
hci_uart_set_proto(), see stack above, fix this by setting
HCI_UART_PROTO_READY bit only when hci_uart_register_dev()
return success.

Reported-by: syzbot+899a33dc0fa0dbaf06a6@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Signed-off-by: Kefeng Wang <wangkefeng.wang@huawei.com>
Reviewed-by: Jeremy Cline <jcline@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Marcel Holtmann <marcel@holtmann.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tset_bit(HCI_UART_PROTO_READY, &hu->flags);', '\t\tclear_bit(HCI_UART_PROTO_READY, &hu->flags);'], 'added_lines': ['\tset_bit(HCI_UART_PROTO_READY, &hu->flags);']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.5. There is a use-after-free issue when hci_uart_register_dev() fails in hci_uart_set_proto() in drivers/bluetooth/hci_ldisc.c.

code_evidence: Line 9 sets HCI_UART_PROTO_READY before hci_uart_register_dev(hu) is called on line 10. If registration fails, lines 11-13 clear the bit and return the error, but the protocol state was already published while hu->proto was assigned on line 8.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function enables a race where memory is freed while another thread still references it, matching CWE-416. A mere missing synchronization (CWE-362) is the race mechanism, but the supported weakness is the resulting use-after-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The READY flag is exposed before device registration succeeds. A concurrent receive path (flush_to_ldisc) that tests the bit can proceed into the protocol receive handler (h5_recv) while set_proto is still failing; on the error path the protocol is torn down/freed, leaving the concurrent reader operating on freed protocol state. Root cause is premature publication of the flag; consequence is a use-after-free race.

Bug-Debian: https://github.com/tats/w3m/issues/12 [CVE-2016-9424]
Origin: https://anonscm.debian.org/cgit/collab-maint/w3m.git/commit/?id=a25fd09f74fb83499396935a96d63bb7cb8e2c58
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (parsedtag_get_value(tag, ATTR_TEXTAREANUMBER, &i))', '    if (parsedtag_get_value(tag, ATTR_SELECTNUMBER, &i))'], 'added_lines': ['    if (parsedtag_get_value(tag, ATTR_TEXTAREANUMBER, &i)', '\t&& i >= 0 && i < max_textarea)', '    if (parsedtag_get_value(tag, ATTR_SELECTNUMBER, &i)', '\t&& i >= 0 && i < max_select)']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Tatsuya Kinoshita w3m fork before 0.5.3-31. w3m doesn't properly validate the value of tag attribute, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap buffer overflow crash) and possibly execute arbitrary code via a crafted HTML page.

code_evidence: Attribute TEXTAREANUMBER is parsed into integer i and, without any bound check, used directly to index textarea_str[i]; the assigned value is stored into item->value/init_value.
Similarly SELECTNUMBER is parsed into i and used to index select_option[i] with no range validation, taking .first and assigning it to item->select_option.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked index produces a memory access outside the intended array bounds, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds read/write within a memory buffer. if (parsedtag_get_value(tag, ATTR_TEXTAREANUMBER, &i))
item->value = item->init_value = textarea_str[i];

commit_msg:
Fix OCSP_basic_verify signer certificate validation

The function `OCSP_basic_verify` validates the signer certificate on an OCSP
response. The internal function, ocsp_verify_signer, is responsible for this
and is expected to return a 0 value in the event of a failure to verify.
Unfortunately, due to a bug, it actually returns with a postive success
response in this case. In the normal course of events OCSP_basic_verify
will then continue and will fail anyway in the ocsp_check_issuer function
because the supplied "chain" value will be empty in the case that
ocsp_verify_signer failed to verify the chain. This will cause
OCSP_basic_verify to return with a negative result (fatal error). Normally
in the event of a failure to verify it should return with 0.

However, in the case of the OCSP_NOCHECKS flag being used, OCSP_basic_verify
will return with a positvie result. This could lead to callers trusting an
OCSP Basic response when it should not be.

CVE-2022-1343

Fixes #18053

Reviewed-by: Paul Dale <pauli@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Matt Caswell <matt@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        ret = X509_STORE_CTX_get_error(ctx);', '                       "Verify error: %s", X509_verify_cert_error_string(ret));'], 'added_lines': ['        int err = X509_STORE_CTX_get_error(ctx);', '', '                       "Verify error: %s", X509_verify_cert_error_string(err));']}
description: The function `OCSP_basic_verify` verifies the signer certificate on an OCSP response. In the case where the (non-default) flag OCSP_NOCHECKS is used then the response will be positive (meaning a successful verification) even in the case where the response signing certificate fails to verify. It is anticipated that most users of `OCSP_basic_verify` will not use the OCSP_NOCHECKS flag. In this case the `OCSP_basic_verify` function will return a negative value (indicating a fatal error) in the case of a certificate verification failure. The normal expected return value in this case would be 0. This issue also impacts the command line OpenSSL "ocsp" application. When verifying an ocsp response with the "-no_cert_checks" option the command line application will report that the verification is successful even though it has in fact failed. In this case the incorrect successful response will also be accompanied by error messages showing the failure and contradicting the apparently successful result. Fixed in OpenSSL 3.0.3 (Affected 3.0.0,3.0.1,3.0.2).

code_evidence: X509_verify_cert() returns a non-positive value on failure, but the failure branch overwrites ret with X509_STORE_CTX_get_error(ctx), which is a positive X509_V_ERR_* code, then jumps to end and returns that positive value instead of a failure indicator.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function is the certificate-validation routine for OCSP signers, and its return-value handling causes a failed certificate verification to be reported as success, matching CWE-295 improper certificate validation. The flaw is the incorrect failure signaling, not merely an error-reporting issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error code from the store context is assigned to the function's return variable ret, converting a verification failure into a positive-looking result. Trigger: a signer certificate whose chain fails X509_verify_cert(). Consequence: callers (notably OCSP_basic_verify with OCSP_NOCHECKS) treat the signer certificate as validated, so an improperly validated certificate is accepted.

commit_msg: Fix arbitrary heap exposure problem
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        state->object_nl = strdup(RSTRING_PTR(object_nl));'], 'added_lines': ['        state->object_nl = fstrndup(RSTRING_PTR(object_nl), len);']}
description: Ruby through 2.2.7, 2.3.x through 2.3.4, and 2.4.x through 2.4.1 can expose arbitrary memory during a JSON.generate call. The issues lies in using strdup in ext/json/ext/generator/generator.c, which will stop after encountering a '\0' byte, returning a pointer to a string of length zero, which is not the length stored in space_len.

code_evidence: Line 6 computes len as the full byte length of the Ruby string, including any embedded NUL bytes. Line 14 uses strdup, which copies only up to the first '\0' and allocates a shorter buffer, yet line 15 records the original len as object_nl_len.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function establishes a buffer whose recorded length exceeds its actual allocation, enabling later reads outside the intended boundary, which matches CWE-119. The trigger is an object_nl string containing a NUL byte; using a length-aware copy (fstrndup) preserves the full buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: strdup stops at an embedded NUL byte, so state->object_nl points to a buffer shorter than the len stored in object_nl_len. Later JSON generation trusts object_nl_len and reads past the allocated buffer, exposing adjacent heap memory. Root cause is the length mismatch between the NUL-terminated copy and the recorded length; the out-of-bounds read is the consequence.

description: In Singular before 4.3.1, a predictable /tmp pathname is used (e.g., by sdb.cc), which allows local users to gain the privileges of other users via a procedure in a file under /tmp. NOTE: this CVE Record is about sdb.cc and similar files in the Singular interface that have predictable /tmp pathnames; this CVE Record is not about the lack of a safe temporary-file creation capability in the Singular language.

Consequence: the fopen(...,"w") and subsequent write/read operate on the attacker-chosen path, supporting local privilege or data-manipulation attacks (classic symlink/temp-file race).

commit_msg:
Fix integer overflow in rwpng.h (CVE-2016-5735)

Reported by Choi Jaeseung 
Found with Sparrow (http://ropas.snu.ac.kr/sparrow)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['', "    // For overflow safety reject images that won't fit in 32-bit", '    if (mainprog_ptr->width > INT_MAX/mainprog_ptr->height) {', '        png_destroy_read_struct(&png_ptr, &info_ptr, NULL);', '        return PNG_OUT_OF_MEMORY_ERROR;  /* not quite true, but whatever */', '    }'], 'added_lines': ["    // For overflow safety reject images that won't fit in 32-bit", '    if (rowbytes > INT_MAX/mainprog_ptr->height) {', '        png_destroy_read_struct(&png_ptr, &info_ptr, NULL);', '        return PNG_OUT_OF_MEMORY_ERROR;', '    }', '']}
description: Integer overflow in the rwpng_read_image24_libpng function in rwpng.c in pngquant 2.7.0 allows remote attackers to have unspecified impact via a crafted PNG file, which triggers a buffer overflow.

code_evidence: Lines 31-32 read attacker-controlled width and height from the PNG IHDR. Lines 33-36 check width > INT_MAX/height, but this guards the width*height product, not the actual allocation size.
Line 73 obtains rowbytes from libpng after transformations (expansion, filler, strip_16); line 74 computes malloc(rowbytes * mainprog_ptr->height) with no overflow check on that product.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The multiplication rowbytes * height can exceed the integer range and wrap, producing a too-small allocation size; this is exactly an integer overflow used as a memory-allocation size, matching CWE-190. It is not merely a memory-corruption weakness (CWE-787), since the root cause is the unchecked size arithmetic.

evidence_lines.code:
rowbytes = png_get_rowbytes(png_ptr, info_ptr);
if ((mainprog_ptr->rgba_data = malloc(rowbytes * mainprog_ptr->height)) == NULL) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The size passed to malloc is rowbytes * height, both derived from the crafted PNG. The only overflow guard validates width*height, so a large height with a rowbytes that makes the product wrap to a small value passes the check. malloc then allocates a small buffer while png_read_image writes height rows of rowbytes, causing a heap buffer overflow.

description: uWebSockets 18.11.0 and 18.12.0 has a stack-based buffer overflow in uWS::TopicTree::trimTree (called from uWS::TopicTree::unsubscribeAll). NOTE: the vendor's position is that this is "a minor issue or not even an issue at all" because the developer of an application (that uses uWebSockets) should not be allowing the large number of triggered topics to accumulate

code_evidence: Guards drain when numTriggeredTopics reaches 64 before the segment loop, but the array is only indexed inside the loop and after it.
Inside the loop, terminatingWildcardChild is appended to triggeredTopics[numTriggeredTopics++] with no capacity check at the point of the write.
After the loop, iterator is likewise appended via triggeredTopics[numTriggeredTopics++] without checking the bound.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The append writes triggeredTopics[numTriggeredTopics++] beyond the array's capacity, which is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). This is not merely a logic error: the unchecked index directly causes memory beyond the intended buffer to be modified.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The fixed-size triggeredTopics array is written using the incremented numTriggeredTopics index at the append sites, but the only drain/check occurs before those appends can raise the counter. When many distinct triggered topics accumulate, numTriggeredTopics exceeds 64 and the writes at the append sites go past the array end, corrupting adjacent stack memory.

description: vim is vulnerable to Heap-based Buffer Overflow

code_evidence: After eval1(), *arg is advanced past whitespace/linebreak, then dereferenced at **arg and compared to ')'. On the error path (line 21 false) emsg sets ret=FAIL, but line 26 unconditionally does ++*arg, advancing past the NUL terminator when the closing paren is missing.

The patch moves the increment inside the success branch, confirming the missing-constraint cause rather than a generic parse error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the pointer increment at line 26 executes regardless of whether the ')' check succeeded, so on a missing closing paren it skips the terminating NUL. The trigger is a malformed lambda/expression lacking ')'; subsequent parsing reads beyond the heap-allocated input string, producing an out-of-bounds read (illegal memory access).

description: The ISAKMP parser in tcpdump before 4.9.2 could enter an infinite loop due to bugs in print-isakmp.c, several functions.

code_evidence: Line 23 returns a pointer advanced by ntohs(e.len), the attacker-controlled length field copied from the packet at line 12. Lines 14 and 18 only guard printing; they do not constrain the returned advancement. If e.len is 0 (or small), the caller's iteration over payloads advances by zero or a tiny amount, so the same payload is re-parsed endlessly.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-835 fits because the missing lower-bound check on e.len makes the caller's loop exit condition unreachable, matching the reported infinite loop. This is not merely an out-of-bounds read: the defect is the non-advancing iteration, which the commit fixes by validating length before dissection.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function advances the parse cursor by the untrusted ISAKMP payload length without ensuring it is at least the header size (>= 4). Trigger: a crafted Notification/Nonce payload with a length field of 0 or < 4. Consequence: the caller's payload-walking loop makes no forward progress, causing an infinite loop and CPU exhaustion (DoS).

commit_msg:
Don't treat the packet length as unsigned.

The scanf family of functions are as annoyingly bad at handling unsigned
numbers as strtoul() is - both of them are perfectly willing to accept a
value beginning with a negative sign as an unsigned value.  When using
strtoul(), you can compensate for this by explicitly checking for a '-'
as the first character of the string, but you can't do that with
sscanf().

So revert to having pkt_len be signed, and scanning it with %d, but
check for a negative value and fail if we see a negative value.

Bug: 12394
Change-Id: I4b19b95f2e1ffc96dac5c91bff6698c246f52007

commit_msg:
block, bfq: fix use-after-free in bfq_idle_slice_timer_body

In bfq_idle_slice_timer func, bfqq = bfqd->in_service_queue is
not in bfqd-lock critical section. The bfqq, which is not
equal to NULL in bfq_idle_slice_timer, may be freed after passing
to bfq_idle_slice_timer_body. So we will access the freed memory.

In addition, considering the bfqq may be in race, we should
firstly check whether bfqq is in service before doing something
on it in bfq_idle_slice_timer_body func. If the bfqq in race is
not in service, it means the bfqq has been expired through
__bfq_bfqq_expire func, and wait_request flags has been cleared in
__bfq_bfqd_reset_in_service func. So we do not need to re-clear the
wait_request of bfqq which is not in service.

description: fluidsynth is a software synthesizer based on the SoundFont 2 specifications. A use after free violation was discovered in fluidsynth, that can be triggered when loading an invalid SoundFont file.

code_evidence: At the invalid-global-zone branch, izone aliases the current zone z via fluid_list_get(p2); the code removes it from start_of_zone_list and calls delete_zone(izone), freeing the SFZone while p2 still points at the now-freed list node.
After the branch, line 154 unconditionally executes p2 = fluid_list_next(p2), dereferencing the freed list element to obtain the next node.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function frees a zone and then reuses the associated list node pointer after free. This is a temporal memory-safety flaw, distinct from an out-of-bounds read, since the memory was valid but has been released.

evidence_lines.code: p2 = fluid_list_next(p2);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the current zone is freed (delete_zone) but iteration continues using the stale p2 pointer. Trigger: loading an invalid SoundFont with a second, invalid global zone. Consequence: use-after-free access at line 154, enabling read of freed memory, crash, or potential code execution.

commit_msg:
Fix memory leak

As reported by https://github.com/tbeu/matio/issues/186
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['            size_t j;', '            for ( j = 0; j < i; j++ ) {', '                free(functions[i]);', '            }']}
description: A memory leak was discovered in matio 1.5.21 and earlier in Mat_VarReadNextInfo5() in mat5.c via a crafted file. This issue can potentially result in DoS.

code_evidence: Line 11 allocates matvar->data and line 14 aliases it as an array of matvar_t* pointers. The loop at lines 15-19 stores each Mat_VarReadNextInfo result into functions[i] and breaks on the first NULL at lines 17-19. On the error path at line 21, only matvar->data (line 22) is freed; the individual functions[0..i-1] objects already stored are never released.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-401 fits because allocated memory (the functions[i] matvar_t objects) is not released after its effective lifetime on the error path, leaving it unreachable. This is a missing-release leak, not a use-after-free or double-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error branch frees the pointer array but not the per-element matvar_t objects already allocated by Mat_VarReadNextInfo. Trigger: a crafted file where a later Mat_VarReadNextInfo returns NULL after earlier elements succeeded. Consequence: the earlier element allocations become unreachable, leaking memory and enabling resource-consumption DoS across repeated reads.

commit_msg:
Fix #69975: PHP segfaults when accessing nvarchar(max) defined columns

The SQL Server Native Client 11.0 and maybe other ODBC drivers report
NVARCHAR(MAX) columns as SQL_WVARCHAR with size 0. This causes too small a
buffer to be emalloc'd, likely causing a segfault in the following. As we don't
know the real size of the column data, we treat such colums as
SQL_WLONGVARCHAR.

The related bug #67437 suggests that some drivers report a size of ~4GB. It is
not certain that this is really the case (there might be some integer overflow
involved, and anyway, there has been no feedback), so we do not cater for this
now. However, it would not be hard to treat all sizes above a certain threshold
in a similar way, i.e. as SQL_WLONGVARCHAR.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\t/* Workaround for drivers that report NVARCHAR(MAX) columns as SQL_WVARCHAR with size 0 (bug #69975) */', '\t\t\t\tif (result->values[i].coltype == SQL_WVARCHAR && displaysize == 0) {', '\t\t\t\t\tresult->values[i].coltype = SQL_WLONGVARCHAR;', '\t\t\t\t\tresult->values[i].value = NULL;', '\t\t\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t\t\t}', '']}
description: The odbc_bindcols function in ext/odbc/php_odbc.c in PHP before 5.6.12 mishandles driver behavior for SQL_WVARCHAR columns, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) in opportunistic circumstances by leveraging use of the odbc_fetch_array function to access a certain type of Microsoft SQL Server table.

code_evidence: For SQL_WVARCHAR (line 40) the driver-reported octet length is read into displaysize (46-47); the code then emalloc's displaysize+1 (61) and binds that buffer (62-63) without checking whether displaysize is 0 or otherwise implausible.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-20 fits because the code fails to validate an input-derived property (the column display/octet size) before using it to size a buffer. This is improper validation of metadata rather than a separate memory-safety root cause; the crash is the consequence of the missing size check.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the driver-supplied column size (metadata) is trusted without validating that it is nonzero/plausible. Trigger: a driver reports NVARCHAR(MAX) as SQL_WVARCHAR with size 0, so a 1-byte buffer is allocated and bound; subsequent fetch writes column data into it, causing a crash. Consequence is availability impact (segfault/DoS), not code execution in this function.

description: Buffer overflow in the Get8BIMProperty function in MagickCore/property.c in ImageMagick before 6.9.5-4 and 7.x before 7.0.2-6 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read, memory leak, and crash) via a crafted image.

At [99,101,102] CopyMagickMemory copies (size_t) count bytes from info and length is reduced by MagickMin(count,length), so an attacker-controlled count larger than the remaining profile causes an out-of-bounds read.

Consequence: CopyMagickMemory reads past the profile buffer, and count is used as a loop/offset, producing out-of-bounds reads, memory errors and a crash (DoS).

description: MPEG4Extractor.cpp in libstagefright in mediaserver in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-04-01 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read and memory corruption) via a crafted media file, aka internal bug 27208621.

Before the patch, the only guard was CHECK(dstOffset + 4 <= mBuffer->size()), a debug-only assertion that does not account for nalLength and is compiled out in release builds. mBuffer->size() is the fixed MediaBuffer capacity, while dstOffset and nalLength derive from attacker-controlled sample data.

Trigger: a crafted MPEG-4 sample whose NAL units cause dstOffset + 4 + nalLength to exceed mBuffer->size(). Consequence: the memcpy writes past the destination buffer, corrupting memory and potentially enabling code execution or a crash.

commit_msg:
Avoid negative integer overflow when `chunkLength == 0`.

This fixes #789.

(cherry picked from commit 8cd95e221889e41e9cc153e2cfb5a7b41c7bc7a4)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                    while (iccOffset < 80 && iccOffset < chunkLength) {', '                        if (chunkData.pData_[iccOffset++] == 0x00) {', '                            break;', '                        }', '                    }', '                    profileName_ = std::string(reinterpret_cast<char*>(chunkData.pData_), iccOffset - 1);', "                    ++iccOffset;  // +1 = 'compressed' flag"], 'added_lines': ['                    do {', '                      enforce(iccOffset < 80 && iccOffset < chunkLength, Exiv2::kerCorruptedMetadata);', '                    } while(chunkData.pData_[iccOffset++] != 0x00);', '', '                    profileName_ = std::string(reinterpret_cast<char *>(chunkData.pData_), iccOffset-1);', "                    ++iccOffset; // +1 = 'compressed' flag"]}
description: An integer overflow in Exiv2 through 0.27.1 allows an attacker to cause a denial of service (SIGSEGV) via a crafted PNG image file, because PngImage::readMetadata mishandles a zero value for iccOffset.

code_evidence: iccOffset is a uint32_t initialized to 0 and advanced only by the loop over chunkData.pData_. If chunkLength is 0 the while condition (iccOffset < chunkLength) is false immediately, so iccOffset stays 0. Line 52 then computes iccOffset - 1 (0 - 1) in unsigned arithmetic, wrapping to 0xFFFFFFFF, and constructs profileName_ with that length from a zero-length buffer. Line 53 increments and enforces iccOffset <= chunkLength, and line 54 uses the wrapped offset as the source and size for zlibToDataBuf.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The core defect is an unsigned integer wraparound (0 - 1) used as an offset/size, matching CWE-190's integer-overflow/wraparound semantics and its note on offsets and sizes. It is not merely a bounds-check gap; the arithmetic itself produces the invalid value that enables the crash.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop guard permits iccOffset to remain 0, and the subsequent unsigned subtraction iccOffset - 1 wraps to a huge value. Trigger: an iCCP chunk with chunkLength == 0 in a crafted PNG drives readMetadata down this path. Consequence: an enormous std::string length and offset are used, causing out-of-bounds reads and a SIGSEGV denial of service (the patch replaces the guard with a do/enforce check).

commit_msg:
Fix integer overflows in internal memalign and malloc functions [BZ #22343]

When posix_memalign is called with an alignment less than MALLOC_ALIGNMENT
and a requested size close to SIZE_MAX, it falls back to malloc code
(because the alignment of a block returned by malloc is sufficient to
satisfy the call).  In this case, an integer overflow in _int_malloc leads
to posix_memalign incorrectly returning successfully.

Upon fixing this and writing a somewhat thorough regression test, it was
discovered that when posix_memalign is called with an alignment larger than
MALLOC_ALIGNMENT (so it uses _int_memalign instead) and a requested size
close to SIZE_MAX, a different integer overflow in _int_memalign leads to
posix_memalign incorrectly returning successfully.

Both integer overflows affect other memory allocation functions that use
_int_malloc (one affected malloc in x86) or _int_memalign as well.

This commit fixes both integer overflows.  In addition to this, it adds a
regression test to guard against false successful allocations by the
following memory allocation functions when called with too-large allocation
sizes and, where relevant, various valid alignments:
malloc, realloc, calloc, reallocarray, memalign, posix_memalign,
aligned_alloc, valloc, and pvalloc.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '  /* Check for overflow.  */', '  if (nb > SIZE_MAX - alignment - MINSIZE)', '    {', '      __set_errno (ENOMEM);', '      return 0;', '    }']}
description: The malloc implementation in the GNU C Library (aka glibc or libc6), from version 2.24 to 2.26 on powerpc, and only in version 2.26 on i386, did not properly handle malloc calls with arguments close to SIZE_MAX and could return a pointer to a heap region that is smaller than requested, eventually leading to heap corruption.

code_evidence: checked_request2size converts the requested bytes into chunk size nb, then line 15 computes nb + alignment + MINSIZE as the argument to _int_malloc without any overflow check. If nb is near SIZE_MAX, this sum wraps to a small value, so _int_malloc allocates a small chunk even though the caller requested a much larger size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function performs an arithmetic size calculation that can wrap before allocation, matching CWE-190 integer overflow/wraparound. The downstream undersized allocation and heap corruption are consequences; the defect itself is the unchecked addition.

evidence_lines.code:
checked_request2size (bytes, nb);
m = (char *) (_int_malloc (av, nb + alignment + MINSIZE));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the padding addition nb + alignment + MINSIZE is performed in size_t with no upper-bound check. Trigger: a memalign/posix_memalign call with a size close to SIZE_MAX (and alignment above MALLOC_ALIGNMENT). The addition wraps, a too-small chunk is returned, and the caller writes beyond it, causing heap corruption.

commit_msg:
enip: use wmem for copied addresses

When we copy an address from pinfo into connInfo->O2T.ipaddress, a
shallow copy is not sufficient. connInfo->O2T.ipaddress is kept across
packets whereas pinfo is valid only for the current packet.

Use wmem with file scope for the copied address. This fixes a
use-after-free error when we access the address in a subsequent packet.

Bug: 14470
Change-Id: I8b74037020189485485a506af6510cb45828e3c4
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/26248
Reviewed-by: Martin Kaiser <wireshark@kaiser.cx>
Petri-Dish: Martin Kaiser <wireshark@kaiser.cx>
Tested-by: Petri Dish Buildbot
Reviewed-by: Anders Broman <a.broman58@gmail.com>
(cherry picked from commit 177962a5b4a05759b40fb6fc07a4a6eec306a9bf)
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/30941
Petri-Dish: Pascal Quantin <pascal.quantin@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Pascal Quantin <pascal.quantin@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            copy_address_shallow(&connInfo->O2T.ipaddress, &pinfo->src);', '            copy_address_shallow(&connInfo->T2O.ipaddress, &pinfo->dst);'], 'added_lines': ['            copy_address_wmem(wmem_file_scope(), &connInfo->O2T.ipaddress, &pinfo->src);', '            copy_address_wmem(wmem_file_scope(), &connInfo->T2O.ipaddress, &pinfo->dst);']}
description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.11, the ENIP dissector could crash. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-enip.c by changing the memory-management approach so that a use-after-free is avoided.

code_evidence: copy_address_shallow stores only the data pointer of pinfo->src into connInfo->O2T.ipaddress, which is retained in the connection record beyond the current packet.
copy_address_shallow likewise retains pinfo->dst pointer in connInfo->T2O.ipaddress; both pinfo addresses are packet-scoped and freed after the packet.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code references memory after it has been freed: a shallow copy aliases pinfo-owned memory that does not outlive the packet, and the stale pointer is later accessed. This matches CWE-416; the fix uses wmem file-scope copies to give the stored address its own lifetime.

evidence_lines.code: copy_address_shallow(&connInfo->O2T.ipaddress, &pinfo->src);
copy_address_shallow(&connInfo->T2O.ipaddress, &pinfo->dst);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The persistent connection state (connInfo, stored in file-scope structures) keeps shallow copies of packet-scoped pinfo addresses. Once the packet's pinfo memory is freed, later packets that read connInfo->O2T/T2O.ipaddress dereference dangling pointers, causing a use-after-free that can crash the ENIP dissector.

commit_msg: Fix issue with invalid component ids (#7)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        }', '        ', '        // Make sure component is unique', '        for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) {', '            if (decoder->scan_components[i] == decoder->scan_components[j]) {', '                ok_jpg_error(jpg, OK_JPG_ERROR_INVALID, "Invalid SOS segment (component ids)");', '                return false;', '            }']}
description: A heap-based buffer overflow vulnerability in the function ok_jpg_decode_block_subsequent_scan() ok_jpg.c:1102 of ok-file-formats through 2020-06-26 allows attackers to cause a Denial of Service (DOS) via a crafted jpeg file.

code_evidence: The loop iterates over decoder->num_scan_components, reading a component id C from the input buffer at src[0] and searching decoder->components. If a matching id is found, the index j is stored in decoder->scan_components[i] and component_found is set. There is no check that the same component id is not selected more than once across iterations of the outer loop; the inner loop only validates presence, not uniqueness.

commit_msg:
Copying fixes (#2289)

We didn't have an OverriddenVisitor in the copying code, and sadly unimplemented visitors just return null. That explains the crash in #2288

The missing visitors were push and pop.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  struct Copier : public Visitor<Copier, Expression*> {', '      return Visitor<Copier, Expression*>::visit(curr);'], 'added_lines': ['  struct Copier : public OverriddenVisitor<Copier, Expression*> {', '      return OverriddenVisitor<Copier, Expression*>::visit(curr);', '    Expression* visitPush(Push* curr) { return builder.makePush(curr->value); }', '    Expression* visitPop(Pop* curr) { return builder.makePop(curr->type); }']}
description: An issue was discovered in Binaryen 1.38.32. Two visitors in ir/ExpressionManipulator.cpp can lead to a NULL pointer dereference in wasm::LocalSet::finalize in wasm/wasm.cpp. A crafted input can cause segmentation faults, leading to denial-of-service, as demonstrated by wasm2js.

code_evidence: The Copier struct derives from Visitor<Copier, Expression*> rather than OverriddenVisitor, so dispatch falls back to the base Visitor::visit implementation.

copy() first returns any custom result, then delegates to Visitor<Copier, Expression*>::visit(curr); for expressions without an overridden visit method (e.g. Push/Pop), the unimplemented base visitor yields a NULL Expression* that is propagated as the copy result.
The Copier instantiation and copier.copy(original) then pass this NULL through to builder consumers such as LocalSet::finalize, which dereferences the expected non-null value.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function returns a NULL Expression* for unhandled node kinds and that value is subsequently dereferenced, matching CWE-476 (NULL pointer dereference). This is distinct from a type-confusion or use-after-free, since the defect is the missing non-null result.

evidence_lines.code: struct Copier : public Visitor<Copier, Expression*> {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the visitor base class lacks overrides for Push/Pop, so visit() returns null instead of a copied expression. Trigger: a crafted wasm input containing Push/Pop expressions processed by flexibleCopy. Consequence: the null copy flows into finalize and is dereferenced, causing a segfault/DoS.

commit_msg:
Sonivox: sanity check numSamples.

Bug: 26366256
Change-Id: I066888c25035ea4c60c88f316db4508dc4dab6bc
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (numSamples <= 0) {', '        ALOGE("b/26366256");', '        return;', '    }']}
description: Sonivox in mediaserver in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-04-01 does not check for a negative number of samples, which allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code or cause a denial of service (memory corruption) via a crafted media file, related to arm-wt-22k/lib_src/eas_wtengine.c and arm-wt-22k/lib_src/eas_wtsynth.c, aka internal bug 26366256.

code_evidence: Line 11 reads numSamples directly from pWTIntFrame->numSamples with no validation of sign or range.

Line 23 uses the unvalidated numSamples as the loop bound via while (numSamples--); lines 24-27 compute and write to *pOutputBuffer++, and lines 29-31 advance pSamples by acc0, so the iteration count directly drives output-buffer writes and sample-pointer reads.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked sample count drives out-of-bounds reads/writes on pOutputBuffer and pSamples, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operations. The underlying cause is the missing negative-value check on numSamples, but the supported consequence is buffer-bound violation.

evidence_lines.code: numSamples = pWTIntFrame->numSamples;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: numSamples from the media-controlled WT frame is used as a loop count without rejecting negative values. commit_msg:
Prevent over long nonces in ChaCha20-Poly1305

ChaCha20-Poly1305 is an AEAD cipher, and requires a unique nonce input for
every encryption operation. RFC 7539 specifies that the nonce value (IV)
should be 96 bits (12 bytes). OpenSSL allows a variable nonce length and
front pads the nonce with 0 bytes if it is less than 12 bytes. However it
also incorrectly allows a nonce to be set of up to 16 bytes. In this case
only the last 12 bytes are significant and any additional leading bytes are
ignored.

It is a requirement of using this cipher that nonce values are unique.
Messages encrypted using a reused nonce value are susceptible to serious
confidentiality and integrity attacks. If an application changes the
default nonce length to be longer than 12 bytes and then makes a change to
the leading bytes of the nonce expecting the new value to be a new unique
nonce then such an application could inadvertently encrypt messages with a
reused nonce.

Additionally the ignored bytes in a long nonce are not covered by the
integrity guarantee of this cipher. Any application that relies on the
integrity of these ignored leading bytes of a long nonce may be further
affected.

Any OpenSSL internal use of this cipher, including in SSL/TLS, is safe
because no such use sets such a long nonce value. However user
applications that use this cipher directly and set a non-default nonce
length to be longer than 12 bytes may be vulnerable.

CVE-2019-1543

Fixes #8345

Reviewed-by: Paul Dale <paul.dale@oracle.com>
Reviewed-by: Richard Levitte <levitte@openssl.org>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/8406)

(cherry picked from commit 2a3d0ee9d59156c48973592331404471aca886d6)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (arg <= 0 || arg > CHACHA_CTR_SIZE)'], 'added_lines': ['        if (arg <= 0 || arg > CHACHA20_POLY1305_MAX_IVLEN)']}
description: ChaCha20-Poly1305 is an AEAD cipher, and requires a unique nonce input for every encryption operation. RFC 7539 specifies that the nonce value (IV) should be 96 bits (12 bytes). OpenSSL allows a variable nonce length and front pads the nonce with 0 bytes if it is less than 12 bytes. However it also incorrectly allows a nonce to be set of up to 16 bytes. In this case only the last 12 bytes are significant and any additional leading bytes are ignored. It is a requirement of using this cipher that nonce values are unique. Messages encrypted using a reused nonce value are susceptible to serious confidentiality and integrity attacks. If an application changes the default nonce length to be longer than 12 bytes and then makes a change to the leading bytes of the nonce expecting the new value to be a new unique nonce then such an application could inadvertently encrypt messages with a reused nonce. Additionally the ignored bytes in a long nonce are not covered by the integrity guarantee of this cipher. Any application that relies on the integrity of these ignored leading bytes of a long nonce may be further affected. Any OpenSSL internal use of this cipher, including in SSL/TLS, is safe because no such use sets such a long nonce value. However user applications that use this cipher directly and set a non-default nonce length to be longer than 12 bytes may be vulnerable. OpenSSL versions 1.1.1 and 1.1.0 are affected by this issue. Due to the limited scope of affected deployments this has been assessed as low severity and therefore we are not creating new releases at this time. Fixed in OpenSSL 1.1.1c (Affected 1.1.1-1.1.1b). Fixed in OpenSSL 1.1.0k (Affected 1.1.0-1.1.0j).

This permits a 13-16 byte nonce length to be set for the ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD cipher.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function permits a nonce length that violates the ChaCha20-Poly1305 specification, making the deployed AEAD construction operate with a risky/incorrect cryptographic parameter. This is a misuse of a cryptographic algorithm rather than a memory-safety flaw, so CWE-327 fits.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the nonce-length setter accepts values above the 12-byte nonce size defined for ChaCha20-Poly1305. Trigger: an application sets a non-default IV length of 13-16 bytes; only the trailing 12 bytes are then significant and leading bytes are ignored. Supported consequence: nonce uniqueness expectations can be broken, enabling nonce reuse and weakening the cipher's confidentiality and integrity guarantees.

Kafka: Be more strict when dissecting varints.

The Kafka dissector uses the return value of tvb_get_varint to advance
the packet offset in many places. If tvb_get_varint fails it returns 0,
which means our offset isn't guaranteed to advance. Stop dissection
whenever that happens. Fixes #17811.

if (len == 0) {

val = 0;

return offset+len+(gint)val;

Fix security vulnerability with FractionalMax(AVG)Pool with illegal pooling_ratio

PiperOrigin-RevId: 483486453
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  for (std::size_t i = 0; i < pooling_ratio.size(); ++i) {', '    if (pooling_ratio[i] < 1) {', '      return errors::InvalidArgument(', '          "pooling_ratio cannot be smaller than 1, got: ", pooling_ratio[i]);', '    }', '  }', '']}
description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. The security vulnerability results in FractionalMax(AVG)Pool with illegal pooling_ratio. Attackers using Tensorflow can exploit the vulnerability. They can access heap memory which is not in the control of user, leading to a crash or remote code execution. We have patched the issue in GitHub commit 216525144ee7c910296f5b05d214ca1327c9ce48. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.11.0. We will also cherry pick this commit on TensorFlow 2.10.1.

code_evidence: The loop divides each input dimension by pooling_ratio[i] and floors the result without checking that pooling_ratio[i] is at least 1. A pooling_ratio below 1 (or zero) inflates the computed dimension, and the only guard rejects negative values, not oversized/illegal ones.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the missing pooling_ratio validation lets an oversized output shape reach downstream buffer allocation, causing writes past the intended buffer. The added patch loop confirming pooling_ratio >= 1 corroborates the missing constraint; this is an out-of-bounds write, not merely an input-validation or integer issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: absence of a lower-bound constraint on pooling_ratio before computing output dimensions. Trigger: an attacker supplies a pooling_ratio element below 1, producing an inflated output dimension that downstream kernel allocation/access assumes to be valid, yielding heap memory written outside the intended buffer. Consequence: out-of-bounds write leading to crash or potential remote code execution.

commit_msg:
usb/redir: avoid dynamic stack allocation (CVE-2021-3527)

Use autofree heap allocation instead.

Fixes: 4f4321c11ff ("usb: use iovecs in USBPacket")
Reviewed-by: Philippe Mathieu-Daudé <philmd@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Gerd Hoffmann <kraxel@redhat.com>

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    uint8_t buf[p->iov.size];'], 'added_lines': ['    g_autofree uint8_t *buf = g_malloc(p->iov.size);']}
description: A flaw was found in the USB redirector device (usb-redir) of QEMU. Small USB packets are combined into a single, large transfer request, to reduce the overhead and improve performance. The combined size of the bulk transfer is used to dynamically allocate a variable length array (VLA) on the stack without proper validation. Since the total size is not bounded, a malicious guest could use this flaw to influence the array length and cause the QEMU process to perform an excessive allocation on the stack, resulting in a denial of service.

code_evidence: Line 5 declares a variable-length array on the stack sized by p->iov.size, a value derived from the guest-supplied USB packet, with no upper bound check.
Lines 9-10 record that same p->iov.size as the packet length and copy that many bytes into buf, so the unbounded size directly controls the stack allocation and the copy.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates a resource (stack buffer) sized by attacker-influenced input without imposing any size restriction, matching CWE-770's allocation without limits. The consequence is resource-exhaustion DoS; the weakness is the missing bound, not a memory-safety overflow (e.g., CWE-121) since the VLA matches the copied length.

evidence_lines.code: uint8_t buf[p->iov.size];

interrupt_packet.length    = p->iov.size;
usb_packet_copy(p, buf, p->iov.size);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the stack VLA length is taken directly from p->iov.size with no validation or limit. Trigger: a malicious guest sends a bulk/interrupt-out packet whose iov size is very large, causing an excessive stack allocation and memory copy, resulting in denial of service of the QEMU process.

nbd: convert to use qio_channel_yield

In the client, read the reply headers from a coroutine, switching the
read side between the "read header" coroutine and the I/O coroutine that
reads the body of the reply.

In the server, if the server can read more requests it will create a new
"read request" coroutine as soon as a request has been read.  Otherwise,
the new coroutine is created in nbd_request_put.

Reviewed-by: Stefan Hajnoczi <stefanha@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Fam Zheng <famz@redhat.com>
