description: An assertion-failure flaw was found in Qemu before 2.10.1, in the Network Block Device (NBD) server's initial connection negotiation, where the I/O coroutine was undefined. This could crash the qemu-nbd server if a client sent unexpected data during connection negotiation. A remote user or process could use this flaw to crash the qemu-nbd server resulting in denial of service.

code_evidence: The receive coroutine unconditionally assigns itself to client->recv_coroutine and calls nbd_update_can_read before any request data is parsed. The assertion g_assert(qemu_in_coroutine()) and this self-registration occur during connection negotiation, driven by client-controlled connection state rather than validated request content.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-617 fits because an assert()/g_assert in the negotiation path is reachable from remote client input and terminates the server. The weakness is the reachable assertion causing exit, not a memory-safety bug or unchecked buffer copy.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the coroutine state (recv_coroutine) is established/updated during negotiation without guarding against unexpected client data, leaving the I/O coroutine undefined (NULL) at a point where the negotiation path expects it. Trigger: a client sends unexpected data during initial connection negotiation, reaching the assertion in this negotiation path. Consequence: the g_assert fails, aborting the qemu-nbd server (DoS) rather than handling the bad input gracefully.

commit_msg:
With write operation on psi files replacing old trigger with a new one,
the lifetime of its waitqueue is totally arbitrary. Overwriting an
existing trigger causes its waitqueue to be freed and pending poll()
will stumble on trigger->event_wait which was destroyed.
Fix this by disallowing to redefine an existing psi trigger. If a write
operation is used on a file descriptor with an already existing psi
trigger, the operation will fail with EBUSY error.
Also bypass a check for psi_disabled in the psi_trigger_destroy as the
flag can be flipped after the trigger is created, leading to a memory
leak.

Fixes: 0e94682b73bf ("psi: introduce psi monitor")
Reported-by: syzbot+cdb5dd11c97cc532efad@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Suggested-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
Analyzed-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Suren Baghdasaryan <surenb@google.com>
Signed-off-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
Reviewed-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers@google.com>
Acked-by: Johannes Weiner <hannes@cmpxchg.org>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20220111232309.1786347-1-surenb@google.com
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tnew = psi_trigger_create(&psi_system, buf, nbytes, res);', '\tif (IS_ERR(new))', '\t\treturn PTR_ERR(new);', '\tseq = file->private_data;', '\tpsi_trigger_replace(&seq->private, new);'], 'added_lines': ['\tseq = file->private_data;', '', '\t/* Allow only one trigger per file descriptor */', '\tif (seq->private) {', '\t\tmutex_unlock(&seq->lock);', '\t\treturn -EBUSY;', '\t}', '', '\tnew = psi_trigger_create(&psi_system, buf, nbytes, res);', '\tif (IS_ERR(new)) {', '\t\tmutex_unlock(&seq->lock);', '\t\treturn PTR_ERR(new);', '\t}', '', '\tsmp_store_release(&seq->private, new);']}
description: A flaw was found in the Linux kernel's implementation of Pressure Stall Information. While the feature is disabled by default, it could allow an attacker to crash the system or have other memory-corruption side effects.

code_evidence: psi_trigger_create() allocates a new trigger before the existing seq->private is inspected, so a fresh trigger is built even when one is already installed.
Under seq->lock, psi_trigger_replace(&seq->private, new) unconditionally swaps in the new trigger, discarding the previously stored pointer without any check that seq->private was NULL.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unconditional replacement frees the old trigger while other code can still hold references to it, matching CWE-416 (use of memory after it has been freed). This differs from a mere race on the pointer, since the core defect is discarding live, still-referenced state.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: A second write to the same psi file descriptor creates a new trigger and replaces the old one; the replacement drops the prior trigger, whose waitqueue is freed while pending poll() callers may still reference trigger->event_wait. The missing guard on seq->private lets the overwrite occur, producing a use-after-free of the freed trigger's waitqueue.

description: In GNOME libgda through 6.0.0, gda-web-provider.c does not enable TLS certificate verification on the SoupSessionSync objects it creates, leaving users vulnerable to network MITM attacks. NOTE: this is similar to CVE-2016-20011.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Creating TLS-capable sessions without enabling certificate validation is exactly improper certificate validation (CWE-295): the client fails to verify the peer certificate. This is a certificate-validation failure, not merely a missing-encryption issue, since the https scheme is used but trust is not checked.

evidence_lines.code:
cdata->worker_session = soup_session_new ();
cdata->front_session = soup_session_new_with_options ("max-conns-per-host", 1, NULL);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the sessions used for the provider's front/worker HTTP(S) traffic are constructed with default options that do not enable system CA verification. Trigger: a USE_SSL connection causes the provider to build https:// URLs and send messages through these sessions to a remote host. Consequence: an attacker positioned on the network can present a forged certificate and intercept the session, bypassing authentication (MITM).

commit_msg:
The Layer 2 Update frame is used to update bridges when a station roams
to another AP even if that STA does not transmit any frames after the
reassociation. This behavior was described in IEEE Std 802.11F-2003 as
something that would happen based on MLME-ASSOCIATE.indication, i.e.,
before completing 4-way handshake. However, this IEEE trial-use
recommended practice document was published before RSN (IEEE Std
802.11i-2004) and as such, did not consider RSN use cases. Furthermore,
IEEE Std 802.11F-2003 was withdrawn in 2006 and as such, has not been
maintained amd should not be used anymore.

Sending out the Layer 2 Update frame immediately after association is
fine for open networks (and also when using SAE, FT protocol, or FILS
authentication when the station is actually authenticated by the time
association completes). However, it is not appropriate for cases where
RSN is used with PSK or EAP authentication since the station is actually
fully authenticated only once the 4-way handshake completes after
authentication and attackers might be able to use the unauthenticated
triggering of Layer 2 Update frame transmission to disrupt bridge
behavior.

Fix this by postponing transmission of the Layer 2 Update frame from
station entry addition to the point when the station entry is marked
authorized. Similarly, send out the VLAN binding update only if the STA
entry has already been authorized.

Signed-off-by: Jouni Malinen <jouni@codeaurora.org>
Reviewed-by: Johannes Berg <johannes@sipsolutions.net>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>

description: An exploitable denial-of-service vulnerability exists in the Linux kernel prior to mainline 5.3. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by triggering AP to send IAPP location updates for stations before the required authentication process has completed. This could lead to different denial-of-service scenarios, either by causing CAM table attacks, or by leading to traffic flapping if faking already existing clients in other nearby APs of the same wireless infrastructure. An attacker can forge Authentication and Association Request packets to trigger this vulnerability.

code_evidence: In the IEEE80211_STA_AUTHORIZED case, the transition from ASSOC sets WLAN_STA_AUTHORIZED and then immediately invokes ieee80211_check_fast_xmit/check_fast_rx and increments multicast accounting; the code does not gate the Layer 2 update on the RSN 4-way handshake having completed, so a station reaching the authorized state can trigger update behavior tied to association rather than full authentication.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-287 fits because the function's transition to AUTHORIZED is accepted without proving the claimed authenticated identity, enabling use of unauthenticated station state. This is improper authentication, not merely a state-machine logic bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the state machine treats the AUTHORIZED transition as sufficient to enable station forwarding/update behavior without verifying that RSN authentication (4-way handshake) actually completed. Trigger: an attacker forges Authentication/Association frames to drive a station to the authorized state, causing Layer 2 update/fast-path activation prematurely. Consequence: bridge disruption and denial of service via CAM-table manipulation or traffic flapping.

commit_msg:
Release "3.0.6": Fix crashes in Array for "integer overflow #10"

FossilOrigin-Name: 50642d64b8f0a4e62df68e59fcb2ef0923c3dbec8fc8a15d38b1ddbe655c38d6
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    n = Jsi_ObjGetLength(interp, obj);'], 'added_lines': ['    n = jsi_SizeOfArray(interp, obj);']}
description: Integer overflow vulnerability in function Jsi_ObjSetLength in jsish before 3.0.6, allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary code.

code_evidence: Line 14 obtains the array length n; lines 15-16 convert the attacker-supplied start value to Jsi_Number nstart and cast it to int istart, and lines 19-20 compute istart = (n+istart) for negative values without bounding the arithmetic.
Lines 31-36 similarly cast the attacker-supplied end value to int iend and compute iend = (n+iend) for negatives; line 40 then computes nsiz = iend-istart+1 from these unvalidated int values.
Line 45 passes the possibly wrapped/overflowed nsiz to Jsi_ObjArraySizer, and line 46 only logs an error when the sizer returns <= 0.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the function performs size arithmetic on attacker-controlled integers (n+istart, iend-istart+1) that can overflow or wraparound, and the resulting value is then used for memory sizing. A plain bounds-check weakness (CWE-129) is less precise since the core defect is the overflow in the length computation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: attacker-controlled start/end numbers are cast to int and combined with array length n without range checks, so the derived slice size nsiz at line 40 can overflow or wrap to a small/negative value. Trigger: passing extreme start/end arguments to Array.slice. Supported consequence: the wrapped size is used for allocation/sizing, leading to memory-safety issues such as out-of-bounds access in the subsequent copy loop.

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. The implementations of the `Minimum` and `Maximum` TFLite operators can be used to read data outside of bounds of heap allocated objects, if any of the two input tensor arguments are empty. This is because the broadcasting implementation(https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/0d45ea1ca641b21b73bcf9c00e0179cda284e7e7/tensorflow/lite/kernels/internal/reference/maximum_minimum.h#L52-L56) indexes in both tensors with the same index but does not validate that the index is within bounds. The fix will be included in TensorFlow 2.5.0. We will also cherrypick this commit on TensorFlow 2.4.2, TensorFlow 2.3.3, TensorFlow 2.2.3 and TensorFlow 2.1.4, as these are also affected and still in supported range.

code_evidence: Eval dispatches on the output tensor type and calls TFLiteOperation for each type without first checking whether input1 or input2 contains any elements.
The int8 branch, like the other branches, invokes TFLiteOperation with op_context directly; no guard on tensor element counts precedes it.
The int64 branch similarly forwards op_context to TFLiteOperation, so an empty input tensor reaches the broadcasting implementation.
Only the unsupported-type default returns an error; all supported types fall through to return kTfLiteOk with no empty-input check.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the function allows empty tensors to reach the broadcasting implementation that indexes beyond the intended buffer, causing a read of memory outside the allocated object. This is an out-of-bounds read, not a write or an arithmetic flaw.

evidence_lines.code:
}
return kTfLiteOk;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: Eval lacks a guard for zero-element input tensors before calling TFLiteOperation. Trigger: a model supplies an empty input1 or input2 to a Minimum/Maximum operator. The broadcasting code then indexes both tensors at the same index without validating bounds, reading past the end of the empty heap buffer; the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds heap read (possible crash or memory disclosure).

description: Istio 1.4.x before 1.4.9 and Istio 1.5.x before 1.5.4 contain the following vulnerability when telemetry v2 is enabled: by sending a specially crafted packet, an attacker could trigger a Null Pointer Exception resulting in a Denial of Service. This could be sent to the ingress gateway or a sidecar, triggering a null pointer exception which results in a denial of service. This also affects servicemesh-proxy where a null pointer exception flaw was found in servicemesh-proxy. When running Telemetry v2 (not on by default in version 1.4.x), an attacker could send a specially crafted packet to the ingress gateway or proxy sidecar, triggering a denial of service.

code_evidence: onStart invokes wasm_->onStart_ only when the callback exists, but unconditionally uses wasm_ to copy the root_id and vm_configuration strings and passes this into the VM callback. The function does not check that the VM context has been created before entering this path; the patch adds the in_vm_context_created_ = true flag after the call, indicating the guard state is set here rather than verified.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The supported consequence is a NULL pointer dereference causing a crash, matching CWE-476. The function's missing context-creation guard, rather than an unrelated memory corruption, is the relevant weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that onStart can call into the VM (copyString and onStart_) without a prior check that the VM context exists. A crafted packet or startup sequence reaching this path while the context is not initialized can pass invalid state into the VM, leading to a null dereference and a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
KEYS: Remove key_type::match in favour of overriding default by match_preparse

A previous patch added a ->match_preparse() method to the key type.  This is
allowed to override the function called by the iteration algorithm.
Therefore, we can just set a default that simply checks for an exact match of
the key description with the original criterion data and allow match_preparse
to override it as needed.

The key_type::match op is then redundant and can be removed, as can the
user_match() function.

Signed-off-by: David Howells <dhowells@redhat.com>
Acked-by: Vivek Goyal <vgoyal@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tmatch_data->cmp = asymmetric_key_cmp;']}
description: The KEYS subsystem in the Linux kernel before 3.18 allows local users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and system crash) via vectors involving a NULL value for a certain match field, related to the keyring_search_iterator function in keyring.c.

code_evidence: The function sets match_data->lookup_type to KEYRING_SEARCH_LOOKUP_ITERATE and returns 0 without ever initializing match_data->cmp. The iteration search path subsequently invokes the comparison callback, so cmp remains NULL when a caller relies on this preparse function.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing assignment leaves cmp NULL, and the iteration path dereferences/calls it, matching CWE-476's NULL pointer dereference. The fix adds match_data->cmp = asymmetric_key_cmp, confirming the uninitialized pointer is the defect rather than a generic logic error.

evidence_lines.code:
match_data->lookup_type = KEYRING_SEARCH_LOOKUP_ITERATE;
return 0;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: asymmetric_key_match_preparse leaves the match_data->cmp function pointer uninitialized while selecting the ITERATE lookup type. Trigger: a keyring search iteration invokes cmp on match_data. Consequence: a NULL function-pointer call, causing a NULL pointer dereference and kernel crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
A security advisory (TALOS-2019-0857/CVE-2019-5068) found that
creating shared memory regions with permission mode 0777 could allow
any user to access that memory.  Several Mesa drivers use shared-
memory XImages to implement back buffers for improved performance.

This path changes the shmget() calls to use 0600 (user r/w).

Tested with legacy Xlib driver and llvmpipe.

Cc: mesa-stable@lists.freedesktop.org
Reviewed-by: Kristian H. Kristensen <hoegsberg@google.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['   shminfo->shmid = shmget(IPC_PRIVATE, size, IPC_CREAT|0777);'], 'added_lines': ['   /* 0600 = user read+write */', '   shminfo->shmid = shmget(IPC_PRIVATE, size, IPC_CREAT | 0600);']}
description: An exploitable shared memory permissions vulnerability exists in the functionality of X11 Mesa 3D Graphics Library 19.1.2. An attacker can access the shared memory without any specific permissions to trigger this vulnerability.

code_evidence: shmget(IPC_PRIVATE, size, IPC_CREAT|0777) creates a private shared-memory segment with mode 0777, granting read/write access to all users on the system rather than restricting it to the creating user.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-732 covers assigning permissions to a security-critical resource that allow access by a wider set of actors than required. Here the mode 0777 on the shared-memory segment is exactly such an over-permissive assignment; it is not a missing authorization check (CWE-285) but an insecure permission value at creation.

evidence_lines.code: shminfo->shmid = shmget(IPC_PRIVATE, size, IPC_CREAT|0777);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the permission argument to shmget uses 0777, so the shared-memory back buffer is world-readable/writable. Trigger: any local user attaches to the IPC_PRIVATE segment (e.g., via shmat) while the Mesa client runs. Supported consequence: unintended actors can read or modify the graphics back-buffer contents, exposing or corrupting application data.

description: Gobby 0.4.11 allows a NULL pointer dereference in the D-Bus handler for certain set_language calls.

code_evidence: Line 3 only guards m_current_view with g_assert, which aborts rather than returning; when NDEBUG is set the assertion is compiled out entirely, leaving no check. Lines 4-6 then unconditionally pass GTK_TEXT_BUFFER(m_current_view->get_text_buffer()) to gtk_text_buffer_copy_clipboard, dereferencing m_current_view through ->get_text_buffer().
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences a pointer expected to be valid but which can be NULL, matching CWE-476. The g_assert is not a real NULL check because it aborts (and vanishes under NDEBUG), so it does not prevent the dereference; this is a NULL dereference, not merely an assertion failure.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: m_current_view is assumed non-NULL; the only guard is a g_assert that aborts on failure and is removed under NDEBUG. Trigger: on_copy is invoked (e.g., via D-Bus) when no document/view is open, so m_current_view is NULL. Consequence: the member call at line 5 dereferences NULL, causing a crash (DoS).

commit_msg: ac3dmx: add remain size check (fixes #2627)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t', '\t\tif (!ctx->in_seek) {', '\t\t\t'], 'added_lines': ['', '\t\tif (!ctx->in_seek && remain >= ctx->hdr.framesize) {', '']}
description: Out-of-bounds Read in GitHub repository gpac/gpac prior to 2.2.2.

code_evidence: At line 116 the guard only checks !ctx->in_seek before allocating a frame buffer and copying ctx->hdr.framesize bytes from sync at line 120. It does not verify that remain (the bytes left in the AC3 buffer from line 66) is at least ctx->hdr.framesize. The while(remain) loop at line 78 can reach this block with remain smaller than the frame size, so memcpy reads past the end of the ac3_buffer allocation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because memcpy at line 120 reads past the end of the intended buffer when remain < ctx->hdr.framesize. The patch adds exactly this remain >= framesize constraint to the condition at line 116, confirming the missing bound is the weakness rather than an out-of-bounds write, which would be CWE-787.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the frame-copy path lacks a bound check that remain >= ctx->hdr.framesize before memcpy. Trigger: a truncated or malformed AC3 stream whose parsed header declares a frame size larger than the remaining buffered data. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read of up to framesize bytes from the buffer, leaking memory or crashing.

description: In Wireshark 2.4.0 to 2.4.3 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.11, the JSON, XML, NTP, XMPP, and GDB dissectors could crash. This was addressed in epan/tvbparse.c by limiting the recursion depth.

code_evidence: Line 15 increments tt->recursion_depth and rejects only when it exceeds TVBPARSE_MAX_RECURSION_DEPTH, but the original error exits at lines 19, 29 and 31 return without decrementing, so the counter leaks upward across calls. Line 24 looks up a value_wanted from the key map; when absent and no other condition exists, line 31 returns -1 without balancing the increment. The fix decrements on each early return and once at line 33, keeping depth consistent.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 requires operations reading/writing outside a buffer's intended boundary; this function's defect is an unbalanced recursion counter leading to resource/stack exhaustion and crash, not a memory-boundary violation. The code shows no out-of-bounds index or pointer arithmetic, so CWE-119 is not directly supported; the weakness is closer to uncontrolled recursion/resource exhaustion.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the recursion-depth guard is incremented per cond_hash entry but not decremented on the several error/return paths, so the counter monotonically grows. Trigger: repeated hash-condition evaluation on attacker-controlled dissector input exhausts the depth budget, causing later parsing to abort or recurse unboundedly, yielding a crash/DoS. The consequence is availability loss, not a direct out-of-bounds buffer access.

commit_msg:
gmarkup: Fix unvalidated UTF-8 read in markup parsing error paths

When formatting the error messages for markup parsing errors, the parser
was unconditionally reading a UTF-8 character from the input buffer —
but the buffer might end with a partial code sequence, resulting in
reading off the end of the buffer by up to three bytes.

Fix this and add a test case, courtesy of pdknsk.

Signed-off-by: Philip Withnall <withnall@endlessm.com>

https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/glib/issues/1462
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  char_str (g_utf8_get_char (utf8), buf);'], 'added_lines': ['  gunichar c = g_utf8_get_char_validated (utf8, -1);', '  if (c == (gunichar) -1 || c == (gunichar) -2)', '    {', '      gchar *temp = g_strdup_printf ("\\\\x%02x", (guint)(guchar)*utf8);', '      memset (buf, 0, 8);', '      memcpy (buf, temp, strlen (temp));', '      g_free (temp);', '    }', '  else', '    char_str (c, buf);']}
description: GNOME GLib 2.56.1 has an out-of-bounds read vulnerability in g_markup_parse_context_parse() in gmarkup.c, related to utf8_str().

code_evidence: Line 5 calls g_utf8_get_char(utf8) unconditionally; this routine decodes a UTF-8 character without a length bound and may read up to several bytes past the end of a buffer that terminates with a partial multibyte sequence.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect is a read beyond the intended buffer boundary, matching CWE-125. It is a read, not a write or buffer overflow, so out-of-bounds read is the precise classification.

evidence_lines.code: char_str (g_utf8_get_char (utf8), buf);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decoder is invoked on a pointer with no length limit or validation of the trailing bytes. Trigger: an input buffer ending in an incomplete UTF-8 sequence. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read of up to three bytes past the buffer, potentially exposing adjacent memory or crashing.

commit_msg: added option to disable trivial auth methods
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [''], 'added_lines': ['\tcli_ses.is_trivial_auth = 0;']}
description: An issue was discovered in Dropbear through 2020.81. Due to a non-RFC-compliant check of the available authentication methods in the client-side SSH code, it is possible for an SSH server to change the login process in its favor. This attack can bypass additional security measures such as FIDO2 tokens or SSH-Askpass. Thus, it allows an attacker to abuse a forwarded agent for logging on to another server unnoticed.

code_evidence: The function builds an SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST for the password method, embedding cli_opts.username and the password, then sends it. The added state change cli_ses.is_trivial_auth = 0 (in the patch after line 30) records that this was a non-trivial password authentication attempt, which is the client-side fix for a server that could otherwise manipulate the authentication-method negotiation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-287 fits because the flaw is an improper authentication decision: the client does not adequately prove/constrain the authentication claim path, allowing an attacker to alter the login process. The state flag is the code-level evidence that the auth method was not reliably classified, enabling the bypass.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the client's authentication flow let a malicious SSH server influence which authentication method is used, so the client could be steered into a trivial method instead of the user's intended password/FIDO2/askpass path. Trigger: a server advertising/manipulating available auth methods. Consequence: bypass of additional security measures (e.g., FIDO2, SSH-Askpass) and agent-forwarding abuse for unnoticed login to another server.

The UAF is because:

 mount(pid: 921)               | cifsd(pid: 923)
-------------------------------|-------------------------------
                               | cifs_demultiplex_thread
SMB2_negotiate                 |

  compound_send_recv           |

    wait_for_response          |

1. After send request to server, wait the response until
    mid->mid_state != SUBMITTED;
2. Receive response from server, and set it to mid;
3. Set the mid state to RECEIVED;
4. Kill the process, the mid state already RECEIVED, get 0;
5. Handle and release the negotiate response;
6. UAF.

description: A use-after-free flaw was found in smb2_is_status_io_timeout() in CIFS in the Linux Kernel. After CIFS transfers response data to a system call, there are still local variable points to the memory region, and if the system call frees it faster than CIFS uses it, CIFS will access a free memory region, leading to a denial of service.

code_evidence: Lines 12-15 conditionally invoke server->ops->handle_cancelled_mid when resp_buf is set, MID_WAIT_CANCELLED is flagged, and mid_state is MID_RESPONSE_RECEIVED. The patch widens this to also accept MID_RESPONSE_READY, gating the callback on the buffer still being valid.

Lines 19 and 21 release resp_buf via cifs_buf_release or cifs_small_buf_release after the callback; the callback runs before this free, but a waiter that observed RECEIVED could proceed to free the buffer concurrently.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The callback dereferences resp_buf after another thread may have freed it via cifs_buf_release, matching CWE-416's reuse of freed memory. This is a lifetime/ordering race rather than a pure double-free (CWE-415), since the defect is use after release.

evidence_lines.code:
if (midEntry->resp_buf && (midEntry->mid_flags & MID_WAIT_CANCELLED) &&
midEntry->mid_state == MID_RESPONSE_RECEIVED &&
server->ops->handle_cancelled_mid)
server->ops->handle_cancelled_mid(midEntry, server);

cifs_buf_release(midEntry->resp_buf);
cifs_small_buf_release(midEntry->resp_buf);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: A synchronous caller waiting on the mid can see MID_RESPONSE_RECEIVED, return, and release resp_buf while cifsd still invokes the cancelled-mid callback that dereferences the same buffer. The missing MID_RESPONSE_READY state let the waiter free memory before the receive path finished using it, producing a read-after-free and crash/DoS.

In the client, read the reply headers from a coroutine, switching the
read side between the "read header" coroutine and the I/O coroutine that

description: Race conditions in opa-fm before 10.4.0.0.196 and opa-ff before 10.4.0.0.197.

code_evidence: The caller-supplied client_path is copied verbatim into hdl->c_path with strcpy, with no creation or exclusive reservation of the file at this point.
The handle is published to the caller via *p_hdl and marked HSM_COM_C_STATE_IN without atomically acquiring ownership of the client_path resource.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is a timing window over a shared filesystem resource (the client_path) with no atomic exclusive acquisition, matching CWE-362's non-atomic access to a shared resource. It is not merely a path-traversal issue; the defect is the race/exclusivity gap, though CWE-377 (insecure temp file) is the closer child.

strcpy(hdl->s_path,server_path);
strcpy(hdl->c_path,client_path);

hdl->client_state = HSM_COM_C_STATE_IN;
*p_hdl = hdl;

Trigger: a local attacker pre-creates or symlinks the well-known client path. Consequence: the client operates on an attacker-controlled file, enabling data exposure or corruption.

There is a race between the assignment of `table->data` and write value
to the pointer of `table->data` in the __do_proc_doulongvec_minmax() on
the other thread.

                                        proc_sys_write
  hugetlb_sysctl_handler                  proc_sys_call_handler
  hugetlb_sysctl_handler_common             hugetlb_sysctl_handler

      proc_doulongvec_minmax

            *i = val;  // corrupt CPU1's stack

description: A race condition between hugetlb sysctl handlers in mm/hugetlb.c in the Linux kernel before 5.8.8 could be used by local attackers to corrupt memory, cause a NULL pointer dereference, or possibly have unspecified other impact, aka CID-17743798d812.

code_evidence: The handler mutates the caller-supplied ctl_table in place: it assigns table->data = &tmp (a pointer to this invocation's stack local) and table->maxlen before passing the shared table to proc_doulongvec_minmax(). If two threads execute this handler concurrently on the same sysctl table, one thread's write to table->data can occur after the other thread has already read table->data inside __do_proc_doulongvec_minmax(), causing that thread to write through a stale pointer into another thread's stack.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a classic race condition: a shared resource (the ctl_table) is accessed by concurrent code sequences without exclusive access or synchronization, violating atomicity/exclusivity. It is not merely a missing bounds check; the defect is the unsynchronized shared-state mutation across concurrent invocations, matching CWE-362.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the shared ctl_table object is modified with no synchronization, so the assignment of table->data and the subsequent read of table->data by the proc handler are not atomic with respect to concurrent invocations. Trigger: two local threads racing on the same hugetlb sysctl write. Consequence: memory corruption of another thread's stack, leading to a NULL-pointer dereference/crash or other impact.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\t\tbits = (m_distance >= COUNTOF(distanceExtraBits)) ? distanceExtraBits[29] : distanceExtraBits[m_distance];'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\t\tif (m_distance >= COUNTOF(distanceExtraBits))', '\t\t\t\t\t\tthrow BadDistanceErr();', '\t\t\t\t\tbits = distanceExtraBits[m_distance];', '\t\t\t\t\t// TODO: this surfaced during fuzzing. What do we do???', '\t\t\t\t\tCRYPTOPP_ASSERT(m_distance < COUNTOF(distanceStarts));', '\t\t\t\t\tif (m_distance >= COUNTOF(distanceStarts))', '\t\t\t\t\t\tthrow BadDistanceErr();']}
description: Crypto++ (aka cryptopp) through 5.6.5 contains an out-of-bounds read vulnerability in zinflate.cpp in the Inflator filter.

code_evidence: At DISTANCE_BITS, m_distance is used to index distanceExtraBits[73] and distanceStarts[79]. Only a CRYPTOPP_ASSERT guards the bound at [72]; in release builds it is compiled out. The ternary at [73] clamps the extra-bits lookup to distanceExtraBits[29], but the subsequent distanceStarts[m_distance] at [79] is indexed with the unvalidated m_distance, and m_distance is attacker-influenced because it comes from distanceDecoder.Decode at [66].
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Indexing distanceStarts with an unchecked attacker-controlled index reads past the end of a fixed array, which is a read past the end of an intended buffer, matching CWE-125. The related CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write) does not apply because the faulty operation is a read used to compute a distance, not a write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: m_distance from the Huffman distance decoder is not range-checked against COUNTOF(distanceStarts) before indexing, since the assert at [72] is non-enforcing. Trigger: a crafted DEFLATE stream yields a distance code >= 30. Consequence: an out-of-bounds read of distanceStarts at [79], causing address-sanitizer findings or crash. The clamp at [73] only fixes the distanceExtraBits lookup, not the distanceStarts read.

commit_msg:
Allow fuse device clones to refer to be distinguished.  This patch just
adds the infrastructure by associating a separate "struct fuse_dev" with
each clone.

Signed-off-by: Miklos Szeredi <mszeredi@suse.cz>
Reviewed-by: Ashish Samant <ashish.samant@oracle.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\t\tstruct fuse_conn *fc = fuse_get_conn(old);', '\t\t\t\tif (fc) {', '\t\t\t\t\terr = fuse_device_clone(fc, file);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\t\tstruct fuse_dev *fud = fuse_get_dev(old);', '\t\t\t\tif (fud) {', '\t\t\t\t\terr = fuse_device_clone(fud->fc, file);']}
description: Memory leak in the cuse_channel_release function in fs/fuse/cuse.c in the Linux kernel before 4.4 allows local users to cause a denial of service (memory consumption) or possibly have unspecified other impact by opening /dev/cuse many times.

code_evidence: The ioctl handler obtains a reference to the caller-supplied fd via fget(old) at line 9, then resolves the associated fuse connection with fuse_get_conn(old) at line 12. When a connection is found (line 13), it locks fuse_mutex and calls fuse_device_clone(fc, file) at line 15 to create a cloned device, then unlocks and releases the file reference with fput(old) at line 18. The function itself performs no resource-accounting or cleanup of the object created by fuse_device_clone; it relies entirely on the callee and later release paths.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-399 (Resource Management Errors) is the target category for improper management of system resources; the code's clone-on-ioctl flow with no corresponding resource release supports that categorization. A more specific descendant such as CWE-772 (missing release) would be narrower, but the target label is the resource-management category.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the clone path acquires and clones the connection but the paired resource ownership/cleanup is not balanced in the release path, so repeated FUSE_DEV_IOC_CLONE calls on /dev/cuse accumulate unreleased fuse_dev/connection resources. Trigger: a local user repeatedly opens the device and issues the clone ioctl. Supported consequence: unbounded memory consumption leading to denial of service.

description: omx/OMXNodeInstance.cpp in libstagefright in mediaserver in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-08-01 does not validate the buffer port, which allows attackers to gain privileges via a crafted application, aka internal bug 28816827.

code_evidence: Line 6 resolves the buffer header from the caller-supplied buffer id without validating portIndex; line 7 immediately dereferences header->pAppPrivate, so a header found for an unexpected/absent port yields an invalid pointer dereference.
Line 8 passes header and portIndex to OMX_FreeBuffer, using the unvalidated port association.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unchecked header dereference performs an operation on a memory location outside the intended buffer, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. description: The NetKVM Windows Virtio driver allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (guest crash) via a crafted length value in an IP packet, as demonstrated by a value that does not account for the size of the IP options.

code_evidence: The function gates UDP header access only on len >= ipHeaderSize + sizeof(UDPHeader), without checking the IP header's own declared or actual size.

When the length check passes, pUdpHeader is derived from the caller-supplied ipHeaderSize and udp_length is read from that location; datagramLength is captured but never compared against the remaining buffer (len - udpDataStart).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is missing validation of attacker-controlled packet length/offset metadata before use, which is improper input validation (CWE-20). It is not a simple out-of-bounds read alone, since the defect is the absent consistency check on ipHeaderSize and datagramLength.

evidence_lines.code:
if (len >= udpDataStart)
{

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the parser validates only that the buffer covers a fixed minimum, not that ipHeaderSize accounts for IP options or that datagramLength fits the available data. A crafted packet with an inconsistent length value passes the check and the parser proceeds on a header offset/length that was never validated, letting malformed metadata reach later processing and crash the guest (supported consequence: DoS).

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tpriv->tx_buff[*txbd_curr].skb = skb;'], 'added_lines': ['', '\t/* Make sure info word is set */', '\twmb();', '', '\tpriv->tx_buff[*txbd_curr].skb = skb;']}
description: An issue was discovered in drivers/net/ethernet/arc/emac_main.c in the Linux kernel before 4.5. A use-after-free is caused by a race condition between the functions arc_emac_tx and arc_emac_tx_clean.

code_evidence: The transmit buffer's skb pointer is published at line 26 before the descriptor data and info word are fully initialized, so the descriptor is visible to arc_emac_tx_clean() before FOR_EMAC is set.
The descriptor index is advanced and the queue state is rechecked with barriers, but the ordering that makes the descriptor consumable is not enforced before the skb is stored.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: This is a concurrent access ordering flaw: the shared descriptor is exposed to another code sequence before initialization is complete, violating exclusivity/atomicity. CWE-362 fits the race; the use-after-free is the downstream consequence, not the primary weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: arc_emac_tx() writes priv->tx_buff[*txbd_curr].skb before the descriptor's data/info fields are completed, creating a window in which arc_emac_tx_clean() sees a non-null data pointer but no FOR_EMAC bit, treats the buffer as completed, and frees the skb while arc_emac_tx() is still submitting it. Trigger: concurrent TX submission and completion cleanup (e.g., heavy traffic). Consequence: use-after-free of the skb, leading to kernel crash/instability.

commit_msg:
There is a possible data race as shown below:

thread-A in nci_request()       | thread-B in nci_close_device()
                                | mutex_lock(&ndev->req_lock);
test_bit(NCI_UP, &ndev->flags); |
...                             | test_and_clear_bit(NCI_UP, &ndev->flags)
mutex_lock(&ndev->req_lock);    |
                                |

This race will allow __nci_request() to be awaked while the device is
getting removed.

Similar to commit e2cb6b891ad2 ("bluetooth: eliminate the potential race
condition when removing the HCI controller"). this patch alters the
function sequence in nci_request() to prevent the data races between the
nci_close_device().

Signed-off-by: Lin Ma <linma@zju.edu.cn>
Fixes: 6a2968aaf50c ("NFC: basic NCI protocol implementation")
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20211115145600.8320-1-linma@zju.edu.cn
Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!test_bit(NCI_UP, &ndev->flags))', '\t\treturn -ENETDOWN;', '', '\trc = __nci_request(ndev, req, opt, timeout);'], 'added_lines': ['\t/* check the state after obtaing the lock against any races', '\t * from nci_close_device when the device gets removed.', '\t */', '\tif (test_bit(NCI_UP, &ndev->flags))', '\t\trc = __nci_request(ndev, req, opt, timeout);', '\telse', '\t\trc = -ENETDOWN;']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in nci_request in net/nfc/nci/core.c in NFC Controller Interface (NCI) in the Linux kernel. This flaw could allow a local attacker with user privileges to cause a data race problem while the device is getting removed, leading to a privilege escalation problem.

code_evidence: The NCI_UP state check is performed outside the req_lock critical section, so it is not synchronized with concurrent state changes.
The lock is acquired only after the check, and __nci_request is invoked under the lock without re-validating NCI_UP.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the function has a check-then-lock sequence that lacks atomicity over the shared ndev->flags state, allowing an interfering concurrent sequence to modify it. The unsynchronized state access, not merely the later use, is the supported weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!test_bit(NCI_UP, &ndev->flags))
return -ENETDOWN;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the NCI_UP flag test is not protected by req_lock, so another thread such as nci_close_device can clear NCI_UP between the test and lock acquisition. Trigger: concurrent device removal while a request is in flight. Consequence: __nci_request may run on a device being torn down, producing the described use-after-free/data race.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    \t/* Make sure the BYE reason does not exceed:', '    \t * - the size of the available buffer', "    \t * - the declared reason's length", '    \t * - the actual packet size', '    \t */', '        reason.slen = PJ_MIN(reason.slen, size-9);', '']}
description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in C language implementing standard based protocols such as SIP, SDP, RTP, STUN, TURN, and ICE. In affected versions if the incoming RTCP BYE message contains a reason's length, this declared length is not checked against the actual received packet size, potentially resulting in an out-of-bound read access. This issue affects all users that use PJMEDIA and RTCP. A malicious actor can send a RTCP BYE message with an invalid reason length. Users are advised to upgrade as soon as possible. There are no known workarounds.

code_evidence: Guarded only by size > 8, the function reads the declared reason length byte at pkt+8 and uses PJ_MIN against the buffer size, not against the received packet size.
It then copies reason.slen bytes from pkt+9 without verifying that size-9 bytes are actually present, so a declared length larger than the packet causes pj_memcpy to read past the packet end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the missing size-9 bound lets the copy read memory past the intended packet buffer. This is an out-of-bounds read, not a write, since the destination buffer is bounded by sizeof(peer_sdes_buf_).

evidence_lines.code:
pj_memcpy(sess->stat.peer_sdes_buf_, ((pj_uint8_t*)pkt+9),
reason.slen);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the attacker-controlled reason length is never clamped to the actual received packet size. Trigger: a BYE packet with size > 8 whose reason length byte exceeds size-9. Consequence: out-of-bounds read from pkt beyond the packet buffer during the copy.

description: Simple Desktop Display Manager (SDDM) before 0.10.0 allows local users to gain root privileges because code running as root performs write operations within a user home directory, and this user may have created links in advance (exploitation requires the user to win a race condition in the ~/.Xauthority chown case, but not other cases).

It then calls addCookie on that path and chown()s it to pw->pw_uid/pw->pw_gid, performing privileged write and ownership operations inside a directory the unprivileged user controls.

CWE-264 covers such management of permissions and privileges; it is not merely an authentication failure, since authentication succeeds before the unsafe privileged file operation.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: privileged code writes and chowns a file in the user's home directory without ensuring the path is not a pre-created symlink or otherwise user-controlled. Trigger: an authenticated local user pre-creates ~/.Xauthority as a link to a root-owned target before login completes. Consequence: the root-executed addCookie/chown operations follow the link, allowing the user to corrupt or take ownership of root files and gain privileges.

commit_msg:
Doing a "get_user_pages()" on a copy-on-write page for reading can be
ambiguous: the page can be COW'ed at any time afterwards, and the
direction of a COW event isn't defined.

Yes, whoever writes to it will generally do the COW, but if the thread
that did the get_user_pages() unmapped the page before the write (and
that could happen due to memory pressure in addition to any outright
action), the writer could also just take over the old page instead.

End result: the get_user_pages() call might result in a page pointer
that is no longer associated with the original VM, and is associated
with - and controlled by - another VM having taken it over instead.

So when doing a get_user_pages() on a COW mapping, the only really safe
thing to do would be to break the COW when getting the page, even when
only getting it for reading.

At the same time, some users simply don't even care.

For example, the perf code wants to look up the page not because it
cares about the page, but because the code simply wants to look up the
physical address of the access for informational purposes, and doesn't
really care about races when a page might be unmapped and remapped
elsewhere.

This adds logic to force a COW event by setting FOLL_WRITE on any
copy-on-write mapping when FOLL_GET (or FOLL_PIN) is used to get a page
pointer as a result.

The current semantics end up being:

 - __get_user_pages_fast(): no change. If you don't ask for a write,
   you won't break COW. You'd better know what you're doing.

 - get_user_pages_fast(): the fast-case "look it up in the page tables
   without anything getting mmap_sem" now refuses to follow a read-only
   page, since it might need COW breaking.  Which happens in the slow
   path - the fast path doesn't know if the memory might be COW or not.

 - get_user_pages() (including the slow-path fallback for gup_fast()):
   for a COW mapping, turn on FOLL_WRITE for FOLL_GET/FOLL_PIN, with
   very similar semantics to FOLL_FORCE.

If it turns out that we want finer granularity (ie "only break COW when
it might actually matter" - things like the zero page are special and
don't need to be broken) we might need to push these semantics deeper
into the lookup fault path.  So if people care enough, it's possible
that we might end up adding a new internal FOLL_BREAK_COW flag to go
with the internal FOLL_COW flag we already have for tracking "I had a
COW".

Alternatively, if it turns out that different callers might want to
explicitly control the forced COW break behavior, we might even want to
make such a flag visible to the users of get_user_pages() instead of
using the above default semantics.

But for now, this is mostly commentary on the issue (this commit message
being a lot bigger than the patch, and that patch in turn is almost all
comments), with that minimal "enable COW breaking early" logic using the
existing FOLL_WRITE behavior.

[ It might be worth noting that we've always had this ambiguity, and it
  could arguably be seen as a user-space issue.

  You only get private COW mappings that could break either way in
  situations where user space is doing cooperative things (ie fork()
  before an execve() etc), but it _is_ surprising and very subtle, and
  fork() is supposed to give you independent address spaces.

  So let's treat this as a kernel issue and make the semantics of
  get_user_pages() easier to understand. Note that obviously a true
  shared mapping will still get a page that can change under us, so this
  does _not_ mean that get_user_pages() somehow returns any "stable"
  page ]

Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Tested-by: Christoph Hellwig <hch@lst.de>
Acked-by: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>

You'll get _a_ COW page, but", '\t * not necessarily the one you intended to get depending on what', '\t * COW event happens after this. COW may break the page copy in a', '\t * random direction.']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.7.3, related to mm/gup.c and mm/huge_memory.c. The get_user_pages (aka gup) implementation, when used for a copy-on-write page, does not properly consider the semantics of read operations and therefore can grant unintended write access, aka CID-17839856fd58.

code_evidence: gup_flags starts as FOLL_GET and FOLL_WRITE is added only when the caller passes write; a read-only request therefore does not force a COW break.
The fast path calls gup_pgd_range under local_irq_save/restore with those flags, so a read-only gup_fast() can return a page pointer without breaking COW first.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The returned page is a shared resource accessed without a synchronization step that excludes concurrent COW modification, which is the timing-window violation described by CWE-362. The race is between the GUP lookup and a later COW event; the fix forces the break early rather than addressing a separate memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: A read-only fault-follow in the fast GUP path obtains a page for a COW mapping without exclusive ownership of that page. Before the caller uses it, a concurrent writer (or unmap/remap under memory pressure) can trigger COW in either direction, so the returned page may no longer belong to the original VM and may be controlled by another address space. The root cause is the missing forced COW break for FOLL_GET read-only requests; the consequence is a stale or foreign page reference used by the caller.

structs to userspace without initializing all members of these
structs. Clear out this memory to prevent information leaks.

Fixes: 423400e64d377 ("scsi: aacraid: Include HBA direct interface")
Fixes: c799d519bf088 ("scsi: aacraid: Retrieve HBA host information ioctl")
Signed-off-by: Seth Forshee <seth.forshee@canonical.com>
Reviewed-by: Johannes Thumshirn <jthumshirn@suse.de>
Signed-off-by: Martin K. Petersen <martin.petersen@oracle.com>

description: An issue was discovered in drivers/scsi/aacraid/commctrl.c in the Linux kernel before 4.13. There is potential exposure of kernel stack memory because aac_send_raw_srb does not initialize the reply structure.

code_evidence: A stack-allocated struct aac_srb_reply reply is declared at line 402 and only partially written: status at 403; in the fast-response branch srb_status, scsi_status, data_xfer_length, sense_data_size and sense_data are set, but in the non-fast branch the same fields are assigned from err while other members of the struct remain uninitialized. The whole struct is then copied to userspace via copy_to_user(user_reply, &reply, sizeof(struct aac_srb_reply)) at lines 419-420, so uninitialized stack bytes are disclosed to the caller.

That is a direct information exposure, matching CWE-200, rather than an out-of-bounds read or a different root-cause weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the reply struct on the stack is not fully initialized before being copied to user space. Trigger: a CAP_SYS_ADMIN caller issues a raw SRB to a native device; the code copies sizeof(struct aac_srb_reply) bytes including padding/unwritten members. Consequence: kernel stack memory contents leak to userspace, an information exposure (confidentiality loss).

commit_msg:
usb: max-3421: Prevent corruption of freed memory

The MAX-3421 USB driver remembers the state of the USB toggles for a
device/endpoint. To save SPI writes, this was only done when a new
device/endpoint was being used. Unfortunately, if the old device was
removed, this would cause writes to freed memory.

To fix this, a simpler scheme is used. The toggles are read from
hardware when a URB is completed, and the toggles are always written to
hardware when any URB transaction is started. This will cause a few more
SPI transactions, but no causes kernel panics.

Fixes: 2d53139f3162 ("Add support for using a MAX3421E chip as a host driver.")
Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Mark Tomlinson <mark.tomlinson@alliedtelesis.co.nz>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20210625031456.8632-1-mark.tomlinson@alliedtelesis.co.nz
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t/* save the old end-points toggles: */', '\t\tu8 hrsl = spi_rd8(hcd, MAX3421_REG_HRSL);', '\t\tint rcvtog = (hrsl >> MAX3421_HRSL_RCVTOGRD_BIT) & 1;', '\t\tint sndtog = (hrsl >> MAX3421_HRSL_SNDTOGRD_BIT) & 1;', '\t\tint epnum = usb_endpoint_num(&urb->ep->desc);', '', "\t\t/* no locking: HCD (i.e., we) own toggles, don't we? */", '\t\tusb_settoggle(urb->dev, epnum, 0, rcvtog);', '\t\tusb_settoggle(urb->dev, epnum, 1, sndtog);', '']}
description: drivers/usb/host/max3421-hcd.c in the Linux kernel before 5.13.6 allows physically proximate attackers to cause a denial of service (use-after-free and panic) by removing a MAX-3421 USB device in certain situations.

code_evidence: After urb_done, curr_urb is cleared and the URB is unlinked and given back to the USB core via usb_hcd_giveback_urb, which allows the completion handler to release the URB and its endpoint/device references. The function keeps no copy of the endpoint toggle state before this point; subsequent toggle handling for the same endpoint/device relied on cached state that could outlive the freed device.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is reuse of a device/endpoint object after it has been freed, matching CWE-416. The fix reads toggles from hardware and writes them on each transaction, removing the stale cached reference; this is a use-after-free, not merely a null dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the driver deferred writing endpoint toggle state to hardware and cached it keyed on device/endpoint, so when a device was removed its freed memory remained referenced by the toggle bookkeeping. Trigger: removing the MAX-3421 USB device, or completing a URB after the device is gone, causes the driver to access freed device/endpoint state, producing a kernel panic (DoS).

This allows a user to call static methods or access static members without running the class initialization method, and may allow a user to observe uninitialized values.

((J9RAMStaticFieldRef *)&ramCP[cpIndex])->flagsAndClass = ramStaticFieldRef->flagsAndClass;

commit_msg:
Fix STARTTLS response injection attack.

Thanks again to Damian Poddebniak and Fabian Ising from the Münster
University of Applied Sciences for reporting this issue.  Their
summary in ticket 248 states the issue clearly:

  We found another STARTTLS-related issue in Mutt. Unfortunately, it
  affects SMTP, POP3 and IMAP.

  When the server responds with its "let's do TLS now message", e.g. A
  OK begin TLS\r\n in IMAP or +OK begin TLS\r\n in POP3, Mutt will
  also read any data after the \r\n and save it into some internal
  buffer for later processing. This is problematic, because a MITM
  attacker can inject arbitrary responses.

  There is a nice blogpost by Wietse Venema about a "command
  injection" in postfix (http://www.postfix.org/CVE-2011-0411.html).
  What we have here is the problem in reverse, i.e. not a command
  injection, but a "response injection."

This commit fixes the issue by clearing the CONNECTION input buffer in
mutt_ssl_starttls().

To make backporting this fix easier, the new functions only clear the
top-level CONNECTION buffer; they don't handle nested buffering in
mutt_zstrm.c or mutt_sasl.c.  However both of those wrap the
connection *after* STARTTLS, so this is currently okay.  mutt_tunnel.c
occurs before connecting, but it does not perform any nesting.

This warns the user that something', '       weird is going on.', '    */', '    mutt_error _("Warning: clearing unexpected buffered data before STARTTLS");', '    mutt_sleep (0);', '    mutt_socket_clear_buffered_input (conn);', '  }']}
description: Mutt before 1.14.4 and NeoMutt before 2020-06-19 have a STARTTLS buffering issue that affects IMAP, SMTP, and POP3. When a server sends a "begin TLS" response, the client reads additional data (e.g., from a man-in-the-middle attacker) and evaluates it in a TLS context, aka "response injection."

Merge pull request from GHSA-8hcp-hm38-mfph

* Check hostname during TLS transport selection

* remove the code in create_request that has been moved

description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in C language implementing standard based protocols such as SIP, SDP, RTP, STUN, TURN, and ICE. In version 2.10 and earlier, PJSIP transport can be reused if they have the same IP address + port + protocol. However, this is insufficient for secure transport since it lacks remote hostname authentication. Suppose we have created a TLS connection to `sip.foo.com`, which has an IP address `100.1.1.1`. If we want to create a TLS connection to another hostname, say `sip.bar.com`, which has the same IP address, then it will reuse that existing connection, even though `100.1.1.1` does not have certificate to authenticate as `sip.bar.com`. The vulnerability allows for an insecure interaction without user awareness. It affects users who need access to connections to different destinations that translate to the same address, and allows man-in-the-middle attack if attacker can route a connection to another destination such as in the case of DNS spoofing.

code_evidence: When the target address list is empty, the destination host name is copied into tdata->dest_info.name before resolution; this name is used for transport selection/reuse, so it must reflect the actual requested hostname for TLS authentication.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is failure to properly validate/associate the certificate with the intended hostname during secure transport reuse, which is improper certificate validation (CWE-295) rather than a generic spoofing issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the destination hostname associated with the TX data is not reliably bound to the requested destination when transport reuse is considered, allowing a TLS connection established for one hostname to be matched to another hostname sharing the same IP/port/protocol. Trigger: two destinations resolving to the same address. Consequence: TLS certificate/hostname authentication is bypassed, enabling man-in-the-middle.

commit 2dcab5984841 ("sctp: avoid BUG_ON on sctp_wait_for_sndbuf")
attempted to avoid a BUG_ON call when the association being used for a
sendmsg() is blocked waiting for more sndbuf and another thread did a
peeloff operation on such asoc, moving it to another socket.

As Ben Hutchings noticed, then in such case it would return without
locking back the socket and would cause two unlocks in a row.

Further analysis also revealed that it could allow a double free if the
application managed to peeloff the asoc that is created during the
sendmsg call, because then sctp_sendmsg() would try to free the asoc
that was created only for that call.

This patch takes another approach. It will deny the peeloff operation
if there is a thread sleeping on the asoc, so this situation doesn't
exist anymore. This avoids the issues described above and also honors
the syscalls that are already being handled (it can be multiple sendmsg
calls).

Joint work with Xin Long.

Fixes: 2dcab5984841 ("sctp: avoid BUG_ON on sctp_wait_for_sndbuf")
Cc: Alexander Popov <alex.popov@linux.com>
Cc: Ben Hutchings <ben@decadent.org.uk>
Signed-off-by: Marcelo Ricardo Leitner <marcelo.leitner@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Xin Long <lucien.xin@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: David S. Miller <davem@davemloft.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t/* If there is a thread waiting on more sndbuf space for', '\t * sending on this asoc, it cannot be peeled.', '\t */', '\tif (waitqueue_active(&asoc->wait))', '\t\treturn -EBUSY;']}
description: net/sctp/socket.c in the Linux kernel through 4.10.1 does not properly restrict association peel-off operations during certain wait states, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (invalid unlock and double free) via a multithreaded application.  NOTE: this vulnerability exists because of an incorrect fix for CVE-2017-5986.

code_evidence: sctp_do_peeloff resolves the association by id and returns -EINVAL when none exists; it does not check whether another thread is sleeping on asoc->wait.
The only style guard rejects non-UDP sockets; it does not prevent peeloff while a concurrent sendmsg is blocked waiting for sndbuf space on the same association.
The function then creates a new socket and migrates the association to it via sctp_sock_migrate, moving the asoc out from under the blocked sender.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing waitqueue check permits the association to be migrated and freed while another path still holds a reference and frees it on resume, producing the double free of the same memory described by CWE-415. It is not merely a race on a lock; the supported consequence is repeated free of one object.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!sctp_style(sk, UDP))
return -EINVAL;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: peeloff is allowed on an association that a concurrent sendmsg is blocked on (waitqueue_active(&asoc->wait) is not checked). Trigger: a multithreaded application peels off the asoc while another thread sleeps in sctp_wait_for_sndbuf. Consequence: the blocked sendmsg resumes after the asoc was migrated/freed, leading to invalid unlock and double free of the asoc.

commit_msg:
DO NOT MERGE mm-video-v4l2: venc: add checks before accessing heap pointers

Heap pointers do not point to user virtual addresses in case
of secure session.
Set them to NULL and add checks to avoid accesing them

Bug: 28815329
Bug: 28920116

Change-Id: I94fd5808e753b58654d65e175d3857ef46ffba26
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (venc_handle->is_secure_session()) {', '        DEBUG_PRINT_ERROR("logging secure input buffers is not allowed!");', '        return -1;', '    }', '']}
description: The secure-session feature in the mm-video-v4l2 venc component in mediaserver in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-08-01 mishandles heap pointers, which allows attackers to gain privileges via a crafted application, aka internal bug 28815329.

code_evidence: Line 21 casts pbuffer->pBuffer to a raw char pointer and the metadatamode==1 branch mmaps fd then fwrite's m_sVenc_cfg.input_height rows of input_width bytes, advancing ptemp by stride, plus a chroma loop starting at pvirt+(stride*scanlines).
The else branch iterates over temp = pbuffer->pBuffer for the same row/chroma counts and advances by stride without validating that the buffer actually contains stride*scanlines bytes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The loops perform fwrite reads at addresses ptemp/temp advanced by stride for height and height/2 iterations; if the buffer is smaller than the configured dimensions, the read crosses the buffer's intended boundary, matching CWE-119. This is an out-of-bounds read driven by unchecked size assumptions, not an integer overflow or a null dereference.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function writes image rows from a heap/user buffer (or mmap'd fd) to a file using dimensions from m_sVenc_cfg, but never checks that the underlying buffer's size matches stride*scanlines. In secure sessions pBuffer does not point to user virtual memory; the added guard prevents logging there, but within the logging path the loop bounds are derived from configured width/height rather than the actual buffer length, so a mismatched or secure buffer leads to reads past the intended boundary.

commit_msg:
gsocketclient: Fix criticals

This ensures the parent GTask is kept alive as long as an enumeration
is running and trying to connect.

Closes #1646
Closes #1649
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  if (g_task_return_error_if_cancelled (data->task))', '        return;', '      enumerator_next_async (data);'], 'added_lines': ['  if (task_completed_or_cancelled (data->task))', '        {', '          g_object_unref (data->task);', '          return;', '        }', '      enumerator_next_async (data, FALSE);']}
description: gio/gsocketclient.c in GNOME GLib 2.59.2 does not ensure that a parent GTask remains alive during the execution of a connection-attempting enumeration, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (g_socket_client_connected_callback mishandling and application crash) via a crafted web site, as demonstrated by GNOME Web (aka Epiphany).

code_evidence: The cancellation check only tests g_task_return_error_if_cancelled, returning and unreffing the task when cancelled, but does not distinguish a completed task from a cancelled one.
When address is NULL and connection attempts are still pending, the function returns without unref'ing data->task, leaving the parent GTask unowned.
When create_socket fails, the address is unreffed and enumerator_next_async(data) is called without a completion flag, so the enumeration proceeds while the task may already be completed.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-754 fits because the function fails to check for the unusual condition that the parent GTask is already completed during an asynchronous enumeration, leading to an application crash. This is an improper check for an exceptional state, not a memory-safety flaw like use-after-free.

evidence_lines.code:
if (data->connection_attempts)
return;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The callback does not properly check whether the parent GTask has already been completed or cancelled before continuing the enumeration and connection setup. A crafted web site triggers connection attempts that complete the task while the enumerator callback still runs, so the callback mishandles the finished task and the application crashes.

commit_msg:
x86: don't wrongly trigger linear page table assertion

_put_page_type() may do multiple iterations until its cmpxchg()
succeeds. It invokes set_tlbflush_timestamp() on the first
iteration, however. Code inside the function takes care of this, but
- the assertion in _put_final_page_type() would trigger on the second
  iteration if time stamps in a debug build are permitted to be
  sufficiently much wider than the default 6 bits (see WRAP_MASK in
  flushtlb.c),
- it returning -EINTR (for a continuation to be scheduled) would leave
  the page inconsistent state (until the re-invocation completes).
Make the set_tlbflush_timestamp() invocation conditional, bypassing it
(for now) only in the case we really can't tolerate the stamp to be
stored.

This is part of XSA-240.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['#ifdef CONFIG_PV_LINEAR_PT', '            if ( ptpg && PGT_type_equal(x, ptpg->u.inuse.type_info) )', '                 * linear_pt_count lives in. Unvalidated page table pages,', '                 * however, should occur during domain destruction only', '                 * anyway.  Updating of linear_pt_count luckily is not', '                 * necessary anymore for a dying domain.', '                ASSERT(page_get_owner(page)->is_dying);', '                ASSERT(page->linear_pt_count < 0);', '                ASSERT(ptpg->linear_pt_count > 0);', '                ptpg = NULL;', '#else /* CONFIG_PV_LINEAR_PT */', '            BUG_ON(ptpg && PGT_type_equal(x, ptpg->u.inuse.type_info));', '#endif', '', '            set_tlbflush_timestamp(page);'], 'added_lines': ['            if ( !ptpg || !PGT_type_equal(x, ptpg->u.inuse.type_info) )', '                 * linear_pt_count lives in. Pages (including page table ones),', "                 * however, don't need their flush time stamp set except when", '                 * the last reference is being dropped. For page table pages', '                 * this happens in _put_final_page_type().', '                set_tlbflush_timestamp(page);', '            else', '                BUG_ON(!IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_PV_LINEAR_PT));']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.9.x allowing x86 PV guest OS users to cause a denial of service (unbounded recursion, stack consumption, and hypervisor crash) or possibly gain privileges via crafted page-table stacking.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function's control flow only manages page type reference counts and TLB flush timestamps; no allocation, tracking, or throttling of a limited resource that could be exhausted is shown, so CWE-400 is not directly supported.

commit_msg:
fix: crash when too many elements in delayed output (as slurs)

The size of the temporary buffer used for delayed output was not correct.
Now, this buffer is allocated from the heap with the same size as the
output normal buffer.

Issue #16.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tchar *outbuf_sav, *mbf_sav, tmpbuf[20 * 1024];'], 'added_lines': ['\tchar *outbuf_sav, *mbf_sav, *tmpbuf;', '\ttmpbuf = malloc(outbufsz);', '\tif (!tmpbuf) {', '\t\terror(1, NULL, "Out of memory for delayed outbuf - abort");', '\t\texit(EXIT_FAILURE);', '\t}', '\tfree(tmpbuf);']}
description: Stack-based buffer overflow in the delayed_output function in music.c in abcm2ps through 8.13.20 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact.

code_evidence: A fixed-size stack buffer tmpbuf[20 * 1024] is declared and made the active output buffer via mbf = outbuf = tmpbuf, so all output generated during draw_systems is written through this 20 KB region.

draw_systems(indent) writes generated output into the redirected outbuf, and a2b("%s", tmpbuf) then treats tmpbuf as a NUL-terminated string; neither step bounds the amount written to the fixed 20 KB stack array.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes data beyond the end of the intended stack buffer, matching CWE-787's out-of-bounds write. This is the direct cause; a stack-buffer-overflow label would describe the same defect, but the target CWE-787 captures the out-of-bounds write itself.

evidence_lines.code:
line_height = draw_systems(indent);
a2b("%s", tmpbuf);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: delayed output is redirected into a fixed 20 KB stack buffer with no capacity limit. Trigger: input producing delayed output larger than 20 KB (e.g., many elements such as slurs) causes draw_systems to write past tmpbuf's end. Supported consequence: stack corruption leading to crash/DoS and potentially code execution.

commit_msg:
avcodec/dnxhd_parser: Do not return invalid value from dnxhd_find_frame_end() on error

Fixes: Null pointer dereference

Fixes: CVE-2017-9608
Found-by: Yihan Lian
Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
(cherry picked from commit 611b35627488a8d0763e75c25ee0875c5b7987dd)
Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michael@niedermayer.cc>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['                dctx->remaining = avpriv_dnxhd_get_frame_size(cid);', '                if (dctx->remaining <= 0) {', '                    dctx->remaining = dnxhd_get_hr_frame_size(cid, dctx->w, dctx->h);', '                    if (dctx->remaining <= 0)', '                        return dctx->remaining;'], 'added_lines': ['                int remaining;', '                remaining = avpriv_dnxhd_get_frame_size(cid);', '                if (remaining <= 0) {', '                    remaining = dnxhd_get_hr_frame_size(cid, dctx->w, dctx->h);', '                    if (remaining <= 0)', '                        continue;', '                dctx->remaining = remaining;']}
description: The dnxhd decoder in FFmpeg before 3.2.6, and 3.3.x before 3.3.3 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference) via a crafted mov file.

code_evidence: On error, dnxhd_find_frame_end() returns the negative frame-size value from avpriv_dnxhd_get_frame_size()/dnxhd_get_hr_frame_size() via 'return dctx->remaining;'. The parser caller treats a negative return as a valid consumed-byte count, producing an invalid pointer/index state that leads to a NULL dereference downstream.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The committed fix changes 'return dctx->remaining;' to 'continue', confirming the returned invalid negative value caused the NULL dereference reported in CVE-2017-9608, matching CWE-476.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error path returns a negative value instead of signaling error via END_NOT_FOUND/continue. Trigger: a crafted mov with an invalid cid so both frame-size lookups return <= 0. Consequence: the caller misinterprets the negative return, causing a NULL pointer dereference (DoS).

commit_msg:
Bug 706057: Fix use-after-free in getOwnPropertyDescriptor.

getOwnPropertyDescriptor should create the descriptor object by
using [[DefineOwnProperty]], and not by looking through the prototype
chain where it may invoke getters and setters on the Object.prototype.

If there exists an Object.prototype.get property with a setter, that method is
invoked when it shouldn't. A malicious getter here can delete the property
currently being processed in getOwnPropertyDescriptor, and we'll end up
with a use-after-free bug.

Avoid this problem by following the spec and use js_defproperty rather than
js_setproperty to define own properties in getOwnPropertyDescriptor and
related functions.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\t\tjs_setproperty(J, -2, "value");', '\t\t\tjs_setproperty(J, -2, "writable");', '\t\t\tjs_setproperty(J, -2, "get");', '\t\t\tjs_setproperty(J, -2, "set");', '\t\tjs_setproperty(J, -2, "enumerable");', '\t\tjs_setproperty(J, -2, "configurable");'], 'added_lines': ['\t\t\tjs_defproperty(J, -2, "value", 0);', '\t\t\tjs_defproperty(J, -2, "writable", 0);', '\t\t\tjs_defproperty(J, -2, "get", 0);', '\t\t\tjs_defproperty(J, -2, "set", 0);', '\t\tjs_defproperty(J, -2, "enumerable", 0);', '\t\tjs_defproperty(J, -2, "configurable", 0);']}
description: A logical issue in O_getOwnPropertyDescriptor() in Artifex MuJS 1.0.0 through 1.3.x before 1.3.2 allows an attacker to achieve Remote Code Execution through memory corruption, via the loading of a crafted JavaScript file.

code_evidence: Builds the descriptor object then uses js_setproperty to define 'value' and 'writable' on it; js_setproperty walks the prototype chain, so an attacker-supplied setter on Object.prototype for these keys is invoked during descriptor construction.
Same pattern for 'get' and 'set' properties when the reference has accessor descriptors, again invoking inherited setters while ref is still in use.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The re-entrant setter frees the js_Property that ref points to, and subsequent use of ref results in use-after-free memory corruption that can lead to out-of-bounds writes and remote code execution, matching CWE-787's out-of-bounds write consequence.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: js_setproperty performs prototype-chain assignment instead of defining an own property, so a malicious Object.prototype setter for 'value'/'get'/'set' executes re-entrantly. That setter can delete the property currently referenced by ref, and the function then continues using the freed ref, leading to memory corruption and potential code execution.

commit_msg:
hwmon: (xgene) Fix use after free bug in xgene_hwmon_remove due to race condition

In xgene_hwmon_probe, &ctx->workq is bound with xgene_hwmon_evt_work.
Then it will be started.

If we remove the driver which will call xgene_hwmon_remove to clean up,
there may be unfinished work.

The possible sequence is as follows:

Fix it by finishing the work before cleanup in xgene_hwmon_remove.

CPU0                  CPU1

                    |xgene_hwmon_evt_work
xgene_hwmon_remove   |
kfifo_free(&ctx->async_msg_fifo);|
                    |
                    |kfifo_out_spinlocked
                    |//use &ctx->async_msg_fifo
Fixes: 2ca492e22cb7 ("hwmon: (xgene) Fix crash when alarm occurs before driver probe")
Signed-off-by: Zheng Wang <zyytlz.wz@163.com>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20230310084007.1403388-1-zyytlz.wz@163.com
Signed-off-by: Guenter Roeck <linux@roeck-us.net>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tcancel_work_sync(&ctx->workq);']}
description: A use-after-free flaw was found in xgene_hwmon_remove in drivers/hwmon/xgene-hwmon.c in the Hardware Monitoring Linux Kernel Driver (xgene-hwmon). This flaw could allow a local attacker to crash the system due to a race problem. This vulnerability could even lead to a kernel information leak problem.

code_evidence: xgene_hwmon_remove obtains ctx from platform_get_drvdata, then unregisters the hwmon device and frees the async_msg_fifo via kfifo_free without first synchronizing with the work item bound to ctx->workq that may still be executing and accessing ctx->async_msg_fifo.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The fifo is freed at line 5 while an unsynchronized concurrent work item may still reference it, which is exactly use-after-free (CWE-416). This is not merely a missing-lock issue; the freed object is subsequently accessed.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: remove path frees ctx->async_msg_fifo while the xgene_hwmon_evt_work work item can concurrently run kfifo_out_spinlocked on the same fifo. Trigger: driver removal racing with pending/running work. Consequence: use-after-free of the fifo memory, potentially causing crash or memory disclosure.
