commit_msg:
When opening files for write, ensure they aren't symbolic links

Issue #1048 identified that if, for example, a non privileged user
created a symbolic link from /etc/keepalvied.data to /etc/passwd,
writing to /etc/keepalived.data (which could be invoked via DBus)
would cause /etc/passwd to be overwritten.

This commit stops keepalived writing to pathnames where the ultimate
component is a symbolic link, by setting O_NOFOLLOW whenever opening
a file for writing.

This might break some setups, where, for example, /etc/keepalived.data
was a symbolic link to /home/fred/keepalived.data. If this was the case,
instead create a symbolic link from /home/fred/keepalived.data to
/tmp/keepalived.data, so that the file is still accessible via
/home/fred/keepalived.data.

There doesn't appear to be a way around this backward incompatibility,
since even checking if the pathname is a symbolic link prior to opening
for writing would create a race condition.

Signed-off-by: Quentin Armitage <quentin@armitage.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tfp = fopen(file_name, "a");'], 'added_lines': ['\tfp = fopen_safe(file_name, "a");']}
description: keepalived 2.0.8 didn't check for pathnames with symlinks when writing data to a temporary file upon a call to PrintData or PrintStats. This allowed local users to overwrite arbitrary files if fs.protected_symlinks is set to 0, as demonstrated by a symlink from /tmp/keepalived.data or /tmp/keepalived.stats to /etc/passwd.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function writes thread dump data to a file via fopen and does not itself manage, store, or disclose sensitive information; the described symlink overwrite issue is a file-write/arbitrary-file-overwrite weakness, not CWE-200 information exposure.

commit_msg:
Fix #78338: Array cross-border reading in PCRE

We backport r1092 from pcre2.

(cherry picked from commit 8947fd9e9fdce87cd6c59817b1db58e789538fe9)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['GETCHARINC(c, cc);'], 'added_lines': ['c = *cc++;']}
description: An out-of-bounds read was discovered in PCRE before 10.34 when the pattern \X is JIT compiled and used to match specially crafted subjects in non-UTF mode. Applications that use PCRE to parse untrusted input may be vulnerable to this flaw, which would allow an attacker to crash the application. The flaw occurs in do_extuni_no_utf in pcre2_jit_compile.c.

code_evidence: Line 8 uses GETCHARINC to advance cc while decoding a character; the patch replaced it with a single-byte read c = *cc++, changing how cc advances relative to multi-byte sequences.

The loop condition at line 10 checks cc < end_subject, but the backward scan at lines 19-22 decrements bptr and dereferences *bptr only after verifying bptr > start_subject, so the boundary handling around the initial forward read is the relevant concern.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the weakness is reading data past the end of the intended buffer during subject scanning, matching the out-of-bounds read description. It is distinct from an out-of-bounds write, since only reads occur here.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is the forward character read/advance at line 8 not being bounded consistently with end_subject, so for specially crafted non-UTF subjects the pointer can move past the subject end and subsequent reads access memory beyond the buffer. The trigger is a \X match against an untrusted subject in non-UTF mode; the supported consequence is an out-of-bounds read leading to a crash (DoS).

commit_msg:
coredump: fix race condition between mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm() and core dumping

The core dumping code has always run without holding the mmap_sem for
writing, despite that is the only way to ensure that the entire vma
layout will not change from under it.  Only using some signal
serialization on the processes belonging to the mm is not nearly enough.
This was pointed out earlier.  For example in Hugh's post from Jul 2017:

  https://lkml.kernel.org/r/alpine.LSU.2.11.1707191716030.2055@eggly.anvils

  "Not strictly relevant here, but a related note: I was very surprised
   to discover, only quite recently, how handle_mm_fault() may be called
   without down_read(mmap_sem) - when core dumping. That seems a
   misguided optimization to me, which would also be nice to correct"

In particular because the growsdown and growsup can move the
vm_start/vm_end the various loops the core dump does around the vma will
not be consistent if page faults can happen concurrently.

Pretty much all users calling mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm() and then
taking the mmap_sem had the potential to introduce unexpected side
effects in the core dumping code.

Adding mmap_sem for writing around the ->core_dump invocation is a
viable long term fix, but it requires removing all copy user and page
faults and to replace them with get_dump_page() for all binary formats
which is not suitable as a short term fix.

For the time being this solution manually covers the places that can
confuse the core dump either by altering the vma layout or the vma flags
while it runs.  Once ->core_dump runs under mmap_sem for writing the
function mmget_still_valid() can be dropped.

Allowing mmap_sem protected sections to run in parallel with the
coredump provides some minor parallelism advantage to the swapoff code
(which seems to be safe enough by never mangling any vma field and can
keep doing swapins in parallel to the core dumping) and to some other
corner case.

In order to facilitate the backporting I added "Fixes: 86039bd3b4e6"
however the side effect of this same race condition in /proc/pid/mem
should be reproducible since before 2.6.12-rc2 so I couldn't add any
other "Fixes:" because there's no hash beyond the git genesis commit.

Because find_extend_vma() is the only location outside of the process
context that could modify the "mm" structures under mmap_sem for
reading, by adding the mmget_still_valid() check to it, all other cases
that take the mmap_sem for reading don't need the new check after
mmget_not_zero()/get_task_mm().  The expand_stack() in page fault
context also doesn't need the new check, because all tasks under core
dumping are frozen.

Link: http://lkml.kernel.org/r/20190325224949.11068-1-aarcange@redhat.com
Fixes: 86039bd3b4e6 ("userfaultfd: add new syscall to provide memory externalization")
Signed-off-by: Andrea Arcangeli <aarcange@redhat.com>
Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Suggested-by: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Acked-by: Peter Xu <peterx@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Mike Rapoport <rppt@linux.ibm.com>
Reviewed-by: Oleg Nesterov <oleg@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Acked-by: Jason Gunthorpe <jgg@mellanox.com>
Acked-by: Michal Hocko <mhocko@suse.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\t/* no task can run (and in turn coredump) yet */', '\t\tVM_WARN_ON(!mmget_still_valid(mm));']}
description: The coredump implementation in the Linux kernel before 5.0.10 does not use locking or other mechanisms to prevent vma layout or vma flags changes while it runs, which allows local users to obtain sensitive information, cause a denial of service, or possibly have unspecified other impact by triggering a race condition with mmget_not_zero or get_task_mm calls. This is related to fs/userfaultfd.c, mm/mmap.c, fs/proc/task_mmu.c, and drivers/infiniband/core/uverbs_main.c.

code_evidence: After the wait loop ends, the function reads release_new_ctx->mm and acquires mm->mmap_sem for writing before walking the vma list and clearing vm_userfaultfd_ctx/vm_flags. The added VM_WARN_ON(!mmget_still_valid(mm)) asserts the mm remains valid, but it is only a warning, not a lock; the mmap_sem write lock does not exclude a concurrent core-dump reader that runs without the write lock.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is improper synchronization: the write-side lock is not the same exclusion used by the coredump reader, so the shared vma state is modified without a consistent locking discipline. This matches CWE-667 (Improper Locking) rather than a pure data race, since the defect is the mismatched lock usage around a shared resource.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The userfaultfd release path mutates vma layout/flags under mmap_sem for writing, while core dumping reads the same vma list without the write lock. A concurrent mmget_not_zero/get_task_mm caller can race with this mutation, yielding an inconsistent vma walk; the warning does not prevent the race, so the consequence is sensitive data exposure or DoS.

commit_msg:
Remove support for pre-authentication compression. Doing compression
early in the protocol probably seemed reasonable in the 1990s, but
today it's clearly a bad idea in terms of both cryptography (cf.
multiple compression oracle attacks in TLS) and attack surface.

Moreover, to support it across privilege-separation zlib needed
the assistance of a complex shared-memory manager that made the
required attack surface considerably larger.

Prompted by Guido Vranken pointing out a compiler-elided security
check in the shared memory manager found by Stack
(http://css.csail.mit.edu/stack/); ok deraadt@ markus@

NB. pre-auth authentication has been disabled by default in sshd
for >10 years.

description: The shared memory manager (associated with pre-authentication compression) in sshd in OpenSSH before 7.4 does not ensure that a bounds check is enforced by all compilers, which might allows local users to gain privileges by leveraging access to a sandboxed privilege-separation process, related to the m_zback and m_zlib data structures.

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The shown function only parses key/cipher state and calls ssh_packet_set_compress_state; it contains no direct out-of-bounds memory access, and the described bounds-check compiler-elision flaw is in the separate shared-memory manager (m_zback/m_zlib), not in this function's code.

commit_msg: Add check after call strtok_r
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (l2byte == NULL)', '        err(-1, "Hex buffer must contain something");']}
description: An issue found in TCPprep v.4.4.3 allows a remote attacker to cause a denial of service via the macinstring function.

code_evidence: strtok_r(string, ",", &token) returns NULL when l2string is empty or begins with a comma; the code then passes l2byte directly to sscanf without a NULL check.

The while loop increments numbytes only after a non-NULL token; the first databyte is copied at index 0 but numbytes is not incremented for it, so the bounds check at numbytes + 1 > hexlen compares the wrong count.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-617 fits: a reachable NULL state from attacker-controlled input causes an abnormal process exit via an unchecked dereference, matching a reachable assertion-style crash condition. The missing first-byte counter is a separate bounds flaw, not the labeled assertion issue.

l2byte = strtok_r(string, ",", &token);
sscanf(l2byte, "%x", &value);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the return value of strtok_r at line 14 is dereferenced at line 15 without verifying it is non-NULL, and the byte counter is not advanced for the first token. Trigger: a crafted hex string (empty or leading comma) makes l2byte NULL and sscanf(NULL, ...) crashes; a multi-byte string can also overflow hex because the first byte is not counted. Supported consequence: remote denial of service (crash) as described in the commit context.

commit_msg: Lock down search_path in SPI calls
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t/* SPI calls must be qualified otherwise they are unsafe */', '\tres = SPI_exec("SET search_path TO pg_catalog, pg_temp", 0);', '\tres = SPI_exec("RESET search_path", 0);'], 'added_lines': ['\t/* Lock down search_path */', '\tres = SPI_exec("SET LOCAL search_path TO pg_catalog, pg_temp", 0);']}
description:
TimescaleDB, an open-source time-series SQL database, has a privilege escalation vulnerability in versions 2.8.0 through 2.9.2. During installation, TimescaleDB creates a telemetry job that is runs as the installation user. The queries run as part of the telemetry data collection were not run with a locked down `search_path`, allowing malicious users to create functions that would be executed by the telemetry job, leading to privilege escalation. In order to be able to take advantage of this vulnerability, a user would need to be able to create objects in a database and then get a superuser to install TimescaleDB into their database. When TimescaleDB is installed as trusted extension, non-superusers can install the extension without help from a superuser.

Version 2.9.3 fixes this issue. As a mitigation, the `search_path` of the user running the telemetry job can be locked down to not include schemas writable by other users. The vulnerability is not exploitable on instances in Timescale Cloud and Managed Service for TimescaleDB due to additional security provisions in place on those platforms.

code_evidence: Line 33 sets search_path with session-level SET (not SET LOCAL), so the altered path persists for the duration of the SPI session; the error branch on lines 34-35 only checks res < 0.
Lines 36-38 build and execute a query referencing unqualified objects (bgw_job_stat, bgw_job, and operators/functions) resolved via the current search_path.
Line 83 resets search_path only after the loop; if execution errors earlier, the RESET is skipped and the path remains altered for the session.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function fails to constrain the privilege context (search_path) under which the telemetry query executes, letting an unprivileged actor influence code run with the job owner's privileges. That is improper privilege management/handling of the execution context (CWE-269), matching the described privilege-escalation impact via an unintended sphere of control.

evidence_lines.code:
res = SPI_exec("RESET search_path", 0);
res = SPI_finish();

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the telemetry query runs with a search_path that is set at session scope and only reset on the success path, so objects and functions in the query are resolved from attacker-writable schemas. Trigger: a malicious user creates same-named objects/functions in a schema earlier in the search_path; the telemetry job, running as the installing user, resolves and executes them. Supported consequence: the attacker's code executes with the telemetry job's higher privileges, i.e., privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
Fix buffer overrun in creating key transport blob according to RFC 9189, 4.2.4.1

Resolves: CVE-2022-29242
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if ((*out_len = i2d_PSKeyTransport_gost(pst, out ? &out : NULL)) > 0)'], 'added_lines': ['    int res_len = 0;', '    res_len = i2d_PSKeyTransport_gost(pst, NULL);', '    if (res_len <= 0) {', '        GOSTerr(GOST_F_PKEY_GOST2018_ENCRYPT, ERR_R_ASN1_LIB);', '        goto err;', '    }', '', '    if (out == NULL) {', '        *out_len = res_len;', '    } else {', '        if ((size_t)res_len > *out_len) {', '            GOSTerr(GOST_F_PKEY_GOST2018_ENCRYPT, GOST_R_INVALID_BUFFER_SIZE);', '            goto err;', '        }', '        if ((*out_len = i2d_PSKeyTransport_gost(pst, &out)) > 0)', '            ret = 1;', '        else', '            GOSTerr(GOST_F_PKEY_GOST2018_ENCRYPT, ERR_R_ASN1_LIB);', '    }', '']}
description: GOST engine is a reference implementation of the Russian GOST crypto algorithms for OpenSSL. TLS clients using GOST engine when ciphersuite `TLS_GOSTR341112_256_WITH_KUZNYECHIK_CTR_OMAC` is agreed and the server uses 512 bit GOST secret keys are vulnerable to buffer overflow. GOST engine version 3.0.1 contains a patch for this issue. Disabling ciphersuite `TLS_GOSTR341112_256_WITH_KUZNYECHIK_CTR_OMAC` is a possible workaround.

code_evidence: The original code passes the caller-supplied output buffer 'out' and its length '*out_len' directly to i2d_PSKeyTransport_gost, which serializes the key transport blob of variable length (dependent on key_len and cipher) into 'out' without first comparing the serialized size against '*out_len'. If the caller's buffer is smaller than the encoded blob, the ASN.1 encoder writes past the end.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function copies an encoded input structure into the output buffer without verifying the destination size first, matching CWE-120's 'buffer copy without checking size of input'. The later patch adds exactly this comparison (res_len > *out_len), confirming the missing constraint was the root cause rather than an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).

evidence_lines.code:
if ((*out_len = i2d_PSKeyTransport_gost(pst, out ? &out : NULL)) > 0)
ret = 1;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the serialized length is computed only while writing into the caller's buffer, so no size check occurs before the copy. Trigger: a caller (TLS client with 512-bit GOST key / large key transport blob) supplies an output buffer smaller than the encoded PSKeyTransport_gost. Supported consequence: out-of-bounds write into the caller's buffer, i.e. a classic buffer overflow.

commit_msg: Fix denial-of-service attack when reading corrupt PDF files.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    else if (_pdfioDictGetValue(dict, key + 1))', '    {', '      _pdfioFileError(pdf, "Duplicate dictionary key \'%s\'.", key + 1);', '      return (NULL);', '    }', '    PDFIO_DEBUG("_pdfioDictRead: Reading value for \'%s\'.\\n", key + 1);', '']}
description: PDFio is a C library for reading and writing PDF files. In versions prior to 1.1.0 a denial of service (DOS) vulnerability exists in the pdfio parser. Crafted pdf files can cause the program to run at 100% utilization and never terminate. The pdf which causes this crash found in testing is about 28kb in size and was discovered via fuzzing. Anyone who uses this library either as a standalone binary or as a library can be DOSed when attempting to parse this type of file. Web servers or other automated processes which rely on this code to turn pdf submissions into plaintext can be DOSed when an attacker uploads the pdf. Please see the linked GHSA for an example pdf. Users are advised to upgrade. There are no known workarounds for this vulnerability.

commit_msg:
Unsquashfs: fix write outside destination directory exploit

An issue on Github (https://github.com/plougher/squashfs-tools/issues/72)
shows how some specially crafted Squashfs filesystems containing
invalid file names (with '/' and ..) can cause Unsquashfs to write
files outside of the destination directory.

This commit fixes this exploit by checking all names for
validity.

In doing so I have also added checks for '.' and for names that
are shorter than they should be (names in the file system should
not have '\0' terminators).

Signed-off-by: Phillip Lougher <phillip@squashfs.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '\t\t\t/* check name for invalid characters (i.e /, ., ..) */', '\t\t\tif(check_name(dire->name, dire->size + 1) == FALSE) {', '\t\t\t\tERROR("File system corrupted: invalid characters in name\\n");', '\t\t\t\tgoto corrupted;', '\t\t\t}', '']}
description: squashfs_opendir in unsquash-1.c in Squashfs-Tools 4.5 stores the filename in the directory entry; this is then used by unsquashfs to create the new file during the unsquash. The filename is not validated for traversal outside of the destination directory, and thus allows writing to locations outside of the destination.

That unvalidated name is then copied verbatim with strcpy into the directory entry list, which unsquashfs later uses to create files under the destination directory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-22 fits because an externally supplied pathname is intended to stay under the destination directory but is not constrained against '/' and '..' elements, enabling traversal. It is distinct from a plain buffer overflow: the defect is missing pathname limitation, not memory corruption.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function accepts a crafted filename from the Squashfs directory table and stores it without neutralizing path separators or parent-directory components. Trigger: a malicious filesystem image containing a name such as '../x' or an absolute path. Consequence: unsquashfs writes the extracted file outside the destination directory.

Factor out logic that attempts to only consult the environment when it's
safe to do so into its own function, and use secure_getenv() instead of
getenv() if it's available.  Original report from
https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=1332508

Consequence: the privileged process consumes attacker-controlled configuration, enabling privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
Fix buffer overrun due to integer overflow in bcmath

Summary: scale gets passed around as an int inside the library.

Reviewed By: mxw

Differential Revision: D3624520

description: Integer overflow in bcmath in Facebook HHVM before 3.15.0 allows attackers to have unspecified impact via unknown vectors, which triggers a buffer overflow.

code_evidence: The scale parameter is typed int64_t and only checked with 'if (scale < 0) scale = BCG(bc_precision);'. No upper bound is enforced, so a very large positive scale passes through unchanged into the bcmath routines (bc_init_num/SCOPE_EXIT setup below).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is an unchecked integer input used in size arithmetic that can wrap, matching CWE-190 (Integer Overflow or Wraparound). It is not merely a bounds/validation issue (CWE-20) because the security consequence flows from the numeric wraparound feeding memory sizing.

evidence_lines.code:
int64_t scale ) {
if (scale < 0) scale = BCG(bc_precision);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: scale is accepted as an int64_t without an upper-bound check, so an oversized scale is used later in size/allocation computations inside bcmath. Trigger: a caller supplies a huge positive scale value to bcpow. Consequence: an integer overflow in those downstream size calculations, which the commit describes as leading to a buffer overrun. The overflow is the cause; the buffer overrun is the resulting impact.

description: TensorFlow is an open source platform for machine learning. Prior to versions 2.12.0 and 2.11.1, if the stride and window size are not positive for `tf.raw_ops.AvgPoolGrad`, it can give a floating point exception. A fix is included in TensorFlow version 2.12.0 and version 2.11.1.

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the constructor validates only the length of ksize_ and stride_, not the sign of their elements, so zero or negative window/stride values are accepted. Trigger: a caller supplies non-positive ksize or strides to AvgPoolGrad. Supported consequence: downstream pooling arithmetic can divide by zero or otherwise fault, producing a floating point exception.

commit_msg:
Fix stack data disclosure when returning static files smaller than
16KiB. It could also cause to return partially incorrect file ending in
case of file not being rounded up to 16KiB.

Thanks to Gynvael Coldwind and hebi for discovering and preparing
report.

Line 9 reads into 'buf' via is.read, but the loop condition only checks gcount() > 0, and line 12 wraps the buffer with asio::buffer(buf) using the full sizeof(buf) rather than the actual bytes read (gcount).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-908 applies because the code uses a resource (stack buffer) that was not initialized; only gcount() bytes are valid but the full buffer is transmitted. This is the direct cause of the memory disclosure, distinct from an out-of-bounds read since the access stays within the declared buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the buffer is sized to the requested length (16384) instead of the number of bytes actually read, so when a static file is smaller than 16 KiB the remainder of 'buf' is uninitialized stack memory. Trigger: serving a static file smaller than 16 KiB. Consequence: uninitialized stack contents are written to the socket, disclosing sensitive memory and returning a partially incorrect file ending.

commit_msg:
xhci: limit the number of link trbs we are willing to process

Needed to avoid we run in circles forever in case the guest builds
an endless loop with link trbs.

Reported-by: Li Qiang <liqiang6-s@360.cn>
Tested-by: P J P <ppandit@redhat.com>
Signed-off-by: Gerd Hoffmann <kraxel@redhat.com>
Message-id: 1476096382-7981-1-git-send-email-kraxel@redhat.com
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    uint32_t link_cnt = 0;', '            if (++link_cnt > TRB_LINK_LIMIT) {', '                return 0;', '            }']}
description: The xhci_ring_fetch function in hw/usb/hcd-xhci.c in QEMU (aka Quick Emulator) allows local guest OS administrators to cause a denial of service (infinite loop and QEMU process crash) by leveraging failure to limit the number of link Transfer Request Blocks (TRB) to process.

code_evidence: The function wraps its fetch logic in an unbounded `while (1)` loop [5]. Each iteration performs a guest-controlled `pci_dma_read` [7] and, when the fetched TRB is a link TRB [19,25], sets `ring->dequeue = xhci_mask64(trb->parameter)` [26]. Because the next loop iteration reads from this guest-supplied address, a guest can construct a chain of link TRBs that redirect back to each other, causing the loop to iterate indefinitely without any counter or bound limiting the number of link TRBs processed. Non-link TRBs return at [24], but a self-referencing or cyclic link chain never takes that path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-770 fits because the code consumes a reusable resource (loop iterations / CPU time) on behalf of the guest without imposing any limit on the number of link TRBs processed, matching an unbounded allocation of processing resources leading to DoS. The missing throttle is the specific defect, not merely a logic error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the loop processes an unbounded number of guest-controlled link TRBs because `ring->dequeue` is reassigned from guest data [26] with no iteration limit. Trigger: a guest builds a cyclic/endless chain of link TRBs. Consequence: the host QEMU process spins forever, consuming CPU and causing a denial of service (hang/crash).

description: TensorFlow is an end-to-end open source platform for machine learning. commit_msg:
AES: move look-up tables to .data section and unshare between processes

* cipher/rijndael-internal.h (ATTR_ALIGNED_64): New.
* cipher/rijndael-tables.h (encT): Move to 'enc_tables' structure.
(enc_tables): New structure for encryption table with counters before
and after.

(do_decrypt): Change '&dec_tables' to 'dec_tables.T'.
* cipher/cipher-gcm.c (prefetch_table): Make inline; Handle input
with length not multiple of 256.
(prefetch_enc, prefetch_dec): Modify pre- and post-table counters
to unshare look-up table pages between processes.
--

GnuPG-bug-id: 4541
Signed-off-by: Jussi Kivilinna <jussi.kivilinna@iki.fi>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  /* Modify counters to trigger copy-on-write and unsharing if physical pages', '   * of look-up table are shared between processes.  Modifying counters also', '   * causes checksums for pages to change and hint same-page merging algorithm', '   * that these pages are frequently changing.  */', '  dec_tables.counter_head++;', '  dec_tables.counter_tail++;', '', '  /* Prefetch look-up tables to cache.  */']}
description: In Libgcrypt 1.8.4, the C implementation of AES is vulnerable to a flush-and-reload side-channel attack because physical addresses are available to other processes. (The C implementation is used on platforms where an assembly-language implementation is unavailable.) NOTE: the vendor's position is that the issue report cannot be validated because there is no description of an attack

code_evidence: prefetch_dec prefetches the entire dec_tables structure, including its encryption look-up tables, into the CPU cache via prefetch_table; the function itself performs no access control or page-isolation check before touching the shared table memory.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The shared physical look-up table pages are a resource exposed to the wrong control sphere (other processes), matching CWE-668: a resource crosses process boundaries without intended isolation. It is not merely improper input validation; the weakness is the cross-sphere sharing of the table resource.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the AES decryption table pages are shared between processes (shared physical pages), so cache state for those pages is a cross-process resource. Trigger: prefetch_dec (or an attacker's own use of the same shared pages) drives the table into cache; a co-resident process observing cache timing (flush-and-reload) infers key-dependent table accesses. Consequence: disclosure of secret key material through the side channel. The function is the prefetching site that exercises the shared resource; it does not itself modify counters to unshare pages in this version.

commit_msg:
Q.931: fix use-after-free (write) of "q931_pi"

The dissect_q931_number_ie (and indirectly dissect_q931_cause_ie_unsafe)
write to the "q931_pi" structure which seems private to the q931
dissector, but can in fact be called through other dissectors (isup) as
well. Normally this structure is initialized in "dissect_q931_pdu" and
invalidated at the end of the function, but a malformed packet can
prevent the cleanup. In the next packet, a different dissector can thus
trigger a use-after-free via "dissect_q931_number_ie".

Rename "dissect_q931_cause_ie_unsafe" since "unsafe" meant that external
dissectors could not call it directly (see commit a83a87e9ca).

Based on commit 197ceddab109, it seems that the intended purpose of the
structure is to provide information to the VoIP Calls dialog, but it
would only be used when called through dissect_q931_pdu. Dissectors like
isup have their own routines to provide call information, but as a
side-effect of code sharing the problematic code path was reached.

description: In Wireshark 2.6.0, 2.4.0 to 2.4.6, and 2.2.0 to 2.2.14, the Q.931 dissector could crash. This was addressed in epan/dissectors/packet-q931.c by avoiding a use-after-free after a malformed packet prevented certain cleanup.

Consequence: use-after-free write leading to crash or memory corruption.

It is possible to cause an out-of-bounds write in versions of Contiki-NG prior to 4.6 when transmitting a 6LoWPAN packet with a chain of extension headers. Unfortunately, the written header is not checked to be within the available space, thereby making it possible to write outside the buffer. The problem has been patched in Contiki-NG 4.6. Users can apply the patch for this vulnerability out-of-band as a workaround.

The only pre-existing guard at line 143 is conditioned on ip_len == 0 and compares against sizeof(uip_buf) rather than the actual destination buffer size, so it does not cover the ip_len != 0 path.
memcpy at line 147 copies len bytes from hc06_ptr to exthdr+2, and lines 149-151 advance ip_payload by the computed header length, with no bound check before the write.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes exthdr fields and memcpy data to a computed offset without validating available space, directly matching CWE-787 (write past the end of the intended buffer). This is a write-side overflow, not an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) or mere integer issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the extension-header write path lacks a bounds check against the real destination buffer size; the existing check is gated on ip_len == 0 and uses uip_buf. Trigger: a 6LoWPAN packet carrying a chain of extension headers with attacker-controlled len values drives ip_payload past the buffer end. Consequence: out-of-bounds write of header fields and copied payload, corrupting memory.

commit_msg:
gnttab: correct maptrack table accesses

In order to observe a consistent (limit,pointer-table) pair, the reader
needs to either hold the maptrack lock (in line with documentation) or
both sides need to order their accesses suitably (the writer side
barrier was removed by commit dff515dfea ["gnttab: use per-VCPU
maptrack free lists"], and a read side barrier has never been there).

Make the writer publish a new table page before limit (for bounds
checks to work), and new list head last (for racing maptrack_entry()
invocations to work). At the same time add read barriers to lockless
readers.

Additionally get_maptrack_handle() must not assume ->maptrack_head to
not change behind its back: Another handle may be put (updating only
->maptrack_tail) and then got or stolen (updating ->maptrack_head).

This is part of XSA-218.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>

commit_msg:
Fix invalid handling of verify errors in libssl

In the event that X509_verify() returned an internal error result then
libssl would mishandle this and set rwstate to SSL_RETRY_VERIFY. This
subsequently causes SSL_get_error() to return SSL_ERROR_WANT_RETRY_VERIFY.
That return code is supposed to only ever be returned if an application
is using an app verify callback to complete replace the use of
X509_verify(). Applications may not be written to expect that return code
and could therefore crash (or misbehave in some other way) as a result.

CVE-2021-4044

Reviewed-by: Tomas Mraz <tomas@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    if (s->ctx->app_verify_callback != NULL)', '    else'], 'added_lines': ['    if (s->ctx->app_verify_callback != NULL) {', '    } else {', '        /* We treat an error in the same way as a failure to verify */', '        if (i < 0)', '            i = 0;', '    }']}
description: Internally libssl in OpenSSL calls X509_verify_cert() on the client side to verify a certificate supplied by a server. That function may return a negative return value to indicate an internal error (for example out of memory). Such a negative return value is mishandled by OpenSSL and will cause an IO function (such as SSL_connect() or SSL_do_handshake()) to not indicate success and a subsequent call to SSL_get_error() to return the value SSL_ERROR_WANT_RETRY_VERIFY. This return value is only supposed to be returned by OpenSSL if the application has previously called SSL_CTX_set_cert_verify_callback(). Since most applications do not do this the SSL_ERROR_WANT_RETRY_VERIFY return value from SSL_get_error() will be totally unexpected and applications may not behave correctly as a result. The exact behaviour will depend on the application but it could result in crashes, infinite loops or other similar incorrect responses. This issue is made more serious in combination with a separate bug in OpenSSL 3.0 that will cause X509_verify_cert() to indicate an internal error when processing a certificate chain. This will occur where a certificate does not include the Subject Alternative Name extension but where a Certificate Authority has enforced name constraints. This issue can occur even with valid chains. By combining the two issues an attacker could induce incorrect, application dependent behaviour. Fixed in OpenSSL 3.0.1 (Affected 3.0.0).

joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function contains no loop or iteration construct; the CVE-2021-4044 defect is mishandling of a negative X509_verify_cert return, not an unreachable loop exit condition.

joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because the code releases resources on the normal path (lines 195-209) but not on these error returns, leaving allocated memory unreleased after its effective lifetime. This is missing release of a resource, not a buffer overflow or use-after-free.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function allocates line via AcquireQuantumMemory at entry and holds token, newstr and name during iteration. Several early error returns inside the savedolen > 0 block exit the function without freeing these buffers. Triggering a TellBlob or SeekBlob failure (e.g., on a malformed or truncated 8BIM stream) causes those allocations to be abandoned, so repeated processing leaks memory and can exhaust resources.

commit_msg:
Handle typeof applied to empty in InstSimplify

Summary:
Do not simplify `typeof` if it is applied to an invalid type. This
handles a case like the one in the added test, where `typeof` is called
on a literal empty in unreachable code.

Reviewed By: kodafb

Differential Revision: D31000173

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['          llvm_unreachable("Invalid literal kind.");'], 'added_lines': ['          break;']}
description: A type confusion vulnerability could be triggered when resolving the "typeof" unary operator in Facebook Hermes prior to v0.10.0. Note that this is only exploitable if the application using Hermes permits evaluation of untrusted JavaScript. Hence, most React Native applications are not affected.

code_evidence: For TypeofKind, the code switches on operand->getKind() and handles known literal kinds, but the default branch calls llvm_unreachable("Invalid literal kind.") instead of returning nullptr. An operand kind not enumerated (e.g. an empty literal) reaches this default, so the function assumes a type invariant that the caller did not guarantee.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accesses the operand under an assumed kind set; an operand of a different kind is misinterpreted as unreachable, matching CWE-843's incompatible-type handling. This is distinct from a generic missing null check, as the flaw is the wrong assumption about the operand's type/kind.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the typeof path treats any unrecognized operand kind as impossible and aborts via llvm_unreachable rather than declining to simplify. Trigger: typeof applied to a literal whose kind is not among the handled cases. Supported consequence: a crash/DoS or undefined behavior from the unreachable path, since the operand kind is incompatible with the assumed literal set.

commit_msg:
epan: Add a boundary check to get_t61_string.

Add a boundary check to make sure we don't go past the end of "ptr".

Bug: 15373
Change-Id: I85394e8e6e477b47919362af146051cc8911254b
Reviewed-on: https://code.wireshark.org/review/31440
Reviewed-by: Gerald Combs <gerald@wireshark.org>

description: In Wireshark 2.6.0 to 2.6.5 and 2.4.0 to 2.4.11, the RTSE dissector and other ASN.1 dissectors could crash. This was addressed in epan/charsets.c by adding a get_t61_string length check.

code_evidence: The loop iterates while i < length, but line 11 enters the two-byte T.61 branch for any byte with high nibble 0xc0 without checking that a following byte exists; on the final iteration i == length-1, so c points to the last byte.

Line 13 then reads c[1] (an out-of-bounds read past ptr+length), and lines 15/19 likewise dereference c[1]. Line 22 increments c and i to consume the second byte, but the loop condition is evaluated against i < length rather than i+1 < length, so the boundary is never enforced.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences c[1] beyond the end of the intended buffer, which is exactly an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125). This is a read-past-end rather than an out-of-bounds write, so CWE-787 would not fit.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the two-byte branch is taken based solely on the lead byte's high nibble, with no check that i+1 < length before dereferencing c[1]. Trigger: a T61 string whose last byte has (byte & 0xf0) == 0xc0. Consequence: c[1] reads one byte past the supplied buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read and potential crash in the dissector.

dm: virtio: check for paddr_guest2host return value

paddr_guest2host can return NULL, but code paths in virtio
are not checking the return value.
_vq_record() initializes iov_base pointer using paddr_guest2host()
but there is nothing in the flow that checks for NULL.
Chane _vq_record to return -1 in case the address translation
has failed.

Tracked-On: #5452
Signed-off-by: Tomas Winkler <tomas.winkler@intel.com>
Acked-by: Wang, Yu1 <yu1.wang@intel.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!vb)', '\t\tgoto error;', '', '\treturn;', '', 'error:', '\tvq->flags = 0;', '\tpr_err("%s: vq enable failed\\n", __func__);']}
description: ACRN through 2.2 has a devicemodel/hw/pci/virtio/virtio.c NULL Pointer Dereference.

code_evidence: Line 12 stores the result of paddr_guest2host() in vb without any NULL check. Lines 13-18 immediately derive vq->desc, vq->avail and vq->used from vb and perform pointer arithmetic on it, so a NULL return propagates into later accesses.

Trigger: the guest supplies a pfn/phys for which translation fails and returns NULL. The unchecked pointer is stored into the vq structures and later dereferenced, causing a NULL pointer dereference and possible crash of the device model.

commit_msg:
avcodec/mpeg4videodec: Check for bitstream overread in decode_vol_header()

Fixes out of array read
Fixes: 08e48e9daae7d8f8ab6dbe3919e797e5-asan_heap-oob_157461c_5295_cov_1266798650_firefing.mpg
Found-by: Mateusz "j00ru" Jurczyk and Gynvael Coldwind
Signed-off-by: Michael Niedermayer <michaelni@gmx.at>

description: A vulnerability, which was classified as problematic, was found in FFmpeg 2.0. This affects the function decode_vol_header of the file libavcodec/mpeg4videodec.c. The manipulation leads to memory corruption. It is possible to initiate the attack remotely. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue.

code_evidence: At line 176 the code reads a bitstream flag and immediately enters the complexity-estimation block without verifying remaining bits.
Line 177 records get_bits_count(gb) as pos, then line 178 reads 2 bits via get_bits(gb,2) even when fewer than 2 bits remain, so the bit reader advances beyond the buffer.
Within that block, loops at lines 139-144 and 157-162 call get_bits(gb,8) up to 64 times each, further consuming bits past the end of the input buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The patch adds a get_bits_left(gb) < 4 guard precisely because the code reads bits past the intended buffer; the reported impact is out-of-array read/memory corruption from unchecked bitstream consumption. This matches CWE-787's out-of-bounds access on the bitstream buffer, though the observed access is a read rather than the write emphasized by the CWE name.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: decode_vol_header consumes bits for the complexity-estimation fields without checking get_bits_left(gb) before the flag at line 176 and the get_bits calls at 178, 139 and 157. Trigger: a truncated VOL header that ends just before this block. Consequence: the bit reader runs off the end of the input buffer, yielding an out-of-bounds read/memory corruption rather than a bounds-checked error return.

commit_msg:
Fixed frame allocation from an awaited frame.

njs_function_frame_save() is used to save the awaited frame when "await"
instruction is encountered. The saving was done as a memcpy() of
existing runtime frame.

njs_function_frame_alloc() is used to alloc a new function frame, this
function tries to use a spare preallocated memory from the previous
frame first.  Previously, this function might result in "use-after-free"
when invoked from a restored frame saved with njs_function_frame_save().
Because njs_function_frame_save() left pointers to the spare memory of
the original frame which may be already free when saved frame is
restored.

The fix is to erase fields for the spare memory from the saved frame.

This closes #469 issue on Github.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    native->size = 0;', '    native->free = NULL;', '    native->free_size = 0;']}
description: nginx njs 0.7.2 is affected suffers from Use-after-free in njs_function_frame_alloc() when it try to invoke from a restored frame saved with njs_function_frame_save().

code_evidence: The saved frame is a shallow struct copy of vm->active_frame, so native->size, native->free and native->free_size are inherited from the original frame.
The function then rewrites native->arguments, native->local and native->temp to point into the copied frame's own storage, but it never clears the inherited spare-memory fields.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because a saved frame keeps and later uses a reference to memory that may have been freed, exactly the reuse-after-free pattern.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the restored frame retains the original frame's spare-memory pointers (native->free, free_size, size) after the shallow copy. Trigger: njs_function_frame_alloc() later reuses that spare memory, which may already have been freed. Consequence: use-after-free read/write through the stale spare pointer.

description: Stack-based buffer overflow in MapServer before 6.0.6, 6.2.x before 6.2.4, 6.4.x before 6.4.5, and 7.0.x before 7.0.4 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) or execute arbitrary code via vectors involving WFS get feature requests.

commit_msg:
x86/pv: Remove unsafe bits from the mod_l?_entry() fastpath

All changes in writeability and cacheability must go through full
re-validation.

Rework the logic as a whitelist, to make it clearer to follow.

This is XSA-182

Reported-by: Jérémie Boutoille <jboutoille@ext.quarkslab.com>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Tim Deegan <tim@xen.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        /* Fast path for identical mapping and presence. */', '        if ( !l4e_has_changed(ol4e, nl4e, _PAGE_PRESENT) )'], 'added_lines': ['        /* Fast path for sufficiently-similar mappings. */', '        if ( !l4e_has_changed(ol4e, nl4e, ~FASTPATH_FLAG_WHITELIST) )']}
description: The PV pagetable code in arch/x86/mm.c in Xen 4.7.x and earlier allows local 32-bit PV guest OS administrators to gain host OS privileges by leveraging fast-paths for updating pagetable entries.

code_evidence: Presence path validates only L4_DISALLOW_MASK and then enters the fast path when l4e_has_changed(ol4e, nl4e, _PAGE_PRESENT) is false; this ignores changes to writeability/cacheability bits.
The fast path calls adjust_guest_l4e and UPDATE_ENTRY without re-validating the modified flags, so a guest-controlled nl4e differing only in non-present bits bypasses full re-validation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The fast path fails to enforce the intended access-control policy on pagetable permissions, allowing a guest administrator to obtain writeability/cacheability the policy should restrict. This improper restriction of access matches CWE-284; the specific permission-bypass behavior is the mechanism, not a different weakness class.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the fast-path change test masks only _PAGE_PRESENT, so changes to writeability/cacheability flags are not detected and skip get_page_from_l4e and full re-validation. Trigger: a 32-bit PV guest administrator supplies an L4 entry differing only in those flags. Consequence: the entry is installed with insufficiently validated permissions, enabling privilege escalation into the host.

commit_msg: Fix bug #72241: get_icu_value_internal out-of-bounds read
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static void get_icu_disp_value_src_php( char* tag_name, INTERNAL_FUNCTION_PARAMETERS) ', '\t\t&loc_name, &loc_name_len , ', '\t'], 'added_lines': ['static void get_icu_disp_value_src_php( char* tag_name, INTERNAL_FUNCTION_PARAMETERS)', '\t\t&loc_name, &loc_name_len ,', '']}
description: The get_icu_value_internal function in ext/intl/locale/locale_methods.c in PHP before 5.5.36, 5.6.x before 5.6.22, and 7.x before 7.0.7 does not ensure the presence of a '\0' character, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (out-of-bounds read) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted locale_get_primary_language call.

code_evidence: Input locale string is parsed via zend_parse_parameters into loc_name/loc_name_len; length is bounded but no check that the buffer is NUL-terminated is performed.
The do-while loop drives ICU uloc_getDisplay* functions; on U_BUFFER_OVERFLOW_ERROR status is reset and the loop continues, with buflen compared against disp_name_len to size the buffer.
After the loop, intl_convert_utf16_to_utf8 consumes disp_name with length buflen, which may exceed the actual valid data if ICU did not write a terminating character.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The defect causes reading beyond the intended buffer boundary (disp_name) during conversion, matching CWE-125 Out-of-bounds Read. It is a read-side memory-safety issue, not a write overflow (CWE-787), because the unsafe operation is consuming data past the allocated/written region.

evidence_lines.code:
intl_convert_utf16_to_utf8( &utf8value, &utf8value_len, disp_name, buflen, &status );
efree( disp_name );

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function does not ensure the ICU display-name buffer is NUL-terminated before conversion, and the overflow-retry loop's length bookkeeping can leave buflen inconsistent with written data. A crafted locale_get_primary_language call triggers ICU to fill the buffer without a trailing terminator, so the UTF-16-to-UTF-8 conversion reads past the end of disp_name, causing an out-of-bounds read and denial of service.

commit_msg:
Fix buffer overflow in extract_status_code()

Issue #960 identified that the buffer allocated for copying the
HTTP status code could overflow if the http response was corrupted.

This commit changes the way the status code is read, avoids copying
data, and also ensures that the status code is three digits long,
is non-negative and occurs on the first line of the response.

Signed-off-by: Quentin Armitage <quentin@armitage.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tchar *buf_code;', '\tchar *begin;', '\tsize_t inc = 0;', '\tint code;', '', '\t/* Allocate the room */', '\tbuf_code = (char *)MALLOC(10);', "\twhile (buffer < end && *buffer++ != ' ') ;", '\tbegin = buffer;', "\twhile (buffer < end && *buffer++ != ' ')", '\t\tinc++;', '\tstrncat(buf_code, begin, inc);', '\tcode = atoi(buf_code);', '\tFREE(buf_code);'], 'added_lines': ['\tunsigned long code;', "\twhile (buffer < end && *buffer != ' ' && *buffer != '\\r')", '\t\tbuffer++;', '\tbuffer++;', "\tif (buffer + 3 >= end || *buffer == ' ' || buffer[3] != ' ')", '\t\treturn 0;', '\tcode = strtoul(buffer, &end, 10);', '\tif (buffer + 3 != end)', '\t\treturn 0;']}
description: keepalived before 2.0.7 has a heap-based buffer overflow when parsing HTTP status codes resulting in DoS or possibly unspecified other impact, because extract_status_code in lib/html.c has no validation of the status code and instead writes an unlimited amount of data to the heap.

code_evidence: A 10-byte heap buffer is allocated via MALLOC(10) at line 8. Lines 9-12 scan for space-delimited tokens without bounding the token length relative to the allocation; inc accumulates the full status-code field length. Line 13 calls strncat(buf_code, begin, inc), copying inc bytes into the 10-byte heap buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the function writes data past the end of an intended heap buffer. This is a direct out-of-bounds write, not merely an out-of-bounds read or integer issue.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the destination buffer is fixed at 10 bytes but the copy length inc is derived from the attacker-controlled HTTP response with no upper bound. Trigger: a corrupted response containing a long status-code token. Consequence: strncat writes past the heap allocation, causing heap buffer overflow, DoS, and possible memory corruption.

commit_msg:
xenoprof: limit consumption of shared buffer data

Since a shared buffer can be written to by the guest, we may only read
the head and tail pointers from there (all other fields should only ever
be written to). Furthermore, for any particular operation the two values
must be read exactly once, with both checks and consumption happening
with the thus read values. (The backtrace related xenoprof_buf_space()
use in xenoprof_log_event() is an exception: The values used there get
re-checked by every subsequent xenoprof_add_sample().)

Since that code needed touching, also fix the double increment of the
lost samples count in case the backtrace related xenoprof_add_sample()
invocation in xenoprof_log_event() fails.

Where code is being touched anyway, add const as appropriate, but take
the opportunity to entirely drop the now unused domain parameter of
xenoprof_buf_space().

This is part of XSA-313.

Reported-by: Ilja Van Sprundel <ivansprundel@ioactive.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: George Dunlap <george.dunlap@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Wei Liu <wl@xen.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static int xenoprof_add_sample(struct domain *d, xenoprof_buf_t *buf,', '    size = xenoprof_buf(d, buf, event_size);', '    if ( xenoprof_buf_space(d, buf, size) > 0 )'], 'added_lines': ['static int xenoprof_add_sample(const struct domain *d,', '                               const struct xenoprof_vcpu *v,', '    xenoprof_buf_t *buf = v->buffer;', '    size = v->event_size;', '    if ( xenoprof_buf_space(head, tail, size) > 0 )']}
description: An issue was discovered in xenoprof in Xen through 4.13.x, allowing guest OS users (without active profiling) to obtain sensitive information about other guests. Unprivileged guests can request to map xenoprof buffers, even if profiling has not been enabled for those guests. These buffers were not scrubbed.

code_evidence: head, tail, and size are read directly from the guest-writable shared buffer via xenoprof_buf(d, buf, ...) and stored in locals.
The sanity check compares head/tail against size, but size itself comes from the shared buffer and may be attacker-controlled or uninitialized.
The write path uses head as an index into event_log[head] and then updates event_head, relying on the guest-provided values.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function consumes guest-writable buffer metadata without ensuring it is initialized/validated against trusted state, matching CWE-909 (Missing Initialization of Resource): the critical resource (buffer metadata) is not established by the hypervisor before use. This differs from a pure bounds-check weakness because the trusted size is never initialized from v->event_size here.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The shared buffer's head, tail, and size fields are trusted before being validated against the trusted v->event_size. A guest can supply inconsistent or malicious size/head values, causing out-of-bounds or incorrect indexing into event_log during sample writes; the fix switches size to the trusted per-vcpu value and re-checks space with the already-read head/tail.

commit_msg:
DO NOT MERGE omx: check buffer port before using

Bug: 28816827
Change-Id: I3d5bad4a1ef96dec544b05bb31cc6f7109aae0a5
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['OMX_BUFFERHEADERTYPE *OMXNodeInstance::findBufferHeader(OMX::buffer_id buffer) {', '    return mBufferIDToBufferHeader.valueAt(index);'], 'added_lines': ['OMX_BUFFERHEADERTYPE *OMXNodeInstance::findBufferHeader(', '        OMX::buffer_id buffer, OMX_U32 portIndex) {', '    OMX_BUFFERHEADERTYPE *header = mBufferIDToBufferHeader.valueAt(index);', '    BufferMeta *buffer_meta =', '        static_cast<BufferMeta *>(header->pAppPrivate);', '    if (buffer_meta->getPortIndex() != portIndex) {', '        CLOGW("findBufferHeader: buffer %u found but with incorrect port index.", buffer);', '        android_errorWriteLog(0x534e4554, "28816827");', '        return NULL;', '    }', '    return header;']}
description: omx/OMXNodeInstance.cpp in libstagefright in mediaserver in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-08-01 does not validate the buffer port, which allows attackers to gain privileges via a crafted application, aka internal bug 28816827.

code_evidence: The function looks up a caller-supplied buffer id in mBufferIDToBufferHeader under mBufferIDLock and returns the stored header without checking which port the header belongs to. The only guard is buffer == 0 and index < 0; there is no validation that the header's port matches the caller's intended port.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The missing port validation lets a buffer operation target a header outside its intended port/buffer boundary, matching CWE-119's out-of-bounds memory operation. The fix adds a port-index check, confirming the weakness is improper restriction of buffer operations; the id-not-found path alone is not the flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: findBufferHeader resolves a buffer id to a header solely by key, so a buffer id valid for one port can be returned for a request on a different port. Trigger: a crafted application supplies a buffer/port combination that passes the id lookup but mismatches the port. Consequence: callers operate on a header whose buffer belongs to another port, leading to out-of-bounds reads/writes on the wrong memory buffer.

commit_msg:
In parse_identifier, it doesn't stop copying '*pcur'
untill encounter the NULL. As the 'ret' has a

commit_msg:
win: fix unsavory rwlock fallback implementation

Before this patch an uv_mutex_t (backed by a critical section) could be
released by a tread different from the thread that acquired it, which is
not allowed. This is fixed by using a semaphore instead.

Note that the affected code paths were used on Windows XP and Windows
Server 2003 only.

Fixes: https://github.com/libuv/libuv/issues/515
PR-URL: https://github.com/libuv/libuv/pull/516
Reviewed-By: Ben Noordhuis <info@bnoordhuis.nl>
Reviewed-By: Saúl Ibarra Corretgé <saghul@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['  int err;', '  err = uv_mutex_init(&rwlock->fallback_.read_mutex_);', '  if (err)', '    return err;', '  err = uv_mutex_init(&rwlock->fallback_.write_mutex_);', '  if (err) {', '    uv_mutex_destroy(&rwlock->fallback_.read_mutex_);', '    return err;', '  }', ''], 'added_lines': ['  /* Initialize the semaphore that acts as the write lock. */', '  HANDLE handle = CreateSemaphoreW(NULL, 1, 1, NULL);', '  if (handle == NULL)', '    return uv_translate_sys_error(GetLastError());', '  rwlock->fallback_.write_lock_.sem = handle;', '  /* Initialize the critical section protecting the reader count. */', '  InitializeCriticalSection(&rwlock->fallback_.read_lock_.cs);', '  /* Initialize the reader count. */']}
description: The uv_rwlock_t fallback implementation for Windows XP and Server 2003 in libuv before 1.7.4 does not properly prevent threads from releasing the locks of other threads, which allows attackers to cause a denial of service (deadlock) or possibly have unspecified other impact by leveraging a race condition.

code_evidence: The function initializes the fallback rwlock using two uv_mutex_t instances (read_mutex_ and write_mutex_) with uv_mutex_init, and on failure of the second mutex it destroys the first. The mutex types back these locks with Windows critical sections, which are owned by the acquiring thread.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The lock's synchronization primitive does not enforce correct exclusive ownership across threads, creating a concurrency window where the lock state can be manipulated by a non-owner thread. This is the race-condition/shared-resource synchronization flaw described by CWE-362; it is not merely a generic resource leak.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the write lock is implemented as a thread-owned mutex/critical section, so the lock's ownership is tied to the thread that acquired it. Trigger: one thread acquires the write lock and a different thread attempts to release it, as the rwlock API permits. Consequence: the release is invalid, leading to deadlock/instability (DoS).

Correctly load/initialize classes when using ConstantPool

- do not load classes in the "ifLoaded" calls
- never intitialize classes in the natives
- do not update the constant pool when querying from the natives

Fixes: #12016

[ci skip]

description: In Eclipse Openj9 to version 0.25.0, usage of the jdk.internal.reflect.ConstantPool API causes the JVM in some cases to pre-resolve certain constant pool entries. This allows a user to call static methods or access static members without running the class initialization method, and may allow a user to observe uninitialized values.

code_evidence: The native getClassAt0 forwards to getClassAt with J9_RESOLVE_FLAG_RUNTIME_RESOLVE, which resolves the constant-pool entry at runtime without triggering class initialization (no initialization flag). The wrapper exposes this resolution path to untrusted ConstantPool API callers, so a class reference can be resolved and its static members accessed before the class initializer runs.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-909 fits because the class resource is made usable without its required initialization, allowing observation of uninitialized values. This is missing initialization of a resource, not merely an incorrect resolution flag or a general access-control flaw.

Trigger: a user calls getClassAt0 (via jdk.internal.reflect.ConstantPool) on an entry whose class has not been initialized. Supported consequence: static methods or fields become reachable before initialization, exposing uninitialized/default values (confidentiality read of application data) or inconsistent state.

commit_msg:
PR22205, .debug_line file table NULL filename

The PR22200 fuzzer testcase found one way to put NULLs into .debug_line
file tables.  PR22205 finds another.  This patch gives up on trying to
prevent NULL files in the file table and instead just copes with them.
Arguably, this is better than giving up and showing no info from
.debug_line.  I've also fixed a case where the fairly recent DWARF5
support in handling broken DWARG could result in uninitialized memory
reads, and made a small tidy.

	PR 22205
	* dwarf2.c (concat_filename): Return "<unknown>" on NULL filename.
	(read_formatted_entries): Init "fe".
	(decode_line_info <DW_LNE_define_file>): Use line_info_add_file_name.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['      memset (&fe, 0, sizeof fe);']}
description: dwarf2.c in the Binary File Descriptor (BFD) library (aka libbfd), as distributed in GNU Binutils 2.29, mishandles NULL files in a .debug_line file table, which allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and application crash) via a crafted ELF file, related to concat_filename. NOTE: this issue is caused by an incomplete fix for CVE-2017-15023.

code_evidence: Each iteration declares an uninitialized stack struct fileinfo fe at [36,37,38]; its name, dir, time and size members have indeterminate values until a matching DW_LNCT_* content type assigns them.
Only DW_LNCT_path sets fe.name via stringp [49,50,51]; if the format header omits that content type, fe.name is never written.
fe.name is then passed to the callback at [108,109], so a crafted .debug_line format with no path entry supplies an indeterminate/NULL filename downstream (concat_filename), which dereferences it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Passing an unset/NULL fe.name to a callee that dereferences it matches CWE-476: a pointer expected to be valid is NULL, yielding a crash. This is distinct from an out-of-bounds read, since the defect is an uninitialized/NULL pointer value rather than an index bound violation.

evidence_lines.code:
if (!callback (table, fe.name, fe.dir, fe.time, fe.size))
return FALSE;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: fe is uninitialized and fe.name is only assigned when a DW_LNCT_path content descriptor appears. A crafted ELF whose .debug_line format lacks that entry leaves fe.name indeterminate (NULL), and the callback forwards it to concat_filename, which dereferences it; consequence is a crash (DoS) from the NULL pointer dereference, not memory corruption in this function.

commit_msg:
x86/vvmx: Disallow the use of VT-x instructions when nested virt is disabled

c/s ac6a4500b "vvmx: set vmxon_region_pa of vcpu out of VMX operation to an
invalid address" was a real bugfix as described, but has a very subtle bug
which results in all VT-x instructions being usable by a guest.

The toolstack constructs a guest by issuing:

  XEN_DOMCTL_createdomain
  XEN_DOMCTL_max_vcpus

and optionally later, HVMOP_set_param to enable nested virt.

As a result, the call to nvmx_vcpu_initialise() in hvm_vcpu_initialise()
(which is what makes the above patch look correct during review) is actually
dead code.  In practice, nvmx_vcpu_initialise() first gets called when nested
virt is enabled, which is typically never.

As a result, the zeroed memory of struct vcpu causes nvmx_vcpu_in_vmx() to
return true before nested virt is enabled for the guest.

Fixing the order of initialisation is a work in progress for other reasons,
but not viable for security backports.

A compounding factor is that the vmexit handlers for all instructions, other
than VMXON, pass 0 into vmx_inst_check_privilege()'s vmxop_check parameter,
which skips the CR4.VMXE check.  (This is one of many reasons why nested virt
isn't a supported feature yet.)

However, the overall result is that when nested virt is not enabled by the
toolstack (i.e. the default configuration for all production guests), the VT-x
instructions (other than VMXON) are actually usable, and Xen very quickly
falls over the fact that the nvmx structure is uninitialised.

In order to fail safe in the supported case, re-implement all the VT-x
instruction handling using a single function with a common prologue, covering
all the checks which should cause #UD or #GP faults.  This deliberately
doesn't use any state from the nvmx structure, in case there are other lurking
issues.

This is XSA-278

Reported-by: Sergey Dyasli <sergey.dyasli@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Reviewed-by: Sergey Dyasli <sergey.dyasli@citrix.com>

commit_msg:
x86/EPT: ept_set_middle_entry() related adjustments

ept_split_super_page() wants to further modify the newly allocated
table, so have ept_set_middle_entry() return the mapped pointer rather
than tearing it down and then getting re-established right again.

Similarly ept_next_level() wants to hand back a mapped pointer of
the next level page, so re-use the one established by
ept_set_middle_entry() in case that path was taken.

Pull the setting of suppress_ve ahead of insertion into the higher level
table, and don't have ept_split_super_page() set the field a 2nd time.

This is part of XSA-328.

Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Roger Pau Monné <roger.pau@citrix.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    unsigned long mfn;', '    ept_entry_t *ept_entry, e;', '        if ( !ept_set_middle_entry(p2m, ept_entry) )', '        else', '            e = atomic_read_ept_entry(ept_entry); /* Refresh */', '', '    if ( is_epte_superpage(&e) )', '    mfn = e.mfn;', '    *table = map_domain_page(_mfn(mfn));'], 'added_lines': ['    ept_entry_t *ept_entry, *next = NULL, e;', '        next = ept_set_middle_entry(p2m, ept_entry);', '        if ( !next )', '        /* e is now stale and hence may not be used anymore below. */', '    else if ( is_epte_superpage(&e) )', '    *table = next ?: map_domain_page(_mfn(e.mfn));']}
description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.13.x, allowing Intel guest OS users to gain privileges or cause a denial of service because of non-atomic modification of a live EPT PTE. When mapping guest EPT (nested paging) tables, Xen would in some circumstances use a series of non-atomic bitfield writes. Depending on the compiler version and optimisation flags, Xen might expose a dangerous partially written PTE to the hardware, which an attacker might be able to race to exploit. A guest administrator or perhaps even an unprivileged guest user might be able to cause denial of service, data corruption, or privilege escalation. Only systems using Intel CPUs are vulnerable. Systems using AMD CPUs, and Arm systems, are not vulnerable. Only systems using nested paging (hap, aka nested paging, aka in this case Intel EPT) are vulnerable. Only HVM and PVH guests can exploit the vulnerability. The presence and scope of the vulnerability depends on the precise optimisations performed by the compiler used to build Xen. If the compiler generates (a) a single 64-bit write, or (b) a series of read-modify-write operations in the same order as the source code, the hypervisor is not vulnerable. For example, in one test build using GCC 8.3 with normal settings, the compiler generated multiple (unlocked) read-modify-write operations in source-code order, which did not constitute a vulnerability. We have not been able to survey compilers; consequently we cannot say which compiler(s) might produce vulnerable code (with which code-generation options). The source code clearly violates the C rules, and thus should be considered vulnerable.

code_evidence: The entry at the computed index is read via atomic_read_ept_entry() into local e, but the present-bit check and the subsequent superpage test occur on that snapshot.

When the entry is not present, ept_set_middle_entry() installs a new middle table entry into the live EPT PTE, and the code then re-reads it with atomic_read_ept_entry() so e is refreshed before being used below.
The table pointer is unmapped and then remapped from e.mfn, relying on the value read from the entry to select the next level page.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-362 fits because the shared live EPT PTE is accessed and modified without ensuring exclusive, atomic update, creating a timing window for concurrent interference. This is a race on shared state, not merely a stale read or a memory-safety bug.

evidence_lines.code:
ept_entry = (*table) + index;
e = atomic_read_ept_entry(ept_entry);

unmap_domain_page(*table);
*table = map_domain_page(_mfn(mfn));

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The live EPT PTE is updated by ept_set_middle_entry() and then read back non-atomically relative to hardware/other walkers. Because the PTE is modified via multiple writes rather than one atomic store, a concurrent EPT walk (hardware or another vCPU) can observe a partially written entry, leading to data corruption, DoS, or privilege escalation.

soc: qcom: aoss: Fix missing put_device call in qmp_get

The reference taken by 'of_find_device_by_node()' must be released when
not needed anymore.
Add the corresponding 'put_device()' in the error handling paths.

Fixes: 8c75d585b931 ("soc: qcom: aoss: Expose send for generic usecase")
Signed-off-by: Miaoqian Lin <linmq006@gmail.com>
Reviewed-by: Stephen Boyd <swboyd@chromium.org>
Signed-off-by: Bjorn Andersson <bjorn.andersson@linaro.org>
Link: https://lore.kernel.org/r/20220108095931.21527-1-linmq006@gmail.com
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\treturn qmp ? qmp : ERR_PTR(-EPROBE_DEFER);'], 'added_lines': ['\tif (!qmp) {', '\t\tput_device(&pdev->dev);', '\t\treturn ERR_PTR(-EPROBE_DEFER);', '\t}', '\treturn qmp;']}
description: In the Linux kernel before 5.17.2, drivers/soc/qcom/qcom_aoss.c does not release an of_find_device_by_node reference after use, e.g., with put_device.

code_evidence: of_find_device_by_node() at line 11 acquires a device reference tied to pdev, and of_node_put at line 12 only releases the node reference, not the device. When platform_get_drvdata returns NULL, line 16 returns ERR_PTR(-EPROBE_DEFER) without ever calling put_device(&pdev->dev), leaking the device reference on this error path.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-772 fits because the acquired device resource outlives its effective lifetime on the error path; the missing put_device is the direct cause. This is a resource-lifetime leak, not a use-after-free, since no stale reference is dereferenced.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the device reference taken by of_find_device_by_node is not dropped when the driver data is not yet available. Trigger: qmp_get is called before the QMP platform device is bound, so platform_get_drvdata returns NULL and the -EPROBE_DEFER path executes. Consequence: the device reference and its associated memory are never released, accumulating across repeated probe deferrals.

happened.  In other words, do _not_ restart when finding that
between unlocking the child and locking the parent the former got
into __dentry_kill().  Skip the killed siblings instead...

Signed-off-by: Al Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tlist_del(&dentry->d_child);'], 'added_lines': ['\t__list_del_entry(&dentry->d_child);']}
description: The d_walk function in fs/dcache.c in the Linux kernel through 3.17.2 does not properly maintain the semantics of rename_lock, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (deadlock and system hang) via a crafted application.

code_evidence: __d_drop(dentry) removes the dentry from the hash, then __list_del_entry(&dentry->d_child) unlinks it from the parent's d_subdirs list and marks DCACHE_DENTRY_KILLED; the fix replaces list_del with __list_del_entry so rename_lock semantics are preserved while d_walk observes the killed state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The faulty list/hash maintenance under rename_lock lets the walker loop/retry indefinitely, exhausting CPU and hanging the system, which is the availability impact of CWE-400; it is not a memory-corruption or authorization flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the dentry is detached from the child list before DCACHE_DENTRY_KILLED is set, so a concurrent d_walk can see an inconsistent state and retry rename_lock under conditions other than an actual rename. Trigger: a local application racing dentry teardown against d_walk. Consequence: deadlock and system hang (availability loss).

description: Bytecode Alliance wasm-micro-runtime (aka WebAssembly Micro Runtime or WAMR) before 1.3.0 can have an "double free or corruption" error for a valid WebAssembly module because push_pop_frame_ref_offset is mishandled.

code_evidence: The function delegates all reference/offset stack bookkeeping to wasm_loader_push_pop_frame_offset and wasm_loader_push_pop_frame_ref, each returning bool checked here. No free() call, ownership transfer, or deallocation appears in this function; the only operations are loader stack pushes/pops and early false returns on failure.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-415 requires a free() invoked twice on one address. This function contains no free() and no pointer-ownership operation, so it does not directly support the target weakness; the double free, if real, is in the helper functions it calls, not in this code.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function itself neither allocates nor frees memory; it only sequences pop/push helpers and propagates their failure. Any double free would originate inside the referenced loader helpers or their interaction, not in these lines. The function's contribution is limited to invoking the combined helpers whose internal mishandling of frame references is the described defect; the consequence (double free/corruption) is not demonstrated by this body.

If alloc_disk fails in pcd_init_units, cd->disk will be
NULL, however in pcd_detect and pcd_exit, it's not check
this before free.It may result a NULL pointer dereference.

Also when register_blkdev failed, blk_cleanup_queue() and

Reported-by: Hulk Robot <hulkci@huawei.com>

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tif (!cd->disk)', '\t\t\tcontinue;', '']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.9. There is a NULL pointer dereference for a cd data structure if alloc_disk fails in drivers/block/paride/pf.c.

code_evidence: The loop iterates all PCD_UNITS entries unconditionally. cd->disk is only accessed inside the cd->present branch at lines 7-9, but lines 11-13 dereference cd->disk->queue and pass cd->disk to put_disk regardless of present or NULL state. If alloc_disk failed during initialization, cd->disk is NULL, so blk_cleanup_queue(cd->disk->queue) dereferences a NULL pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function directly dereferences a pointer (cd->disk->queue) that can be NULL, matching CWE-476. This is a missing validity check rather than a use-after-free or resource leak, which are distinct weaknesses.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: pcd_exit lacks a NULL check on cd->disk before using it outside the present guard. Trigger: an entry whose alloc_disk failed leaves cd->disk NULL while cleanup still runs. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference, causing a kernel crash (DoS) during module exit.

commit_msg: Bug 698916: Indirect object numbers must be in range.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tif (num < 0 || num > PDF_MAX_OBJECT_NUMBER)', '\t\tfz_throw(ctx, FZ_ERROR_SYNTAX, "object number out of range");']}
description: In Artifex MuPDF 1.12.0, the pdf_read_new_xref function in pdf/pdf-xref.c allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (segmentation violation and application crash) via a crafted pdf file.

code_evidence: Line 20 assigns the parsed integer token directly to num without any bounds check before it is used as an object number.
Lines 112-113 store num into the caller-provided *onum, propagating the unchecked value outward for later indexing/offset computation.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because an unchecked input-derived value flows into memory-addressing logic, enabling out-of-bounds operations and a crash. The root cause is the missing range validation on the object number, which is a precondition for the out-of-bounds access rather than an integer overflow or type-confusion weakness.

evidence_lines.code:
num = buf->i;
tok = pdf_lex(ctx, file, buf);

if (onum) *onum = num;
if (ogen) *ogen = gen;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The function parses an indirect object number from attacker-controlled PDF input and accepts any integer, including negative or oversized values, without validating it against PDF_MAX_OBJECT_NUMBER. Downstream code that uses this number to index object tables or compute memory offsets can then operate outside intended buffer bounds, producing a segmentation violation and crash.
