diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    tabstop_set(curbuf->b_p_vsts, &curbuf->b_p_vsts_array);', '    tabstop_set(curbuf->b_p_vts,  &curbuf->b_p_vts_array);'], 'added_lines': ['    (void)tabstop_set(curbuf->b_p_vsts, &curbuf->b_p_vsts_array);', '    (void)tabstop_set(curbuf->b_p_vts,  &curbuf->b_p_vts_array);']}
description: vim is vulnerable to Heap-based Buffer Overflow

code_evidence: didset_options2 frees curbuf->b_p_vsts_array and curbuf->b_p_vts_array, then calls tabstop_set with those option strings and the just-freed array pointers to rebuild them. The return value is ignored, so a failure inside tabstop_set (e.g. a negative or oversized tabstop value) leaves the freed pointer dangling or partially rebuilt without any error being surfaced.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function drives heap buffer allocation for tabstop arrays via tabstop_set on attacker-controlled option values, and ignoring the failure return permits the heap buffer to be left in an unsafe state that is subsequently written/read out of bounds. This is a heap-based buffer overflow (CWE-122) rather than a mere integer issue, since the resulting unsafe operation targets a heap-allocated buffer.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: tabstop_set parses a user-controlled 'vartabstop'/'varsofttabstop' value and allocates/rewrites the heap array, but its failure return is discarded. Trigger: a value that makes tabstop_set fail after the prior array was freed. Consequence: the stale/freed heap buffer is later used, giving invalid memory access consistent with a heap-based overflow or use-after-free.

commit_msg:
VP8: disallow thread count changes

Currently allocations are done at encoder creation time. Going from
threaded to non-threaded would cause a crash.

Bug: chromium:1486441
Change-Id: Ie301c2a70847dff2f0daae408fbef1e4d42e73d4
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['  if (cpi->initial_width) {', '    // TODO(https://crbug.com/1486441): Allow changing thread counts; the', '    // allocation is done once in vp8_create_compressor().', '    oxcf->multi_threaded = cpi->oxcf.multi_threaded;', '  }']}
description: Heap buffer overflow in vp8 encoding in libvpx in Google Chrome prior to 117.0.5938.132 and libvpx 1.13.1 allowed a remote attacker to potentially exploit heap corruption via a crafted HTML page. (Chromium security severity: High)

code_evidence: Lines 12-15 snapshot last_w/last_h/prev_number_of_layers and then overwrite cpi->oxcf with the caller-supplied *oxcf, adopting new Width/Height/thread settings without re-validating allocation state.
Lines 151-156 react to a changed number_of_layers by resetting temporal state and calling vp8_reset_temporal_layer_change, but never reconcile thread-count-dependent buffers.
Lines 158-161 only capture initial_width/height once; subsequent reconfiguration is not tied to the one-time allocation done in vp8_create_compressor.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The described Chromium bug is a heap buffer overflow where writes exceed allocated thread buffers, matching CWE-787's out-of-bounds write. It is not merely a logic error; the config change causes memory access past the buffer end.

evidence_lines.code:
if (cpi->oxcf.number_of_layers != prev_number_of_layers) {
vp8_reset_temporal_layer_change(cpi, oxcf, prev_number_of_layers);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: configuration changes (thread count/layer count) are accepted after encoder allocation, while per-thread buffers are sized only at creation. Trigger: an attacker-controlled page invokes encoding then changes thread count via vp8_change_config, leaving stale sizing. Consequence: writes into undersized thread buffers, heap corruption.

commit_msg: fixed #2138
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\t\tout_ptr = gf_malloc(sizeof(u8) * (1 + data_size * 2) );', '\t\t\tout_size = gf_base16_encode((u8*) data, (u32) data_size, out_ptr, 1 + (u32) data_size * 2);', '\t\t\tout_size = gf_base64_encode((u8*) data, (u32) data_size, out_ptr, 1 + (u32) data_size * 2);'], 'added_lines': ['\t\tu32 size64 = (u32) data_size * 2 + 3;', '\t\tout_ptr = gf_malloc(sizeof(char) * size64);', '\t\t\tout_size = gf_base16_encode((u8*) data, (u32) data_size, out_ptr, size64);', '\t\t\tout_size = gf_base64_encode((u8*) data, (u32) data_size, out_ptr, size64);']}
description: GPAC 2.0 allows a heap-based buffer overflow in gf_base64_encode. It can be triggered via MP4Box.

code_evidence: Line 27 obtains an attacker-controlled array buffer and its size from argv[0]; line 29 allocates 1 + data_size*2 bytes, computed in size_t but sized for base16 output.
Lines 36-37 call gf_base64_encode with the same 1 + data_size*2 output limit, though base64 requires ~ceil(data_size/3)*4 bytes plus padding/terminator.
Line 44 writes a NUL terminator at out_ptr[out_size], which can lie past the allocation when the encoder reports a size beyond the buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function allocates a buffer too small for the base64 output and lets the encoder write beyond it, which is a direct out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The root cause is the incorrect size constraint rather than a read overrun or integer-only flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The output buffer is sized using the base16 bound (1 + 2*data_size) but reused for base64 encoding, whose worst-case output exceeds that bound. Supplying an ArrayBuffer through the JS binding triggers gf_base64_encode to write past the heap allocation, and the out_ptr[out_size] terminator further writes out of bounds, yielding heap corruption or crash.

diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['static int search_old_relocation(struct reloc_struct_t *reloc_table, ut32 addr_to_patch, int n_reloc) {'], 'added_lines': ['static int search_old_relocation (struct reloc_struct_t *reloc_table,', '\t\t\t\t  ut32 addr_to_patch, int n_reloc) {']}
description: The relocs function in libr/bin/p/bin_bflt.c in radare2 1.2.1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (heap-based buffer overflow and application crash) or possibly have unspecified other impact via a crafted binary file.

code_evidence: The loop condition i < n_reloc bounds the index solely by the caller-supplied n_reloc, and line 4 dereferences reloc_table[i] without any check that n_reloc matches the allocated length of reloc_table.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the function performs buffer access using an unvalidated length, allowing reads outside the intended reloc_table boundary; the missing bounds check is the direct defect, and the out-of-bounds read is the supported consequence rather than an unrelated issue.

evidence_lines.code:
for (i = 0; i < n_reloc; i++) {
if (addr_to_patch == reloc_table[i].data_offset) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the function trusts the n_reloc count and indexes reloc_table[i] up to n_reloc-1 without validating it against the table's actual allocation size. Trigger: a crafted binary makes the caller pass a count larger than the allocated relocation table. commit_msg:
Merge pull request from GHSA-cv8x-p47p-99wr

* - Avoid SSL socket parent/listener getting destroyed during handshake by increasing parent's reference count.
- Add missing SSL socket close when the newly accepted SSL socket is discarded in SIP TLS transport.

* - Fix silly mistake: accepted active socket created without group lock in SSL socket.
- Replace assertion with normal validation check of SSL socket instance in OpenSSL verification callback (verify_cb()) to avoid crash, e.g: if somehow race condition with SSL socket destroy happens or OpenSSL application data index somehow gets corrupted.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['', '    /* Detach from SSL instance */', '    if (ossock->ossl_ssl) {', '\tSSL_set_ex_data(ossock->ossl_ssl, sslsock_idx, NULL);', '    }', '']}
description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in C language implementing standard based protocols such as SIP, SDP, RTP, STUN, TURN, and ICE. In PJSIP before version 2.11.1, there are a couple of issues found in the SSL socket. First, a race condition between callback and destroy, due to the accepted socket having no group lock. Second, the SSL socket parent/listener may get destroyed during handshake. Both issues were reported to happen intermittently in heavy load TLS connections. They cause a crash, resulting in a denial of service. These are fixed in version 2.11.1.

code_evidence: The function reads ossock->ossl_ssl and calls SSL_shutdown/SSL_in_init on it without any locking, while another thread could concurrently destroy or reset the SSL instance.

Only the write_mutex protects the ssl_state assignment; the SSL object access and the subsequent ssl_close_sockets call are performed outside that lock, leaving a window between the SSL_shutdown block and the close.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function accesses a shared SSL resource outside the mutex that guards the socket state, creating a timing window for an interfering concurrent sequence, which matches CWE-362 (race condition with improper synchronization).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the SSL instance is dereferenced and shut down without holding the socket's lock, so a concurrent destroy/reset path can free or detach the SSL object between the check and use. Trigger: heavy concurrent TLS connect/close activity. Consequence: use-after-free/race leading to a crash and denial of service.

commit_msg:
userfaultfd: shmem/hugetlbfs: only allow to register VM_MAYWRITE vmas

After the VMA to register the uffd onto is found, check that it has
VM_MAYWRITE set before allowing registration.  This way we inherit all
common code checks before allowing to fill file holes in shmem and
hugetlbfs with UFFDIO_COPY.

The userfaultfd memory model is not applicable for readonly files unless
it's a MAP_PRIVATE.

Link: http://lkml.kernel.org/r/20181126173452.26955-4-aarcange@redhat.com
Fixes: ff62a3421044 ("hugetlb: implement memfd sealing")
Signed-off-by: Andrea Arcangeli <aarcange@redhat.com>
Reviewed-by: Mike Rapoport <rppt@linux.ibm.com>
Reviewed-by: Hugh Dickins <hughd@google.com>
Reported-by: Jann Horn <jannh@google.com>
Fixes: 4c27fe4c4c84 ("userfaultfd: shmem: add shmem_mcopy_atomic_pte for userfaultfd support")
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Cc: "Dr. David Alan Gilbert" <dgilbert@redhat.com>
Cc: Mike Kravetz <mike.kravetz@oracle.com>
Cc: Peter Xu <peterx@redhat.com>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: Andrew Morton <akpm@linux-foundation.org>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\t\tWARN_ON(!(vma->vm_flags & VM_MAYWRITE));']}
description: The userfaultfd implementation in the Linux kernel before 4.19.7 mishandles access control for certain UFFDIO_ ioctl calls, as demonstrated by allowing local users to write data into holes in a tmpfs file (if the user has read-only access to that file, and that file contains holes), related to fs/userfaultfd.c and mm/userfaultfd.c.

code_evidence: The loop validates each VMA in the requested range with BUG_ON and vma_can_userfault(cur), but it never checks whether the VMA has VM_MAYWRITE. This validation block is the authorization gate for the range before any unregister work begins.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-863 fits because the function performs an authorization check (vma_can_userfault plus range validation) that is incomplete: it fails to verify VM_MAYWRITE, allowing unauthorized modification of read-only file data. This is an incorrect authorization check rather than a memory-safety flaw like CWE-787, since the weakness is the missing permission constraint, not an out-of-bounds write.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the range-validation loop accepts any VMA that satisfies vma_can_userfault but omits the VM_MAYWRITE permission constraint, so a read-only file VMA (e.g. a tmpfs file opened read-only, containing holes) passes validation. Trigger: a local user invokes the UFFDIO unregister/registration path over such a VMA; the added WARN_ON(!(vma->vm_flags & VM_MAYWRITE)) confirms the missing check. Supported consequence: the userfaultfd memory model is applied to a non-writable mapping, enabling writes into file holes despite lacking write authorization, i.e. an access-control bypass.

commit_msg:
Bing-Jhong Billy Jheng reported null-ptr-deref in unix_stream_sendpage()
with detailed analysis and a nice repro.

unix_stream_sendpage() tries to add data to the last skb in the peer's
recv queue without locking the queue.

If the peer's FD is passed to another socket and the socket's FD is
passed to the peer, there is a loop between them.  If we close both
sockets without receiving FD, the sockets will be cleaned up by garbage
collection.

The garbage collection iterates such sockets and unlinks skb with
FD from the socket's receive queue under the queue's lock.

So, there is a race where unix_stream_sendpage() could access an skb
locklessly that is being released by garbage collection, resulting in
use-after-free.

To avoid the issue, unix_stream_sendpage() must lock the peer's recv
queue.

Note the issue does not exist in 6.5+ thanks to the recent sendpage()
refactoring.

This patch is originally written by Linus Torvalds.

description:
A use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux kernel's af_unix component can be exploited to achieve local privilege escalation.

The unix_stream_sendpage() function tries to add data to the last skb in the peer's recv queue without locking the queue. Thus there is a race where unix_stream_sendpage() could access an skb locklessly that is being released by garbage collection, resulting in use-after-free.

We recommend upgrading past commit 790c2f9d15b594350ae9bca7b236f2b1859de02c.

code_evidence: After unix_state_lock(other) at line 34, the code reads the peer's receive queue via skb_peek_tail at line 47 and may append frags to that skb at line 61, all without holding other->sk_receive_queue.lock. The queue lock is only taken at line 73, after the skb has already been accessed and modified.
The skb obtained from skb_peek_tail is dereferenced and mutated (skb_append_pagefrags, skb->len/data_len/truesize) before any queue lock is acquired, so a concurrent lock-holding unlink can free it.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function dereferences and writes to an skb that garbage collection can concurrently free, which is exactly CWE-416 (use after free). This is not merely a missing-lock logic flaw; the lockless access to released memory is the supported weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unix_stream_sendpage() accesses and modifies the tail skb of the peer's receive queue without the queue's spinlock. Trigger: a peer socket loop cleaned up by garbage collection unlinks that skb under the queue lock while sendpage reads/updates it locklessly. Consequence: use-after-free of the skb, leading to a crash or potential privilege escalation.

description: Out-of-bounds Read in GitHub repository gpac/gpac prior to 2.3-DEV.

code_evidence: buflen is decreased by 6 without first checking it is at least 6, so a short input makes the unsigned buflen wrap to a huge value.
The loop bound is this wrapped buflen, and each iteration reads pbuffer[0..3] for the start code without ensuring four bytes remain.
After matching the sequence start code, pbuffer is advanced by 4 and then indexes pbuffer[0] through pbuffer[6] are read with no bounds check.
The bitrate fields read pbuffer[4], pbuffer[5] and pbuffer[6], i.e. bytes beyond the nominal 4-byte start-code window.
The extension-start branch likewise reads pbuffer[0] through pbuffer[3] after advancing pbuffer, without verifying remaining length.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function reads pbuffer beyond the intended buffer bounds because of the missing length check, matching CWE-125 (out-of-bounds read). This is a read overrun, not a write, so CWE-787 does not apply.

evidence_lines.code:
buflen -= 6;
for (ix = 0; ix < buflen; ix++, pbuffer++) {

scode = ((u32)pbuffer[0] << 24) | (pbuffer[1] << 16) | (pbuffer[2] << 8) |
pbuffer[3];

pbuffer += sizeof(u32);
switch ((pbuffer[0] >> 4) & 0xf) {

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: buflen is reduced by 6 before any length validation, and the loop and subsequent field reads index pbuffer without rechecking the remaining buffer. Trigger: a caller supplies a buffer shorter than the 6 bytes the function assumes. Consequence: reads past the end of the supplied buffer, which can crash or disclose adjacent memory.

description: tif_pixarlog.c in libtiff 4.0.6 has out-of-bounds write vulnerabilities in heap allocated buffers. Reported as MSVR 35094, aka "PixarLog horizontalDifference heap-buffer-overflow."

code_evidence: swapbuff is a fixed 32-byte stack buffer (line 8). bytes_per_pixel is computed from caller-supplied bps and spp (line 14). For bps/8 in {8,4,3,2} the loop copies bytes_per_pixel bytes into swapbuff via _TIFFmemcpy (lines 23,25) without any bound relating bytes_per_pixel to sizeof(swapbuff).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Writing more bytes than the destination swapbuff can hold is a write past the end of an intended buffer, matching CWE-787. The patch's added check in the diff confirms the missing bound; the flaw is an out-of-bounds write rather than an out-of-bounds read.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: bytes_per_pixel derived from bps*spp is used as the copy length into the fixed-size stack array swapbuff with no size check. Trigger: a caller passing a large spp (or bps) yields bytes_per_pixel > 32, so _TIFFmemcpy at line 23 writes past swapbuff. description: In ImageMagick 7.0.8-3 Q16, ReadDIBImage and WriteDIBImage in coders/dib.c allow attackers to cause an out of bounds write via a crafted file.

code_evidence: bytes_per_line is computed at line 49 and dib_info.image_size as bytes_per_line*image->rows at line 56, but the allocation uses dib_info.image_size as the count with sizeof(*pixels).
The pixel buffer is allocated with AcquireQuantumMemory(dib_info.image_size, sizeof(*pixels)) and zeroed for dib_info.image_size bytes.
Each raster loop writes via q=pixels+(image->rows-y-1)*bytes_per_line and then advances q up to bytes_per_line bytes per row (padding loops at lines 114-115, 136-137, 166-167, 194-195).
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function writes padding bytes beyond the allocated pixel buffer, which is an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787). The root cause is an allocation size mismatch/overflow rather than a read past the buffer, so CWE-787 fits the supported consequence.

evidence_lines.code:
bytes_per_line=4*((image->columns*dib_info.bits_per_pixel+31)/32);
dib_info.image_size=(unsigned int) (bytes_per_line*image->rows);

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The allocation count derives from dib_info.image_size, a 32-bit unsigned computed as bytes_per_line*image->rows, which can wrap for large dimensions, while the per-row write offset uses the full bytes_per_line*image->rows. A crafted image with large columns/rows makes the allocated buffer smaller than the row-padding writes, so the padding loops write past the end of the heap buffer, corrupting memory or crashing.

code_evidence: The loop iterates over HTTPS service parameters and, before writing the key/len header, checks only `context->ptr - start > rrs->len` and `_dns_left_len(context) <= 0`. It then writes 4 header bytes and, for the listed key cases, `memcpy(context->ptr, param->value, param->len)` followed by advancing `context->ptr` by param->len, with no check that param->len fits the remaining output buffer.

commit_msg:
DH_check(): Do not try checking q properties if it is obviously invalid

If  |q| >= |p| then the q value is obviously wrong as q
is supposed to be a prime divisor of p-1.

We check if p is overly large so this added test implies that
q is not large either when performing subsequent tests using that
q value.

Otherwise if it is too large these additional checks of the q value
such as the primality test can then trigger DoS by doing overly long
computations.

Fixes CVE-2023-3817

Reviewed-by: Paul Dale <pauli@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Matt Caswell <matt@openssl.org>
(Merged from https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/21551)
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['    int ok = 0, r;', '    if (dh->q) {'], 'added_lines': ['    int ok = 0, r, q_good = 0;', '    if (dh->q != NULL) {', '        if (BN_ucmp(dh->p, dh->q) > 0)', '            q_good = 1;', '        else', '            *ret |= DH_CHECK_INVALID_Q_VALUE;', '    }', '', '    if (q_good) {']}
description:
Issue summary: Checking excessively long DH keys or parameters may be very slow.

Impact summary: Applications that use the functions DH_check(), DH_check_ex()
or EVP_PKEY_param_check() to check a DH key or DH parameters may experience long
delays. Where the key or parameters that are being checked have been obtained
from an untrusted source this may lead to a Denial of Service.

The function DH_check() performs various checks on DH parameters. After fixing
CVE-2023-3446 it was discovered that a large q parameter value can also trigger
an overly long computation during some of these checks. A correct q value,
if present, cannot be larger than the modulus p parameter, thus it is
unnecessary to perform these checks if q is larger than p.

An application that calls DH_check() and supplies a key or parameters obtained
from an untrusted source could be vulnerable to a Denial of Service attack.

The function DH_check() is itself called by a number of other OpenSSL functions.
An application calling any of those other functions may similarly be affected.
The other functions affected by this are DH_check_ex() and
EVP_PKEY_param_check().

Also vulnerable are the OpenSSL dhparam and pkeyparam command line applications
when using the "-check" option.

The OpenSSL SSL/TLS implementation is not affected by this issue.

The OpenSSL 3.0 and 3.1 FIPS providers are not affected by this issue.

code_evidence: When dh->q is non-NULL, the function unconditionally runs expensive checks on attacker-supplied q: BN_mod_exp with dh->q as exponent (line 27), BN_is_prime_ex(dh->q,...) (line 32), and BN_div(dh->p, dh->q) (line 37). There is no check that q is smaller than p before these operations, so q may be arbitrarily large.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The weakness is unbounded iteration count in the big-number operations whose loop count scales with the unvalidated q size, matching CWE-834's excessive iteration leading to resource-consumption DoS. It is not a memory-safety bug; the harm is computational, not a buffer overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the q-dependent checks execute without validating that |q| < |p|, so an oversized q drives BN_mod_exp, the primality test and the division through many iterations proportional to q's bit length. Trigger: an application calls DH_check on untrusted DH parameters containing a very large q. Supported consequence: excessive CPU consumption, i.e., a denial of service from overly long computations.

description: A vulnerability has been found in Open5GS up to 2.4.10 and classified as problematic. This vulnerability affects unknown code in the library lib/core/ogs-tlv-msg.c of the component UDP Packet Handler. The manipulation leads to denial of service. The exploit has been disclosed to the public and may be used. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. VDB-209686 is the identifier assigned to this vulnerability.

code_evidence: root is allocated via ogs_tlv_get() at line 8, and further nodes are allocated in the loop at lines 14-16. The only exit path is the assert at line 20 followed by return root at line 21; there is no free of root or the linked curr nodes before the assert failure aborts.

code_evidence: Lines 10-11 only normalize a zero nb_packed_samples to 1; there is no upper bound check on the caller-supplied count.
Lines 35-37 accumulate nb_packed_samples into ent->sampleCount and w_currentSampleNum and compute w_LastDTS with ent->sampleDelta * (nb_packed_samples-1), using an unvalidated count.
Lines 62-66 grow stts->entries by only nb_extra (0 or 1) entries, not by the packed sample count, so the entry array capacity is unrelated to the sample count being written.
Line 84 stores nb_packed_samples directly into ent->sampleCount, and line 85 sets sampleDelta from nb_extra, propagating the unbounded count.
Line 91 allocates DTSs sized by stbl->SampleSize->sampleCount+2, while lines 99-108 fill it iterating over stts->nb_entries and ent->sampleCount, which can exceed the SampleSize-derived size.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits: the function performs buffer writes (DTSs[sampNum], entry sample counts) using an input-derived size without verifying it fits the allocated output buffer. This is a classic buffer-copy style overflow rather than an out-of-bounds read or pure integer error.

evidence_lines.code:

nb_packed_samples=1;

ent->sampleCount = nb_packed_samples;
ent->sampleDelta = nb_extra;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The root cause is that nb_packed_samples from the crafted file is never bounded before being used to size and fill sample-table entries and the DTSs array. A large packed-sample count drives the loops at lines 99-108 past the allocation at line 91, causing an out-of-bounds write (buffer overflow) that can crash or corrupt memory.

commit_msg:
DO NOT MERGE mm-video-v4l2: venc: add checks before accessing heap pointers

Heap pointers do not point to user virtual addresses in case
of secure session.
Set them to NULL and add checks to avoid accesing them

Bug: 28815329
Bug: 28920116

Change-Id: I94fd5808e753b58654d65e175d3857ef46ffba26
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['    if (venc_handle->is_secure_session()) {', '        DEBUG_PRINT_ERROR("logging secure output buffers is not allowed!");', '        return -1;', '    }', '']}
description: The secure-session feature in the mm-video-v4l2 venc component in mediaserver in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, and 6.x before 2016-08-01 mishandles heap pointers, which allows attackers to gain privileges via a crafted application, aka internal bug 28815329.

code_evidence: The function uses buffer_addr as the source pointer for fwrite(buffer_addr, buffer_len, 1, m_debug.outfile) with no validation that buffer_addr is a valid user virtual address or that buffer_len matches the actual buffer extent.

When m_debug.outfile is unset, the function also derives the output filename from m_sVenc_cfg dimensions and this pointer, but the write path at line 35 is the direct memory operation on the supplied buffer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-119 fits because the unsafe fwrite reads buffer_len bytes from buffer_addr without confirming the pointer references an in-bounds user buffer, producing an out-of-bounds memory read. It is not merely an access-control issue; the direct buffer operation is the weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the logging path treats buffer_addr/buffer_len as a valid user buffer and passes them directly to fwrite without checking session security or buffer validity. Trigger: a secure session supplies heap pointers that are not user virtual addresses, so fwrite reads from an unintended memory location. Consequence: out-of-bounds read of memory, potentially leaking data or crashing.

commit_msg: mboxlist: fix uninitialised memory use where pattern is "Other Users"
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            if (prefixlen < len) {'], 'added_lines': ['            if (prefixlen <= len) {']}
description: In the mboxlist_do_find function in imap/mboxlist.c in Cyrus IMAP before 3.0.4, an off-by-one error in prefix calculation for the LIST command caused use of uninitialized memory, which might allow remote attackers to obtain sensitive information or cause a denial of service (daemon crash) via a 'LIST "" "Other Users"' command.

code_evidence: The LIST pattern is reduced to commonpat and compared against the namespace prefix, but the branch selection at 112 uses a strict '<' test. When prefixlen equals len (the 'Other Users' prefix matches the namespace exactly), the else branch at 115 executes and copies commonpat+len+1, reading past the validated common prefix into uninitialized stack memory that is then used to build domainpat.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The code fails to correctly validate the derived length property of attacker-supplied LIST input before using it as an offset, matching CWE-20's improper validation of derived quantities such as offsets. The missing constraint is the equality case; the fix changes '<' to '<=' so the exact-prefix input takes the safe branch.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is an off-by-one boundary check: prefixlen == len is routed into the branch that assumes trailing pattern data exists beyond the matched prefix. Triggered by LIST "" "Other Users", the string copy at 117 reads uninitialized bytes from commonpat into domainpat, which is then passed to mboxlist_find_category, causing disclosure of stale memory or a daemon crash.

commit_msg: Replaced unsecure vsprintf function with vsnprintf in server logging functions (fixed issue #222).
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        vsprintf (buffer, format, args);'], 'added_lines': ['        if (vsnprintf(buffer, 255, format, args) >= 255)', "            buffer[255] = '\\0';"]}
description: Buffer Overflow Vulnerability exists in ajaxsoundstudio.com n Pyo < 1.03 in the Server_debug function, which allows remote attackers to conduct DoS attacks by deliberately passing on an overlong audio file name.

code_evidence: A fixed 256-byte stack buffer 'buffer' is declared at line 6. The variadic 'format' argument is passed directly to vsprintf at line 9, which copies the formatted output into 'buffer' without any destination-size bound. The result is then passed to PySys_WriteStdout at line 11.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-120 fits because the copy operation (vsprintf into buffer) writes an input-derived string to a fixed-size output buffer without verifying the input size against that buffer. This is a buffer-copy-without-size-check, distinct from an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: vsprintf at line 9 performs an unbounded formatted copy into the 256-byte stack buffer, with no check that the resulting length is less than 256. Trigger: a caller supplies an overlong audio file name (or other long input) as the format argument, as described for Server_debug. Consequence: the formatted string overflows the stack buffer, corrupting adjacent memory and enabling a crash/DoS and potentially code execution.

commit_msg: Make line_no with too large value(2**20) invalid. Fixes #124
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['          invalid_data = true;', '', '        } else if ((line_no > (2 << 20)) || (line_no < -(2 << 20))) {', '          // Too large value. Assume this is invalid', '          // 2**20 = 1048576 = heuristic value.']}
description: tinyexr 0.9.5 has a integer overflow over-write in tinyexr::DecodePixelData in tinyexr.h, related to OpenEXR code.

code_evidence: line_no and data_len are read from the untrusted chunk and byte-swapped without range validation; only data_len is compared to data_size.
line_no feeds line_no + num_scanline_blocks, and the result determines num_lines used for decoding.
A later int64 subtraction guards against wrap, but the earlier int additions still assume the value fits in int.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the unsafe computation is signed integer addition on an untrusted value whose result is assumed to remain valid. The commit's added 2**20 line_no bound confirms that the vulnerability lies in unchecked integer range, not in the separate size_t(data_len) > data_size check, which is a comparison rather than an overflow.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: attacker-controlled line_no is used in signed int arithmetic (line_no + num_scanline_blocks) before bounds checking, so a very large or negative value can overflow or wrap. Trigger: a crafted EXR chunk with an extreme line_no that passes the data_len check. Consequence: wrapped num_lines or line_no values can mislead DecodePixelData, producing out-of-bounds writes or memory corruption.

In summary, this patch solves those use-after-free by

1. Re-implement the nfc_llcp_find_local(). The current version does not
grab the reference when getting the local from the linked list.  For
example, the llcp_sock_bind() gets the reference like below:

// llcp_sock_bind()

    local = nfc_llcp_find_local(dev); // A
    ..... \
           | raceable
    ..... /
    llcp_sock->local = nfc_llcp_local_get(local); // B

There is an apparent race window that one can  drop the reference
and free the local object fetched in (A) before (B) gets the reference.

2. Some callers of the nfc_llcp_find_local() do not grab the reference
at all. For example, the nfc_genl_llc_{{get/set}_params/sdreq} functions.
We add the nfc_llcp_local_put() for them. Moreover, we add the necessary
error handling function to put the reference.

3. Add the nfc_llcp_remove_local() helper. The local object is removed
from the linked list in local_release() when all reference is gone. This
patch removes it when nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called.

Therefore, every caller of nfc_llcp_find_local() will get a reference
even when the nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called. This promises no
use-after-free for the local object is ever possible.

description: A use-after-free flaw was found in nfc_llcp_find_local in net/nfc/llcp_core.c in NFC in the Linux kernel. This flaw allows a local user with special privileges to impact a kernel information leak issue.

code_evidence: nfc_llcp_find_local(dev) at [29] returns a pointer to the LLCP local object stored in the device's list; the function stores it in local without taking a reference.

On the LTO path, if dev->dep_link_up is set, [36,37] jumps to exit without releasing local, and the exit block at [45,46,47] only unlocks the device and drops the device reference; no nfc_llcp_local_put is performed.
Because no reference is held, a concurrent nfc_llcp_unregister_device can free the local via local_release while this function still holds the raw pointer.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-416 fits because the function operates on a pointer to an LLCP local that can be freed by a concurrent unregister path; the missing reference acquisition and missing put leave a dangling reference in use. This is a lifetime/refcount flaw, not merely a null-check omission.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: nfc_llcp_find_local returns a list pointer without acquiring a kref, and the error path at [36,37] returns before any reference is taken or released. Trigger: concurrent device unregistration frees the local object while nfc_genl_llc_set_params still uses or omits cleanup of it. Consequence: use-after-free of the local object, supporting memory corruption, crash, or information leak.

commit_msg:
Add some sanity checks when checking CRL scores

Note: this was accidentally omitted from OpenSSL 1.0.2 branch.
Without this fix any attempt to use CRLs will crash.

CVE-2016-7052

Thanks to Bruce Stephens and Thomas Jakobi for reporting this issue.

Reviewed-by: Stephen Henson <steve@openssl.org>
Reviewed-by: Rich Salz <rsalz@openssl.org>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['        if (crl_score < best_score)', '        if (crl_score == best_score) {'], 'added_lines': ['        if (crl_score < best_score || crl_score == 0)', '        if (crl_score == best_score && best_crl != NULL) {']}
description: crypto/x509/x509_vfy.c in OpenSSL 1.0.2i allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (NULL pointer dereference and application crash) by triggering a CRL operation.

code_evidence: When crl_score equals best_score, the code enters the tie-break block and calls X509_CRL_get_lastUpdate(best_crl) without checking best_crl; best_crl is initialized to NULL at line 8 and only assigned at line 24 after this comparison.
If the first candidate has score 0 equal to the initial best_score (0), the equal-score branch is taken while best_crl is still NULL, and the NULL pointer is passed to X509_CRL_get_lastUpdate.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Passing a NULL best_crl into X509_CRL_get_lastUpdate is a direct dereference of a pointer expected to be valid, matching CWE-476. The missing guard is a NULL-check omission, not a use-after-free or type confusion.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the tie-break branch dereferences best_crl even though it may still be NULL when no prior CRL has been selected. Trigger: a CRL whose computed score equals the incoming best_score (e.g. 0) on the first iteration. Consequence: NULL pointer dereference and application crash (DoS).

commit_msg: Bug #703 safeguard against corrupt packet lengths in checksum functions
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['            retval = fix_ipv4_checksums(tcpedit, *pkthdr, ip_hdr);', '            retval = fix_ipv6_checksums(tcpedit, *pkthdr, ip6_hdr);'], 'added_lines': ['            retval = fix_ipv4_checksums(tcpedit, *pkthdr, ip_hdr, l2len);', '            retval = fix_ipv6_checksums(tcpedit, *pkthdr, ip6_hdr, l2len);']}
description: Tcpreplay v4.4.1 has a heap-based buffer overflow in do_checksum_math at /tcpedit/checksum.c.

code_evidence: l2len is derived from the packet via tcpedit_dlt_l2len using caplen; only -1 is rejected, so a large l2len relative to caplen can propagate.
IPv4 path checks caplen < l2len + sizeof(*ip_hdr) before obtaining ip_hdr, but the checksum call at 199 receives no length bound.
IPv6 path performs the analogous caplen < l2len + sizeof(*ip6_hdr) check, again without passing a bounded length to the checksum routine.

When fixcsum or needtorecalc is set, fix_ipv4_checksums/fix_ipv6_checksums are invoked with only pkthdr and the header pointer; the checksum math then walks packet data using lengths derived from the packet.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the checksum computation writes past the end of the heap buffer when packet length fields are corrupt and no bound is enforced before the call. This is a write past the buffer end, not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125), matching the out-of-bounds write classification.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: checksum routines are invoked without a validated length bound tying the IP header/payload to caplen, so corrupt or inconsistent packet length fields drive the checksum walk beyond the allocated buffer. Trigger: a crafted packet with corrupt internal length fields reaches do_checksum_math via fix_ipv4_checksums/fix_ipv6_checksums. Consequence: out-of-bounds heap write, potentially code execution or crash.

commit_msg:
Fix jpeg_skip_scanlines() segfault w/merged upsamp

The additional segfault mentioned in #244 was due to the fact that
the merged upsamplers use a different private structure than the
non-merged upsamplers.  jpeg_skip_scanlines() was assuming the latter, so
when merged upsampling was enabled, jpeg_skip_scanlines() clobbered one
of the IDCT method pointers in the merged upsampler's private structure.

For reasons unknown, the test image in #441 did not encounter this
segfault (too small?), but it encountered an issue similar to the one
fixed in 5bc43c7821df982f65aa1c738f67fbf7cba8bd69, whereby it was
necessary to set up a dummy postprocessing function in
read_and_discard_scanlines() when merged upsampling was enabled.
Failing to do so caused either a segfault in merged_2v_upsample() (due
to a NULL pointer being passed to jcopy_sample_rows()) or an error
("Corrupt JPEG data: premature end of data segment"), depending on the
number of scanlines skipped and whether the first scanline skipped was
an odd- or even-numbered row.

Fixes #441
Fixes #244 (for real this time)

description: A crafted input file could cause a null pointer dereference in jcopy_sample_rows() when processed by libjpeg-turbo.

code_evidence: Line 7 casts cinfo->upsample to my_upsample_ptr, but this function is the merged-upsample variant whose private structure is my_merged_upsample_ptr. Lines 14-17 then read Cr_r_tab, Cb_b_tab, Cr_g_tab and Cb_g_tab through that wrongly typed pointer, so the field offsets resolve to unrelated members of the merged upsampler's private struct.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-476 fits because the wrong struct cast produces pointer fields that are not valid, and the subsequent indexed reads dereference them, causing a NULL-pointer crash. It is not a simple out-of-bounds read; the defect is an invalid pointer value from a mismatched private-structure type.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause is a type-confusion cast that makes the table-pointer fields read from the wrong offsets in the merged upsampler's private struct. The trigger is any decode that enables merged upsampling and invokes this routine; the misread pointers can be NULL or garbage, and dereferencing them (e.g. Crrtab[cr], Cbgtab[cb]) yields a crash or invalid memory access. The consequence is a NULL-pointer dereference/segfault, as described for jcopy_sample_rows().

commit_msg:
parser: json: fix double-free (#3453)

Signed-off-by: davkor <david@adalogics.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        mp_buf = NULL;', '            flb_free(tmp_out_buf);']}
description: Fluent Bit (aka fluent-bit) 1.7.0 through 1.7,4 has a double free in flb_free (called from flb_parser_json_do and flb_parser_do).

code_evidence: tmp_out_buf aliases mp_buf initially (line 56) and is stored in *out_buf (line 70); after the decoder path may replace tmp_out_buf, mp_buf is freed only when it differs (lines 72-74).

The NULL-key error branch frees mp_buf (line 95) but leaves *out_buf pointing at the same allocation, then returns -1; later code frees tmp_out_buf (line 152), which can equal the already-freed mp_buf, causing a second free.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function calls flb_free on the same heap address more than once (mp_buf at line 95 and tmp_out_buf at line 152 when aliased), which is exactly CWE-415. This is a double free rather than a use-after-free because the repeated operation is free itself.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the error branch at line 95 frees the buffer without clearing the alias *out_buf (or tmp_out_buf), and the normal path at line 152 frees tmp_out_buf unconditionally. Trigger: decoding or parsing reaches the NULL time-key check after the buffer was published to *out_buf, so the same allocation is freed twice; the fix adds flb_free(tmp_out_buf) and mp_buf=NULL. Consequence: heap corruption or crash from double free.

description: PJSIP is a free and open source multimedia communication library written in the C language implementing standard based protocols such as SIP, SDP, RTP, STUN, TURN, and ICE. In various parts of PJSIP, when error/failure occurs, it is found that the function returns without releasing the currently held locks. This could result in a system deadlock, which cause a denial of service for the users. No release has yet been made which contains the linked fix commit. All versions up to an including 2.11.1 are affected. Users may need to manually apply the patch.

commit_msg:
hevc: check that the VCL NAL types are the same for all slice segments of a frame

Fixes possible invalid memory access for mismatching skipped/non-skipped
slice segments.

Found-by: Mateusz "j00ru" Jurczyk and Gynvael Coldwind
Sample-Id: 00001533-google
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        if (s->nal_unit_type != s->first_nal_type) {', '            av_log(s->avctx, AV_LOG_ERROR,', '                   "Non-matching NAL types of the VCL NALUs: %d %d\\n",', '                   s->first_nal_type, s->nal_unit_type);', '            return AVERROR_INVALIDDATA;', '        }', '']}
description: A vulnerability, which was classified as problematic, was found in FFmpeg 2.0. This affects the function decode_nal_unit of the component Slice Segment Handler. The manipulation leads to memory corruption. It is possible to initiate the attack remotely. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue.

code_evidence: hls_slice_header(s) parses the slice header and sets s->nal_unit_type for the current VCL NAL unit without checking that it matches the type of the first slice segment of the frame.
When first_slice_in_pic_flag is set, hevc_frame_start(s) initializes frame state; otherwise a non-first segment proceeds as long as s->ref is set, without verifying the NAL type consistency.

hls_slice_data(s) then decodes slice data using the per-NAL-type-derived state, and hls_slice_data's result ctb_addr_ts drives the is_decoded/restore_tqb_pixels path, so a mismatched skipped/non-skipped segment can corrupt frame state.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The commit explicitly fixes 'possible invalid memory access' from mismatching skipped/non-skipped slice segments, and the added check rejects non-matching NAL types before hls_slice_data. The resulting memory corruption is an out-of-bounds write, matching CWE-787; it is not merely an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) since state-driven decoding can write past buffers.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the decoder accepts a frame's subsequent slice segments whose VCL NAL type differs from the first segment's type, so skipped and non-skipped segments are mixed. Trigger: a crafted bitstream delivers mismatching NAL types across segments of one frame. Consequence: state derived from one segment type is used while decoding another, leading to invalid memory access/memory corruption (CWE-787 out-of-bounds write).

commit_msg:
KGDB and KDB allow read and write access to kernel memory, and thus
should be restricted during lockdown.  An attacker with access to a
serial port (for example, via a hypervisor console, which some cloud
vendors provide over the network) could trigger the debugger so it is
important that the debugger respect the lockdown mode when/if it is
triggered.

Fix this by integrating lockdown into kdb's existing permissions
mechanism.  Unfortunately kgdb does not have any permissions mechanism
(although it certainly could be added later) so, for now, kgdb is simply
and brutally disabled by immediately exiting the gdb stub without taking
any action.

For lockdowns established early in the boot (e.g. the normal case) then
this should be fine but on systems where kgdb has set breakpoints before
the lockdown is enacted than "bad things" will happen.

CVE: CVE-2022-21499
Co-developed-by: Stephen Brennan <stephen.s.brennan@oracle.com>
Signed-off-by: Stephen Brennan <stephen.s.brennan@oracle.com>
Reviewed-by: Douglas Anderson <dianders@chromium.org>
Signed-off-by: Daniel Thompson <daniel.thompson@linaro.org>
Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

For now the', '\t\t\t * answer is simply "don\'t do that". Typically lockdown', '\t\t\t * *will* be applied before the debug core gets started', '\t\t\t * so only developers using kgdb for fairly advanced', '\t\t\t * early kernel debug can be biten by this. Hopefully', '\t\t\t * they are sophisticated enough to take care of', '\t\t\t * themselves, especially with help from the lockdown', '\t\t\t * message printed on the console!', '\t\t\t */', '\t\t\tif (security_locked_down(LOCKDOWN_DBG_WRITE_KERNEL)) {', '\t\t\t\tif (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_KGDB_KDB)) {', '\t\t\t\t\t/* Switch back to kdb if possible... */', '\t\t\t\t\tdbg_kdb_mode = 1;', '\t\t\t\t\tcontinue;', '\t\t\t\t} else {', '\t\t\t\t\t/* ... otherwise just bail */', '\t\t\t\t\tbreak;', '\t\t\t\t}', '\t\t\t}']}
description: KGDB and KDB allow read and write access to kernel memory, and thus should be restricted during lockdown. An attacker with access to a serial port could trigger the debugger so it is important that the debugger respect the lockdown mode when/if it is triggered. joint-evidence.rejection_reason: The function contains no buffer write or index computation; the patch only adds a lockdown check around the gdb stub, so out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) is not supported.

description: Rizin is a UNIX-like reverse engineering framework and command-line toolset. Versions 0.4.0 and prior are vulnerable to out-of-bounds write when parsing DEX files. A user opening a malicious DEX file could be affected by this vulnerability, allowing an attacker to execute code on the user's machine. A patch is available on the `dev` branch of the repository.

Line 7 computes malloc(size + 1); if size is UINT64_MAX the addition wraps to 0, yielding a tiny allocation. Line 12 then writes data[size] = 0, a NUL byte far past the allocated buffer, producing the one-byte OOB write described in the commit.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-787 fits because the function writes the terminator past the end of the intended heap buffer. The underlying flaw is an integer overflow (CWE-190), but the supported and directly observable weakness is the resulting out-of-bounds write, so the target label is appropriate.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: unchecked integer overflow in the allocation-size expression size + 1. Trigger: a DEX string length of UINT64_MAX (or near-wrap value) from rz_buf_uleb128. Consequence: malloc allocates a too-small buffer, and the terminating write at data[size] writes out of bounds, corrupting heap memory and potentially enabling code execution or crash. The missing guard is the UT64_ADD_OVFCHK check added in the patch.

commit_msg:
usb: misc: legousbtower: Fix NULL pointer deference

This patch fixes a NULL pointer dereference caused by a race codition in
the probe function of the legousbtower driver. It re-structures the
probe function to only register the interface after successfully reading
the board's firmware ID.

The probe function does not deregister the usb interface after an error
receiving the devices firmware ID. The device file registered
(/dev/usb/legousbtower%d) may be read/written globally before the probe
function returns. When tower_delete is called in the probe function
(after an r/w has been initiated), core dev structures are deleted while
the file operation functions are still running. If the 0 address is
mappable on the machine, this vulnerability can be used to create a
Local Priviege Escalation exploit via a write-what-where condition by
remapping dev->interrupt_out_buffer in tower_write. A forged USB device
and local program execution would be required for LPE. The USB device
would have to delay the control message in tower_probe and accept
the control urb in tower_open whilst guest code initiated a write to the
device file as tower_delete is called from the error in tower_probe.

This bug has existed since 2003. Patch tested by emulated device.

Cc: stable <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Greg Kroah-Hartman <gregkh@linuxfoundation.org>

description: The tower_probe function in drivers/usb/misc/legousbtower.c in the Linux kernel before 4.8.1 allows local users (who are physically proximate for inserting a crafted USB device) to gain privileges by leveraging a write-what-where condition that occurs after a race condition and a NULL pointer dereference.

code_evidence: The interface and its character device are registered via usb_set_intfdata and usb_register_dev before the firmware version is obtained, exposing the device node to userspace while probe is still running.
usb_control_msg may block for up to 1000 ms; if it fails, the error path calls tower_delete(dev), which frees the dev structure while the already-registered file operations can still access it.
tower_delete frees core dev structures referenced by concurrent tower_read/tower_write, leaving dangling or NULL pointers dereferenced later in those operations.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function supports CWE-476 because the race leaves file-operation code dereferencing dev pointers that have been freed or NULLed by tower_delete, matching a NULL pointer dereference. The added ordering change addresses the use-after-free-like race that produces this NULL dereference; CWE-476 is the specified target.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: registration of the device node occurs before probe completes, and the probe error path tears down dev via tower_delete. Trigger: a crafted USB device delays or fails the get-version control message while a local user opens/writes the device file. Consequence: tower_write/tower_read dereference freed or NULL dev fields (e.g., interrupt_out_buffer), causing a NULL pointer dereference and potential write-what-where privilege escalation.

commit_msg:
posix-timer: Properly check sigevent->sigev_notify

timer_create() specifies via sigevent->sigev_notify the signal delivery for
the new timer. The valid modes are SIGEV_NONE, SIGEV_SIGNAL, SIGEV_THREAD
and (SIGEV_SIGNAL | SIGEV_THREAD_ID).

The sanity check in good_sigevent() is only checking the valid combination
for the SIGEV_THREAD_ID bit, i.e. SIGEV_SIGNAL, but if SIGEV_THREAD_ID is
not set it accepts any random value.

This has no real effects on the posix timer and signal delivery code, but
it affects show_timer() which handles the output of /proc/$PID/timers. That
function uses a string array to pretty print sigev_notify. The access to
that array has no bound checks, so random sigev_notify cause access beyond
the array bounds.

Add proper checks for the valid notify modes and remove the SIGEV_THREAD_ID
masking from various code pathes as SIGEV_NONE can never be set in
combination with SIGEV_THREAD_ID.

Reported-by: Eric Biggers <ebiggers3@gmail.com>
Reported-by: Dmitry Vyukov <dvyukov@google.com>
Reported-by: Alexey Dobriyan <adobriyan@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Thomas Gleixner <tglx@linutronix.de>
Cc: John Stultz <john.stultz@linaro.org>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org

commit_msg:
The ALSA proc helper manages the child nodes in a linked list, but its
addition and deletion is done without any lock.  This leads to a
corruption if they are operated concurrently.  Usually this isn't a
problem because the proc entries are added sequentially in the driver
probe procedure itself.  But the card registrations are done often
asynchronously, and the crash could be actually reproduced with
syzkaller.

This patch papers over it by protecting the link addition and deletion
with the parent's mutex.  There is "access" mutex that is used for the
file access, and this can be reused for this purpose as well.

Reported-by: syzbot+48df349490c36f9f54ab@syzkaller.appspotmail.com
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>
Signed-off-by: Takashi Iwai <tiwai@suse.de>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tlist_del(&entry->list);'], 'added_lines': ['\tp = entry->parent;', '\tif (p) {', '\t\tmutex_lock(&p->access);', '\t\tlist_del(&entry->list);', '\t\tmutex_unlock(&p->access);', '\t}']}
description: An issue was discovered in the Linux kernel before 5.0.10. There is a use-after-free in the sound subsystem because card disconnection causes certain data structures to be deleted too early. This is related to sound/core/init.c and sound/core/info.c.

code_evidence: Lines 11-13 recursively free all child entries via list_for_each_entry_safe and snd_info_free_entry(p), which itself eventually kfree()s each child (line 17).

Line 13 then performs list_del(&entry->list) on the entry being freed, but the parent's children list is modified without holding the parent's access mutex, so a concurrent traversal/addition can race with this unlink and the subsequent kfree.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The unsynchronized list_del followed by kfree lets another thread reference an entry after its memory is released, matching CWE-416. The locking omission is the cause; the use-after-free is the resulting weakness, not merely a generic race condition (CWE-362).
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the linked-list removal of a freed entry is not serialized against concurrent list operations on the parent's children list. Trigger: asynchronous card registration/disconnection causes snd_info_free_entry to run concurrently with another thread traversing or adding to the same list. Consequence: a racing thread can retain or follow a stale list pointer into freed snd_info_entry memory, yielding a use-after-free crash (as reproduced by syzkaller).

wouldn't cleanup the default device in the normal way, but rely on the garbage
collector.

This works (but isn't ideal), *except* when the job replaces the device with
the null device (using the nulldevice operator) - this means that
.uninstallpagedevice doesn't replace the existing device with the nulldevice
(since it is already installed), the device from the graphics ends up being
freed - and as it is the nulldevice, which we rely on, memory corruption
and a segfault can happen.

We avoid this by checking if the current device is the nulldevice, and if so,
restoring it away, before continuing with the device cleanup.

commit_msg:
journalctl: verify sealed log epochs are continuous

Currently empty epochs are not sealed. This allows an attacker to truncate
a sealed log and continue it without any problems showing when verifying the
log.

This partially addresses CVE-2023-31438. One way to extend this change to
address CVE-2023-31438 completely, would be to verify that there is exactly
one seal per epoch (and not sealing when the epoch has not ended yet).

the change also adds a journal-file flag: HEADER_COMPATIBLE_SEALED_CONTINUOUS
this flag indicates that a journal file is sealed continuously and decides whether
any missing crypto epochs should trigger a warning or an error.
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['        journal_file_write_final_tag(*f);']}
description: An issue was discovered in systemd 253. An attacker can truncate a sealed log file and then resume log sealing such that checking the integrity shows no error, despite modifications. NOTE: the vendor reportedly sent "a reply denying that any of the finding was a security vulnerability."

code_evidence: journal_file_rotate archives the current file then opens a new file using the archived path and the predecessor *f as the previous file, without any step validating that the sealed epochs of the archived log are continuous before the new file is created and sealing resumes.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-354 fits because the function proceeds to archive and reopen the journal without validating the integrity-sealing state (epoch continuity) of the existing sealed data, so an integrity check value/chain is effectively not verified before continued use. The missing constraint is validation of seal continuity, not a checksum computation bug.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: rotation archives a sealed journal and immediately reopens/continues it, so a truncated sealed log with missing crypto epochs is carried forward without integrity validation. Trigger: an attacker truncates a sealed log; when rotation later occurs, the new file is linked to the incomplete predecessor and later integrity checking reports no error. Consequence: modification/truncation of sealed log data is not detected, undermining integrity verification.

commit_msg:
libsepol/cil: Check for statements not allowed in optional blocks

While there are some checks for invalid statements in an optional
block when resolving the AST, there are no checks when building the
AST.

OSS-Fuzz found the following policy which caused a null dereference
in cil_tree_get_next_path().
  (blockinherit b3)
  (sid SID)
  (sidorder(SID))
  (optional o
    (ibpkeycon :(1 0)s)
    (block b3
      (filecon""block())
      (filecon""block())))

The problem is that the blockinherit copies block b3 before
the optional block is disabled. When the optional is disabled,
block b3 is deleted along with everything else in the optional.
Later, when filecon statements with the same path are found an
error message is produced and in trying to find out where the block
was copied from, the reference to the deleted block is used. The
error handling code assumes (rightly) that if something was copied
from a block then that block should still exist.

It is clear that in-statements, blocks, and macros cannot be in an
optional, because that allows nodes to be copied from the optional
block to somewhere outside even though the optional could be disabled
later. When optionals are disabled the AST is reset and the
resolution is restarted at the point of resolving macro calls, so
anything resolved before macro calls will never be re-resolved.
This includes tunableifs, in-statements, blockinherits,
blockabstracts, and macro definitions. Tunable declarations also
cannot be in an optional block because they are needed to resolve
tunableifs. It should be fine to allow blockinherit statements in
an optional, because that is copying nodes from outside the optional
to the optional and if the optional is later disabled, everything
will be deleted anyway.

Check and quit with an error if a tunable declaration, in-statement,
block, blockabstract, or macro definition is found within an
optional when either building or resolving the AST.

Signed-off-by: James Carter <jwcart2@gmail.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tstruct cil_tree_node *optional = args->optional;', '\t\t\tgoto exit;', '\t\t}', '\t}', '', '\tif (optional != NULL) {', '\t\tif (parse_current->data == CIL_KEY_TUNABLE ||', '\t\t\tparse_current->data == CIL_KEY_IN ||', '\t\t\tparse_current->data == CIL_KEY_BLOCK ||', '\t\t\tparse_current->data == CIL_KEY_BLOCKABSTRACT ||', '\t\t\tparse_current->data == CIL_KEY_MACRO) {', '\t\t\trc = SEPOL_ERR;', '\t\t\tcil_tree_log(parse_current, CIL_ERR, "%s is not allowed in optionals", (char *)parse_current->data);']}
description: The CIL compiler in SELinux 3.2 has a heap-based buffer over-read in ebitmap_match_any (called indirectly from cil_check_neverallow). This occurs because there is sometimes a lack of checks for invalid statements in an optional block.

code_evidence: The function reads the macro/optional context from args but, before the patch, only guards macro contents; there is no check that statements such as blocks or macros are disallowed inside an optional block.

The macro guard rejects tunable, in, block, blockinherit, blockabstract and macro keywords when macro context is active, showing the intended constraint pattern; the same constraint is absent for optional context.
When the keyword is CIL_KEY_BLOCK or CIL_KEY_BLOCKINHERIT, the code proceeds to cil_gen_block/cil_gen_blockinherit, building AST nodes that can be copied out of an optional before it is disabled.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-125 fits because the supported consequence is reading memory past the intended buffer via a dangling reference from the improperly permitted optional-block contents; the missing validation is the enabling condition, not the read itself.

evidence_lines.code:
struct cil_tree_node *macro = args->macro;
struct cil_tree_node *boolif = args->boolif;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the AST builder lacks a check preventing block, blockinherit, macro and similar statements inside an optional block. Trigger: a crafted policy places a block with blockinherit inside an optional; the block is copied before the optional is disabled, then deleted, leaving a dangling reference. Later error handling reads through that reference, producing an out-of-bounds read (the described null/heap over-read).

description: omx/SimpleSoftOMXComponent.cpp in libstagefright in mediaserver in Android 4.x before 4.4.4, 5.0.x before 5.0.2, 5.1.x before 5.1.1, 6.x before 2016-09-01, and 7.0 before 2016-09-01 does not prevent input-port changes, which allows attackers to gain privileges via a crafted application, aka internal bug 29421804.

code_evidence: onPortEnable accepts a caller-supplied portIndex and enable flag, validates the index against mPorts.size() and transition state, then mutates the addressed port's mDef.bEnabled and mTransition without checking the port direction.

The disable branch clears ownership and notifies buffers based on eDir (lines 9-21), and the enable branch sets ENABLING; both act on whatever port was chosen, so a software (input) port can be enabled/disabled through this API. The patch adds an eDir != OMX_DirOutput guard to reject such requests.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-264 covers weaknesses in permission/access-control management; here the component fails to enforce that only output ports may be enabled/disabled, allowing a caller to perform a restricted operation. This is an access-control omission rather than a memory-safety flaw.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: missing restriction on which port directions may be toggled, so a crafted application can drive input-port enable/disable on a software codec. Trigger: supplying an input portIndex to onPortEnable. Consequence: unauthorized state changes on input ports, enabling privilege escalation per the advisory.

description: GNU Tar through 1.30, when --sparse is used, mishandles file shrinkage during read access, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (infinite read loop in sparse_dump_region in sparse.c) by modifying a file that is supposed to be archived by a different user's process (e.g., a system backup running as root).

code_evidence: The loop at line 9 runs while size_left > 0; size_left is only decremented by bytes_read at line 32. safe_read at line 21 can return 0 (short read / file shrinkage), in which case bytes_read is 0, dumped_size is unchanged, and size_left is not reduced, so the loop condition stays true indefinitely.

commit_msg:
Patch series "Fix several device private page reference counting issues",
v2

This series aims to fix a number of page reference counting issues in
drivers dealing with device private ZONE_DEVICE pages.  These result in
use-after-free type bugs, either from accessing a struct page which no
longer exists because it has been removed or accessing fields within the
struct page which are no longer valid because the page has been freed.

During normal usage it is unlikely these will cause any problems.  However
without these fixes it is possible to crash the kernel from userspace. 
These crashes can be triggered either by unloading the kernel module or
unbinding the device from the driver prior to a userspace task exiting. 
In modules such as Nouveau it is also possible to trigger some of these
issues by explicitly closing the device file-descriptor prior to the task
exiting and then accessing device private memory.

This involves some minor changes to both PowerPC and AMD GPU code. 
Unfortunately I lack hardware to test either of those so any help there
would be appreciated.  The changes mimic what is done in for both Nouveau
and hmm-tests though so I doubt they will cause problems.


This patch (of 8):

When the CPU tries to access a device private page the migrate_to_ram()
callback associated with the pgmap for the page is called.  However no
reference is taken on the faulting page.  Therefore a concurrent migration
of the device private page can free the page and possibly the underlying
pgmap.  This results in a race which can crash the kernel due to the
migrate_to_ram() function pointer becoming invalid.  It also means drivers
can't reliably read the zone_device_data field because the page may have
been freed with memunmap_pages().

Close the race by getting a reference on the page while holding the ptl to
ensure it has not been freed.  Unfortunately the elevated reference count
will cause the migration required to handle the fault to fail.  To avoid
this failure pass the faulting page into the migrate_vma functions so that
if an elevated reference count is found it can be checked to see if it's
expected or not.

description: A vulnerability was found in Linux Kernel. It has been classified as problematic. Affected is an unknown function of the file mm/memory.c of the component Driver Handler. The manipulation leads to use after free. It is possible to launch the attack remotely. It is recommended to apply a patch to fix this issue. The identifier of this vulnerability is VDB-211020.

code_evidence: The fault handler reads vmf->vma and derives mm from vma->vm_mm, then looks up the process by mm; the faulting page vmf->page is never referenced or pinned before use.
The pre-patch call svm_migrate_vram_to_ram(prange, mm, KFD_MIGRATE_TRIGGER_PAGEFAULT_CPU) passes no page reference; the fix passes vmf->page so migrate_vma can validate an elevated reference count.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The root cause is a missing reference/get-page on vmf->page, enabling the page to be freed and subsequently referenced during the fault-driven migration. This is CWE-416 (use after free); it is not merely a missing check, since the freed object is actually reused.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: The CPU fault path migrates a device-private page without taking a reference on the faulting page. A concurrent migration can free the page and possibly its pgmap while svm_migrate_to_ram is still operating, so later access to the page or the migrate_to_ram callback pointer becomes use-after-free, crashing the kernel.

description: _XcursorThemeInherits in library.c in libXcursor before 1.1.15 allows remote attackers to cause denial of service or potentially code execution via a one-byte heap overflow.

code_evidence: Line 22 allocates only strlen(l) bytes, with no space for the terminating NUL that line 37 writes via '*r++ = '\0''. The loop copies token characters into result and inserts ':' separators; after the final token, r points one past the allocated buffer, so the NUL is stored out of bounds.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: Writing the NUL terminator one byte past the malloc'd region is an out-of-bounds write on a heap buffer, matching CWE-119's operation outside intended buffer boundaries. The underlying allocation-size defect is an off-by-one (CWE-193), but the supported consequence is the buffer-boundary violation described by CWE-119.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the heap allocation omits the +1 byte needed for the string terminator. Trigger: any Inherits line in an Xcursor theme file whose value is parsed and copied. Consequence: a one-byte heap overflow at line 37, corrupting adjacent heap metadata and potentially leading to denial of service or code execution.

description: Division-by-zero vulnerabilities in the functions opj_pi_next_cprl, opj_pi_next_pcrl, and opj_pi_next_rpcl in pi.c in OpenJPEG before 2.2.0 allow remote attackers to cause a denial of service (application crash) via crafted j2k files.

The divisor (1 << rpy) / (1 << rpx) and the shifted component values derive directly from these attacker-influenced resolution/level fields; the function lacks any upper bound or zero check before these divisions.

commit_msg:
Because group consistency is non-atomic between parent (filedesc) and children
(inherited) events, it is possible for PERF_FORMAT_GROUP read() to try and sum
non-matching counter groups -- with non-sensical results.

Add group_generation to distinguish the case where a parent group removes and
adds an event and thus has the same number, but a different configuration of
events as inherited groups.

This became a problem when commit fa8c269353d5 ("perf/core: Invert
perf_read_group() loops") flipped the order of child_list and sibling_list.
Previously it would iterate the group (sibling_list) first, and for each
sibling traverse the child_list. In this order, only the group composition of
the parent is relevant. By flipping the order the group composition of the
child (inherited) events becomes an issue and the mis-match in group
composition becomes evident.

That said; even prior to this commit, while reading of a group that is not
equally inherited was not broken, it still made no sense.

(Ab)use ECHILD as error return to indicate issues with child process group
composition.

Fixes: fa8c269353d5 ("perf/core: Invert perf_read_group() loops")
Reported-by: Budimir Markovic <markovicbudimir@gmail.com>
Signed-off-by: Peter Zijlstra (Intel) <peterz@infradead.org>
Link: https://lkml.kernel.org/r/20231018115654.GK33217@noisy.programming.kicks-ass.net
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': [], 'added_lines': ['\tleader->group_generation = parent_event->group_generation;']}
description:
A heap out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the Linux kernel's Linux Kernel Performance Events (perf) component can be exploited to achieve local privilege escalation.

If perf_read_group() is called while an event's sibling_list is smaller than its child's sibling_list, it can increment or write to memory locations outside of the allocated buffer.

We recommend upgrading past commit 32671e3799ca2e4590773fd0e63aaa4229e50c06.

code_evidence: inherit_group() clones the parent leader via inherit_event() and then iterates each sibling, inheriting child counters with leader as the group leader; no group-generation consistency check is performed here.

The loop walks every sibling of the parent event and returns early on errors, but the resulting child group composition is not validated against the parent's generation, so mismatched group sizes can propagate.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: The function builds event groups whose composition can diverge from the parent, enabling subsequent group reads to write past the allocated buffer. That directly matches CWE-787 (write past the end of an intended buffer), rather than a mere logic/inconsistency weakness.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: inherited child event groups are built without tracking whether the parent group's composition changed (group_generation). Trigger: a parent group removes/adds events, leaving a child group with a different sibling count; a later PERF_FORMAT_GROUP read sums mismatched groups. This lets writes/updates target memory beyond the expected group buffer, i.e. an out-of-bounds write.

description: The Linux kernel before 4.15-rc8 was found to be vulnerable to a NULL pointer dereference bug in the __netlink_ns_capable() function in the net/netlink/af_netlink.c file. A local attacker could exploit this when a net namespace with a netnsid is assigned to cause a kernel panic and a denial of service.

evidence_lines.code: net = get_net_ns_by_id(sock_net(skb->sk), netnsid);
if (!netlink_ns_capable(skb, net->user_ns, CAP_NET_ADMIN)) {

commit_msg:
nfsd: check permissions when setting ACLs

Use set_posix_acl, which includes proper permission checks, instead of
calling ->set_acl directly.  Without this anyone may be able to grant
themselves permissions to a file by setting the ACL.

Lock the inode to make the new checks atomic with respect to set_acl.
(Also, nfsd was the only caller of set_acl not locking the inode, so I
suspect this may fix other races.)

This also simplifies the code, and ensures our ACLs are checked by
posix_acl_valid.

The permission checks and the inode locking were lost with commit
4ac7249e, which changed nfsd to use the set_acl inode operation directly
instead of going through xattr handlers.

Reported-by: David Sinquin <david@sinquin.eu>
[agreunba@redhat.com: use set_posix_acl]
Fixes: 4ac7249e
Cc: Christoph Hellwig <hch@infradead.org>
Cc: Al Viro <viro@zeniv.linux.org.uk>
Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
Signed-off-by: J. Bruce Fields <bfields@redhat.com>
diff_line_info: {'deleted_lines': ['\tif (!inode->i_op->set_acl || !IS_POSIXACL(inode))', '\t\treturn nfserr_attrnotsupp;', '', '\thost_error = inode->i_op->set_acl(inode, pacl, ACL_TYPE_ACCESS);', '\t\tgoto out_release;', '\t\thost_error = inode->i_op->set_acl(inode, dpacl,', '\t\t\t\t\t\t  ACL_TYPE_DEFAULT);', 'out_release:'], 'added_lines': ['\tfh_lock(fhp);', '', '\thost_error = set_posix_acl(inode, ACL_TYPE_ACCESS, pacl);', '\t\tgoto out_drop_lock;', '\t\thost_error = set_posix_acl(inode, ACL_TYPE_DEFAULT, dpacl);', 'out_drop_lock:', '\tfh_unlock(fhp);', '']}
description: nfsd in the Linux kernel through 4.6.3 allows local users to bypass intended file-permission restrictions by setting a POSIX ACL, related to nfs2acl.c, nfs3acl.c, and nfs4acl.c.

code_evidence: fh_verify requests NFSD_MAY_SATTR, which authorizes attribute modification but the function then proceeds to change ACLs without any explicit permission check on the ACL-setting path.

The access ACL is written via inode->i_op->set_acl directly, bypassing the set_posix_acl wrapper that enforces inode permission checks, so an actor permitted to set attributes can grant ACL entries beyond their authority.
For directories, the default ACL is similarly written via inode->i_op->set_acl without permission validation, and no inode lock is held, so the check-free write is not atomic.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-284 fits because the function fails to enforce an access-control policy: it changes ACLs without the permission checks the wrapper would perform, enabling privilege escalation via unauthorized permission grants. It is an enforcement failure in the ACL write path rather than a simple validation error.
joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: the ACL path calls the low-level set_acl operation directly instead of the permission-checking set_posix_acl wrapper. Trigger: an NFS client able to pass fh_verify's NFSD_MAY_SATTR check submits an ACL granting itself additional file permissions. Consequence: intended file-permission restrictions are bypassed, letting a local user grant themselves access to a file.

description: Pillow before 3.3.2 allows context-dependent attackers to obtain sensitive information by using the "crafted image file" approach, related to an "Integer Overflow" issue affecting the Image.core.map_buffer in map.c component.

code_evidence: Line 30 computes size = (Py_ssize_t) ysize * stride, where both ysize and stride are attacker-influenced int values from the parsed tuple; the multiplication can wrap before the result is widened.
Line 37 checks offset + size > view.len, but offset is a Py_ssize_t and size may be a wrapped small/negative value, so the bounds check can pass incorrectly.
Lines 48 and 51 use offset + y * stride to compute im->image pointers, so a wrapped offset/size can yield out-of-bounds pointer arithmetic into view.buf.
joint-evidence.cwe_rationale: CWE-190 fits because the defect is an unchecked integer multiplication/addition that can wrap in size and offset calculations used for buffer bounds. This is distinct from CWE-125/787, which describe the resulting out-of-bounds access rather than the arithmetic root cause.

evidence_lines.code: size = (Py_ssize_t) ysize * stride;
if (offset + size > view.len) {

im->image[y] = (char*)view.buf + offset + y * stride;
im->image[ysize-y-1] = (char*)view.buf + offset + y * stride;

joint-evidence.vulnerability_mechanism: Root cause: ysize * stride and offset + size are computed without overflow guards, despite ysize, stride and offset being supplied by the caller. Trigger: a crafted image buffer argument makes the product or sum wrap. Consequence: the view.len bounds check is bypassed and image row pointers point outside the mapped buffer, enabling out-of-bounds reads/writes (memory corruption or information disclosure).
